- **corpus minimisation** — `afl-cmin` reduces the corpus to a path-equivalent minimal set, and `afl-tmin` then shrinks individual inputs. > "afl-cmin -i corpus/ -o corpus_min/ -- ./fuzz_harness @@"
- **CI vs nightly tuning** — The skill carries a two-column profile — a CI short run against a nightly long run — covering duration, mode, calibration flags, corpus caching and parallelism. > "| Setting | CI Short Run | Nightly Long Run |"
- **secondary fuzzer instances** — Nightly runs launch one named `-S` instance per core so several fuzzers explore in parallel. > "# Launch multiple secondary instances for better coverage"
- **corpus caching** — GitHub Actions caches `corpus/` under a commit-SHA key and restores it through the `fuzz-corpus-` prefix, so each run resumes earlier coverage instead of starting cold. > "- name: Restore corpus cache
>         uses: actions/cache@v4
>         with:
>           path: corpus/
>           key: fuzz-corpus-${{ github.sha }}
>           restore-keys: fuzz-corpus-"
- **crash gating** — The job counts files under `*/crashes/*` while excluding `README.txt`, echoes each crash with its byte size, and fails the build. > "CRASHES=$(find findings/ -path "*/crashes/*" -not -name "README.txt" | wc -l)"
- **crash triage** — Each crash is replayed under the ASan binary with `timeout 5`, then deduplicated by stack trace. > "# Deduplicate crashes by stack trace
> afl-collect findings/ crashes_deduped/ -- ./fuzz_harness @@"
- **campaign monitoring** — `afl-whatsup` reports paths, unique crashes and hangs, stability, execs/sec and cycles done. > "# Key metrics to track:
> # - Total paths found (code coverage indicator)
> # - Unique crashes / unique hangs"
- **compliance framing** — The frontmatter tags the practice against NIST AI RMF, ATLAS, NIST CSF and ATT&CK identifiers, so the workflow maps onto an audit story. > "nist_ai_rmf:
> - MEASURE-2.7
> - MAP-5.1
> - MANAGE-2.4
> atlas_techniques:
> - AML.T0070"
RULES:
- Linux CI runners only, because AFL++ has no native Windows support — > "Linux-based CI runners (AFL++ does not support Windows natively)"
- CI exports the fast-calibration settings `AFL_CMPLOG_ONLY_NEW: 1`, `AFL_FAST_CAL: 1` and `AFL_NO_STARTUP_CALIBRATION: 1` — > "AFL_CMPLOG_ONLY_NEW: 1
> AFL_FAST_CAL: 1
> AFL_NO_STARTUP_CALIBRATION: 1"
- The nightly profile turns calibration back off: `AFL_FAST_CAL` and `AFL_NO_STARTUP_CALIBRATION` are `0`, while `AFL_CMPLOG_ONLY_NEW` stays `1` — > "| `AFL_FAST_CAL` | 1 | 0 |"
- Run 30-60 minutes in CI and 4-24 hours nightly — > "| Duration | 30-60 min | 4-24 hours |"
- Run 1-2 parallel instances in CI and `nproc` nightly — > "| Parallel instances | 1-2 | nproc |"
- Pass `-t 5000` as the input timeout, wrap the campaign in `timeout 7200`, and cap the job at `timeout-minutes: 120` — > "timeout 7200 afl-fuzz \
>             -S ci_fuzzer \
>             -i corpus/ \
>             -o findings/ \
>             -t 5000 \
>             -- ./fuzz_harness @@ || true"
- Use `-S` secondaries only; never `-M` in CI — > "| Mode | `-S` (secondary only) | `-S` (no `-M` for CI) |"
- Corpus caching is required in both profiles — > "| Corpus caching | Required | Required |"
- Keep stability above 90% — > "Stability percentage (should be >90%)"
- The harness skips inputs shorter than four bytes — > "if (len < 4) continue;"
WORKFLOW:
1. Build the fuzzing harness (`__AFL_FUZZ_INIT`, `__AFL_INIT`, `__AFL_LOOP(10000)`, reset context per iteration).
2. Compile with instrumentation (`export CC=afl-clang-fast`, `CXX=afl-clang-fast++`, `AFL_USE_ASAN=1`, `-fsanitize=address`, second `-DCMPLOG` binary).
3. Prepare seed corpus (`afl-cmin -i corpus/ -o corpus_min/ -- ./fuzz_harness @@`, then per-file `afl-tmin`).
4. Configure CI/CD (GitHub Actions: install `aflplusplus`, restore corpus cache, build harness, run `afl-fuzz`, gate on crash count, refresh cache via `afl-cmin` from `findings/<fuzzer>/queue/`).
5. Parallel/nightly fuzzing (loop `seq 1 $(nproc)` launching `afl-fuzz -S fuzzer_$i`, `wait`, merge with `afl-cmin -i findings/*/queue/`).
6. Crash triage (replay under ASan, `afl-collect findings/ crashes_deduped/`).
TABLES:
- "Instrumentation Modes" — rows: `afl-clang-fast` (LTO), `afl-clang-fast`, `afl-gcc-fast`, `QEMU mode`, `Frida mode`, `Unicorn mode`; columns: Mode, Use Case, Performance.
- "CI/CD Best Practices for AFL++" — rows: Duration, Mode, `AFL_CMPLOG_ONLY_NEW`, `AFL_FAST_CAL`, `AFL_NO_STARTUP_CALIBRATION`, Corpus caching, Parallel instances; columns: CI Short Run, Nightly Long Run.
ANTI-PATTERNS: Persistent loop without re-initialising target state → init/cleanup the parser context every iteration. Counting `README.txt` as a finding → exclude it (`-not -name "README.txt"`). Using `-M` in CI → `-S` secondaries. Re-running from an uncached corpus → SHA key plus prefix restore.
TOOLING: `apt install aflplusplus`; `afl-cmin -i … -o … -- ./harness @@`; `afl-tmin -i … -o …`; `afl-fuzz -S ci_fuzzer -i corpus/ -o findings/ -t 5000 -- ./fuzz_harness @@`; `afl-collect`; `afl-whatsup findings/`; env `CC`, `CXX`, `AFL_USE_ASAN`, `AFL_CMPLOG_ONLY_NEW`, `AFL_FAST_CAL`, `AFL_NO_STARTUP_CALIBRATION`; `actions/checkout@v4`, `actions/cache@v4`; cron `'0 2 * * *'`.
GOTCHAS: `|| true` after `afl-fuzz` masks the campaign exit — the crash-count step is the real gate. CmpLog without the `-DCMPLOG` binary extracts nothing. A per-commit cache key without `restore-keys: fuzz-corpus-` starts every run cold. State leaking across `__AFL_LOOP` iterations silently corrupts findings.
STRUCTURE: none bundled (only external reference links).

## S105 · fuzzing
SOURCE: `testing/libfuzzer/getting_started.md`; `third_party/fuzztest/src/doc/fuzz-test-macro.md`; `third_party/fuzztest/src/doc/domains-reference.md`; `third_party/fuzztest/src/doc/fixtures.md` (Chromium tree).
PURPOSE: Instructs an agent to add a FuzzTest `FUZZ_TEST` to Chromium, register it in GN, and prove it works by building, running it as a unit test, and running it in fuzzing mode.
CONCEPTS:
- **`FUZZ_TEST`** — The registration macro pairs a suite name with a property function and takes `.WithDomains(...)` for the generators. > "FUZZ_TEST(MyComponentFuzzTest, MyPropertyFunctionDoesNotCrash)
>   .WithDomains(
>       fuzztest::InRange(0, 100),
>       fuzztest::Arbitrary<std::string>()
>   );"
- **property function** — An ordinary C++ function whose parameters are the fuzz inputs, and the author requires a name that states the property rather than a placeholder. > "the property being tested (e.g., "ParseFooDoesNotCrash" or "RoundTripIsLossless")."
- **domains** — Typed input specifications such as `fuzztest::InRange(0, 100)` for bounded integers and `fuzztest::Arbitrary<std::string>()` for arbitrary values; `Constructor` and `Map` build valid objects. > "Use `fuzztest::Constructor` or `fuzztest::Map` to build valid objects."
- **constructor-from-primitives pattern** — When a type has a parsing constructor such as `GURL(string)`, the test takes the primitive and constructs the object inside the test function. > "If the object has a parsing constructor (e.g. `GURL(string)`), accept the primitive and construct it inside your test function."
- **local domain helper** — A small function returning a domain keeps the construction rule in one place. > "auto ArbitraryFoo() {
>     return fuzztest::Constructor<Foo>(fuzztest::InRange(0, 10));
>   }"
- **`fuzztests` list** — A GN variable listing entries as `SuiteName.TestName` on the executable target that builds the test file. > "fuzztests = [
>     "MyComponentFuzzTest.MyPropertyFunctionDoesNotCrash",
>   ]"
- **`test()` vs `source_set()` targets** — Case A adds only the `fuzztests` entry; Case B adds `//third_party/fuzztest:fuzztest` to `deps` and registers on the depending executable. > "**Case B: File is in a `source_set()`:** Add `//third_party/fuzztest:fuzztest` to `deps`."
- **`gn refs`** — The reverse-dependency query used to find the executable `test()` target that owns a file or a source_set. > "Find the executable `test()` target that depends on this `source_set()`:"
- **`autoninja`** — Chromium's build wrapper, used to build the target `gn refs` identified. > "Build the identified target (e.g. `unit_tests` or `browser_tests`):"
- **`gtest_filter` verification** — Running the registered test as an ordinary unit test proves the property holds on ordinary inputs. > "Verify unit tests pass"
- **fuzzing-mode verification** — `--fuzz="Suite.Test" --fuzz_for=10s` runs the property under FuzzTest's mutation. > "Verify fuzzing mode doesn't crash"
- **DEPS `specific_include_rules`** — Chromium's DEPS check blocks the fuzztest include until the nearest DEPS file grants it per file pattern. > "You must allow the `fuzztest` include in the nearest `DEPS` file (usually in the same directory as your test or a parent directory)."
- **fuzz build config** — A dedicated output directory enables fuzzing with `enable_fuzztest_fuzz=true` while keeping `is_debug=false`, `is_asan=true`, `is_component_build=false`, `use_remoteexec=true`. > "gn gen out/fuzz --args='enable_fuzztest_fuzz=true is_debug=false is_asan=true \
> is_component_build=false use_remoteexec=true'"
RULES:
- Register the test in the `fuzztests` list, alphabetically, on the **executable** `test` target — > "You **MUST** register the test in the `fuzztests` list (in alphabetical order) of the **executable** `test` target."
- The work is not finished until the three-command verification sequence has run — > "The task is **incomplete** until you successfully execute this sequence:"
- Fuzz verification uses a ten-second budget — > "--fuzz="MyComponentFuzzTest.MyPropertyFunctionDoesNotCrash" --fuzz_for=10s"
- Case A needs no dependency edits, because the build system adds FuzzTest dependencies itself — > "No dependency changes are needed here. The build system"
- Name the property function for the property, not with a placeholder — > "Use a descriptive name that reflects"
WORKFLOW:
1. Configure output dir: `gn gen out/fuzz --args='enable_fuzztest_fuzz=true is_debug=false is_asan=true is_component_build=false use_remoteexec=true'`.
2. Implement `FUZZ_TEST` in `*_unittest.cc` with fuzztest/gtest includes, property function with invariants, `.WithDomains(...)`.
3. Register in `BUILD.gn` (Case A: `fuzztests = ["Suite.Test"]`; Case B: add `//third_party/fuzztest:fuzztest` dep, find executable via `gn refs … --testonly=true --type=executable --all`, list it there).
4. Verify: `gn refs out/fuzz //path/to/my_component_unittest.cc --type=executable --all`; `autoninja --quiet -C out/fuzz <target_name>`; `./out/fuzz/<target_name> --gtest_filter="Suite.Test"`; `./out/fuzz/<target_name> --fuzz="Suite.Test" --fuzz_for=10s`.
TABLES: none.
ANTI-PATTERNS: Passing a complex type straight to the domain when only primitives are generatable → accept the primitive and construct the object inside the test, or build a domain with `Constructor`/`Map`. Registering on a `source_set()` and expecting it to run → the executable `test()` target must carry the `fuzztests` entry. Ignoring a DEPS build error → add `+third_party/fuzztest` under `specific_include_rules`.
TOOLING: `gn gen`, `gn refs <out> <path> --testonly=true --type=executable --all`, `autoninja --quiet -C out/fuzz <target>`, `--gtest_filter=`, `--fuzz=`, `--fuzz_for=10s`; GN keys `fuzztests`, `deps`, `sources`; DEPS `specific_include_rules` with regex `".*_unittest\\.cc"`.
GOTCHAS: Build fails with `ERROR: include not allowed by DEPS: third_party/fuzztest/...` — the include is silently disallowed until the nearest DEPS file grants it; the fix is the DEPS snippet, not a build-flag change. Omitting the GN registration compiles the file but never fuzzes it. Non-alphabetical listing violates the stated convention.
STRUCTURE: none bundled; four reference paths declared in-tree (`testing/libfuzzer/getting_started.md`, `fuzz-test-macro.md`, `domains-reference.md`, `fixtures.md`).

## S106 · fuzzing-go-expert
SOURCE: OSS-Fuzz infra (`infra/helper.py`), `github.com/AdamKorcz/go-118-fuzz-build/testing`, `../oss-fuzz-engineer/references/structured_seed_generation.md`.
PURPOSE: Gives an agent what it needs to write, build, and validate Go fuzz targets for OSS-Fuzz using the native Go 1.18 fuzzing framework driven by libFuzzer.
CONCEPTS:
- **native Go fuzzing** — The author builds on Go's own fuzzing framework from Go 1.18 rather than a byte-level harness library, and OSS-Fuzz drives it through libFuzzer. > "Go fuzzing uses the native Go fuzzing framework introduced in Go 1.18, which OSS-Fuzz drives via libFuzzer under the hood using `compile_native_go_fuzzer`."
- **`base-builder-go` image** — Go projects start from the dedicated base builder image instead of the generic one. > "Go projects must use the Go base builder image:"
- **`Fuzz` target function** — Targets are ordinary Go test functions named with the `Fuzz` prefix, placed in `_test.go` files or plain `.go` files that import `testing`. > "Go fuzz targets are standard Go test functions with the prefix `Fuzz`, placed in `_test.go` files (or plain `.go` files that import the testing package):"
- **registration shim** — A blank import of the fuzz-build package is what lets OSS-Fuzz hook native fuzzing, so the author writes it into a generated `register.go`. > "the `import _ "github.com/AdamKorcz/go-118-fuzz-build/testing"` blank import is required for OSS-Fuzz to hook into native Go fuzzing — never omit it."
- **seed corpus via `f.Add`** — Representative valid inputs are compiled into the harness so coverage starts from a meaningful state. > "Seed corpus: add representative valid inputs so the fuzzer starts"
- **typed fuzz parameters** — When the target is not purely byte-oriented, the callback signature can take structured types directly. > "Go's fuzzer can mutate `string`, `int`, `bool`, `float64`, etc. directly."
- **`compile_native_go_fuzzer`** — The `build.sh` helper takes the package import path, the function name and the output binary name, and is repeated per target or package. > "Use the `compile_native_go_fuzzer` helper in `build.sh`. It takes the package import path, the function name, and the output binary name:"
- **seed corpus artefacts** — Seeds ship either as individual files in a directory or as a zip, both under `$OUT`. > "Seed corpus entries go in `$OUT/<fuzzer_name>_seed_corpus/` as individual files, or as a zip at `$OUT/<fuzzer_name>_seed_corpus.zip`."
- **dictionary artefacts** — Dictionaries are plaintext token files named after the fuzzer. > "Dictionaries go in `$OUT/<fuzzer_name>.dict` as plaintext token files."
- **structured seed generation** — For format parsers the author prefers scripted seeds, because random mutation rarely clears the parser's early checks. > "For targets that parse a structured format, generating seeds with a script beats hand-picking a few files — random mutation rarely passes the parser's early checks."
- **memory-safety shift** — Because Go is memory-safe, the interesting bug classes are different from C/C++. > "Go is memory-safe, so the focus shifts from memory-corruption bugs to:"
- **crash taxonomy** — What counts as a crash is any unrecovered panic, plus logic bugs, hangs and wrong error handling. > "index out of range, nil pointer dereference, type assertion failures, stack overflows — any unrecovered `panic` is a crash."
- **local iteration via `COPY`** — For fast local loops the author swaps a Dockerfile `git clone` for a copied checkout. > "When iterating locally clone the upstream repo and switch the Dockerfile from `RUN git clone` to `COPY` to avoid network round-trips."
RULES:
- Target the attack surface: parsers, decoders, protocol handlers, serialisation and any API taking untrusted bytes or strings — > "focus on parsers, decoders, protocol handlers, serialisation/deserialisation, and any API that accepts untrusted bytes or strings."
- Handle expected errors and ignore expected error returns, so only genuine panics and unexpected behaviour are findings — > "Only genuine panics and unexpected behaviour are findings."
- Use typed fuzz parameters when the target is not purely byte-oriented — > "when the target is not purely byte-oriented"
- Avoid non-determinism: no random sources, no time, no goroutines, no global state that persists between calls — > "do not use random sources, time, goroutines, or global state that persists between calls."
- Keep the callback fast and hoist expensive setup out of `f.Fuzz` — > "expensive setup (e.g. parsing config, opening files) belongs outside `f.Fuzz(...)`, not inside the inner function."
- Provide meaningful seeds so coverage grows from the start — > "`f.Add(...)` entries should be valid representative inputs so coverage grows from the start."
- Never get stuck: no busy-loops or blocking I/O inside the fuzz function — > "avoid code paths that busy-loop or block on I/O inside the fuzz function."
- Include the registration shim and never omit it — > "is required for OSS-Fuzz to hook into native Go fuzzing — never omit it."
- Validate with a 30-second run — > "run_fuzzer <project> <fuzzer_name> -- -max_total_time=30"
- Run `go vet ./...` and `go build ./...` inside the module before wrapping it in an OSS-Fuzz build — > "Run `go vet ./...` and `go build ./...` inside the module before wrapping in an OSS-Fuzz build to catch compile errors early."
- Treat an instant crash as a harness defect — > "An instant crash almost always means the harness itself is wrong (e.g. missing error handling, bad seed, wrong package path)."
- Document why each entry point was chosen and what bug class it may find — > "Document why each entry point was chosen and what class of bugs it may find."
WORKFLOW:
1. Use the Go base builder image and set `language: go`.
2. Write `Fuzz*` test with `f.Add` seeds and an `f.Fuzz` callback.
3. In `build.sh`: copy the harness into the module, write `register.go` with the blank import, `go mod tidy`, then `compile_native_go_fuzzer <importpath> <FuzzName> <outname>` per target.
4. Ship seeds (`$OUT/…_seed_corpus[.zip]`) and dictionaries (`$OUT/<fuzzer>.dict`), or generate them structurally.
5. Validate: `python3 infra/helper.py build_fuzzers <project>`; `check_build <project>`; `run_fuzzer <project> <fuzzer_name> -- -max_total_time=30`.
TABLES: none.
ANTI-PATTERNS: Omitting the blank import shim → OSS-Fuzz never hooks native fuzzing. Doing config parsing or file opening inside `f.Fuzz` → hoist outside the callback. Spawning goroutines or reading time/rand in the fuzz path → nondeterministic, unreproducible findings. Hand-picking a few seed files for a structured format → generate seeds with a script.
TOOLING: `dockerfile FROM gcr.io/oss-fuzz-base/base-builder-go`; `project.yaml language: go`; `compile_native_go_fuzzer github.com/owner/repo/pkg FuzzMyTarget fuzz_my_target`; `printf`-generated `register.go`; `go mod tidy`, `go vet ./...`, `go build ./...`; `python3 infra/helper.py build_fuzzers|check_build|run_fuzzer`; `-max_total_time=30`; `$SRC`, `$OUT`.
GOTCHAS: Missing registration shim produces a build that compiles but never fuzzes natively. Instant crash signals a harness defect (missing error handling, bad seed, wrong package path) rather than a target bug. `RUN git clone` in the Dockerfile makes iteration slow and network-dependent. `f.Add` seeds are compiled in — stale seeds silently cap initial coverage.
STRUCTURE: `../oss-fuzz-engineer/references/structured_seed_generation.md` (declared, not bundled).

## S107 · fuzzing-jvm-expert
SOURCE: https://github.com/CodeIntelligenceTesting/jazzer ; OSS-Fuzz `infra/helper.py`; `../oss-fuzz-engineer/references/structured_seed_generation.md`.
PURPOSE: Equips an agent to write, build, and validate Jazzer fuzz targets for Java/Kotlin/Scala/Groovy projects in OSS-Fuzz.
CONCEPTS:
- **Jazzer** — The tool wraps libFuzzer and instruments JVM bytecode, which is where coverage guidance comes from. > "JVM fuzzing uses [Jazzer](https://github.com/CodeIntelligenceTesting/jazzer), which wraps libFuzzer and instruments JVM bytecode for coverage guidance."
- **`base-builder-jvm` image** — JVM projects start from their own base builder image with `language: jvm`. > "JVM projects must use the JVM base builder image:"
- **raw-bytes harness** — The simplest target receives the byte array directly in `fuzzerTestOneInput`. > "The simplest Jazzer harness receives raw bytes via `fuzzerTestOneInput`:"
- **`FuzzedDataProvider` harness** — The typed variant splits the stream into values such as `consumeString(64)`, `consumeInt()` and `consumeRemainingAsBytes()`, which the author calls essential for structured targets. > "`FuzzedDataProvider` splits the raw byte stream into typed values, which is essential for targets that require structured input:"
- **expected-exception filtering** — Documented exceptions are caught so they do not become findings. > "Ignore expected exceptions; they are not bugs."
- **`fuzzerInitialize`** — Expensive setup such as config loading or client creation goes into an optional static method Jazzer calls once before fuzzing. > "If initialisation is expensive (loading config, creating DB connections, etc.), put it in an optional static method that Jazzer calls once before fuzzing:"
- **Maven `build.sh` pattern** — The build packages the project skipping tests and javadoc, then composes `ALL_JARS`, `BUILD_CLASSPATH` and `RUNTIME_CLASSPATH` with `xargs printf`. > "The `build.sh` pattern for Maven projects:"
- **per-fuzzer wrapper script** — A generated bash launcher execs `jazzer_driver` with `--agent_path`, `--instrumentation_includes`, `--cp`, `--target_class` and `--jvm_args`. > "Wrapper script that launches jazzer_driver with the right arguments."
- **`mem_settings` pattern** — Memory and stack differ between crash reproduction and fuzzing, chosen by testing whether the arguments contain `-runs=[0-9]+`. > "if [[ \"\$@\" =~ (^| )-runs=[0-9]+($| ) ]]; then
>   mem_settings='-Xmx1900m:-Xss900k'"
- **`instrumentation_includes`** — A package prefix glob such as `com.example.**` scopes instrumentation; the author says without it guidance is impossible. > "to the package prefix of the target library in the wrapper script — without this Jazzer cannot guide fuzzing."
- **Jazzer security hooks** — Beyond crashes, the tool detects injection classes through hooks: JDBC for SQL, file APIs for traversal, `Runtime.exec` for command injection. > "- SQL injection (via JDBC hooks)
> - Path traversal (via file API hooks)
> - Command injection (via `Runtime.exec` hooks)"
- **false-positive triage** — Out-of-memory, stack overflow and null pointer errors on invalid input are usually expected, so the project must decide which are real. > "`OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`, and `NullPointerException` on invalid input are usually expected — decide which are genuine bugs for this project."
- **artefact layout** — Seeds are zipped and dictionaries placed under `$OUT`, both named after the fuzzer. > "Place dictionaries at `$OUT/<fuzzer_name>.dict`."
RULES:
- Target the attack surface: parsers, deserializers, protocol handlers, template engines, any API taking untrusted bytes or strings — > "parsers, deserializers (JSON, XML, Protobuf, custom binary formats), network protocol handlers, template engines, and any API that accepts untrusted bytes or strings."
- Catch all documented exception types in `try/catch`, so only unexpected exceptions and crashes are findings — > "wrap calls in `try/catch` for all documented exception types. Only unexpected exceptions and crashes are findings."
- Prefer `FuzzedDataProvider` over raw bytes when the method expects well-formed data — > "for structured input rather than passing raw bytes to methods that expect well-formed data."
- Initialise heavy state once: client connections, complex parsers, loaded schemas — > "client connections, parsers with complex configuration, and loaded schemas should be set up once."
- Avoid `Math.random()`, `System.currentTimeMillis()` and thread spawning in the fuzzing path — > "no `Math.random()`, no `System.currentTimeMillis()` in the fuzzing path, no thread spawning."
- Set `--instrumentation_includes` or coverage guidance is lost — > "without this Jazzer cannot guide fuzzing."
- Use the `mem_settings` pattern so runs do not get OOM-killed while crash reproduction keeps a smaller heap — > "use the `mem_settings` pattern shown above to avoid OOM kills during runs vs. crash reproduction."
- Decide per project which error classes are genuine bugs — > "decide which are genuine bugs for this project."
- Validate with a 30-second run — > "run_fuzzer <project> <fuzzer_name> -- -max_total_time=30"
- Build the project standalone first to prove it compiles — > "Build the project outside the fuzzing harness first (`mvn package` or `gradle build`) to ensure the project itself compiles cleanly."
- Document why each entry point was chosen and what bug class it may find — > "Document why each entry point was chosen and what class of bugs it may find."
WORKFLOW:
1. Use `base-builder-jvm` and `language: jvm`.
2. Write `*Fuzzer.java` with `fuzzerTestOneInput` (bytes or `FuzzedDataProvider`) and optional `fuzzerInitialize`.
3. In `build.sh`: `$MVN package -DskipTests …`, build classpaths, loop `find $SRC -maxdepth 1 -name '*Fuzzer.java'`, `javac -cp $BUILD_CLASSPATH`, copy `.class` to `$OUT`, emit + `chmod u+x` the wrapper.
4. Ship `$OUT/<fuzzer>_seed_corpus.zip` and `$OUT/<fuzzer>.dict`.
5. Validate: `build_fuzzers`, `check_build`, `run_fuzzer … -- -max_total_time=30`.
TABLES:
- `FuzzedDataProvider` methods — rows: `consumeBytes(n)`, `consumeRemainingAsBytes()`, `consumeString(maxLen)`, `consumeAsciiString(maxLen)`, `consumeInt()`/`consumeInt(min, max)`, `consumeLong()`, `consumeBoolean()`, `consumeDouble()`, `pickValue(collection)`; columns: Method, Description.
ANTI-PATTERNS: Reporting `OutOfMemoryError`/`StackOverflowError`/`NullPointerException` from invalid input as bugs → classify which are expected for the project. Passing raw bytes to an API that needs well-formed structured data → use `FuzzedDataProvider`. Re-creating clients/parsers per input → move to `fuzzerInitialize`. Omitting `--instrumentation_includes` → no coverage guidance.
TOOLING: `$MVN package -DskipTests -Dmaven.javadoc.skip=true`; `javac -cp`; `jazzer_driver --agent_path=… --instrumentation_includes=com.example.** --cp=… --target_class=… --jvm_args=…`; `-Xmx1900m:-Xss900k`, `-Xmx2048m:-Xss1024k`; `LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$JVM_LD_LIBRARY_PATH`; `$JAZZER_API_PATH`; `$OUT`, `$SRC`; `python3 infra/helper.py` verbs.
GOTCHAS: An instant crash "usually means a missing JAR on the classpath or an uncaught expected exception" — read `check_build` output. The wrapper's `-runs=` regex branch exists so crash reproduction gets smaller heap/stack than fuzzing. Gradle projects must swap `$MVN package` and adjust JAR paths. `RUN git clone` slows local iteration; switch to `COPY`.
STRUCTURE: `../oss-fuzz-engineer/references/structured_seed_generation.md` (declared, not bundled).

## S108 · fuzzing-memory-unsafe-expert
SOURCE: OSS-Fuzz (`infra/helper.py`, `$LIB_FUZZING_ENGINE`), `compiler-rt`'s `FuzzedDataProvider.h`, repo example harnesses under `projects/…`, `../oss-fuzz-engineer/references/structured_seed_generation.md`.
PURPOSE: Teaches an agent to threat-model a C/C++ project, derive a libFuzzer harness at the real trust boundary, build it inside OSS-Fuzz with sanitizers, and justify that the harness finds maintainer-actionable bugs.
CONCEPTS:
- **threat modelling before code** — The author front-loads four explicit questions — what input is untrusted, where it crosses a trust boundary, what the attacker controls there, what counts as a real bug — and wants the answers written down. > "Before writing a single line of harness code, decide **what you are trying to find and where an attacker's input actually enters the code**."
- **attack-surface taxonomy** — File-format parsers, wire handlers, serialisation/IPC decoders, text and query languages, and decompression codecs each come with named entry points to target. > "Concrete, common attack surfaces in C/C++ projects, and the entry points to target for each:"
- **mutate exactly what the attacker controls** — The harness fuzzes the untrusted bytes and holds trusted configuration constant, set once in `LLVMFuzzerInitialize`. > "Mutate exactly what the attacker controls; fix the rest."
- **enter at the real trust boundary** — Calling a deep internal helper yields crashes the public API would have rejected upstream. > "Enter at the real trust boundary, not below it."
- **reachability** — An entry point reachable in production may be unreachable from the harness without prior state such as a session, handshake, header packet or registered codec. > "An entry point that is untrusted-reachable in production may still be *unreachable* from your harness if getting to the interesting code requires state the harness never sets up"
- **seed-limited vs harness-limited** — Dark files in `summary.json` are diagnosed either as needing a better corpus or as needing the harness to build more state. > "decide whether it is *seed-limited* (a better corpus would reach it — write seeds) or *harness-limited* (no input reaches it as the harness stands — the harness itself must set up more state)."
- **`LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput`** — The libFuzzer entry point that receives the byte array and returns a status code. > "A fuzzing harness is a function that takes a byte array as input and processes it in a way that can trigger bugs or vulnerabilities in the software being tested."
- **`LLVMFuzzerInitialize`** — A one-time hook for `argv`, environment variables and library global initialisation, never per-input work. > "If the harness needs setup that must happen once before fuzzing (parsing `argv`, setting environment variables, initialising a library global), put it in the optional `LLVMFuzzerInitialize` hook"
- **`FuzzedDataProvider`** — It maps one mutation stream onto the several typed parameters a real API expects. > "`FuzzedDataProvider` splits the one input stream into typed values, so libFuzzer's mutations map onto the parameters the target actually expects."
- **sanitizer as bug oracle** — The harness only reaches the memory operations; ASan, UBSan or MSan is what reports the violation, with ASan the default and highest value. > "A C/C++ harness rarely detects a bug by itself — the sanitizer the project is built with is what turns silent memory corruption into a crash the fuzzer can catch."
- **`$LIB_FUZZING_ENGINE` linking** — Linking through the variable keeps the engine swappable between libFuzzer, AFL++, Centipede and the coverage no-op engine. > "Link the harness with **`$LIB_FUZZING_ENGINE`**, not a hardcoded `-fsanitize=fuzzer` — this lets OSS-Fuzz swap the engine"
- **static library build** — A static project build both avoids runtime library-path juggling and guarantees the linked code is instrumented. > "Prefer a **static** project build; it avoids `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` juggling at run time and ensures the linked code is instrumented."
- **thirteen harness characteristics** — Simplicity, coverage, determinism, performance, error handling, true positives, threat-model match, attack-surface coverage, entropy, code structure, code conventions, not getting stuck, and a dictionary. > "The below are characteristics commonly found in good fuzzing harnesses, which contribute to their effectiveness in finding bugs."
- **worked example** — For `img_load(buf, len, opts)` the trusted `opts` is fixed once and all bytes go to the payload. > "The harness therefore fixes `opts` to a representative default once, and feeds the mutated bytes as `buf`/`len`:"
- **reference harnesses** — Existing OSS-Fuzz harnesses are the model: scalars first and string last, lazy static logger with a `size == 0` guard, and `FuzzerTemporaryFile` for fd-only APIs. > "Study existing harnesses before writing your own — they show the idioms above applied to real projects, and matching an established style makes your harness easier for maintainers to accept."
- **structured seed generation** — Seeds are constructed by script from `build.sh` and appended to the corpus, which is reproducible and needs no external samples. > "The most effective approach is a **script that constructs structurally-valid inputs from scratch**, run from `build.sh` and appended to the corpus."
RULES:
- Return `0` in normal cases and `-1` only to reject an input from the corpus — > "Return `0` in all normal cases. Return `-1` to tell libFuzzer to reject an input and not add it to the corpus (rarely needed)."
- Never call `exit()` on bad input, because it aborts the run and breaks coverage tooling — > "Never `exit()` on bad input — it aborts the whole run and breaks coverage tooling."
- Consume typed values in a fixed, documented order so saved crashes still reproduce — > "The mapping from bytes to parameters must be stable, or a saved crash will not reproduce."
- Consume the variable-length "rest of the input" argument last — > "Consume the variable-length / "rest of the input" argument last"
- Bound sizes and indices with `ConsumeIntegralInRange` instead of masking a raw integer — > "rather than masking a raw integer — it wastes fewer inputs and keeps allocations sane."
- Enable MSan only when the whole dependency chain is built under MSan — > "only enable it when the whole dependency chain is built under MSan."
- Compile both the target library and the harness with the OSS-Fuzz flags in `build.sh` — > "`build.sh` must compile both the target library and the harness with the OSS-Fuzz `$CFLAGS`/`$CXXFLAGS`"
- Validate with a 30-second run — > "run the fuzzer for 30 seconds to validate it works"
- Treat an instant crash as a harness defect — > "If a fuzzer runs into a crash instantly, it's very likely wrong."
- When extending a harness, prove existing coverage does not digress — > "always validate that the existing code coverage does not digress."
- Document the design rationale and why the harness should find bugs — > "Always document the rationale for design decisions in the fuzzing harness, and the rationale for why the harness is expected to find bugs."
WORKFLOW:
1. Threat-model the four questions; pick the trust-boundary entry point; decide what is mutated vs fixed.
2. Confirm reachability; add state setup if deep code needs a session/handshake.
3. Write the harness (`LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput`, optional `LLVMFuzzerInitialize`, FDP for structured params).
4. In `build.sh`: static build (`cmake -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF`, `make -j$(nproc)`), then per harness `$CXX $CXXFLAGS -std=c++17 -I… -o "$OUT/${fuzzer}" $LIB_FUZZING_ENGINE libproject.a`; copy seed zips and dicts.
5. Script-generate seeds into the corpus rather than hand-picking samples.
6. Validate: `build_fuzzers`, `run_fuzzer … -- -max_total_time=30`, `check_build`; justify coverage non-regression.
TABLES:
- `FuzzedDataProvider` methods — rows: `ConsumeIntegral<T>()`, `ConsumeIntegralInRange<T>(min, max)`, `ConsumeBool()`, `ConsumeEnum<E>()`, `ConsumeFloatingPoint<T>()`/`...InRange(min, max)`, `ConsumeRandomLengthString(max)`, `ConsumeBytes<T>(count)`/`ConsumeBytesAsString(count)`, `ConsumeRemainingBytes<T>()`/`ConsumeRemainingBytesAsString()`, `remaining_bytes()`; columns: Method, Description.
ANTI-PATTERNS: Fuzzing trusted config alongside the payload → "invents a threat that does not exist and yields rejected findings"; fix it once. Internal helper below the boundary → reproduce the upstream precondition or target the public function. Fuzzing the encoder → target the untrusted direction. Violating the API contract (missing NUL, invalid handle, unallocated buffer) → harness bug, not target bug. Raw `data`/`size` where the API needs typed params → use FDP; FDP on a single opaque buffer "would only add noise". Linking a non-instrumented build → silently disables oracle and coverage.
TOOLING: `#include <fuzzer/FuzzedDataProvider.h>`; `extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const uint8_t *data, size_t size)`; `extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerInitialize(int *argc, char ***argv)`; `cmake -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF`; `$CXX $CXXFLAGS -std=c++17`; `$LIB_FUZZING_ENGINE`; `$OUT/<fuzzer>_seed_corpus.zip`; `$OUT/<fuzzer>.dict`; `python3 infra/helper.py build_fuzzers|check_build|run_fuzzer`; `-max_total_time=30`.
GOTCHAS: `exit()` aborts the run and breaks coverage tooling. `-1` silently drops inputs from the corpus. MSan without full instrumentation false-positives. Non-static linking leaves code uninstrumented — the fuzzer finds nothing and looks "clean". Coverage gaps are ambiguous and need `summary.json` inspection. fd/path-only APIs force the slower `FuzzerTemporaryFile` route.
STRUCTURE: `../oss-fuzz-engineer/references/structured_seed_generation.md` (declared, not bundled); referenced in-tree harnesses `projects/sentencepiece/sample_encode_fuzzer.cc`, `projects/spdlog/fuzz/pattern_fuzzer.cc`, `projects/file/magic_fuzzer_fd.cc`, `projects/vlc/generate_seeds.py` (declared, not bundled).

## S109 · fuzzing-python-expert
SOURCE: https://github.com/google/atheris ; OSS-Fuzz `infra/helper.py`; `../oss-fuzz-engineer/references/structured_seed_generation.md`.
PURPOSE: Tells an agent how to write, build, and validate Atheris fuzz targets for Python projects in OSS-Fuzz, including bytecode instrumentation and local single-input debugging.
CONCEPTS:
- **Atheris** — The tool wraps libFuzzer and instruments Python bytecode, which is what gives coverage-guided fuzzing in Python. > "Python fuzzing uses [Atheris](https://github.com/google/atheris), which wraps libFuzzer and instruments Python bytecode for coverage-guided fuzzing."
- **`base-builder-python` image** — Python projects start from their own base builder image with `language: python`. > "Python projects must use the Python base builder image:"
- **harness file convention** — A target is a `fuzz_<target>.py` file containing `TestOneInput(data)` plus a `main()`. > "A Python fuzz target is a `.py` file (named `fuzz_<target>.py` by convention) that follows this pattern:"
- **`instrument_all()`** — The simple default instruments every loaded module. > "instrument_all()   # instrument all loaded Python modules"
- **`instrument_imports()`** — When `instrument_all()` is too broad, for instance because of C-extension conflicts, a context manager instruments only the modules imported inside it. > "When `instrument_all()` is too broad (e.g. causes conflicts with C extensions), instrument specific modules using the `instrument_imports()` context manager:"
- **`Setup` + `Fuzz` wiring** — `atheris.Setup(sys.argv, TestOneInput, enable_python_coverage=True)` followed by `atheris.Fuzz()` is the standard entry, and the flag adds bytecode-level coverage tracking. > "atheris.Setup(sys.argv, TestOneInput, enable_python_coverage=True)"
- **`atheris.FuzzedDataProvider`** — It splits the raw byte stream into typed values for the target. > "`atheris.FuzzedDataProvider` splits the raw byte stream into typed values:"
- **`compile_python_fuzzer`** — The helper turns each `fuzz_*.py` into a standalone executable in `$OUT`, linking against Atheris and libFuzzer. > "`compile_python_fuzzer` handles linking against Atheris and libFuzzer and produces an executable in `$OUT` named after the `.py` file."
- **exception filtering** — Documented exception types are caught so only unexpected exceptions and hard crashes count as findings. > "wrap target calls in `try/except` for the documented exception types the target raises on bad input. Only unexpected exceptions and hard crashes are findings."
- **memory-safety shift** — Python being memory-safe moves the interesting findings to other classes. > "Python is memory-safe, so the focus is on:"
- **C-extension carryover** — Libraries wrapping C can still corrupt memory, and Atheris surfaces it because libFuzzer runs the whole process. > "Python libraries that wrap C code (e.g. lxml, Pillow, cryptography) can still have memory-corruption bugs in their C layer, which Atheris will surface because libFuzzer runs the whole process."
- **single-input mode** — Atheris can run a harness against one seed file outside libFuzzer, which is how the author debugs. > "Atheris supports running in single-input mode outside libFuzzer."
- **corpus/dictionary artefacts** — Seeds go in a directory or a zip under `$OUT`, and dictionaries are especially valuable for text formats such as JSON, XML, YAML and CSV. > "Place seed files in `$OUT/<fuzzer_name>_seed_corpus/` or zip them as `$OUT/<fuzzer_name>_seed_corpus.zip`."
- **structured seed generation** — Scripted seeds beat hand-picked files because random mutation rarely passes the parser's early checks. > "For targets that parse a structured format, generating seeds with a script beats hand-picking a few files — random mutation rarely passes the parser's early checks."
RULES:
- Instrument the right modules, since without instrumentation coverage guidance is blind — > "Without instrumentation coverage guidance is blind."
- Target the attack surface: parsers, template engines, serialisation, protocol handling, any API taking untrusted strings or bytes — > "parsers, template engines, serialisation (pickle, JSON, YAML, XML), network protocol handling, and any API that accepts untrusted strings or bytes."
- Catch expected exceptions; only unexpected exceptions and hard crashes are findings — > "Only unexpected exceptions and hard crashes are findings."
- Use `FuzzedDataProvider` for structured input rather than raw bytes — > "most Python APIs work on strings, not bytes."
- Import at module level, inside the `instrument_imports()` block when used, so imports are instrumented and not re-executed per iteration — > "imports should happen at module level (inside the `instrument_imports()` block if used) so they are instrumented and not re-executed per iteration."
- Stay fast: no file I/O, network calls or subprocesses inside `TestOneInput` — > "avoid file I/O, network calls, or subprocess invocations inside `TestOneInput`."
- Avoid non-determinism: no `random`, `datetime.now()` or `os.urandom()` — > "no `random`, no `datetime.now()`, no `os.urandom()` inside the fuzz function."
- Pass `enable_python_coverage=True` to `atheris.Setup` — > "pass `enable_python_coverage=True` to `atheris.Setup` for bytecode-level coverage tracking."
- Validate with a 30-second run — > "run_fuzzer <project> <fuzzer_name> -- -max_total_time=30"
- Read an instant crash as an exception raised on every input — > "An instant crash usually means an exception is being raised on every input."
- Install the package locally and iterate before the Docker build — > "Install the package locally (`pip3 install .`) and iterate quickly before going through the Docker build."
- Document why each entry point was chosen and what bug class it may find — > "Document why each entry point was chosen and what class of bugs it may find."
WORKFLOW:
1. Use `base-builder-python` and `language: python`.
2. Write `fuzz_<target>.py`: imports first, `TestOneInput(data)` with FDP and exception filtering, `main()` calling `instrument_all()`, `Setup(...)`, `Fuzz()`.
3. In `build.sh`: `pip3 install .`, then `for fuzzer in $(find $SRC -name 'fuzz_*.py'); do compile_python_fuzzer "$fuzzer"; done`.
4. Ship seed corpus and dictionary artefacts; generate structurally valid seeds for format parsers.
5. Validate: `build_fuzzers`, `check_build`, `run_fuzzer … -- -max_total_time=30`; locally `python3 fuzz_target.py <seed_file>`.
TABLES:
- `atheris.FuzzedDataProvider` methods — rows: `ConsumeBytes(count)`, `ConsumeByteList(count)`, `ConsumeString(count)`, `ConsumeUnicode(count)`, `ConsumeUnicodeNoSurrogates(count)`, `ConsumeInt(nbytes)`, `ConsumeIntInRange(min, max)`, `ConsumeFloat()`, `ConsumeBool()`, `ConsumeIntList(count, nbytes)`, `PickValueInList(lst)`, `ConsumeRemainingBytes()`; columns: Method, Description.
ANTI-PATTERNS: Importing the module under test inside `TestOneInput` → module-level import (inside the `instrument_imports()` block) so it is instrumented and not re-executed per iteration. Using `instrument_all()` when C extensions conflict → switch to `instrument_imports()`. Feeding raw bytes to an API expecting text → consume via FDP. Doing file/network/subprocess work inside `TestOneInput` → hoist it.
TOOLING: `#!/usr/bin/python3`; `import atheris`; `atheris.instrument_all()`; `atheris.Setup(sys.argv, TestOneInput, enable_python_coverage=True)`; `atheris.Fuzz()`; `with atheris.instrument_imports():`; `pip3 install .`; `compile_python_fuzzer "$fuzzer"`; `python3 infra/helper.py build_fuzzers|check_build|run_fuzzer`; `-max_total_time=30`; `$SRC`, `$OUT`.
GOTCHAS: `ConsumeString` "may contain surrogates" — use `ConsumeUnicodeNoSurrogates` for strict text. Instant crash = exception on every input, so debug locally with `python3 fuzz_target.py <seed_file>`. Uninstrumented modules give blind coverage guidance. `RUN git clone` in the Dockerfile slows iteration; prefer `COPY`.
STRUCTURE: `../oss-fuzz-engineer/references/structured_seed_generation.md` (declared, not bundled).

## S110 · fuzzing-rust-expert
SOURCE: OSS-Fuzz `infra/helper.py`; cargo-fuzz + `libfuzzer_sys`; `../oss-fuzz-engineer/references/structured_seed_generation.md`.
PURPOSE: Tells an agent how to write, build, and validate Rust fuzz targets with cargo-fuzz/libFuzzer for OSS-Fuzz, including structured fuzzing via `arbitrary`.
CONCEPTS:
- **cargo-fuzz + `libfuzzer_sys`** — The toolchain is cargo-fuzz with the `libfuzzer_sys` crate, and the `fuzz_target!` macro drives libFuzzer. > "Rust fuzzing uses cargo-fuzz with the `libfuzzer_sys` crate, which drives libFuzzer."
- **`base-builder-rust` image** — Rust projects start from their own base builder image with `language: rust`. > "Rust projects must use the Rust base builder image:"
- **fuzz target location** — Targets live in `fuzz/fuzz_targets/<name>.rs` inside the crate and start with `#![no_main]`. > "Rust fuzz targets live in `fuzz/fuzz_targets/<name>.rs` within the crate being fuzzed."
- **raw-bytes harness** — The minimal harness takes `&[u8]` and lets the fuzzer mutate it each iteration. > "Call into the target. The fuzzer will mutate `data` on every iteration."
- **structured fuzzing with `arbitrary`** — A derived `Arbitrary` struct becomes the closure parameter, which the author prefers when the target expects typed input. > "For structured fuzzing using the `arbitrary` crate (preferred when the target expects typed input):"
- **`fuzz/Cargo.toml`** — It declares `libfuzzer-sys = "0.4"`, an optional `arbitrary` with the derive feature, a path dependency on the crate, and a `[[bin]]` with `test = false`, `doc = false`. > "The `Cargo.toml` for the fuzz directory must declare dependencies:"
- **`cargo fuzz build -O`** — Release optimisation is what makes the campaign fast enough to matter. > "cargo fuzz build -O   # -O enables release optimisations; important for performance"
- **binary collection** — Built targets are copied out of the target-triple release directory into `$OUT`. > "`build.sh` uses `cargo fuzz build` and then copies binaries to `$OUT`:"
- **toolchain pinning** — `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` selects nightly, or a dated nightly when reproducibility matters. > "Or pin to a specific nightly for reproducibility:"
- **in-repo corpus** — Seeds placed in `fuzz/corpus/<target_name>/` are picked up automatically and can be zipped for OSS-Fuzz. > "Place seed files in `fuzz/corpus/<target_name>/` within the repo; they are automatically picked up by cargo-fuzz and can be zipped for OSS-Fuzz."
- **artefacts** — A corpus zip and a dictionary named after the target ship under `$OUT`. > "To ship a corpus with OSS-Fuzz copy a zip to `$OUT/<target_name>_seed_corpus.zip`."
- **setup hoisting** — Expensive or per-process-constant setup is lifted out of the callback with `LazyLock` or `OnceLock`. > "avoid I/O, heavy allocations, or expensive setup inside the callback"
- **unsafe coverage** — Ownership prevents most memory corruption, but `unsafe` blocks remain a genuine memory-bug surface and deserve dedicated harnesses. > "if the crate has `unsafe` blocks, write harnesses that exercise those paths — this is where memory bugs can still occur in Rust."
- **finding taxonomy** — Panics, `unsafe` undefined behaviour, logic errors, hangs and deep-recursion stack overflows are what the campaign reports. > "Rust's ownership model prevents most memory-corruption bugs, but fuzzing still finds:"
RULES:
- Target the attack surface: parsers, deserializers, protocol implementations, `unsafe` blocks, any API taking untrusted bytes — > "parsers, deserializers, protocol implementations, unsafe blocks, and any API that processes untrusted bytes."
- Use structured fuzzing with `arbitrary` when the target expects typed data — > "when the target expects typed data rather than raw bytes — this dramatically improves coverage."
- Let-bind and ignore `Result`/`Option`, because only actual panics are findings — > "`Result` and `Option` should be let-bound and ignored (`let _ = ...`). Only actual panics are findings."
- Never `.unwrap()` or `.expect()` on fuzz-driven fallible operations — > "do not use `.unwrap()` or `.expect()` on fallible operations driven by fuzz input — these create false positives."
- Avoid non-determinism: no `rand`, no system time, no thread spawning — > "no `rand`, no system time, no thread spawning inside the fuzz callback."
- Hoist expensive setup outside the `fuzz_target!` macro with `LazyLock`/`OnceLock` — > "do those outside the `fuzz_target!` macro if needed with `LazyLock` / `OnceLock`."
- Exercise `unsafe` paths where memory bugs can still occur — > "write harnesses that exercise those paths — this is where memory bugs can still occur in Rust."
- Build in release mode with `-O`, since debug-mode fuzzing is much slower — > "fuzzing in debug mode is much slower."
- Validate with a 30-second run — > "run_fuzzer <project> <fuzzer_name> -- -max_total_time=30"
- Run `cargo build` and `cargo test` before adding the harness — > "Run `cargo build` and `cargo test` inside the crate before adding the fuzz harness to catch pre-existing compilation errors."
- For `no_std` crates use libfuzzer-sys's `no_std` feature and keep the harness off `std` — > "If the crate uses `no_std`, use `libfuzzer-sys`'s `no_std` feature and ensure the harness does not rely on `std`."
- Document why each entry point was chosen and what bug class it may find — > "Document why each entry point was chosen and what class of bugs it may find."
WORKFLOW:
1. Use `base-builder-rust` and `language: rust`.
2. Add `fuzz/fuzz_targets/<name>.rs` with `fuzz_target!` (raw bytes or `arbitrary` struct).
3. Fill `fuzz/Cargo.toml` dependencies and `[[bin]]` entries.
4. In `build.sh`: `cd $SRC/<crate-dir>`, `cargo fuzz build -O`, loop `fuzz/fuzz_targets/*.rs` copying from `target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release` to `$OUT/`.
5. Set `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` (pinned nightly) when needed; ship corpus zip and dict.
6. Validate: `build_fuzzers`, `check_build`, `run_fuzzer … -- -max_total_time=30`.
TABLES: none.
ANTI-PATTERNS: `.unwrap()`/`.expect()` on fuzz-driven paths → `if let` or `?`, otherwise every input is a false-positive panic. Fuzzing in debug mode → build with `-O`. Passing raw bytes to a typed API → derive `Arbitrary`. Creating clients/parsers per iteration → hoist into `LazyLock`/`OnceLock`. Hand-picking seed files for a structured format → script-generate seeds, or prefer `arbitrary` when the target takes typed data.
TOOLING: `#![no_main]`; `use libfuzzer_sys::fuzz_target;`; `fuzz_target!(|input: MyInput| …)`; `libfuzzer-sys = "0.4"`; `arbitrary = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }`; `[[bin]] name/path/test = false/doc = false`; `cargo fuzz build -O`; `target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release`; `ENV RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=nightly-2025-07-03`; `fuzz/corpus/<target_name>/`; `$OUT/<target_name>_seed_corpus.zip`; `$OUT/<target_name>.dict`; `python3 infra/helper.py build_fuzzers|check_build|run_fuzzer`; `-max_total_time=30`.
GOTCHAS: An instant crash is usually a `panic!` on every input — audit `.unwrap()` on fuzz-driven paths. Debug-mode arithmetic overflow panics that release builds would not — the `-O` requirement is load-bearing. Unpinned nightly toolchains break reproducibility. `RUN git clone` slows local iteration; switch to `COPY`.
STRUCTURE: `../oss-fuzz-engineer/references/structured_seed_generation.md` (declared, not bundled).

## S112 · offensive-fuzzing
SOURCE: none explicitly (links: github.com/AFLplusplus/AFLplusplus, google/honggfuzz, llvm.org LibFuzzer docs, google/syzkaller, 0vercl0k/wtf, nyx-fuzz/Nyx, awslabs/snapchange, AFLplusplus/LibAFL, aflgo/aflgo, IntelLabs/kAFL, googleprojectzero/Jackalope, rust-fuzz/cargo-fuzz, google/atheris, nautilus-fuzz/nautilus, quic/AFLTriage, mrash/afl-cov, google/clusterfuzz).
PURPOSE: Gives an agent an end-to-end offensive fuzzing methodology — pick a fuzzer type, instrument, write a harness, curate a corpus, fuzz, and triage crashes — across parsers, protocols, kernels, EDR engines, firmware and language runtimes.
CONCEPTS:
- **Fuzzer taxonomy** — the author classifies fuzzers as BlackBox, GreyBox, Snapshot, WhiteBox and Ensemble, and tabulates coverage, speed and tools for each row. > "| Snapshot | Good | Fastest | Nyx, wtf, Snapchange |"
- **GreyBox sub-variants** — within GreyBox the author distinguishes directed, grammar, concolic and kernel work, naming a tool per sub-variant. > "**GreyBox sub-variants:** Directed (AFLGo, UAFuzz), Grammar (AFLSmart, Tlspuffin), Concolic (QSYM, Driller), Kernel (syzkaller, kAFL, wtf)."
- **Eight-stage core workflow chain** — the methodology is an ordered chain from target research through reporting. > "Research target → Choose analyses → Build harness → Seed corpus → Instrument → Fuzz → Triage crashes → Report"
- **Input-surface mapping** — the first stage enumerates every way input reaches the target, not just the obvious entry point. > "Map all input surfaces (files, network, IPC, syscalls, IOCTL)"
- **Harness shapes** — the author supplies harness skeletons per fuzzer, including persistent-mode loops for Honggfuzz and AFL++, and `dlopen`/`dlsym` for Mach IPC libraries. > "**Honggfuzz HF_ITER (persistent mode — preferred for large targets):**"
- **Corpus curation** — seeds come from the project's own test suite, from bug reports and from real-world samples, then are minimized and trimmed. > "Pull from target's test suite, bug reports, and real-world samples"
- **Parallel/ensemble orchestration** — several campaigns share one sync directory, with AFL++ in `-M`/`-S` roles and Honggfuzz reading the primary's queue. > "afl-fuzz -M fuzzer1 -i seeds -o sync_dir -- ./target @@"
- **Unstick levers** — when progress stalls the author escalates through CmpLog, dictionaries, directed fuzzing, concolic help, snapshots and the MOpt scheduler. > "Enable CmpLog: `-c 0` on AFL++ secondaries"
- **Oracle selection matrix** — each bug class is paired with a sanitizer, allocator or differential oracle in a dedicated table. > "| Memory safety | ASan, HWASan (AArch64, lower overhead) |"
- **Property oracles** — for logic bugs the author proposes idempotency, differential comparison and invariant checks instead of sanitizers. > "- Invariants: monotonic lengths, checksum equality, schema validation post-parse"
- **Kernel fuzzing with syzkaller** — a JSON config drives syzkaller, with the syscall list narrowed and kcov filters used to steer coverage. > "Limit `enable_syscalls` to deepen coverage on specific subsystems"
- **EDR/Windows targets** — Windows engines are fuzzed through snapshot breakpoints, filter connection ports and IOCTL buffers, with verifier codes watched. > "Take snapshots after initialization, right before parse/dispatch loop"
- **Cross-platform mpengine.dll on Linux** — the engine is loaded as a library and driven through `HF_ITER` with Intel PT, redirecting the Lua VM function to avoid stability issues. > "Cross-platform mpengine.dll on Linux (loadlibrary + HF_ITER + Intel PT):"
- **Rust pipeline ladder** — Rust targets are escalated through property tests, Miri, `cargo careful`, `cargo fuzz`, loom and coverage. > "cargo fuzz run fuzz_target_1 -- -max_total_time=3600  # 4. libFuzzer crashes"
- **Ecosystem entries** — per-language entry points are listed for Go, Python, Rust, JS engines, Wasm runtimes and smart contracts. > "**Go 1.18+**: `go test -fuzz=Fuzz -run=^$ ./...`"
- **Reproducibility hygiene** — a crash is only reproducible when the machine state and seeds are pinned along with the binary. > "pin CPU governor, disable ASLR only where safe, fix RNG seeds"
- **CI/CD fuzzing** — CI runs a time-boxed smoke campaign, uploads crashes, and relies on ClusterFuzzLite plus corpus caching for continuity. > "Use **ClusterFuzzLite** for persistent continuous fuzzing; cache corpora between runs."
- **Tool index table** — 17 tools are mapped to the use cases they serve. > "| [AFLGo](https://github.com/aflgo/aflgo) | Directed fuzzing to target BB/function |"
RULES:
- Limit `enable_syscalls` so syzkaller goes deep on particular subsystems — > "Limit `enable_syscalls` to deepen coverage on specific subsystems"
- Enable the kernel configs syzkaller needs: `CONFIG_KASAN=y`, `CONFIG_KCFI=y`, `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF=y` — > "Enable `CONFIG_KASAN=y`, `CONFIG_KCFI=y`, `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF=y`"
- Use CmpLog on secondaries via `-c 0`, and `AFL_MAP_SIZE=1048576` with `-L 0` for MOpt — > "`AFL_MAP_SIZE=1048576`, `-L 0` for MOpt scheduler"
- Triage crashes in a fixed order — minimize, symbolize, then hash and bucket — > "afl-tmin -i crash -o crash.min -- ./target @@"
- Record binary hashes and sanitizer options with every crash — > "record binary hashes and sanitizer options with every crash"
- For deterministic repro, pin the CPU governor, fix RNG seeds, and keep input sequences from persistent mode — > "save input sequences in persistent mode"
WORKFLOW:
1. Research target and map all input surfaces; prioritize patched code, complex parsers, new code.
2. Instrument/build (AFL++ `afl-clang-fast`, libFuzzer `-fsanitize=fuzzer,address,undefined -O1 -g`, CmpLog build).
3. Write harness (libFuzzer / HF_ITER / `__AFL_LOOP` / IPC).
4. Build seed corpus (`afl-cmin -i raw_corpus -o seeds -- ./target @@`).
5. Launch (`afl-fuzz -M f1 …`, `-S s1 … -c 0`, `./target_libfuzzer corpus/ -max_total_time=3600 -workers=4`, `-Q` for QEMU, Nyx, ensemble).
6. Monitor and unstick.
7. Triage (`afl-tmin`, `ASAN_OPTIONS=abort_on_error=1:symbolize=1 ./target crash.min 2>asan.log`, `./cov-tool --bbids …`, `./bucket.py --key …`).
TABLES: "Fuzzer Types" (5 rows × Type/Coverage/Speed/Tools); "Oracle Selection" (12 rows × Bug Class/Oracle); "Tool Index" (17 tools × Use Case).
ANTI-PATTERNS: only looking at `copy_from_user` in kernel modules → also check DMA-BUF ops, page fault handlers, VM operation structs, allocation callbacks; stopping at a stalled queue → apply CmpLog/dict/directed/concolic/snapshot escalation ladder.
TOOLING: AFL++ (`afl-fuzz`, `afl-cmin`, `afl-tmin`, `-x dict.txt`, `-c 0`, `-Q`, `AFL_LLVM_CMPLOG=1`, `AFL_TOKEN_FILE`), libFuzzer, Honggfuzz, syzkaller (`syz-extract`, `syz-execprog -repeat=0 -procs=1 -cover=0 -debug`), `scripts/decode_stacktrace.sh`, `addr2line`, gflags, `gdb -ex 'bt'`.
GOTCHAS: sanitizer env defaults differ per sanitizer (`TSAN_OPTIONS=history_size=7`, `MSAN_OPTIONS=track_origins=2`); Windows needs PageHeap + local dumps enabled to get usable crashes; snapshot harnesses must be taken after init, right before parse/dispatch; KCFI requires Clang 18; syzkaller crash decode requires `vmlinux` and matching modules.

## S113 · aflpp
SOURCE: AFLplusplus/AFLplusplus (github), docs `fuzzing_in_depth.md`, blog.ritsec.club AFL internals, USENIX WOOT'20 paper, Trail of Bits cURL blog, LiveOverflow videos.
PURPOSE: Tells an agent how to install, compile with, harness, run, monitor and parallelize AFL++ campaigns on C/C++ targets.
CONCEPTS:
- **Instrumentation modes** — LTO mode is tried first for performance and instrumentation, LLVM mode is the fallback, and the GCC plugin covers projects that require GCC. > "- **LTO mode** (`afl-clang-lto`): Best performance and instrumentation. Try this first."
- **Wrapper script (`./afl++ host|docker`)** — one script switches between a bare-metal invocation and a `docker run` of the AFL++ image, normalizing both behind a mode argument. > "Create a wrapper script to run AFL++ on host or Docker:"
- **Docker mode details** — the container is run `--privileged` with the repo mounted at `/src`, and its name derives from the wrapper PID so parallel instances stay distinct. > "parallel instances get distinct container names rather than colliding on a single `afl_fuzzing`"
- **System configuration** — `afl-system-config` is run against the host kernel after each reboot for up to 15% more executions per second, and `afl-persistent-config` adds `mitigations=off` for maximum performance. > "Run after each reboot for up to 15% more executions per second:"
- **Harness rules table** — a Do/Don't table states that the harness resets global state, handles edge cases, stays deterministic, frees memory and validates input size. > "| Reset global state between runs | Rely on state from previous runs |"
- **Build flags table** — four flags are documented, from `-DNO_MAIN=1` for libFuzzer-style harnesses to `-fsanitize=fuzzer-no-link` for libraries. > "| `-DNO_MAIN=1` | Skip main function when using libFuzzer harness |"
- **Corpus lifecycle** — a campaign needs a minimal non-empty seed, then representative real inputs, then `afl-cmin` minimization of the queue. > "AFL++ requires at least one non-empty seed file:"
- **Campaign statistics** — the status output is read through execs/sec, cycles done, corpus count, saved crashes and stability. > "| **stability** | % of stable edges (should be near 100%) |"
- **Output directory anatomy** — `out/default/` holds `cmdline`, `crashes/`, `hangs/`, `queue/`, `fuzzer_stats` and `plot_data`, with testcase names encoding source, time and exec count. > "├── queue/           # Test cases reproducing final fuzzer state"
- **Environment variables that matter** — the author separates the variables worth setting from the niche ones, covering tmpfs, calibration, test cache, exit conditions and the UI. > "AFL++ has [many environment variables](https://aflplus.plus/docs/env_variables/), but most are niche."
- **Variables to avoid** — three variables are flagged as harmful by default, each with the reason. > "| `AFL_DISABLE_TRIM` | Trimming is valuable, don't disable without reason |"
- **Multi-core topology** — a campaign is one `-M primary` plus N `-S secondaryNN` instances writing into a shared output directory. > "Start secondary fuzzers (as many as you have cores):"
- **Asymmetrical fuzzing** — one instance runs with ASan while the rest run without sanitizers, following a stated ratio. > "2. Asymmetrical fuzzing (e.g., one ASan job, rest without sanitizers)"
- **CMPLOG/RedQueen** — the target is rebuilt with `AFL_LLVM_CMPLOG=1` and the instance runs with `-c0` to solve hard path constraints. > "CMPLOG/RedQueen is the best path constraint solving mechanism available in any fuzzer."
- **Sanitizer integration** — `AFL_USE_ASAN=1` and `AFL_USE_UBSAN=1` compile flags catch corruption that does not crash immediately. > "Sanitizers are essential for finding memory corruption bugs that don't cause immediate crashes."
- **Input styles** — the skill covers stdin, file input via `@@`, argument fuzzing through `argv-fuzz-inl.h` and `AFL_INIT_ARGV()`, and persistent mode. > "AFL++ can fuzz programs reading from stdin without a libFuzzer harness:"
- **Performance tuning table** — core count, persistent mode speed, input-size limit and ASan ratio are presented with their impact. > "| Persistent mode | 10-20x faster than fork server |"
- **Troubleshooting table** — six symptoms are mapped to cause and fix, from low exec/sec to Docker virtualization loss. > "| Low stability (<85%) | Non-deterministic code | Fuzz a program via stdin or file inputs, or create such a harness |"
RULES:
- A campaign needs at least one non-empty seed file — > "AFL++ requires at least one non-empty seed file:"
- Set `AFL_TMPDIR=/dev/shm` so the campaign writes to tmpfs — > "Every campaign should use tmpfs — SSDs will thank you, and it's faster"
- Set `AFL_FAST_CAL=1` for slow targets (e.g. >10 ms/exec), which speeds calibration ~2.5x — > "Speeds up calibration ~2.5x — use when targets are slow (e.g., >10 ms/exec)"
- Leave `AFL_TESTCACHE_SIZE` near its 50 MB default; 50-250 MB is the stated good range — > "cache test cases in memory (default: 50 MB, good range: 50-250 MB)"
- In CI, bound the campaign with `AFL_EXIT_ON_TIME=3600` (1 hour with no new paths) or `AFL_EXIT_WHEN_DONE=1` — > "Unbounded fuzzing in CI wastes resources. Set time limits or use exit conditions."
- Backgrounded fuzzers need `</dev/null`, otherwise the job is stopped and never fuzzes — > "The `</dev/null` is required, not decorative."
- Do not pass `-m` with ASan, because ASan reserves 20TB of virtual memory — > "Memory limit (`-m`) is not supported with ASan due to 20TB virtual memory reservation."
- A `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` harness is the efficient style only when stability is at least 85% — > "If a fuzzing campaign has at least 85% stability then this is the most efficient fuzzing style"
- Defaults: `-G` max input length 1048576 bytes, `-t` 1000 ms, `-m 0` (unlimited) — > "| `-G 4000` | Maximum test input length (default: 1048576 bytes) |"
- The GCC version must match the one used to compile the AFL++ GCC plugin — > "GCC version must match the version used to compile the AFL++ GCC plugin."
- The harness returns 0; non-zero is reserved — > "Return 0 (non-zero reserved for future use)"
- Monitor with `watch -n5` because every tick starts a container — > "Every tick starts a container, which is why the interval is 5 seconds rather than 1"
WORKFLOW:
1. Choose install method (Ubuntu/Debian repos — match `lld` to clang, e.g. `apt install afl++ lld-17`; Docker Hub `aflplusplus/aflplusplus:stable`; Docker from source; from source with `LLVM_CONFIG`).
2. Create `./afl++` wrapper and `chmod +x`.
3. `./afl++ host afl-system-config` after each reboot; optionally `afl-persistent-config` + `update-grub` + reboot.
4. Write `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` harness, compile (`./afl++ docker afl-clang-fast++ -DNO_MAIN=1 -O2 -fsanitize=fuzzer harness.cc main.cc -o fuzz`).
5. Create seeds, run `./afl++ docker afl-fuzz -i seeds -o out -- ./fuzz`.
6. Optionally `afl-cmin`, `afl-whatsup`, `afl-plot`.
7. Scale: start `-M primary` then `-S secondaryNN`, monitor with `watch -n5 --color ./afl++ docker afl-whatsup state/`, stop with `kill $(jobs -p)`.
TABLES: "When to Use" (AFL++ vs libFuzzer vs LibAFL × Best For/Complexity); Installation methods (4 × Method/When/Supported Compilers); Harness Rules (Do/Don't); Build Flags (4 × Flag/Purpose); Interpreting Output (5 × Output/Meaning); Fuzzer Options (4); Environment Variables to Avoid (3 × Variable/Why); Common Sanitizer Issues (3); Tips and Tricks (5 × Tip/Why); Performance Tuning (4 × Setting/Impact); Troubleshooting (6 × Problem/Cause/Solution); Related Skills and Related Fuzzers.
ANTI-PATTERNS: `docker run -ti` in CI/agent contexts → drop `-t` (avoid "the input device is not a TTY"); leaving `AFL_DISABLE_TRIM` set → keep trimming; running all cores with ASan → 1 ASan job per 4-8; relying on `docker ps` COMMAND column → use `--no-trunc`.
TOOLING: `afl-clang-fast++`, `afl-g++-fast`, `afl-clang-lto`, `afl-fuzz`, `afl-cmin`, `afl-whatsup`, `afl-plot`, `afl-system-config`, `afl-persistent-config`, `LLVM_CONFIG`, `AFL_LLVM_CMPLOG`, `AFL_USE_ASAN`, `AFL_USE_UBSAN`, `AFL_FINAL_SYNC`, `argv-fuzz-inl.h`.
GOTCHAS: wrapper word-splits args, so `-x "my dict.dict"` breaks; `$$` gives distinct container names or parallel instances collide; `docker ps` truncation; `watch` can't run inside the container; Docker virtualization costs performance.
