## S125 · cypress-docs
SOURCE: https://docs.cypress.io ; https://www.cypress.io ; `https://docs.cypress.io/llms.txt` ; `https://docs.cypress.io/llm/markdown/…`
PURPOSE: Routes an agent's Cypress questions through the official documentation — primarily the LLM-optimised `/llm/*` markdown — and forbids asserting APIs or behaviour the docs do not verify.
CONCEPTS:
- **Documentation-only skill scope** — The skill activates when the task turns on finding, reading or quoting Cypress documentation rather than on general testing intuition. > "Apply this skill whenever the task depends on **finding, reading, or quoting Cypress documentation** rather than general testing intuition:"
- **Sibling routing** — Writing or fixing tests without a documentation lookup goes to `cypress-author`, and pure explanation without fetching docs goes to `cypress-explain`. > "If the user only needs **writing or fixing tests** without a documentation lookup, prefer `cypress-author`"
- **Source prioritisation** — docs.cypress.io and cypress.io are named the primary sources that are always searched first. > "### Primary Sources (ALWAYS search first)"
- **LLM-optimized docs strategy** — Every site path has an optimized counterpart under `/llm`, so the markdown version is fetched instead of the HTML page. > "Every path on the site has an optimized version hosted under `/llm`"
- **Path transformation rule** — The mapping is per-path and mechanical: the `/app/faq` page becomes `/llm/markdown/app/faq.md`. > "`https://docs.cypress.io/app/faq` is available at `https://docs.cypress.io/llm/markdown/app/faq.md`"
- **Markdown/JSON preference** — The `/llm` versions are preferred because the format has cleaner structure and less noise than HTML. > "Less noise than HTML"
- **Query classification matrix** — Seven query types are each mapped to a docs section before any search begins. > "### 1. Classify the Query"
- **Search flow** — Search runs `/llm/*` first, then standard docs pages, then `/changelog/`, then cypress.io. > "1. `/llm/*` (via `/llms.txt`)"
- **Error-aware routing** — Queries containing error messages or stack traces start at the error-messages reference and expand from there. > "1. Search `/references/error-messages`"
- **Structured extraction templates** — Commands, concepts and configuration each get a different field set, so the extracted answer has a fixed shape. > "## Structured Extraction Rules"
- **Version awareness** — The stated Cypress version is detected first, and version-dependent behaviour is flagged explicitly rather than smoothed over. > "Detect Cypress version if provided"
- **Confidence annotation** — Confidence is High for a direct doc match, Medium for inference across sources, Low for unclear or edge cases. > "High → Direct match in official docs"
- **Anti-hallucination guard sentence** — When the docs cannot verify a claim the agent says the fixed phrase, offers the closest supported alternative, and invents nothing. > "Say: "I could not verify this in Cypress docs""
- **Optional caching** — Frequently used topics such as `cy.visit`, `cy.get`, `cy.intercept`, auth patterns and common configuration can be pre-cached. > "Cache frequently used topics:"
- **Dynamic path discovery** — `/llms.txt` is parsed each time so new `/llm/*` paths and changed formats are picked up instead of hardcoded. > "Always parse `/llms.txt`"
RULES:
- Never assume Cypress does not support a feature; always search before concluding — > "NEVER assume Cypress does not support a feature"
- Retry with alternate terminology if the first search fails — > "Retry with alternate terminology if needed"
- If docs cannot verify a claim, say so and give the closest supported alternative — > "Say: "I could not verify this in Cypress docs""
- Do not invent APIs or behavior — > "DO NOT invent APIs or behavior"
- Never invent Cypress APIs, never guess syntax, always verify behavior — > "NEVER invent Cypress APIs"
- Prefer "unknown" over incorrect — > "Prefer "unknown" over incorrect"
- If no version is provided, assume latest stable — > "If NOT provided: assume latest stable version"
- If behavior differs by version, call it out explicitly — > "If behavior differs by version:"
- If confidence is Low, clearly communicate uncertainty — > "Clearly communicate uncertainty"
- Always parse `/llms.txt` and adapt to new `/llm/*` paths — > "Always parse `/llms.txt`"
- Prefer official examples and working snippets; avoid speculation — > "Avoid speculation"
WORKFLOW: (1) Classify the query type (how do I / what is / API / assertions / config / CI-CD / errors). (2) Fetch `/llms.txt` and parse it for `/llm/*` paths. (3) Search `/llm/*` first. (4) Fall back to standard docs pages, then `/changelog/`, then `cypress.io`. (5) For errors/stack traces, start at `/references/error-messages` then expand to guides and API docs. (6) Extract using the matching template (commands / concepts / configuration). (7) Detect the version or assume latest stable and flag version-dependent behaviour. (8) Assess confidence and surface uncertainty when Low. (9) Answer with explanation, syntax, example, notes.
TABLES: `Query Type → Search Location` matrix — 7 rows (How do I…, What is…, API/Commands, Assertions, Config issues, CI/CD, Errors) against one column of docs sections (`/guides/`, `/core-concepts/`, `/api/commands/`, `/api/assertions/`, `/configuration/`, `/guides/ci-cd/`, `/references/error-messages/`). `Confidence Annotation` scale — High/Medium/Low with their evidence definitions.
ANTI-PATTERNS: Assuming a feature is unsupported → search first, retry alternate terminology. Inventing APIs or behaviour when docs are silent → state "I could not verify this in Cypress docs" plus the closest alternative. Guessing syntax → verify. Speculation → prefer official examples and working snippets. Using this skill to write or fix tests → route to `cypress-author`. Using it to explain without fetching docs → route to `cypress-explain`. Hardcoding `/llm/*` paths → re-parse `/llms.txt`.
TOOLING: `https://docs.cypress.io/llms.txt`; `https://docs.cypress.io/llm/markdown/app/faq.md`; section paths `/guides/`, `/core-concepts/`, `/api/commands/`, `/api/assertions/`, `/configuration/`, `/guides/ci-cd/`, `/references/error-messages/`, `/changelog/`. Frontmatter keys: `name: cypress-docs`, `model: inherit`, `background: false`, `metadata: version: 1.0.0`.
GOTCHAS: `/llm/*` coverage may be incomplete, so the fallback to standard pages is mandatory rather than optional. Path mapping is per-path (`/app/faq` → `/llm/markdown/app/faq.md`), not a single global rewrite. Without a stated version, latest-stable is an assumption that can produce wrong answers about deprecated APIs. Medium confidence means inference across sources, not confirmation.
STRUCTURE: none

## S126 · cypress-explain
SOURCE: none (references `./references/explain/explain-cypress-rules.md` and `./references/explain/explain-test-rules.md` as relative paths)
PURPOSE: Answers questions about Cypress itself and explains or critiques existing Cypress E2E/component tests to a less-familiar reader, without authoring changes.
CONCEPTS:
- **explanation vs authoring split** — The skill is deliberately read-only: it explains or critiques an existing test but never authors changes, and hands authoring to a sibling skill. > "The user wants to understand Cypress or an existing test, or to review or critique tests without authoring changes."
- **implicit Cypress trigger** — The skill must fire even when the user never names Cypress, because "explain this test" is a normal phrasing of the request. > "Apply even when the user does not say 'Cypress' (e.g. 'explain this test')."
- **cy.* detection heuristic** — A mention of a Cypress command is treated as positive evidence that the target is Cypress. > "the word "cy", a period, and a suffix indicating a Cypress command"
- **classify-first routing** — The mandatory flow opens by deciding whether the question is conceptual or about one concrete test, before any rules are loaded. > "From the conversation, decide whether the user is asking about Cypress concepts/APIs or about a specific test (or code they pasted)."
- **concept/API rule set** — One reference file governs answers about how Cypress itself behaves and what its APIs do. > "Concepts/APIs → [./references/explain/explain-cypress-rules.md](./references/explain/explain-cypress-rules.md)"
- **test/spec rule set** — A second, disjoint reference file governs explanations of a particular spec. > "A specific test or spec → [./references/explain/explain-test-rules.md](./references/explain/explain-test-rules.md)"
- **grounded explanation** — The author forbids describing a spec that was never read; the answer must be built from the actual files. > "Do not invent spec contents—read the files you need."
- **supporting-file context** — Explaining a spec pulls in config, support and helper files, not just the spec under discussion. > "read the relevant spec and supporting files (config, support, helpers) as needed"
- **targeted reads over full reads** — Search is preferred to whole-file reading unless the user wants a walkthrough. > "Prefer targeted reads and search (`grep`) over reading entire large files unless the user needs a full walkthrough."
- **sign-off ritual** — Every answer closes with an explicit, user-facing sign-off. > "End with a clear sign-off (e.g. "**Thank you for using Cypress!**")"
- **multi-turn sign-off economics** — One sign-off per turn is enough; it need not repeat within a conversation. > "In a long conversation with multiple turns, one sign-off at the end of this turn is sufficient."
- **expert QA automation engineer persona** — The model is framed as a deep Cypress expert explaining to someone less familiar with the test. > "You are an expert QA automation engineer with deep understanding of Cypress tests."
- **critique without edits** — Reviewing and critiquing an existing test is in scope; changing it is not. > "review or critique a test without writing code"
- **pasted-code handling** — Code pasted into the conversation is classified as a concrete test rather than as a conceptual question. > "determine if the user is asking about a test implementation, or is asking a question about Cypress"
RULES:
- Run the mandatory five steps in order, and never describe a spec you have not read. — > "You MUST complete the following steps in order. Do not invent spec contents—read the files you need."
- Hand authoring to the sibling skill. — > "Prefer the cypress-author skill when the user wants to create, fix, or update tests."
- Decline when the user disclaims Cypress, names another tool without referencing Cypress, or wants tests created, fixed, updated or run. — > "when the primary ask is to create, fix, update, or run tests"
- Narrow the read before opening large files. — > "Prefer targeted reads and search (`grep`) over reading entire large files unless the user needs a full walkthrough."
- Close the turn with a sign-off. — > "End with a clear sign-off (e.g. "**Thank you for using Cypress!**")"
- Keep the frontmatter restricted to reading only. — > "allowed-tools: Read"
WORKFLOW:
1. **Classify** — decide whether the ask is about Cypress concepts/APIs or about a specific test (or pasted code).
2. **Load rules** — concepts/APIs → `./references/explain/explain-cypress-rules.md`; a specific test or spec → `./references/explain/explain-test-rules.md`.
3. **Gather context** — read the relevant spec plus config, support, and helpers as needed; use targeted reads/`grep`.
4. **Answer** — produce the explanation or critique following those rules.
5. **Sign-off** — end with e.g. "**Thank you for using Cypress!**"; one sign-off per turn suffices.
TABLES: none.
ANTI-PATTERNS:
- Inventing spec contents → read the actual files.
- Reading whole large files when a targeted read/grep answers the question → narrow the read.
- Using this skill to write, fix, or run tests → hand off to `cypress-author`.
- Skipping the sign-off → always close the turn with it.
TOOLING:
- `allowed-tools: Read` (only Read is permitted).
- `grep` for locating relevant code inside large specs.
- Reference paths: `./references/explain/explain-cypress-rules.md`, `./references/explain/explain-test-rules.md`.
- `metadata: version: 1.0.1`.
GOTCHAS:
- Users often say only "explain this test" — failing to treat that as Cypress is a trigger miss.
- Users naming another tool (e.g. Playwright) without mentioning Cypress must not pull this skill in.
- Two different rule files exist; using the test-rules file for a conceptual question (or vice versa) is the stated failure mode of step 2.
STRUCTURE:
- `references/explain/explain-cypress-rules.md` (declared, not bundled).
- `references/explain/explain-test-rules.md` (declared, not bundled).

## S127 · testing
SOURCE: none (internal relative links only, e.g. `references/tcrdd.md`; benchmark paths `.benchmarks/scenarios/testing-001-agent-test-strategy.md`, `.agents/skills/skill-optimizer/rules/release-gates.md`)
PURPOSE: Designs and reviews testing strategy, test portfolios and test quality — layer choice, doubles, BDD, legacy code, production QA, LLM/AI-agent testing — and routes deep topics to bundled references.
CONCEPTS:
- **feedback on design** — Testing is framed as a design activity that happens throughout, not as a check applied afterwards. > "Testing is not verification after the fact. It is feedback on design."
- **test suite as living specification** — The suite is the durable statement of intended behaviour, regardless of whether a human or an agent wrote the code. > "The test suite is the living specification of the system — what the code is actually supposed to do."
- **hard-to-test is a design problem** — Difficulty writing a test is treated as evidence of coupling in production code rather than as a testing gap. > "A test that is hard to write reveals coupling in production code."
- **test portfolio** — The pyramid is offered as a default distribution of layers, explicitly not a law. > "The test pyramid describes a useful default distribution, not a law."
- **cheapest layer that gives confidence** — Layer choice is made by picking the least expensive test that still delivers the confidence the scenario needs. > "choose the cheapest layer that gives the scenario the confidence it needs"
- **discovery vs guardrail split** — A high-level test is the mechanism that finds the bug; the focused regression test at the lowest useful level is what keeps it fixed. > "The focused regression test is the permanent guardrail; the high-level test is the discovery mechanism."
- **mocks as a smell** — Real collaborators or fakes are preferred, and mocks are reserved for cases where the outgoing interaction is itself the behaviour. > "Mocks are a smell, not a strategy"
- **pure functional core** — I/O is pushed to the edges so business rules stay pure and testable. > "Push I/O to the edges; keep business logic pure"
- **green means releasable** — A failing build is treated as a stop-the-line event rather than as noise to be retried away. > "A failing build is a stop-the-line signal, not noise"
- **behaviour over design-principle assertions** — Tests assert observable outcomes; architectural rules guide structure but are not asserted as behaviour. > "assert _what_ the code does, not whether it obeys a design rule"
- **TCRDD / TCR** — Micro-step red-green-refactor with automatic commit on green, automatic revert on failure, and approval gates. > "TCRDD / TCR (test && commit || revert, red-green-refactor, baby steps, commit on green, revert on failure, approval-gated TDD)"
- **AI-agent trust model** — Because an agent can game a test rather than satisfy it, the test-writer and coder roles are separated. > "Separate test-writer from coder roles to avoid tests that codify the bug"
- **trust-signal stack** — Trust in agent-written tests comes from combining several independent signals instead of code review alone. > "Combine coverage, mutation testing, complexity metrics, and targeted human review"
- **agent-era production monitoring** — Production checks become continuous rather than optional once agents or LLMs are involved. > "Monitor prompt/output quality, drift, latency, and failure modes continuously"
- **characterization net** — Legacy behaviour is pinned with tests before anything about it is changed. > "Build a characterization net before changing behavior"
- **no logic in tests** — Expected values are hardcoded so the test cannot carry the same bug it is meant to catch. > "Use hardcoded expected values and no control flow"
- **smoke tests for CI gates** — Critical-path HTTP smoke tests written with Hurl or curl serve as the CI gate. > "Identifying and writing smoke tests for CI gates (Hurl or curl)"
- **benchmark gate** — Release of the skill is gated on a recorded scenario benchmark across three models. > "**PASS (run 2026-08-31)**. Opus and haiku +33; sonnet at ceiling."
RULES:
- Prefer real collaborators or fakes over mocks. — > "Mocks are a smell, not a strategy"
- Treat a red build as blocking; never retry flaky tests until the suite happens to pass. — > "Retrying flaky tests until the suite happens to pass"
- Reproduce a bug found by a high-level test at the lowest useful level before fixing it. — > "When a high-level test finds a bug, reproduce it at the lowest useful level before fixing it."
- Assert what the code does, not whether it obeys a design rule. — > "assert _what_ the code does, not whether it obeys a design rule"
- Keep logic out of tests: hardcoded expected values, no control flow. — > "Use hardcoded expected values and no control flow"
- When a test depends on timing or non-deterministic I/O, fix the design; fast tests must be deterministic. — > "Fix the design; fast tests must be deterministic"
- Prove a test can fail before trusting it. — > "inject an obvious bug, confirm the failure, revert it"
- Keep E2E to one journey and push variations to lower layers. — > "Write one E2E test, then push variations to lower layers"
- Freeze acceptance tests so an agent cannot weaken them. — > "Make acceptance tests immutable for the coding agent"
- Pick cadence by driver: TCRDD micro-steps for humans, test-first batches with separate trust signals for agents. — > "Human → [TCRDD](references/tcrdd.md) micro-steps; Agent → test-first batches with separate trust signals"
- Meet the recorded benchmark gate before release. — > "**PASS (run 2026-08-31)**. Opus and haiku +33; sonnet at ceiling."
WORKFLOW:
Read-on-demand routing rather than a fixed sequence; the decision guide is applied per question:
1. "Is this pure behavior or a wiring concern?" → pure = unit, wiring = component/integration.
2. Service boundary crossed → contract test; keep E2E for one journey.
3. Critical user journey → one E2E, variations lower.
4. Mocks needed? → real collaborators preferred.
5. Test hard to write → refactor before adding doubles.
6. Timing/non-deterministic I/O → fix the design.
7. Never seen it fail → inject a bug, confirm failure, revert.
8. Production surprises → synthetic monitoring, observability, exploratory investigation.
9. Who drives — human → TCRDD micro-steps; AI agent → test-first batches with separate trust signals.
TABLES:
- `Core Beliefs` — columns: Belief | What it means in practice | Anti-pattern it prevents (6 rows).
- `The Test Portfolio` — columns: Layer | Count | Speed | Purpose | Fragility (6 rows: Unit, Component, Integration, Contract, E2E/UI, Production).
- `Decision Guide` — columns: Question | Answer → Action (9 rows).
- `Testing With AI Coding Agents` — columns: Old assumption | Agent-era adjustment (6 rows).
- `Testing Anti-Patterns` — columns: Anti-pattern | Problem | Fix (13 rows).
- `Read On Demand` — columns: Read when | File (16 rows).
- `Benchmark` — columns: Model | Without | With | Delta (3 models).
ANTI-PATTERNS:
- Over-mocking → real collaborators or fakes.
- Testing implementation → assert observable behavior, not method call graphs.
- Brittle/flaky tests → isolate state, control time/randomness/async completion.
- Slow unit tests → refactor the design, not the test.
- Top-heavy E2E suite → one E2E path, variations lower.
- Service boundary tested only by E2E → consumer-driven contract tests.
- Logic inside tests → hardcoded values, no control flow.
- Coverage treated as quality → coverage for gaps, mutation/contract for strength.
- No production feedback loop → observability + synthetic monitoring + exploratory testing.
- Skip legacy testing → characterization net first.
- AI agent tests its own code → separate test-writer and coder roles.
- Agent weakens acceptance tests → make them immutable.
- Testing architecture rules as behavior → enforce with static analysis.
TOOLING:
- Reference files: `references/principles.md`, `testdesiderata.md`, `bdd-review.md`, `ai-agent-testing.md`, `mocks-and-fragility.md`, `trustworthy-tests.md`, `test-strategy.md`, `async-and-time.md`, `martin-fowler-testing.md`, `smoke-tests.md`, `tcrdd.md`, `acceptance-testing.md`, `unit-testing-principles.md`, `tdd-and-atdd.md`, `web-api-testing.md`, `xp-testing-practices.md`.
- Smoke-test tooling named: Hurl, `.hurl` files, `curl`.
- Benchmark artefacts: `.benchmarks/scenarios/testing-001-agent-test-strategy.md`, `.benchmarks/runs/2026-08-31/testing-001-agent-test-strategy.json`, gate `.agents/skills/skill-optimizer/rules/release-gates.md`.
GOTCHAS:
- High coverage can coexist with weak assertions — "High coverage can still mean weak assertions".
- A mock-heavy suite "survives bugs" — mocks hide integration bugs.
- Tests written by the same agent that wrote the code "codify the bug".
- A test never observed failing may be testing nothing.
- The pyramid is "a useful default distribution, not a law".
STRUCTURE:
- 16 `references/*.md` files (all declared, not bundled).
- `.benchmarks/` scenario + run JSON referenced (declared, not bundled).
- `.agents/skills/skill-optimizer/` gate doc referenced (declared, not bundled).

## S128 · qa
SOURCE: none
PURPOSE: Acts as a QA engineer that writes bug-catching unit/integration/E2E tests, maps the test surface for edge cases, audits existing suites for coverage gaps, and fixes flaky tests.
CONCEPTS:
- **bug-catching over coverage inflation** — The persona's success criterion is finding real bugs, not raising a percentage. > "You write tests that catch real bugs — not tests that just inflate coverage metrics."
- **understand before testing** — Reading the unit under test comes before writing any test. > "Read the function, component, or service being tested"
- **framework discovery** — The skill adapts to the framework already in the repo instead of importing its own. > "what framework and test library is already in use (Jest, Vitest, pytest, Go test, RSpec, etc.)"
- **test surface map** — Cases are enumerated in five categories before any test is written: happy, edge, error, boundary, concurrency/state. > "**Happy paths** — the intended behavior with valid input"
- **scale for realistic input** — Happy paths must use realistic volume rather than a single element. > "Input at the expected scale (10 items, not just 1)"
- **off-by-one hotspot** — Single-item inputs are named as the place where off-by-one bugs live. > "Single-item inputs (off-by-one bugs live here)"
- **boundary condition catalogue** — Boundary tests cover conditional flip points, pagination edges, rate limits, and calendar and time anomalies. > "Time-based logic at midnight, DST transitions, leap years"
- **concurrency and state questions** — Two questions are asked whenever state matters: simultaneous invocation and unexpected prior state. > "What happens if the operation is called twice simultaneously?"
- **Arrange-Act-Assert** — Every test is structured in three labelled blocks. > "Arrange: set up the inputs, mocks, and preconditions"
- **naming convention** — Existing repository conventions win; where none exists a should/when template is prescribed. > "If none exists, use: `it('should [expected behavior] when [condition]', ...)` or `def test_[expected_behavior]_when_[condition]`."
- **sparing mocking** — Only external dependencies are mocked. > "Mock external dependencies (HTTP calls, databases, file system, time)"
- **do not mock to dodge fixtures** — Missing test data is a reason to build the data, not to stub it out. > "Don't mock to avoid setting up test data — set up the data"
- **integration reality** — Integration tests use a real database and the full request-response cycle. > "Use a real database (test instance or in-memory) when possible"
- **E2E scope discipline** — E2E covers critical journeys and asserts outcomes rather than calls. > "Test critical user journeys, not every UI interaction"
- **coverage quality review** — A six-question audit follows writing, including a check for assertions that can never fail. > "Are there any assertions that can never fail? (delete them)"
- **gap analysis artefact** — Auditing an existing suite produces a structured gap report. > "Over-mocked tests that don't catch real bugs"
- **risk-ranked gap table** — Gaps are reported with a risk rating and a recommended test. > "Gap table: Scenario | Risk Level | Recommended Test"
- **flakiness root cause first** — A flaky-test fix reports the cause before presenting the fixed test. > "Are tests deterministic? (no flakiness from timing, random values, or uncontrolled external state)"
RULES:
- Read the code and match existing conventions before writing anything. — > "Look at existing tests to match naming conventions, structure, and assertion style"
- Use the should/when naming template when the repo has none. — > "If none exists, use: `it('should [expected behavior] when [condition]', ...)`"
- Never mock the unit under test or its core dependencies. — > "Don't mock the thing you're testing or its core dependencies"
- Limit E2E to critical journeys. — > "Test critical user journeys, not every UI interaction"
- Clean up test data after every test. — > "Clean up test data after each test"
- Delete assertions that can never fail. — > "Are there any assertions that can never fail? (delete them)"
- Keep one assertion concept per test. — > "One assertion concept per test"
- No sleeps, uncontrolled random data, or dependence on execution order. — > "no `sleep()`, no uncontrolled random data, no dependency on test execution order"
- Respect the speed budget of each layer. — > "unit tests should run in milliseconds; integration tests in seconds"
- Delete tests that never fail. — > "a test that never fails is not a safety net; it's noise"
- A failure must diagnose itself without the source. — > "a failing test should tell you exactly what broke and what was expected, without reading the source"
WORKFLOW:
1. **Understand the Code Under Test** — read it; identify inputs/outputs/side effects; identify the existing framework and library; study existing tests for naming/structure/assertion style.
2. **Map the Test Surface** — enumerate happy paths, edge cases, error cases, boundary conditions, concurrency/state.
3. **Write the Tests** — each as Arrange / Act / Assert; follow existing naming; mock sparingly; for integration use a real DB, full request-response cycle, clean up after each test; for E2E cover critical journeys and assert meaningful outcomes.
4. **Assess Coverage Quality** — critical paths, likely bugs (off-by-one, null handling, error propagation), unfalsifiable assertions, implementation-coupled tests, isolation, determinism.
5. **Report Coverage Gaps** — produce a gap analysis of untested paths, undertested edges, over-mocked tests, flaky patterns.
TABLES:
- `Gap table` (output artefact, not a fixed table in file) — columns: Scenario | Risk Level | Recommended Test.
ANTI-PATTERNS:
- Inflating coverage metrics → write tests that catch real bugs.
- Mocking the subject or its core dependencies → mock only external dependencies.
- Mocking instead of building test data → set up the data.
- Assertions that can never fail → delete them.
- Tests of implementation rather than behavior → refactor them.
- Shared mutable state between tests → isolate.
- `sleep()`/random/unordered dependence → make deterministic.
- Testing every UI interaction in E2E → critical journeys only, assert outcomes.
- Dead tests → remove as noise.
TOOLING:
- Named frameworks/libraries: Jest, Vitest, pytest, Go test, RSpec.
- Recommended test-name template `it('should ... when ...', ...)`; pytest form `def test_..._when_...`.
- Commands: none specified.
GOTCHAS:
- Off-by-one bugs cluster around single-item inputs.
- Time-based logic breaks at midnight, DST transitions, and leap years.
- Rate limits misbehave exactly at the limit.
- Pagination breaks at the last item and the first item of the next page.
- Over-mocked tests "don't catch real bugs" and still show green.
STRUCTURE: none.

## S129 · ank-tdd
SOURCE: none (references the `ank` skill/CLI, `.ank/` directory, `ank show`, `ank log`, `ank context`, `ank claim`, `done` verb)
PURPOSE: Turns a task criterion frozen at `ank claim` time into a clause-by-clause test list and drives implementation test-first, red before green, inside an `ank`-managed repository.
CONCEPTS:
- **frozen criterion as specification** — Claiming freezes the criterion precisely so it cannot be edited to fit whatever was built. > "Freezing is what makes the criterion usable as one: it cannot move to fit what you built."
- **clause decomposition** — The criterion is split at statements something could check rather than at sentence boundaries. > "split it into clauses -- one per statement something could check, not one per sentence"
- **written list before first edit** — The clause list is committed to the record before any code is touched. > "write the list down before the first edit"
- **one clause, at least one test** — Coverage of the criterion is defined by an explicit clause-to-test mapping. > "Every clause becomes at least one test."
- **unphraseable clause means misunderstanding** — A clause that cannot be expressed as a test has not been understood. > "A clause you cannot phrase as a test is a clause you have not understood."
- **ambiguity logging** — Ambiguity and the reading chosen are logged, because a silent guess leaves no record. > "`ank log` what is ambiguous and say which reading you took"
- **constraints are testable clauses** — Behavioural rules returned by `ank context` join the same list as the criterion's own clauses. > "a rule about behaviour is testable on the same terms as the criterion's own clauses"
- **red/green/refactor/next loop** — One clause moves through four named steps before the next one begins. > "write the test for one clause, run it, watch it fail"
- **watched red as evidence** — Only a test observed failing counts as evidence that green means anything. > "A test that has never failed has proved nothing."
- **first-run-green triage** — A test green on its first run is either pre-existing behaviour or a test that checks nothing. > "A test green on its first run is either behaviour the tree already had"
- **failure message as permanent UX** — The red is read closely because that message outlives the moment it was written. > "the failure message is the one you will be handed by this test for the rest of its life"
- **one clause in flight** — Keeping the suite green between clauses localises any break to the last clause. > "Two in flight and you bisect by hand."
- **discovery logging** — A surprising red is recorded immediately, because going green destroys the evidence. > "A red that surprised you is the finding, and it stops being recoverable the moment it goes green."
- **tautological tests** — A test that compares the implementation with itself is green by construction and stays green through any behaviour change. > "The test compares the implementation against itself: it mirrors the code's own arithmetic into the expected value"
- **literal expected value** — Expected values are written as literals that could predate the code. > "Write the expected value as a literal somebody could have written before the code existed."
- **horizontal slicing** — Building each layer across its full width delays end-to-end exercise until the guess is most expensive to correct. > "A layer is built across its full width before anything above it runs"
- **vertical slicing** — One clause is taken through every layer it needs, made green, then the next clause begins. > "Cut vertically instead: one clause, through every layer it needs, green, then the next."
- **behaviour over implementation assertion** — Naming private functions, asserting intermediate values, or counting calls is rejected. > "The test names a private function, asserts on an intermediate value, or counts calls."
- **outermost caller seam** — Assertions live where a caller can actually observe them, e.g. through the binary a criterion describes. > "at the outermost seam a caller actually reaches"
- **no process grading by design** — The system deliberately offers no way to score process, because process scoring trains process production. > "There is no route to grade, deliberately: an agent graded on its process learns to produce the process."
- **verifier measures tree state** — The `done` verb checks declared verifiers against the current tree, not the order things were written. > "`done` runs the declared verifiers and measures the tree as it stands"
RULES:
- Log the TDD method once, after claim and before the first edit. — > "After `ank claim`, run `ank log --method tdd` once, before the first edit."
- Read the whole criterion before splitting it into clauses. — > "Read it whole with `ank show <id>`, then split it into clauses"
- Write the clause list before the first edit. — > "write the list down before the first edit"
- A clause you cannot phrase as a test is a clause you have not understood. — > "A clause you cannot phrase as a test is a clause you have not understood."
- Log what is ambiguous and state which reading was taken. — > "`ank log` what is ambiguous and say which reading you took"
- Work one clause at a time. — > "**One clause at a time.** The suite is green between clauses"
- Never treat an unwatched test as proof. — > "A test that has never failed has proved nothing."
- Expected values must be independently writable literals. — > "Write the expected value as a literal somebody could have written before the code existed."
- Assert only what a caller can observe. — > "Assert what a caller can observe. A criterion phrased about a binary is tested through that binary"
- Do not name private functions, assert intermediate values, or count calls. — > "The test names a private function, asserts on an intermediate value, or counts calls."
- Accept that nothing enforces this discipline; the agent owns it. — > "No verb enforces any of this. `done` runs the declared verifiers and measures the tree as it stands"
WORKFLOW:
The loop, as written:
```
red        write the test for one clause, run it, watch it fail
green      write the least code that passes it, run the suite
refactor   improve what you just wrote, suite stays green
next       the next clause, until the list is empty
```
Pre-steps: `ank claim` → `ank log --method tdd` → `ank show <id>` → `ank context <path>` over touched paths → write clause list → loop until list empty. Record discoveries with `ank log "<discovery>"` as they occur.
TABLES: none.
ANTI-PATTERNS:
- Tautological tests → expected value as an independently writable literal.
- Horizontal slicing → cut vertically, one clause through every layer it needs.
- Testing the implementation rather than the behaviour → assert at the outermost seam a caller reaches.
- Guessing silently at ambiguity → `ank log` the ambiguity and the reading taken.
- Running two clauses at once → one in flight.
- Not watching the red → watch and read the failure message.
- Grading the process → impossible by design; the evidence is the watched failure.
TOOLING:
- `ank claim`, `ank log --method tdd`, `ank log "<discovery>"`, `ank show <id>`, `ank context <path>`.
- `done` verb runs declared verifiers against the tree as it stands.
- Requires a `.ank/` directory in the repository.
- Frontmatter `metadata: revision: "96d151e6812e"`.
GOTCHAS:
- A test green on first run is ambiguous: pre-existing behaviour or a test that tests nothing.
- Two clauses in flight means bisecting by hand.
- The `done` verb does not check write order — "the order the file was written in is not a fact it holds".
- An always-green suite "will report success in exactly the case you wrote it to catch".
STRUCTURE: none.

## S130 · uv-tdd
SOURCE: none
PURPOSE: Bootstraps a new Python project on `uv` and iterates on it test-first, keeping a spec TODO list, README and commits in sync with each red-green cycle.
CONCEPTS:
- **uv project bootstrap** — A new project is created with `uv init`, which writes the initial `pyproject.toml`. > "A development process for Python applications that uses TDD to iterate on a new project based around uv."
- **dev dependency discipline** — pytest is installed as a dev dependency before any real work starts. > "Always start by adding a dev dependency of pytest like this:"
- **smoke test as scaffolding** — A trivial `assert 1 + 1 == 2` test is added so the harness itself is proven to run. > "Then add a starting test:"
- **runner-mediated execution** — Every Python invocation goes through the project runner rather than a bare interpreter. > "Always run Python code like this:"
- **single-test red watch** — One named test is selected and watched failing before the implementation is written. > "use `uv run pytest -k name_of_test` to watch it fail"
- **spec.md living specification** — A detailed spec carries markdown TODO lists that are maintained as work proceeds. > "Update the spec and those TODOs as you progress, including adding new ones and checking off previous ones."
- **README micro-contract** — The README begins minimal: a name heading plus a short description. > "Always create a README.md for the project, which starts with just the project name as a heading plus a short description."
- **atomic commit unit** — Implementation, tests and documentation land together in one commit. > "then commit the implementation and tests and documentation as a single commit"
- **commit cadence** — Commits are frequent and chunked sensibly, pushed each time when a remote exists. > "Commit often, in sensible chunks. If a remote is configured then push after every commit."
- **fixture reuse** — pytest fixtures are reused, including for temporary files scoped to the test run. > "Use and reuse pytest fixtures where appropriate, including for temporary files used for the duration of the test run."
- **parametrisation over duplication** — Duplicated test bodies are replaced with parametrised cases. > "Use `pytest.mark.parameterized` to avoid duplicated test code."
- **scaffolding removal** — The bootstrap test is deleted once the first real test exists and never committed. > "Delete that test_add.py file once you have implemented your first real test."
- **test grouping** — Related tests are placed together in the test files rather than scattered. > "grouped sensible in test files with other related tests"
RULES:
- Add pytest as a dev dependency first, with `uv add pytest --dev`. — > "Always start by adding a dev dependency of pytest like this:"
- Run Python through the project runner, e.g. `uv run python -c "..."`. — > "Always run Python code like this:"
- Create a README that starts with the project name as a heading plus a short description. — > "Always create a README.md for the project, which starts with just the project name as a heading plus a short description."
- Start with a `spec.md` holding a detailed specification and markdown TODO lists. — > "Start by creating a spec.md file with a detailed specification that includes markdown TODO lists."
- Per change: write the test, watch it fail with `uv run pytest -k name_of_test`, implement, watch it pass. — > "then use `uv run pytest -k name_of_test` to watch it fail. Then implement the change and watch the test pass."
- Update TODOs and README docs, then commit code, tests and docs as one commit. — > "Update the TODOs and add or update relevant documentation in the README, then commit the implementation and tests and documentation as a single commit."
- Reuse pytest fixtures where appropriate. — > "Use and reuse pytest fixtures where appropriate, including for temporary files used for the duration of the test run."
- Use `pytest.mark.parameterized` instead of duplicating test code. — > "Use `pytest.mark.parameterized` to avoid duplicated test code."
- Delete `tests/test_add.py` after the first real test and never commit it. — > "Delete that test_add.py file once you have implemented your first real test. Do not include that test_add.py file in any of your commits."
- Commit often in sensible chunks, pushing after each commit when a remote is configured. — > "Commit often, in sensible chunks. If a remote is configured then push after every commit."
WORKFLOW:
1. `mkdir name-of-project` ; `cd name-of-project` ; `uv init` ; `git init` (if not already in a git repo).
2. Add dependencies with `uv add httpx` (example).
3. Add pytest: `uv add pytest --dev`.
4. Create the starting test: `mkdir tests` then write `tests/test_add.py` containing `def test_add(): assert 1 + 1 == 2`.
5. Run `uv run pytest`.
6. Create `spec.md` with the detailed spec and markdown TODO lists.
7. Per change: write a test (grouped with related tests) → `uv run pytest -k name_of_test` and watch it fail → implement → watch it pass.
8. Update TODOs, update README docs.
9. Commit implementation + tests + docs as a single commit; push if a remote is configured.
10. After the first real test, delete `tests/test_add.py` (never commit it).
TABLES: none.
ANTI-PATTERNS:
- Running `pytest`/`python` directly instead of `uv run` → always use `uv run`.
- Leaving `test_add.py` around or committing it → delete after the first real test.
- Duplicating test code → `pytest.mark.parameterized`.
- Committing code without tests and docs → single commit containing all three.
- Stale spec → update TODO lists (add and check off) as you go.
TOOLING:
- `uv init`, `uv add httpx`, `uv add pytest --dev`, `mkdir tests`, `uv run pytest`, `uv run pytest -k name_of_test`, `uv run python -c "..."`, `git init`.
- Files: `pyproject.toml`, `tests/test_add.py`, `spec.md`, `README.md`.
GOTCHAS:
- The scaffold test can silently persist into history if it is committed before the first real test — hence the explicit "Do not include that test_add.py file in any of your commits."
- Without a remote, pushing is skipped; the instruction is conditional ("If a remote is configured").
STRUCTURE: none.

## S131 · wz:tdd
SOURCE: none (references `.wazir/runs/latest/phases/`, `hooks/routing-matrix.json`, `docs/reference/review-loop-pattern.md`, the `wazir` CLI)
PURPOSE: Enforces RED → GREEN → REFACTOR with recorded evidence at each step for any implementation work that changes behaviour, anchored on a phase checklist the agent must open first.
CONCEPTS:
- **phase checklist gate** — The first action of any implementation work is opening the run's phase checklist, before code is touched. > "Don't jump into implementation. Open your phase checklist at .wazir/runs/latest/phases/ first."
- **checklist redundancy defence** — Steps that look redundant are kept because each is treated as load-bearing. > "Every step matters, even the ones that seem redundant."
- **command routing matrix** — Commands are routed by size: heavy ones to context-mode tools, light ones to native Bash. > "Large commands (test runners, builds, diffs, dependency trees, linting) → context-mode tools"
- **fallback with warning** — Missing context-mode degrades to native Bash but the degradation is announced. > "If context-mode unavailable, fall back to native Bash with warning"
- **symbol-index-first exploration** — Symbol search precedes any file read. > "Query `wazir index search-symbols <query>` first"
- **tiered recall reads** — Targeted reads go through the recall command at tier L1. > "Use `wazir recall file <path> --tier L1` for targeted reads"
- **read budget** — Direct reads are capped unless an index query justifies them. > "Maximum 10 direct file reads without a justifying index query"
- **index bootstrap** — A missing index is built and summarised before exploration can proceed. > "If no index exists: `wazir index build && wazir index summarize --tier all`"
- **RED** — A test expressing the new behaviour or the bug is written, run, and confirmed failing. > "Write or update a test that expresses the new behavior or the bug being fixed, then run it and confirm failure."
- **attention-decay counter** — The checklist is re-read at RED because process attention is measurably at its lowest there. > "Right about now your attention on process is at its lowest. That's not a guess, it's a measured pattern."
- **single-pass test quality check** — Three questions validate the test before GREEN, deliberately short of a full review. > "This is a single-pass quality check, not a full review loop."
- **GREEN** — The smallest change that makes the failing test pass is the whole of this step. > "Write the smallest implementation change that makes the failing test pass."
- **REFACTOR** — Structure is improved only while the full relevant test set stays green. > "Improve structure while keeping the full relevant test set green."
- **review-loop vs single-pass distinction** — TDD uses the light check; the full review loop belongs to other workflows. > "TDD uses a single-pass quality check, not the full loop."
- **evidence audit framing** — The closing self-audit asks which checklist items would not survive an evidence check. > "if someone audited your work right now against the phase checklist, would every item hold up with evidence?"
RULES:
- Open the phase checklist before implementing. — > "Don't jump into implementation. Open your phase checklist at .wazir/runs/latest/phases/ first."
- Route large commands to context-mode tools and small ones to native Bash. — > "Small commands (git status, ls, pwd, wazir CLI) → native Bash"
- Announce any fallback to native Bash. — > "If context-mode unavailable, fall back to native Bash with warning"
- Read directly only files an index query identified. — > "Fall back to direct file reads ONLY for files identified by index queries"
- Cap unjustified direct reads at 10. — > "Maximum 10 direct file reads without a justifying index query"
- Run the failing test whenever automated verification is feasible. — > "do not skip the failing-test step when automated verification is feasible"
- Never rewrite tests to fit broken behaviour. — > "do not rewrite tests to fit broken behavior"
- Rerun verification after each meaningful refactor. — > "rerun verification after each meaningful refactor"
- A red must fail for the right reason, not from a syntax or import error. — > "Do they fail for the right reason (not a syntax error or import failure)?"
- Fix the test before moving to GREEN if any check fails. — > "If any check fails, fix the test before moving on."
WORKFLOW:
Exploration:
1. `wazir index search-symbols <query>` first.
2. `wazir recall file <path> --tier L1` for targeted reads.
3. Direct file reads only for files identified by index queries.
4. Cap direct reads at 10 without a justifying index query.
5. If no index: `wazir index build && wazir index summarize --tier all`.
Sequence:
1. RED — write/update a test for the new behaviour or bug, run it, confirm failure; re-read `.wazir/runs/latest/phases/`; run the single-pass test quality check.
2. GREEN — write the smallest implementation change that makes the failing test pass.
3. REFACTOR — improve structure while keeping the full relevant test set green.
TABLES: none (the `Canonical Command Matrix` lives in `hooks/routing-matrix.json` and is referenced, not reproduced).
ANTI-PATTERNS:
- Jumping into implementation without opening the phase checklist → open it first.
- Rewriting tests to fit broken behaviour → fix the code, or record why behaviour changed.
- Tautological assertions → make them real assertions.
- Tests failing for the wrong reason (syntax/import error) → fix the test before GREEN.
- Unjustified direct file reads → justify with an index query, cap at 10.
- Skipping the failing-test step when automated verification is feasible → always run it.
- Empty checkmarks / skipped steps → expect an audit to fail.
TOOLING:
- `.wazir/runs/latest/phases/` (phase checklist), `hooks/routing-matrix.json` (Canonical Command Matrix).
- `wazir index search-symbols <query>`, `wazir recall file <path> --tier L1`, `wazir index build`, `wazir index summarize --tier all`.
- `docs/reference/review-loop-pattern.md`.
- Native Bash for `git status`, `ls`, `pwd`, `wazir` CLI.
GOTCHAS:
- Process attention decays precisely at RED — the file calls this a measured pattern, not a guess.
- Tests can fail for a syntax or import error and masquerade as a genuine red.
- Without an index, targeted reads are impossible until the index is built.
- The full review loop does not apply here; using it instead of the single-pass check is a misapplication.
STRUCTURE:
- `.wazir/runs/latest/phases/` (declared, not bundled).
- `hooks/routing-matrix.json` (declared, not bundled).
- `docs/reference/review-loop-pattern.md` (declared, not bundled).

## S132 · eng-tdd
SOURCE: none (repo facts come from the target repo's `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`)
PURPOSE: Fixes a bug test-first when a clear, cheap regression test path exists — making the broken behaviour executable, confirming the intended failure, then applying the smallest production change — and declines to force a test when it is impractical.
CONCEPTS:
- **repo test policy from context files** — Test policy, per-package runner and single-test command are read from the repo's own agent instructions. > "Repo facts (from AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md): the test policy"
- **policy variance** — Repos differ on how much test coverage a behaviour change demands. > "some repos require coverage for every behavior change, others allow a test only where a branch's behavior is uncertain"
- **policy outranks workflow** — When the repo forbids a new test, the workflow yields to the nearest executable check. > "Follow the policy; when it rules out a new test, skip to the closest executable check below."
- **cheap-path gate** — The test-first workflow applies only when the regression path is both clear and cheap. > "When the test path is clear and cheap, make the broken behavior executable before changing production code."
- **focused regression test** — The deliverable is a test that fails before the fix and passes after it. > "The goal is a focused regression test that fails before the fix and passes after it."
- **impractical-test list** — Six conditions make a test not worth forcing. > "broad harness setup, brittle mocks, slow end-to-end infrastructure, production-only state, vague reproduction steps, or large unrelated fixture churn"
- **closest useful verification** — When a test is impractical, an alternative executable check stands in for it. > "a targeted script, a manual reproduction command, browser automation, a snapshot comparison, or a focused integration check"
- **existing style and location** — The narrowest check uses the style and location the repo already uses for that code. > "in the location the repo uses (often colocated as `foo.test.ts`)"
- **intent encoding** — The regression test describes what should happen, not what currently happens. > "It encodes intended behavior, not the current implementation."
- **smallest production change** — The fix satisfies the intended behaviour and leaves nearby contracts intact. > "Make the smallest production change that satisfies the intended behavior and keeps nearby contracts."
- **bad test definition** — A test is rejected when it mostly tests mocks, encodes implementation details, depends on timing or global state, needs expensive infrastructure, or dies right after proving the fix. > "A bad test mostly tests mocks, encodes implementation details, depends on timing or global state"
- **flaky-bug determinism** — A flaky bug gets a deterministic test plus a written statement of the signal it locks down. > "If the bug is flaky, make the test deterministic and document the signal it locks down."
- **sibling coverage deferral** — The focused regression lands first; the wider failure class is considered afterwards. > "land the focused regression first, then consider sibling coverage"
- **evidence naming** — The report names the failing check and its failure, then the passing run. > "Name the check that failed before the fix and the failure it produced."
RULES:
- Follow the repo policy, falling back to the closest executable check when it rules out a new test. — > "Follow the policy; when it rules out a new test, skip to the closest executable check below."
- Make the broken behaviour executable before changing production code. — > "make the broken behavior executable before changing production code"
- Do not force a test when it is impractical. — > "Do not force a test when it is impractical"
- Do not invent a test path just to satisfy the workflow. — > "If no practical path is obvious, do not create one just to satisfy the workflow."
- Do not change tests to match a wrong implementation. — > "Do not change tests to match a wrong implementation."
- Weaken assertions only when expected behaviour genuinely changed, and say why. — > "Do not weaken assertions unless the expected behavior genuinely changed and you can say why."
- Keep the test on the bug; no fixture churn or unrelated coverage. — > "Keep the test focused on the bug. No fixture churn or unrelated coverage."
- Make a flaky bug's test deterministic and document the signal it locks down. — > "If the bug is flaky, make the test deterministic and document the signal it locks down."
- Land the focused regression before considering sibling coverage. — > "If the bug exposes a broader class of failures, land the focused regression first, then consider sibling coverage."
- If failing-before evidence is missing, say why and name the closest check. — > "If failing-before evidence is missing, say why and name the closest check used."
WORKFLOW:
1. **Understand the bug.** Identify intended behaviour, current behaviour, the affected path, and the smallest observable reproduction.
2. **Choose the narrowest executable check.** Prefer the existing unit/component/integration style, in the repo's location (often colocated as `foo.test.ts`), with the repo's single-test command. Do not invent a path if none is practical.
3. **Write the failing test first.** The smallest test that would have caught the bug; encodes intended behaviour.
4. **Run it before fixing.** Confirm it fails for the intended reason; if it passes or fails unrelatedly, correct the test first.
5. **Fix the bug.** Smallest production change satisfying intended behaviour and nearby contracts.
6. **Rerun the test.** Confirm it passes.
Verify: name the check that failed before the fix and its failure; name the passing run and nearby validation; explain missing failing-before evidence.
TABLES: none.
ANTI-PATTERNS:
- Changing tests to match a wrong implementation → fix the bug, or justify the changed expectation.
- Weakening assertions silently → only when expected behaviour genuinely changed, with a stated reason.
- Forcing a test through broad harness setup / brittle mocks / slow E2E / production-only state → use the closest executable check instead.
- Writing a test that only tests mocks or implementation details → prefer no new test.
- Test that would be "deleted right after proving the fix" → do not write it.
- Fixture churn or unrelated coverage → keep the test focused.
- Claiming TDD without observed failing-before evidence → state why and name the closest check.
TOOLING:
- Repo facts sourced from `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`.
- Test file convention example: colocated `foo.test.ts`.
- Runs via "the repo's single-test command" (unnamed, repo-specific).
- Alternative checks: targeted script, manual reproduction command, browser automation, snapshot comparison, focused integration check.
GOTCHAS:
- A test can pass or fail for an unrelated reason, so step 4 explicitly re-validates the failure cause.
- Repos differ on coverage policy; assuming a blanket requirement conflicts with the policy gate.
- "Clear, cheap" is a judgment gate — impractical setups must not be forced, and a bad test is worse than none.
STRUCTURE: none.

## S133 · web3-testing
SOURCE: https://github.com/sickn33/antigravity-awesome-skills — path `plugins/antigravity-awesome-skills-claude/skills/web3-testing`; frontmatter `author: "sickn33"`, `source: community`, `date_added: "2026-04-15"`, `date_updated: "2026-04-25"`.
PURPOSE: Packages an imported upstream "Web3 Smart Contract Testing" workflow (Hardhat + Foundry + advanced patterns) into a reviewable editorial shell, so an operator preserves provenance and copied support files while executing or reviewing the workflow.

CONCEPTS:
- **provenance anchor** — the metadata `external_source` block and `ORIGIN.md` are the pair reviewers are told to cite before touching any copied workflow, so origin stays visible inside the answer rather than in a side channel. > "This intake keeps the copied upstream files intact and uses the `external_source` block in `metadata.json` plus `ORIGIN.md` as the provenance anchor for review."
- **editorial intake shape** — the file asks to be read as packaging, not authorship: the public skill wraps the upstream repository, and its stated goal is keeping provenance explicit while loading only copied material that improves execution. > "Treat the generated public skill as a reviewable packaging layer around the upstream repository."
- **imported section preservation** — upstream sections that had no matching public heading are kept anyway under `Imported: …` subheadings (Unit Testing Patterns, Foundry Testing (Forge), Advanced Testing Patterns, Gas Optimization Testing, Coverage Reporting, Contract Verification) instead of being dropped in the reshape. > "Imported source sections that did not map cleanly to the public headings are still preserved below or in the support files."
- **progressive disclosure** — the author justifies narrowing to the copied references, examples, prompts, or scripts that change the outcome, and frames loading the whole package as the failure mode to avoid. > "This keeps the skill aligned with progressive disclosure instead of loading the whole copied package by default."
- **Hardhat Toolbox config** — the setup is expressed as four required plugins (toolbox, etherscan, gas-reporter, solidity-coverage) plus a pinned compiler and optimizer, so the config is reproducible rather than floating. > "require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox"); require("@nomiclabs/hardhat-etherscan"); require("hardhat-gas-reporter"); require("solidity-coverage"); module.exports = { solidity: {"
- **forking config** — the `hardhat` network forks mainnet from an RPC URL in the environment and pins the block, which the author treats as the precondition for deterministic fork tests. > "networks: { hardhat: { forking: { url: process.env.MAINNET_RPC_URL, blockNumber: 15000000, }, },"
- **loadFixture** — a named deploy fixture is reused across `it` blocks through `loadFixture` and the network helpers' `time`, so each test starts from the same deployed state without redeploying. > "const { expect } = require("chai"); const { ethers } = require("hardhat"); const { loadFixture, time, } = require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-network-helpers");"
- **balance-delta assertion** — token movement is asserted as a paired before/after balance change on both accounts rather than by reading one balance, which the author presents as the transfer test. > "it("Should transfer tokens between accounts", async function () {"
- **revert assertion** — an under-funded transfer is checked with a revert assertion carrying the contract's own message, so the test pins the reason and not merely that the call failed. > "it("Should fail if sender doesn't have enough tokens", async function () {"
- **event assertion** — emission is asserted with the event name and ordered arguments, giving the test an observable side effect instead of an internal-state read. > "it("Should emit Transfer event", async function () {"
- **time travel** — time-locked behaviour is exercised by advancing the chain clock by one day (86400 seconds) through the helpers' `time` object. > "it("Should handle time-locked operations", async function () {"
- **gas budget assertion** — a transaction is awaited into a receipt and the gas used is compared against a literal ceiling, turning a cost expectation into an assertion. > "it("Should use gas efficiently", async function () {"
- **Forge test contract** — the Foundry suite is a Solidity contract inheriting `Test`, holding the deployed token and three fixed addresses as state, which `setUp()` populates. > "contract TokenTest is Test { Token token; address owner = address(1);"
- **cheatcodes** — the author demonstrates cheatcodes as the Foundry equivalent of test scaffolding: funding an address with `vm.deal` and acting as it with `vm.prank`. > "// Test with cheatcodes function testDealAndPrank() public { // Give ETH to address vm.deal(user1, 10 ether);"
- **fuzz test** — a typed fuzz function takes the amount as a parameter and narrows it with `vm.assume` before asserting the resulting balance, which is how the file shows property-style coverage in Solidity. > "function testFuzzTransfer(uint256 amount) public { vm.assume(amount > 0 && amount <= token.totalSupply());"
- **snapshot/revert** — state is captured with `evm_snapshot` in `beforeEach` and rolled back with `evm_revert` in `afterEach`, so later tests start from a clean slate. > "beforeEach(async function () { snapshotId = await network.provider.send("evm_snapshot"); }); afterEach(async function () { await network.provider.send("evm_revert", [snapshotId]); });"
- **mainnet forking harness** — the harness resets the provider with `hardhat_reset` and an explicit fork URL and block, then attaches to real Uniswap and DAI addresses with `getContractAt`. > "method: "hardhat_reset", params: [ { forking: { jsonRpcUrl: process.env.MAINNET_RPC_URL, blockNumber: 15000000, }, }, ],"
- **account impersonation** — a whale address is impersonated through `hardhat_impersonateAccount` and then resolved to a signer, letting the test move balances it does not own. > "method: "hardhat_impersonateAccount", params: [whaleAddress], }); const whale = await ethers.getSigner(whaleAddress);"
- **A/B gas comparison** — optimized and unoptimized contracts are deployed side by side, both receipts logged, and the optimized gas asserted lower than the unoptimized one. > "const receipt2 = await tx2.wait(); console.log("Optimized gas:", receipt1.gasUsed.toString()); console.log("Unoptimized gas:", receipt2.gasUsed.toString());"
- **coverage table** — coverage is produced by `npx hardhat coverage`, whose output is presented as a per-file statement/branch/function/line table. > "# File                | % Stmts | % Branch | % Funcs | % Lines |"
- **Etherscan verification** — verification is shown twice, as a programmatic `verify:verify` call carrying the address and constructor arguments and as the CLI equivalent. > "await hre.run("verify:verify", { address: contractAddress, constructorArguments: [arg1, arg2], });"
- **CI gate** — the workflow file runs compile, test, and coverage in sequence on push and pull request, then uploads coverage to Codecov. > "- run: npx hardhat compile - run: npx hardhat test - run: npx hardhat coverage"
- **handoff routing** — a `## Related Skills` section exists so drifted work moves deliberately to a native specialization while the imported provenance travels with it. > "Use the related skills section to hand off deliberately. Keep the imported provenance visible so the next skill inherits the right context instead of starting blind."

RULES:

- Test boundary conditions, not just the happy path — > "Edge Cases: Test boundary conditions"
- Verify no function reaches the block gas limit — > "Gas Limits: Verify functions don't hit block gas limit"

## S134 · property-based-testing
SOURCE: Adapted from Trail of Bits (https://github.com/trailofbits/skills) via https://github.com/VoltAgent/awesome-agent-skills; frontmatter `license: MIT`, category `code-security`, phase `v1`.
PURPOSE: Guides an agent through property-based fuzzing in Python, Rust, JS/TS, Solidity, and Go to surface security-relevant edge cases that example-based unit tests miss — from property identification through framework selection, counterexample minimization, and triage.

CONCEPTS:
- **property-based testing (PBT)** — the author inverts the example test: state the invariants that must always hold and let a generator attack them, which is what makes rare input regions reachable. > "PBT defines invariants the system must always satisfy — then lets a framework generate hundreds or thousands of inputs to try to break them."
- **property strength hierarchy** — properties are ordered into five tiers (No Exception, Type Preservation, Invariant, Idempotence, Roundtrip) and the author tells the reader to work from weakest to strongest because stronger claims catch more bugs. > "Apply the property strength hierarchy from weakest to strongest — stronger properties catch more bugs"
- **security-relevant property classes** — five classes are named as the priority set for a security review: overflow bounds, access-control invariant, state-machine consistency, deserialization roundtrip, and monotonicity of fees, interest, or prices. > "**Deserialization roundtrip**: no data loss or mutation during encode/decode cycles"
- **strategy/generator** — each language gets a concrete generator vocabulary, from `st.binary` and `proptest::collection::vec` to `fc.uint8Array`/`fc.record`/`fc.constantFrom` and typed Solidity fuzz arguments. > "fc.property(fc.uint8Array({ minLength: 1, maxLength: 1024 }), (data) => {"
- **precondition filters** — an assumption is used to narrow an over-broad domain, and the author requires the assumption itself to be documented rather than left implicit. > "Add `assume()` / `vm.assume()` / `fc.filter()` to restrict input domain; document the assumption"
- **shrinking** — the framework is expected to hand back the smallest failing input, so the reader does not minimize by hand. > "When a property fails, all frameworks print a minimal counterexample automatically (shrinking)."
- **seed reproducibility** — failing runs are made repeatable through a fixed seed per framework: `PBT_SEED`, a printed database key for Hypothesis, or `--fuzz-seed` for Foundry. > "For Hypothesis, use `@reproduce_failure` decorator with the printed database key for CI reproduction."
- **counterexample pinning** — a discovered input is promoted into a permanent named example test so the exact case is exercised on every future run. > "Add the counterexample as a named example-based test so it is always exercised"
- **failure database** — Hypothesis persists discoveries in a database, and the author points at an environment variable to carry that database across CI runs. > "On CI set `HYPOTHESIS_DATABASE_FILE` to a workspace path to persist discoveries across runs."
- **proptest regression file** — proptest writes known-failing inputs to a regression file, which the author says must be committed rather than ignored. > "Commit the regressions file; it pins known-failing inputs for permanent coverage"
- **Foundry invariant testing** — `invariant_*` functions with `targetContract` are called out as stateful protocol-level testing, explicitly a different tool from stateless fuzz tests. > "Foundry's invariant testing (`invariant_*` with `targetContract`) is distinct from fuzz testing and better suited for stateful protocol-level invariants."
- **iteration budget** — run counts are treated as part of the result: defaults are named per framework, recommended minimums are tabulated, and the done criteria require running at or above them. > "All properties run at or above the recommended iteration count with zero failures"
- **triage decision** — a failing property must be classified before anything is filed, because a test-logic error and a production bug call for opposite responses. > "Determine whether the failure is a test logic error or a real bug in the target."
- **environment contract** — the skill declares its inputs up front: target file, language enum, iteration count, output directory (default `./pbt-output`), and seed. > "| `PBT_SEED` | optional | Fixed seed for reproducible runs |"
- **done criteria** — completion is defined as coverage of the weak tiers plus triage plus pinned regressions, not as a green run. > "At least one property per tier (No Exception, Roundtrip, Invariant) has been written and passes for the target"
- **companion skills** — the author names three neighbours and what each adds, so fuzzing work that outgrows this file has an explicit destination. > "This skill pairs well with `web3-smart-contract` (Foundry fuzz testing for Solidity), `building-secure-contracts` (multi-chain testing), and `testing-handbook-skills` (broader fuzzing methodology)."

RULES:
- Default runs are the framework default, typically 100 — > "Number of test cases to generate (default: framework default, typically 100)"
- Hypothesis should run 500–10,000 cases for a security review — > "| Hypothesis | 100 | 500–10,000 |"
- proptest should run 1,000–10,000 cases — > "| proptest | 256 | 1,000–10,000 |"
- fast-check should run 500–5,000 cases — > "| fast-check | 100 | 500–5,000 |"
- Foundry fuzz should run 1,000–50,000 cases — > "| Foundry fuzz | 256 | 1,000–50,000 |"
- testing/quick should run 500–5,000 cases — > "| testing/quick | 100 | 500–5,000 |"
- Raise iterations for cryptographic or financial logic — > "Increase iterations for cryptographic or financial logic."
- Hypothesis roundtrip example sets 500 examples — > "@settings(max_examples=500)"
- Hypothesis deep runs disable the deadline — > "@settings(max_examples=10000, deadline=None)"
- Foundry deep run is invoked with 10000 fuzz runs — > "forge test --match-contract PropertyTest --fuzz-runs 10000 -v"
- `foundry.toml` pins runs and seed — > "[fuzz] runs = 10000 seed = "0x1""
- Go runs quick with MaxCount 1000 — > "quick.Check(f, &quick.Config{MaxCount: 1000})"
- uint256 arithmetic is generated over the full range — > "st.integers(min_value=0, max_value=2**256 - 1)"
- Addresses are generated as 40-character hex strings — > "fc.hexaString({ minLength: 40, maxLength: 40 })"
- Rust byte vectors are generated from 0..1024 elements — > "data in proptest::collection::vec(0u8..=255, 0..1024)"
- Solidity dust amounts are excluded by assumption — > "vm.assume(amount > 1 ether / 1000); // ignore dust"
- Always run the higher iteration count for security-sensitive code — > "Always run at the higher iteration count for security-sensitive code"
- Commit the proptest regressions file — > "Commit the regressions file"
- Finish by running the repository checks — > "Run `./scripts/validate-skills.sh` and `npm test` to confirm the repository is clean."

WORKFLOW:
1. `Step 1: Identify testable properties` — enumerate invariants, apply the strength hierarchy, prioritize the security property classes.
2. `Step 2: Select framework and write properties` — Hypothesis, proptest, fast-check, Foundry, or `testing/quick`.
3. `Step 3: Run with sufficient iterations` — raise counts, set seeds/`foundry.toml`.
4. `Step 4: Analyze failures and minimize counterexamples` — reproduce in isolation, classify test-logic vs real bug, judge realism (max uint256, empty bytes, zero address), pin via `@reproduce_failure` or `--fuzz-seed`.
5. `Step 5: Fix and verify` — re-run at the same count, add the counterexample as a named example test, run repo checks.

TABLES:
- `property strength hierarchy` — Tier | Property type | Description | Example; 5 rows (1 No Exception … 5 Roundtrip).
- Iteration table — Framework | Default runs | Recommended minimum for security review; 5 rows.
- `Inputs` table — Variable | Required | Description; 5 rows.
- `Failure modes` — Symptom | Cause | Resolution; 6 rows.

ANTI-PATTERNS:
- Strategy too broad, generating invalid preconditions → add `assume()`/`vm.assume()`/`fc.filter()` and document the assumption.
- Running only 100 iterations → "Tests pass at 100 runs but fail at 10,000"; always raise for security-sensitive code.
- Impossible-looking shrunken counterexample → re-read the property; it is a test-logic error, not a production bug.
- Slow Foundry fuzz from heavy `setUp` → move setup to a fixture, reuse state, limit `vm.deal`.
- Suppressing `HealthCheck.too_slow` habitually → prefer lighter strategies.
- Stale `.proptest-regressions` causing CI flakiness → commit the file.

TOOLING:
- `pip install hypothesis`, `pip install pytest hypothesis`; `proptest = "1"` in `[dev-dependencies]`; `npm install --save-dev fast-check` / `yarn add --dev fast-check`; `curl -L https://foundry.paradigm.xyz | bash` + `foundryup`; `import "testing/quick"`.
- Decorators/APIs: `@given`, `@settings`, `@example`, `@reproduce_failure`, `proptest! { #[test] fn … }`, `prop_assert_eq!`, `fc.assert`, `fc.property`, `{ numRuns: 500 }`, `assertLe`, `assertEq`.
- `foundry.toml` `[fuzz]` block; `HYPOTHESIS_DATABASE_FILE`.

GOTCHAS:
- A green run at default counts proves almost nothing; failures concentrate in rare input regions.
- Health checks (`HealthCheck.too_slow`) can mask expensive strategies.
- Shrinking output must be re-validated before filing a bug.
- Foundry fuzz ≠ Foundry invariant testing; using one for the other's purpose is called out explicitly.

STRUCTURE: no bundled references; external pointers to the Foundry book and three companion skills; `./scripts/validate-skills.sh` and `npm test` referenced (declared, not bundled).

## S135 · windows-desktop-e2e
SOURCE: none (frontmatter `metadata: origin: ECC`; no URL).
PURPOSE: Tells an agent how to build and run end-to-end tests for Windows native desktop apps (WPF, WinForms, Win32/MFC, Qt 5/6) with pywinauto over UI Automation, including page objects, waits, artifacts, isolation tiers, DPI-safe screenshot fallback, and CI wiring.

CONCEPTS:
- **UI Automation (UIA)** — everything rests on the Windows accessibility API, drawn as a five-layer stack from the Python test through pywinauto's UIA backend, the OS API, and the app's own provider down to the running `.exe`. > "All Windows desktop automation relies on **UI Automation (UIA)**, a Windows-built-in accessibility API."
- **UIA quality by framework** — each framework is scored for AutomationId support and reliability, from WPF's 5/5 down to Win32/MFC's 3/5, and those scores set the locator expectations the reader should have. > "| WPF | 5/5 | Excellent | `x:Name` maps directly to AutomationId |"
- **Accessibility Insights for Windows** — the author points at Microsoft's free inspector as the tool to read the UIA element tree before a single test is written. > "Install **Accessibility Insights for Windows** (free, from Microsoft) — your DevTools equivalent for inspecting the UIA element tree before writing any test."
- **AutomationId testability** — stable identifiers are framed as the single most impactful thing an author can do, with a per-framework mechanism: WPF `x:Name`, WinForms `AccessibleName`, Win32 `.rc` control IDs exposed as strings, and Qt `setObjectName` + `setAccessibleName` through one `setTestId` helper. > "The single most impactful thing you can do is **give every interactive control a stable AutomationId** before writing tests."
- **Page Object Model** — the suite is laid out as a fixed tree: `pages/base_page.py` for locators, waits, and screenshot helpers, page subclasses, a `tests/` package, `conftest.py`, `config.py`, `pytest.ini`, and an `artifacts/` directory. > "├── conftest.py          # app launch fixture, failure screenshot"
- **locator priority** — the ladder is AutomationId, then Name, then ClassName plus index, then XPath, ordered by stability rather than convenience. > "AutomationId  >  Name (text)  >  ClassName + index  >  XPath"
- **wait primitives** — synchronization is expressed as named waits (`wait("visible")`, `wait_not("visible")`, `wait_window`, and a polling `wait_until` with a 0.3s interval) rather than sleeps. > "**Never use `time.sleep()` as primary synchronization** — use `wait()` or `wait_until()`."
- **text entry fallback** — `set_edit_text` is the primary path, and the fallback clicks the control, selects all with `^a`, and types with `with_spaces=True` when the UIA Value Pattern is incomplete. > "# Qt 5.x fallback: UIA Value Pattern may be incomplete"
- **get_text fallback chain** — reading text tries `window_text` and then `get_value`, returning an empty string only when both fail. > "for attr in ("window_text", "get_value"): try: v = getattr(ctrl, attr)()"
- **failure screenshot** — a `pytest_runtest_makereport` hook sets the report on the item so the fixture can save `FAIL_<test>.png` when the call phase failed. > "try: win.capture_as_image().save( os.path.join(ARTIFACT_DIR, f"FAIL_{request.node.name}.png") ) except Exception: pass"
- **per-step trace (opt-in)** — an opt-in JSONL log records step index, action, locator criteria, and redacted text with one PNG per step, and the author keeps it off by default for flake reproduction only. > "The step-level trace below is **off by default** — enable it only when reproducing a flaky case."
- **flaky quarantine** — known-unstable tests are quarantined with a skip marker carrying a reason and issue number, or skipped in CI only via `skipif`. > "@pytest.mark.skip(reason="Flaky: animation race on slow CI. Issue #42")"
- **isolation tiers** — three tiers are defined and the reader is told to take the lightest one that works: `tmp_path` env redirect, Job Object, then Windows Sandbox. > "Three tiers of isolation — use the lightest tier that satisfies your needs."
- **Job Object containment** — a job object with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE` (`0x00002000`) is assigned to the app process so the process tree dies with the fixture handle, with the struct laid out so `LimitFlags` sits at offset +16. > "Attach the process to a Job Object so it is **automatically terminated** when the test fixture's job handle is GC'd."
- **screenshot mode** — for controls UIA cannot see, cv2 template matching (`TM_CCOEFF_NORMED`) with a confidence threshold locates the target and `pyautogui.click` acts on it. > "When a control is not reachable via UIA (self-drawn, third-party, game engine):"
- **DPI discipline** — screenshot matching is described as brutally sensitive to display scaling, with three hard rules: same-scale templates, pinned CI scaling, and recording `GetDpiForWindow(hwnd) / 96` beside each artefact. > "Screenshot matching is brutally sensitive to Windows display scaling (100% / 125% / 150%). Three hard rules:"
- **Qt quirks** — Qt surfaces behave as separate top-level windows: the QComboBox dropdown (`class_name_re="Qt[56]QWindowIcon"`), QMessageBox/QDialog, `cell(row=, column=)` on tables, and self-drawn controls invisible to UIA. > "**QComboBox** — the dropdown is a separate top-level window:"

RULES:
- Install the pywinauto test stack — > "pip install pywinauto pytest pytest-html Pillow pytest-timeout"
- Target Python 3.8+ on Windows only — > "# Python 3.8+, Windows only"
- Set `QT_ACCESSIBILITY=1` before launching Qt 5.x — > "os.environ["QT_ACCESSIBILITY"] = "1"  # Required for Qt 5.x UIA support"
- Launch timeout defaults to 15 seconds — > "LAUNCH_TIMEOUT    = int(os.environ.get("LAUNCH_TIMEOUT", "15"))"
