| Test-everything vs skip classes | `An empty test diff on a behavior change is a review finding` (S074) | `Trivial wiring → skip tests` (B003); `Prefer no new test over a bad test` (S048); `Do not force a test when it is impractical` (S132) | yes |
| Coverage targets | 80% gates: `cargo llvm-cov --fail-under-lines 80` (S084), `minBound(80)` (S082), `>80% code coverage` (B008) | `Don't aim for 100% coverage. Instead:` (S038); coverage-vs-mutation articles (Part D, 61–68) | yes |
| Retry on failure | Retry for diagnosis: `Retry only to test a specific transient explanation` (S171) | Never: `Never hide failures with retries, longer timeouts, weaker assertions` (S185); `Never approve if any scenario failed, even if it seems like a flake` (B016) | yes |
| Quarantine flaky tests | `test.fixme(true, 'Flaky - Issue #123')` (S027); `quarantine it visibly with an owner` (S015) | Fix immediately, no quarantine path (S128 self-audit; S025 sleep ban) | yes |
| Mocking depth | Mock at every boundary, fail on unmocked traffic (B019) | `Never mock a data model, DTO, entity, or state object.` (S145); `mocking the CDSS engine (must test real logic)` (S184) | yes |
| E2E placement | E2E only for critical journeys (B017, S014 `Edge cases (too slow)`) | UI-first campaigns: `~40 for a full page with functional + adversarial + a11y` (S075), `100 ... root-cause fixes` via live proof (S175) | yes |
| Test pyramid as allocator | Pyramid tiers with fixed shares (S051, S072 `70% Unit Tests`) | `Is the Test Pyramid Dead?` (article 159); `no one agrees on anything` (158) | yes |

| AI-generated tests | Adopt with guardrails (S038, S011, S127) | Oracle-reliability evidence: `All Smoke, No Alarm` and coverage/mutation independence (articles 40, 48–49) | yes |

| Evidence sufficiency | Green CI is enough (implicit in many framework playbooks) | `Files, test counts, and green CI alone do not prove required rules are covered.` (S080) | yes |

## A000 · AI Agent Testing | IBM
URL: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/ai-agent-testing
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: AI agent testing verifies that agentic systems behave reliably, safely and as intended; because LLM-driven agents are probabilistic, testing must judge reasoning paths and intermediate outputs, not only final answers.
CONCEPTS:
- **AI agent testing** — Evaluating agentic AI systems before deployment, as part of the continuous create/evaluate loop the authors call the agent development lifecycle. > "systems to verify they perform reliably, safely and as intended before deployment."
- **Compounding errors** — Agents run multi-part chains of reasoning and action, so an error at any point can be amplified. > "Agents often run multi-part chains of reasoning and action, meaning errors at any point in the process can be amplified."
- **LLM-as-a-judge** — A second, typically larger model given a rubric scores the tested agent's outputs at several points along its trajectory. > "Typically a larger, more capable model than the one being tested is given a rubric and asked to assess the agent’s response."
- **Three-tiered approach** — Testing runs at three levels — component tests of isolated parts, trajectory tests of the reasoning path, end-to-end tests on realistic tasks — each catching a different failure class. > "Effective agent testing operates along three distinct levels, each designed to catch a different class of failure."
- **Environmental simulation** — Controlled, repeatable stand-ins replace environments that would be expensive or irreversible to test directly. > "Sophisticated environmental simulation solves that challenge by providing controlled and repeatable stand-ins for real-world scenarios."
- **Success rate** — The percentage of test cases in which the agent completes the assigned task. > "The success rate measures the percentage of test cases in which an agent completes an assigned task."
- **Tool accuracy** — Whether the agent selects the correct tools and calls them with the correct parameters. > "Tool accuracy measures whether an agent selects the correct tools for a specific task, and whether it calls on them within the correct parameters."
- **Trajectory evaluations** — Judging whether the reasoning path is coherent and appropriate even when the final answer is correct. > "Evaluating agent trajectory involves assessing whether an agent’s reasoning path is coherent and appropriate, even if the final answer happens to be correct."
- **Latency and cost** — Hard requirements covering time to final output and aggregate token and API consumption per task. > "Latency and cost are generally hard requirements used to determine whether a system is fundamentally usable."
- **Conciseness and coherence** — Whether outputs carry the necessary information and remain logically consistent, independent of accuracy. > "Coherence measures whether the output is logically consistent, well-structured and free of internal contradictions."
- **Evaluation frameworks** — Infrastructure that runs tests, logs trajectories, scores outputs and tracks metrics over time. > "Evaluation frameworks provide the fundamental infrastructure for running tests, logging agent trajectories, scoring outputs and tracking metrics over time."
- **Observability platforms** — Real-time and historical visibility into agent behavior that surfaces anomalies and regressions. > "Observability platforms provide real-time and historical visibility into agent behavior."
- **Agent control plane** — The management layer governing what agents are allowed to do, which also records configuration for reproducibility. > "An agent control plane is the management layer that sits above individual agents, providing centralized visibility and control over how agents are deployed and governed across an organization."
- **In-platform tools** — Vendor-built evaluation built into the deployment platform: tight integration and simple setup, but less flexibility. > "These in-platform tools offer the advantage of tight integration with the deployment environment and simplified setup."
GUIDELINES: Layer tests as `component` → `trajectory` → `end-to-end` rather than relying on exploratory testing alone. Use a rubric-bearing, larger judge model, applied at multiple trajectory points, as a scale aid "not a replacement for human evaluation". Define success criteria before building the agent. Balance test sets: include cases where a trajectory "should" and "shouldn't" happen, single-step and multi-step interactions, varied input phrasing, explicit edge cases, adversarial prompts and empty inputs. Refresh test sets as usage patterns evolve; consider `automated test case generation`. Version and audit testing data; keep gold-standard reference trajectories for multi-step tasks. Run automation when prompts change or tools are added, and as routine monitoring. Apply structured human review to samples "at several tiers of the testing process". Deliberately subject agents to adversarial inputs and edge cases at E2E.
EVIDENCE: IBM Institute for Business Value survey: `80%` of CIOs/CTOs report CEO-driven AI transformation mandates, but only `11%` say they are fully ready for expected agent deployment scale in the next year. No test-outcome experiments reported.
LIMITS: States LLM-as-a-judge is not a replacement for human evaluation; in-platform tools offer less flexibility than standalone frameworks; non-determinism means variance must be evaluated rather than a single snapshot.
TOOLING: ADLC, CI/CD pipelines, evaluation frameworks, observability platforms, agent control planes, IBM watsonx Orchestrate / watsonx.ai, in-platform evaluation tools.
LINKS: IBM Institute for Business Value CXO study; IBM developer tutorial "create evaluation workflow AI agents"; IBM topics on agentic AI, tool calling, AI agent security, AI observability, debugging.

## A001 · Agentic quality assurance: A guide to AI-driven QA - Tricentis
URL: https://www.tricentis.com/learn/agentic-quality-assurance
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Agentic QA replaces fixed-instruction automation with autonomous systems that study an application, decide what to test from goals and risk, generate and run tests, and adjust their approach with little human help — while still requiring human governance.
CONCEPTS:
- **Agentic AI** — Systems that pursue goals, make decisions and change their approach without constant human guidance. > "Agentic AI refers to AI systems that can work on their own to reach specific goals, make decisions, and change their approach without needing constant human guidance."
- **Independence** — The axis separating agentic QA from AI-assisted QA: the agent decides what to test from its goals, limits and what it learns. > "The main difference between AI-assisted QA and agentic QA is independence."
- **Four-phase loop** — Intent input, planning, execution and adaptation repeat continuously. > "Agentic QA works in a continuous cycle, in which it receives input, plans what to test, runs the tests, learns, and delivers insights from the results."
- **Scaling intelligently** — The agent reviews large codebases and concentrates testing on high-risk and recently changed areas. > "Agentic AI can review large codebases and focus testing on the most important parts, like high-risk areas and sections that were recently changed."
- **Adapting to change** — After each update the agent re-assesses risk and updates the tests to match. > "When code is updated, agentic AI reviews the risk again and automatically updates the tests to match."
- **Reducing maintenance burden** — The agent adjusts broken tests itself when an interface changes, instead of leaving the repair to the team. > "agentic AI understands how the application already works and will adjust the test on its own instead of making you fix a test that broke"
GUIDELINES: Define goals and scope; start with one focused area such as `API testing` rather than changing everything at once. `Establish baselines` — record current test coverage, execution time and defect rates to measure improvement. Integrate with existing CI/CD pipelines, test management tools and quality platforms. `Start small and iterate` — small pilot, then expand. Maintain human oversight: QA leaders and engineers regularly review the agent's testing strategies, validate results, feed back. Keep historical test results and defect records clean, because the agent relies on them. Monitor hallucinations by regularly reviewing outputs. `Scale securely` — use `model context protocol (MCP)` to control the agent's access to test data, workflows and systems; keep it within approved permissions and governance policies. Metrics to track: `test coverage`, `defect escape rate`, `testing efficiency`, `maintenance reduction`.
EVIDENCE: Manufacturing ERP case: biweekly releases spent `twenty-five or more hours per cycle` on regression; adding agentic QA to the CI pipeline with natural-language instructions cut regression testing from "over twenty-five hours to under eight hours". Claims teams "can reduce manual test maintenance work by `30% to 50%` within the first year". Anecdote: Meta Superintelligence safety leader's email agent began deleting her entire inbox, cited as evidence outputs/actions must be monitored.
LIMITS: Vendor-authored guide; the maintenance-reduction range is stated without methodology; reliability claim is qualified — trust is built over time with oversight, clear quality goals and controls around critical systems.
TOOLING: Tricentis Tosca (risk-based testing), qTest, SeaLights, MCP, CI pipelines.
LINKS: Tricentis "Agentic Test Automation" blog, SAP/RISE integration announcement, Tosca risk-based testing (risk coverage "90%+"), NVIDIA CES 2025 keynote quote.

## A002 · What Is Agentic Testing? Agentic QA Explained (2026) | QA.tech
URL: https://qa.tech/blog/what-is-agentic-testing
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Agentic testing means an AI agent reasons from a stated goal to a verdict at runtime on the live application, with no script and no selectors; what you maintain shifts from steps to goals, test data and constraints.
CONCEPTS:
- **Goal** — The authored unit: a statement of what should be true, closer to an acceptance criterion than a test case. > "A goal is closer to an acceptance criterion than to a test case."
- **Scripted automation** — Playwright, Cypress or Selenium tests whose explicit steps are tied to selectors. > "A person or a code generator writes explicit steps tied to selectors."
- **AI-assisted automation** — A model drafts the script, but the artefact that runs in CI is still a script. > "A model writes the script for you, from a prompt or a recording."
- **Self-healing automation** — A script with a repair mechanism that guesses which element was meant, with a green-while-checking-nothing risk. > "It is agentic about one thing, finding the button, and scripted about everything else."
- **Autonomous testing** — Describes how little a human is involved, whereas agentic describes how the test runs. > "Agentic describes how the test runs (an agent reasons through it)."
- **Agentic loop** — Every system runs some variant of perceive, plan, act, verify and remember. > "Every agentic testing system runs some version of the same loop."
- **Grounding** — Resolving a step such as clicking submit to one specific element; markup-only resolution misses what a user would see. > "resolve purely by the markup and the agent misses what a user would see"
- **Settling** — Confirming that a request finished and the page stopped moving before the agent looks again. > "The second detail is settling: knowing that a request finished and the page stopped moving before the agent looks again."
- **Step count** — The real cost unit, since runs are billed by work done rather than by test count. > "Steps are what the work actually costs, whatever the invoice is denominated in, so a per-execution price moves the step count into the vendor's margin rather than off your bill."
- **Oracle problem** — A wrong goal makes script and agent confirm the wrong behaviour alike. > "If the goal is wrong because the product spec was wrong, both the script and the agent will happily confirm the wrong behaviour."
GUIDELINES: Author goals, not steps; if the test contains selectors, coordinates or verbatim steps, "it isn't agentic". Treat the remembered path as "a hypothesis, not a contract": on mismatch it must fail its check, fall back to reasoning and still pass. Ask the vendor for its `false-positive rate` "on a suite that is genuinely green". Require a `step budget`, a stop condition that fires before it, and a per-step record (screenshot, reasoning, network/console) so "an engineer who didn't write the goal can open a red run and decide in two minutes". Ask for the `run-one-to-run-ten` step ratio to size memory. Reproducibility default: "re-run a red once automatically, block the merge only on two consecutive fails for the same goal, and quarantine a goal whose flake rate over `30 runs` is above whatever your team already tolerates from its Playwright suite." Start with one frequently broken, never-scripted flow run twice a day for a week; measure what share of reds were real. Define blast radius: allowed hosts, forbidden actions (delete an account, submit a real payment), standing rules. Keep goals exportable to git. Use seeded accounts, a mailbox for one-time codes, and a reusable session. Onboard with one flow before wiring to PRs for one service, leaving the scripted suite in place. Pin explicit checks inside the goal where judgement isn't enough (e.g., a specific request returned a specific status and body).
EVIDENCE: none (vendor's own qualitative findings only, e.g. vision-only model fixated on target position, text-only model couldn't rank prominence, screenshot+HTML combined made the action recogniseable after page change). QA.tech states test cases are capped at "around `50 agent steps`", screen sampling "about once a second", SOC 2 Type 2, EU data at rest, parallel executions capped per environment by default.
LIMITS: Not deterministic; where a flow has two sensible paths both occur. Cannot see anything faster than ~1 Hz (flicker, jank, short transitions); struggles with third-party auth screens fighting automation, CAPTCHAs, real payment instruments, visual-design judgement, and data the agent can't see. Slower per step than replay. Page content and screenshots leave the environment to a model provider.
TOOLING: Browser Use, Stagehand, Skyvern, computer-use models, Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, MCP server, GitHub/GitLab PR integration, CI/CLI/REST API.
LINKS: qa.tech posts on self-healing misconceptions, autonomous testing, flaky tests (two kinds), dynamic testing, regression testing, AI QA testing guide, best agentic QA tools 2026.

## A003 · Agentic testing for modern QA: A practical guide - Tricentis
URL: https://www.tricentis.com/learn/agentic-testing
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Agentic testing lets autonomous AI agents plan and execute tests from intent, observe outcomes and adapt steps without fixed scripts — the goal stays stable while the agent chooses actions.
CONCEPTS:
- **Agentic capabilities** — Planning, tool use and feedback loops that let a system decide, act and learn within guardrails. > "Agentic capabilities are the planning, tool use, and feedback loops that let an AI system decide, act, and learn within guardrails."
- **AI-assisted versus agentic** — AI-assisted testing helps at authoring time; agentic testing takes responsibility for executing and adjusting the test itself. > "AI-assisted testing helps humans write tests faster or summarize results. Agentic testing makes the AI responsible for executing and adjusting the test itself."
- **Perceive and contextualize** — The agent sees the accessibility tree and the rendered pixels the way a user would. > "The accessibility tree and the rendered pixels are “visible” to the agent, just as a user would have visibility."
- **Planning capability** — The agent decomposes a goal into candidate action paths and re-plans mid-run when one fails. > "Should even one of the candidate’s action paths start to fail, the agent has the capability to re-plan mid-run."
- **Action workflows in real time** — The agent clicks, types, navigates and performs tool calls against the running application. > "It actually clicks, types, navigates through, and performs tool calls"
- **Reflect** — The agent compares results against the original intent and decides to continue, retry or escalate. > "After performing an action, the agent can see the results against the original intent."
- **Agentic loop phases** — Intent is defined, the agent plans UI or API steps, acts and observes, then adapts and reports. > "In most implementations we’ve seen, an agentic loop looks something like this"
- **Guardrails** — Allowed scope, a specific test account and environment, and a ceiling on retries. > "A good, well-scoped agent should know what it’s allowed to touch and what is off limits."
- **Intent-based execution** — Tests are written as goals rather than brittle step lists. > "The tester just writes a sentence: “A returning customer logs in and updates their card details and then re-orders their last stock photo.”"
- **UI resilience** — Labels and selectors can move without breaking the test. > "Elements are deciphered using their label, role, and the underlying context."
- **Natural language reporting** — Reports are legible to leads and non-testers without calling in the test engineer. > "The scrum master or product manager doesn’t need to pull in the test engineer every time to understand what went wrong"
- **Lower maintenance cost** — Maintenance shifts from repairing test flows to tightening ambiguous intent. > "Rather, it moves your troubleshooting from “fix my test flow” to a more “let’s tighten the intent” approach."
- **Multi-environment adaptation** — One intent covers staging, UAT and production while guardrails vary by environment. > "the same intent-based test can cover environments across staging, UAT, and production"
- **AI-augmented software test tooling** — Gartner tracks agentic testing tools under this category. > "Gartner is now tracking such tools under a special category called “AI-augmented software test tooling.”"
- **Multi-agent QA** — A predicted arrangement of planning, execution, triage and coordinating agents. > "One agent will plan the coverage. The second will execute. A third will triage the failures with a human QA team."
GUIDELINES: Get started: (1) pick one high-value flow that breaks often and affects revenue; (2) define intent with acceptance criteria in plain language; (3) stabilize test data with safe accounts/datasets; (4) run in a controlled environment, staging then pre-production; (5) "Scale slowly. Add `two or three` more flows once confidence is earned." Write intent like a user story; add `explicit assertions` telling the agent what "done" looks like; instrument runs with logs, screenshots and checkpoints; use guardrails; keep data isolated — "reset accounts or seed data between runs". Set a retry ceiling because "a limitless number of retries will burn through your AI budget". "Autonomy without observability is just automation you can't trust." Guardrails should be implemented from the ground up. Keep a clean test suite — agentic testing "doesn't excuse unclear requirements or unstable environments."
EVIDENCE: Gartner 2026 CIO survey: `17%` of organizations have AI agents deployed; `>60%` plan deployment within two years. Gartner: agentic AI in `40%` of enterprise applications by end of 2026 vs `5%` in 2025; `>1/3` of enterprise apps by 2028 vs `<1%` in 2024; `40%` of agentic AI projects killed by 2027. LTIMindtree case: low-complexity cases `30 mins → 10 mins` (`67%`); high-complexity `2 hours → 20-30 mins` (`83%`); overall `67%` faster execution and `50%` quicker design. Summary figure: design time reduced "by up to `83%`" and automation/execution by `67%`.
LIMITS: Vendor-authored; adoption statistics come from Gartner projections; industry applicability table is illustrative; notes overreliance risk — teams "stop thinking critically about test design once agents take over".
TOOLING: Tricentis Tosca, qTest, Tricentis Agentic Quality Engineering Platform, SAP AI units, agentic-loop diagrams.
LINKS: Gartner Hype Cycle for agentic AI, Gartner AI-augmented software testing tools market, LTM case study, SAP partnership announcement, ISTQB-adjacent acceptance criteria guidance.

## A004 · Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration for Unit Test Generation via Human-Testing-Inspired Workflows
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2607.09101
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: TestAgent emulates the human three-step unit-test workflow — derive requirements, write and refine by execution feedback, review with adequacy metrics — using three collaborating LLM agents, dynamic tool APIs and a test-specialized repository knowledge graph, outperforming LLM and search-based baselines.
CONCEPTS:
- **TestAgent** — Three collaborating agents — requirement planner, test generator, test reviewer — emulate how developers understand, construct and validate unit tests. > "TestAgent designs three specialized agents, namely a requirement planner, a test generator, and a test reviewer, to simulate how developers understand, construct, and validate unit tests."
- **Procedural framework** — A fixed pipeline cannot decide whether to refine tests or re-extract context from real-time feedback. > "Existing approaches typically follow a pre-defined and static generation pipeline that does not adapt the test generation strategy based on real-time feedback"
- **Coarse-grained context extraction** — Fixed rules such as the whole focal method or class miss dependency detail or overflow the input limit. > "Most existing approaches retrieve context using fixed rules (e.g., the entire focal method or the focal class), without explicitly modeling language-specific structures"
- **Knowledge graph** — An entity-level graph of packages, classes, methods and variables with typed dependency edges, built once per project and incrementally maintained. > "we construct an entity-level knowledge graph based on static code analysis to capture the internal semantics and relationships within the project"
- **Tool APIs** — Graph manipulation, information retrieval and runtime interaction tools exposed to every agent for autonomous selection. > "we design a set of tools to facilitate efficient interaction between agents and external resources"
- **search_similar_test_class** — Recommends related tests by dependency-set Jaccard similarity above a threshold, on the premise that tests sharing dependencies share testing logic. > "The intuition is that tests sharing dependencies tend to share testing logic"
- **Voting-based confirmation** — Three different LLMs vote on whether a failing test exposes a real bug. > "employs a voting-based confirmation mechanism among three different LLMs to determine whether a failure exposes a real bug"
- **Requirement planner states** — The planner produces a function summary, then test requirements across normal inputs, boundary cases and exceptional scenarios. > "this agent operates in two internal states: function summary and test requirement"
GUIDELINES: Derive structured test requirements before generating code; store them on the graph so later stages can retrieve them. Iterate generation against execution feedback in a sandbox. Do root-cause analysis on failing tests and require multi-LLM voting confirmation before treating a failure as a defect. Review across coverage, correctness and requirement alignment, and emit actionable suggestions (e.g. new requirements for uncovered scenarios). Expose all tools to every agent and let it select autonomously per state. Ground context in dependency structure rather than lexical code similarity.
EVIDENCE: Six Java projects: `97.46%` execution rate, `92.34%` line coverage, `90.24%` branch coverage, `83.69%` mutation score; beats ChatUniTest and HITS under the same GPT-4o backbone on all six metrics; vs EvoSuite comparable correctness with mutation score `83.69%` vs `43.59%`. Ablation: adding the knowledge graph improves line coverage `22.31%`, branch coverage `24.52%`, mutation score `26.83%`. Qwen3-30B-A3B backbone still beats ChatUniTest with GPT-4o. Python adaptation: `88.85%` line, `78.89%` branch coverage, beating CodaMosa and CoverUp. Detects `154` real-world bugs via non-regression tests at `92.22%` precision. Three benchmarks, six metrics, five baselines, three LLMs, two languages, six RQs, industrial project plus user study.
LIMITS: Extracted text truncates mid Section III-D-2, so generator/reviewer mechanisms and evaluation protocol details are not covered here. Java-centric design (James/SPOON-based graph); Python adaptation reported separately. Traditional tools still achieve high coverage, so coverage alone does not establish usefulness.
TOOLING: GPT-4o, Qwen3-30B-A3B, SPOON, JaCoCo, PITest, Java, Python.
LINKS: ChatUniTest, HITS, EvoSuite, Randoop, AthenaTest/Methods2Test, RepoGraph, AutoCodeRover, SWE-Bench, SWE-Agent, CodaMosa, CoverUp.

## A005 · Tricentis Leads New Era of Agentic AI to Scale Enterprise-Grade Autonomous Software Quality - Tricentis
URL: https://www.tricentis.com/news/tricentis-leads-new-era-of-agentic-ai
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Tricentis announced what it calls two industry firsts — secure remote Model Context Protocol servers for enterprise testing tools and Tricentis Agentic Test Automation — plus a beta of persona-aware AI workflows, framed as an open, hybrid AI strategy.
CONCEPTS:
- **Remote MCP servers** — Secure remote Model Context Protocol servers described as the “UI for AI”, letting agents call enterprise testing tools such as Tosca, NeoLoad and qTest. > "secure remote MCP servers – the “UI for AI” infrastructure that allows AI agents to interact directly with enterprise-grade testing tools"
- **Tricentis Agentic Test Automation** — An AI agent that generates complete test cases from natural-language prompts, analyzes prior runs and adapts to enterprise-specific context. > "the first AI agent capable of generating complete test cases from natural language prompts, analyzing prior test runs, and adapting to enterprise-specific context"
- **Vision AI** — Proprietary visual element interpretation that keeps the agent technology-agnostic across SAP Fiori and web applications. > "Tricentis Agentic Test Automation can also interpret visual elements across platforms, making it technology-agnostic"
- **AI workflows** — Persona-aware, chat-based interfaces for agent-to-agent and human-to-agent work on test cases, test data and manual automation. > "intuitive, persona-aware interfaces that allow users of all skill levels to engage with AI"
- **Build-your-own or vendor agents** — Customers may build their own agents or use Tricentis' rather than following one prescribed model. > "With MCP and Tricentis Agentic Test Automation, we’re giving our customers the flexibility to build their own AI agents or use ours — whichever best fits their strategy."
GUIDELINES: Choose the agent ownership model fit to strategy rather than one prescribed approach ("we're not prescribing a one-size-fits-all approach"). Combine MCP (agents calling enterprise tools) with agentic automation (agents generating and adapting tests). Use visual/AI interpretation to stay technology-agnostic in complex enterprise UI stacks. Start from existing testing history and requirements so the agent can reason from organizational context.
EVIDENCE: Early adopters reported "up to `85%` time savings in test creation and `60%` gains in overall productivity"; no methodology, sample, or measurement basis stated. Generally available in July (2025); beta AI workflows offered via signup.
LIMITS: Company press release; both headline figures are unqualified early-adopter claims; "industry first" is a self-description.
TOOLING: Model Context Protocol (MCP) remote and on-premises servers, Tricentis Tosca, NeoLoad, qTest, SeaLights, Vision AI, Agentic Test Automation (GA July 2025), Claude, OpenAI-powered agents, Cursor.
LINKS: Tricentis webinar on remote MCP/Agentic Test Automation; Tricentis blog "three major steps in AI-powered software testing"; Wolters Kluwer and TTC Global co-development quotes.

## A006 · Autonomous AI and Agentic Testing Agents: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Self-Directed Software Quality Assurance (J Artif Intell Mach Learn & Data Sci)
URL: https://urfjournals.org/open-access/autonomous-ai-and-agentic-testing-agents-a-multi-agent-architecture-for-self-directed-software-quality-assurance.pdf
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: LLM-driven testing agents that perceive, plan, execute, self-heal locators, triage defects and learn from history are best organized as a layered multi-agent architecture with a bounded self-healing decision point and a memory write-back loop inside CI/CD.
CONCEPTS:
- **Test-suite fragility** — One change to a page element, schema or navigation flow invalidates many previously passing tests. > "a single change to a page element, endpoint schema or navigation flow can invalidate large numbers of previously passing tests, a phenomenon widely known as test-suite fragility"
- **Agentic testing agent** — A software entity that perceives state, plans to a testing objective, invokes tools and revises the plan on feedback. > "An agentic testing agent is a software entity that perceives the state of an application, forms a plan consistent with a testing objective"
- **Six-layer architecture** — Application under test, perception and context acquisition, reasoning and planning core, multi-agent execution, tool integration, and reporting with feedback. > "The proposed architecture organizes an autonomous agentic testing system into six cooperating layers"
- **Four perception agents** — UI/DOM, API and log observability, requirement and specification parser, and visual regression agents each emit normalized context. > "Four specialized perception agents extract structured context from the application and its surrounding artifacts."
- **Five execution agents** — Generation, execution, self-healing locator, defect triage/RCA and regression prioritization. > "Five specialized agents perform the concrete work of testing. The test-case generation agent converts a task specification into executable test cases"
- **Reasoning and planning core** — Interprets intent, decomposes goals, retrieves precedent and self-reflects, emitting task specifications rather than acting. > "The planning core does not itself execute browser or API actions; it emits task specifications that are dispatched to the execution layer"
GUIDELINES: Seven-stage cycle per trigger (PR, nightly, scheduled regression): requirement ingestion → test intent and planning → test case generation → autonomous execution → self-healing and retry → root-cause analysis → reporting and learning. Place the `self-healing decision point between execution and reporting` rather than treating locator failures as terminal. Invoke self-healing "only on locator failure rather than on every step". Bound retries and apply rate limiting at the orchestrator to stop runaway self-healing loops delaying the pipeline. Constrain prompts to `structured-output schemas`; log all agent-to-tool interactions for auditability. Expose only three signals to the surrounding pipeline: `aggregate pass rate`, `requirement-coverage estimate`, `root-cause classification summary`, and insert the stage between build/static checks and the quality gate. Persist every outcome (repairs, oracle refinements, flaky classifications) to vector memory. Defer ambiguous cases to humans rather than masking a possible regression. Treat automated triage as `decision-support`, not a fully autonomous gate in safety-critical contexts.
EVIDENCE: Four-week qualitative pilot: web app with `220` scripted UI cases and `60` REST endpoints. `35/35` new user stories got a first-draft test case, most needing only minor assertion edits. `46` cases failed from locator drift after unrelated front-end changes; `39 (85%)` auto-recovered via vision-grounded fallback; `7 (15%)` deferred to human review. `128` failures triaged as regression/environment/flaky with manual review concurring on "the large majority". Implementation in Python (reasoning, generation, triage) and JS/TS (browser execution, self-healing) with Playwright.
LIMITS: Explicitly "exploratory and qualitative rather than a controlled experiment"; figures "indicative of prototype behavior on the two target systems rather than generalizable benchmarks"; the oracle problem persists; LLM non-determinism stresses version-control and audit practices built around static scripts; explainability/trust unresolved for regulated domains; per-step LLM cost motivates selective invocation and caching.
TOOLING: Playwright, Selenium, Appium, OpenAPI, Jenkins, GitHub Actions, vector store, relational defect store, Gherkin, containerized services.
LINKS: Myers; Barr et al. (oracle problem survey); Zhang et al. (ML for testing); Durieux et al. (program repair); Wooldridge & Jennings; Russell & Norvig; Vaswani et al.; Devlin et al.; Brown et al.; Wei et al. (chain-of-thought); Yao et al. (ReAct); Schick et al. (Toolformer); Park et al. (generative agents).

## A007 · Autonomous AI and Agentic Testing Agents: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Self-Directed Software Quality Assurance (Research Square preprint)
URL: https://assets-eu.researchsquare.com/files/rs-10220882/v1/8ef5a321-3e3e-436c-99c7-2fbdfee1e491.pdf?c=1784004764
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Same architecture paper as A006, posted as a preprint under DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10220882/v1: a six-layer, five-execution-agent design for LLM-driven self-directed testing, with a bounded self-healing loop and online memory feedback inside CI/CD.
CONCEPTS:
- **Paradigm comparison table** — Scripted, ML-assisted and agentic testing are compared along test creation, UI-change maintenance, oracle construction, adaptability and learning. > "the principal shift introduced by agentic testing is not any single capability but the combination of goal-directed planning, bounded autonomous repair, and closed-loop memory"
- **Perception layer** — Four agents emit normalized context objects consumed by the reasoning core. > "Four specialized perception agents extract structured context from the application and its surrounding artifacts."
- **Reasoning and planning core** — Interprets intent, decomposes tasks, retrieves precedent and self-reflects, preserving a separation between deliberation and action. > "The planning core does not itself execute browser or API actions; it emits task specifications that are dispatched to the execution layer, preserving a clean separation between deliberation and action"
- **Multi-agent execution layer** — Five agents generate tests, drive execution, heal locators, triage defects and prioritize regression. > "The test-case generation agent converts a task specification into executable test cases, typically expressed in a structured format such as Gherkin or a framework-native scripting language."
- **Bounded autonomy** — Agents act unilaterally only within their declared toolset; other decisions route back to the planning core. > "the execution agent invokes the self-healing agent only on locator failure rather than on every step"
- **Continuous-learning loop** — Outcomes are written back into vector memory to refine planning and locator-repair heuristics. > "results are published to the dashboard, and the outcome — including any newly discovered locator repairs, oracle refinements, or flaky-test classifications — is written back into the vector memory"
GUIDELINES: Attempt each registered locator strategy in `priority order`; only when all deterministic strategies fail, delegate to vision-grounded matching, then persist the recovered locator so later runs are constant-time — "bounds the cost of vision-based matching to the first occurrence of a locator drift". Ground generation prompts in retrieved similar past tests to reduce hallucinated assertions and match project naming/oracle conventions. Bounded retry budget plus rate limiting at the orchestrator. Structured-output/function-calling mode for the reasoning core. Log every agent-to-tool interaction for auditability. Insert the agentic stage between build/static-check and the deployment quality gate, exposing only aggregate pass rate, requirement-coverage estimate and root-cause classification summary. Adopt incrementally alongside existing scripted suites.
EVIDENCE: Four-week pilot, web application with `220` existing scripted UI tests plus `60` REST endpoints: `35/35` new user stories drafted; `46` UI tests hit locator drift; `39 (85%)` auto-recovered without human intervention; `7 (15%)` deferred as structural navigation changes; `128` failures triaged as regression/environment/flaky with manual concurrence for the large majority. Python + JS/TS prototype with Playwright.
LIMITS: Self-described exploratory, qualitative evaluation, not a controlled experiment; no generalizable performance claims; oracle problem not eliminated; non-determinism complicates reproducibility and audit; explainability/trust blocks broader autonomy in regulated domains; bounded autonomy reduces achievable automation; per-step LLM invocation cost. Extracted text ends mid-Section VII.
TOOLING: Playwright, Selenium, Appium, OpenAPI client, GitHub Actions, Jenkins, vector store, relational defect store, Gherkin, structured-output/function-calling LLM APIs.
LINKS: Myers; Barr et al.; Zhang et al.; Durieux et al.; Itkonen & Mäntylä; Wooldridge & Jennings; Russell & Norvig; Vaswani et al.; Devlin et al.; Brown et al.; Wei et al.; Yao et al. (ReAct); Schick et al. (Toolformer); Park et al.

## A008 · Design and Implementation of an AI-Enhanced Multi-Stage Testing Architecture for Scalable Software Quality Assurance
URL: https://oss.cs.fau.de/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Gailler_2026.pdf
TYPE: thesis
THESIS: A bachelor thesis designs and prototypes an architecture combining a standardized context layer with specialized agents (Requirements Review, Governance, AI Governance Review, Test Generation) so that LLM support in a multi-stage test process stays traceable, evidence-backed and human-controlled within an existing PR/CI workflow.
CONCEPTS:
- **SCA Tool starting point** — SCA Tool already has unit, integration and end-to-end tests but only weak traceable links to requirements, systematic gap identification and consistent evaluation. > "Ausgangspunkt ist die bestehende Testlandschaft von SCA Tool, die bereits unterschiedliche Teststufen umfasst, jedoch nur begrenzte Unterstützung für nachvollziehbare Anforderungsbezüge, systematische Testlückenerkennung und einheitliche Auswertung bietet."
- **Multi-stage testing** — Coordinated use of several test levels in one QA process, with the test pyramid as orientation rather than rigid rule. > "Multi-Stage Testing bezeichnet in dieser Arbeit die koordinierte Verwendung mehrerer Teststufen innerhalb eines gemeinsamen Qualitätssicherungsprozesses, mit dem Ziel, Fehler früh zu erkennen und zugleich komplexe Systemabläufe realitätsnah zu prüfen."
- **Shift-left requirement review** — Applying shift-left to requirement review lets later implementation, governance and generation steps build on a more precise requirement base. > "In der entwickelten Architektur wird dieses Prinzip auf die Anforderungsprüfung übertragen: Werden Probleme bereits auf Issue-Ebene erkannt, können die nachfolgenden Implementierungs-, Governance- und Testgenerierungsschritte auf einer präziseren Anforderungsgrundlage aufbauen."
- **Standardized Context Layer** — Requirements, code changes, existing tests and results are merged into one standardized context layer. > "Dazu werden Informationen über Anforderungen, Codeänderungen, vorhandene Tests und Testergebnisse in einer standardisierten Kontextschicht zusammengeführt."
- **Requirements Review Agent** — Checks requirements for testability and traceability. > "Der Requirements Review Agent prüft Anforderungen auf Testbarkeit und Nachvollziehbarkeit."
- **Governance Agent** — Assesses technical and organizational rules plus the existing test coverage. > "Der Governance Agent bewertet technische und organisatorische Vorgaben sowie die vorhandene Testabdeckung."
- **AI Governance Reviewer** — The AI-assisted assessment agent among the four specialized agents. > "Die entwickelte Architektur kombiniert eine standardisierte Kontexterfassung mit spezialisierten Agenten für Requirements Review, Governance, KI-gestützte Bewertung und Test Generation."
- **Test Generation Agent** — Produces suggestions and drafts for suitable tests. > "Der Test Generation Agent erzeugt Vorschläge und Entwürfe für geeignete Tests."
- **Structured artifacts** — Results are delivered as structured artifacts and checked by humans at defined points. > "Die Ergebnisse werden als strukturierte Artefakte bereitgestellt und an definierten Stellen durch Menschen geprüft."
- **Human-in-the-loop** — Human interaction is planned wherever domain decisions, approvals or additional application context are needed. > "Menschliche Interaktion wird insbesondere dort vorgesehen, wo fachliche Entscheidungen, Freigaben oder zusätzlicher Anwendungskontext erforderlich sind."
- **Controlled AI use** — Model output stays bounded by deterministic checks, structured artifacts, evidence references and human-in-the-loop mechanisms. > "Sprachmodelle unterstützen Analyse und Testvorschläge, ihre Ergebnisse bleiben jedoch durch deterministische Prüfungen, strukturierte Artefakte, Evidenzbezüge und Human-in-the-loop-Mechanismen begrenzt."
GUIDELINES: Collect context in a standardized, structured form before invoking any agent. Keep model output non-authoritative: pair every LLM step with `deterministic checks`, `structured artifacts`, `evidence references` and `human-in-the-loop` checkpoints. Reuse existing issue, pull-request, CI and review artifacts and control points rather than adding a parallel process. Define requirements first (functional and non-functional), then the architecture (design goals, data flow, layers). Anchor quality gates in CI; evaluate each stage and each agent separately for cost and runtime, and measure `trigger costs`. Interview-style thesis rule: evaluate via a fully executed demo scenario (Issue #45 / PR #46) against numbered evaluation questions `EF-1` to `EF-9`.
EVIDENCE: Thesis-shaped, not reproduced in the extracted text: evaluation is one demo scenario (Issue #45, PR #46) with evaluation questions EF-1…EF-9, per-stage and per-agent cost/runtime tables with input/output tokens, a first governance pass reporting coverage gaps, and a limitation section on cost measurement. Cited external figure: repository-level context files (e.g. `AGENTS.md`) raise coding-agent inference cost "im Mittel um mehr als `20 %`" without generally improving success rate (Gloaguen et al., 2026).
LIMITS: Single prototypical implementation for one system (SCA Tool); evaluation is a demo scenario, with a dedicated validity discussion (8.4) and explicit cost-measurement limitations (7.6.2); German-language thesis; states the work does not ask whether general-purpose coding agents could do the individual tasks, only how a QA process should be architected. Extracted text ends inside Section 2.4.
TOOLING: LLM providers via a shared provider layer, CI quality gates, PR workflows, `AGENTS.md` repository instructions, general-purpose coding agents with extension/tool mechanisms (Anthropic, GitHub, OpenAI).
LINKS: ISTQB Foundation Level syllabus 2024; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2 and 29119-3; ISO/IEC 25010; Fowler (2012) test pyramid; Wacker (2015); Ouédraogo et al. (2026, 2024) on LLM unit-test quality and test smells; Yang et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2025) on test maintenance; Alshammari et al. (2024) on flaky classification; Pan et al. (2022) on test prioritization; Liu et al. (2024) and Wang et al. (2025) agent surveys; Gloaguen et al. (2026).

## A009 · Software Testing Strategy: How to Decide What to Test When AI Writes the Code
URL: https://shiftasia.com/column/software-testing-strategy-how-to-decide-what-to-test-when-ai-writes-the-code/
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: When AI writes code, human review attention is the scarcest resource, so a testing strategy must be a short, reviewed record of scope, risk and evidence decisions — including code provenance and verification capacity — rather than a filed-away document.
CONCEPTS:
- **Software testing strategy** — A documented set of decisions about objectives, scope, levels and types, environments, test data, automation, roles, defect handling, metrics and release criteria. > "a documented set of decisions about how to test a product to meet its quality goals"
- **Testing process** — Planning, analysis, design, implementation, execution and completion activities under ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2. > "The testing process consists of activities such as planning, analysis, design, implementation, execution, and completion"
- **Test plan** — What is tested in one release, when, and by whom. > "What we test in this release, when, and who does it"
- **Organization-level vs project-level strategy** — 29119-3 separates company-wide rules from a product's adaptation of them; AI usage rules belong at the organizational level. > "ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 separates the organizational test strategy from the project test strategy."
- **Code provenance** — A risk-workshop input recording how much of a module's recent change was AI-generated. > "For AI-assisted projects, add two inputs most risk registers miss: code provenance and change volume."
- **Change volume** — A sudden rise in changes per sprint makes a module less understood and therefore riskier. > "The same goes for a module that has suddenly started receiving three times as many changes per sprint."
- **Independence rule** — For high-risk areas, tests must originate from a source other than the code, such as a human tester, a separate tool, or requirements written before coding. > "For high-risk areas, require that tests originate from a different source than the code, such as a human tester, a separate tool, or tests derived from requirements before coding."
- **Quality gates** — Commit, merge and release gates enforced in the CI/CD pipeline with rigour set per risk tier. > "Typical gates include commit, merge, and release gates, all of which are automated in the CI/CD pipeline."
- **Review load** — A metric counting changes awaiting skilled review and their wait times. > "Additionally, track review load, defined as the number of changes awaiting skilled review and their wait times."
- **Human validation sign-off matrix** — A concise matrix recording which decisions require human judgement. > "Including a concise sign-off matrix in the strategy helps ensure that human oversight is maintained."
- **AI-specific frameworks** — The strategy names the frameworks it aligns with, such as the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 or the EU AI Act for high-risk systems. > "At the strategy level, specify the frameworks you are aligning with, such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, or the EU AI Act for high-risk systems"
GUIDELINES: Seven-step build: understand business/technical risks (workshop with product owners, architects, developers, support leads, QA) → define measurable quality objectives ("No high-severity findings against `OWASP ASVS Level 2` on payment and authentication services") → map risks to activities in both directions → select levels → decide what to automate → define gates → establish metrics. Rule of thumb: "if a statement remains valid next quarter, include it in the strategy. If it references a date or individual, place it in the plan." Raise risk likelihood by `1 point` when a workflow's latest changes were AI-generated. For AI-generated modules, prefer `integration and contract tests` over unit tests, since generated unit tests confirm what code does, not what it should do. Cap change size: above a set number of changed lines, split the PR or require a second human reviewer. Track `defect escape rate`, `change failure rate`, `time to restore service`, share of critical/high-risk areas with current passing tests, plus review load. Keep the document to "a few pages". Allocate a fixed review budget: example team with two senior QA engineers gets about `six days` per release — roughly `3 days` to the two critical workflows, `2 days` to high risk, `1 day` for everything else; cut medium-tier exploratory first, then high-tier exploratory; never cut critical-tier review. Count AI-generated tests as release evidence only after a human approves the assertions. Name frameworks in scope: `NIST AI Risk Management Framework`, `ISO/IEC 42001`, `EU AI Act` for high-risk systems. Review production incidents, tickets and monitoring each release and adjust scores.
EVIDENCE: CISQ 2022: cost of poor software quality in the US "no less than `$2.41 trillion`"; locating and fixing bugs is the highest single cost in the SDLC. GitClear 2025 analysis of `211 million` changed lines: duplicated code blocks became `eight times` more frequent and copy-pasted lines surpassed moved lines. Google DORA 2025: each `25%` increase in AI adoption linked to a `7.2%` decline in delivery stability; DORA 2024 found AI adoption linked to lower delivery stability and that small batch sizes and solid testing still matter. Worked example: 7 workflows scored likelihood×impact 1-5 (reimbursement payout `4×5=20`, admin permissions `4×5=20`, receipt AI extraction `16`, approval routing `16`, SSO `10`, expense submission `6`, reporting `6`).
LIMITS: Vendor/consultancy column with an explicit services pitch; prescribes thresholds qualitatively ("a set number of changed lines") rather than numerically; the risk-scoring example is hypothetical, with the +1 AI-provenance adjustment an asserted heuristic.
TOOLING: CI/CD pipelines with commit/merge/release gates, contract tests, security scans, self-healing locators, Playwright MCP (event banner).
LINKS: CISQ 2022 cost-of-poor-quality report; ISTQB glossary; ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-2/-3; ISO/IEC 25010; OWASP ASVS; DORA 2024 report; GitClear AI code quality 2025; NIST AI RMF; ISO/IEC 42001; EU AI Act; Shift Asia guides on risk-based testing, generative-AI testing, self-healing automation, AI-generated code testing.

## A010 · The Test Pyramid 2.0: AI-assisted testing across the pyramid
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12713685
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Proposes "The Test Pyramid 2.0", a conceptual framework that embeds a security-testing practice into each of five test layers (SAST, security controls validation, IAST, DAST, pen/chaos) and adds AI capabilities (test generation, coverage analysis, data synthesis, anomaly detection, risk prioritization) at every layer.
CONCEPTS:
- **Test Pyramid 2.0** — Five-layer pyramid (unit, component, integration, UI/API, manual/exploratory) extending the original three-layer model, with a DevSecOps security practice and AI techniques embedded in every layer. > "we operate on a pyramid with five layers that incorporate various testing methodologies used across the industry and academia today"
- **pyramid principle** — Tests become broader, fewer and more expensive to execute as you move up the pyramid, keeping fast feedback at the bottom and essential behavioural checks at the top. > "The basic principle is that tests become broader, fewer, and more expensive to execute as we move up the pyramid."
- **ChatUniTest** — LLM-based test-generation framework evaluated on four Java projects against the evolutionary tool EvoSuite. > "Compared to the overall coverage of 38.2% achieved by EvoSuite, the LLM-based solution yielded 59.6%."
- **coverage-guided RL fine-tuning** — A 7B-parameter model fine-tuned on test-coverage feedback and deployed as a custom unit-testing agent. > "the authors used test-coverage guided RL to fine-tune a model with 7B params and deployed a custom unit-testing agent"
- **chain-of-thought + RL from coverage feedback** — Zhang et al. optimise LLM unit-test generation with chain-of-thought prompts plus coverage-based reinforcement learning. > "researchers optimized LLMs for unit test generation via chain-of-thought (CoT) prompt and reinforcement learning (RL) from coverage feedback"
- **SAST at Layer-1** — Static analysis aligned with unit tests because of its frequency, proximity to source and fast execution, which makes security a default part of the developer workflow. > "Embedding SAST at this foundational level aligns with shift-left principles and ensures that security becomes a default part of the developer workflow, not a delayed checkpoint."
- **Security Controls Validation (SCV)** — DevSecOps practice verifying that access-control policies, data-handling rules and configuration settings themselves are functional, enforced and resilient; the proposed home for policy-as-code. > "SCV ensures that the security mechanisms themselves are functional, enforced, and resilient in production"
- **IAST at Layer-3** — Runtime instrumentation during integration tests, giving runtime-verified vulnerability detection with full code-level context. > "IAST uniquely provides accurate, runtime-verified vulnerability detection with full code-level context."
- **test data fidelity** — Integration scenarios need test entities in a valid prior state, so the framework calls for LLM/ML synthesis of those states. > "This often requires that test entities exist in a specific (and valid) state before testing begins."
- **Software Defect Prediction (SDP)** — ML over historical bug patterns, change frequency and dependency graphs to flag risky components, paired with explainable AI for stakeholders. > "researchers propose a lightweight approach for ML-based Software Defect Prediction (SDP), along with the use of explainable AI to provide feedback to stakeholders"
- **DAST at Layer-4** — Dynamic application security testing is attached to the UI/API layer of the pyramid. > "From bottom to top: Unit Testing with SAST, Component Tests with Security Controls Validation, Integration Testing with IAST, UI/API-level Testing with DAST"
- **pen/chaos tests at Layer-5** — Penetration and chaos testing sit in the manual/exploratory top layer. > "Component Tests with Security Controls Validation, Integration Testing with IAST, UI/API-level Testing with DAST, and Manual/Exploratory with Pen/Chaos Tests"
- **defect leakage** — The reduction the framework claims to deliver, alongside efficiency and resilience. > "integrate the latest advances in AI and DevSecOps principles into engineering workflows to achieve greater efficiency, reduce defect leakage, and create more resilient systems"
GUIDELINES:
- Obtain "close to 100% coverage" at the unit layer.
- Embed SAST in Layer-1 so security is "a default part of the developer workflow, not a delayed checkpoint".
- Codify security policy-as-code in Layer-2 "given the cost of executing tests in the higher layers".
- Place IAST in Layer-3, where runtime context exists but remediation is still cheap.
- Use AI defect prediction together with automated test generation to "close the loop between prediction and prevention" and avoid wasted cycles in low-risk areas.
- Have industry and academia adopt AI tools that "detect outdated or broken tests and proactively update them before execution".
EVIDENCE:
- ChatUniTest 59.6% coverage vs EvoSuite 38.2% across four Java projects.
- gpt-3.5-turbo with prompt engineering/fine-tuning/RAG generating "up to 85% relevant tests".
- Coverage-guided RL 7B agent: coverage increase rate 0.41 vs 0.3 for o3-mini/o4.
- IntelliJ GPT-3.5 plugin trial: test group averaged 28 code smells vs control 20, and detected 25 refactored code smells.
- TaRGET (CLM test repair): 66.1% exact match, 80% plausible repair.
- Deep-learning impact analysis: precision up to 97.2%.
- RL test-case prioritization: NRPA > 0.96.
- LLM misconfiguration detection: precision 72.88%, recall 88.18%, F1 79.75%.
- CNN anomaly detection: accuracy 95.88%, recall 91.23%, false positive rate 2.34%.
- Privilege-escalation detection up to 97%; insecure API invocation up to 88%.
- GPT-4 test data: 63 case studies, 69% executability.
- SDP precision up to 0.981.
- LLM input mutation found 9 unknown zero-days vs 3 or 4 for baseline tools.
LIMITS: Presented by the authors as a "conceptual framework"; no empirical evaluation of the framework itself is reported. Cited evidence is drawn from heterogeneous third-party studies with different subjects and metrics.
TOOLING: EvoSuite, ChatUniTest, SAST, IAST, DAST, PaC/Rego, o3-mini/o4, Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o, Qwen3:30b, IntelliJ IDEA, GPT-3.5.
LINKS: Cohn (2009) Test Pyramid; Vocke (2018); Chen et al. (2024); Adu (2024); Takerngsaksiri et al. (2025); Baqar and Khanda (2025); Russell et al. (2018); Santos et al. (2021); Klieber and Flynn (2024); Saboor Yaraghi et al. (2025); Pathik and Sharma (2022); Bagherzadeh et al. (2022); Romeo et al. (2025); Nobi et al. (2022); Wen et al. (2025); Behjati et al. (2019); Baudry et al. (2024); Long et al. (2024); Madeyski and Stradowski (2025); Wang et al. (2025); Chang et al. (2025); Mehmood et al. (2023); Basheer et al. (2024); Meng et al. (2024).

## A011 · AI Shift Left - Diego Pacheco Tech Substack
URL: https://diegopachecotech.substack.com/p/ai-shift-left
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: AI coding agents make code review the binding bottleneck, so quality work — review, testing, requirements discovery and observability — must shift left onto the engineer's machine and into agents' own loops, while organisations are more likely to "accumulate" AI departments and tools than to truly transform.
CONCEPTS:
- **AI Shift Left** — Extending classic shift left so that code review, requirements and monitoring also move onto the engineer's machine and into local agent sessions. > "I think we need to shift left for AI. We need the code review to happen on the engineer’s machine."
- **code review bottleneck** — More people write code than review it, so agentic throughput widens the gap whatever the real productivity gain. > "So does not matter how much actual productivity AI gave to you or not, the code review is a bottleneck."
- **prompt request** — Submitting a stored prompt instead of code; rejected because it demands one-shot-quality models while LLMs are non-deterministic and English is not a context-free grammar. > "This is a recent idea: you just store the prompt, and instead of submitting the code, you submit the prompt."
- **systems thinking** — A holistic view of complex problems as interconnected systems rather than isolated incidents; engineering, Claude's code, XP and Kanban are all systems. > "Systems thinking is a holistic, analytical approach that views complex problems as interconnected systems rather than isolated incidents, focusing on relationships, patterns, and underlying structures"
- **TDD loop** — Write a failing test, make it pass, refactor, repeat; cited as a system agents imitate only until they stop fixing their own mistakes. > "We have a loop in TDD: first, you write a test, it fails, then you make it pass, you refactor the code, and you repeat the loop."
- **self-regulating system** — Gas Town, a multi-agent arrangement of collaborating roles that deliberately avoids mimicking the traditional waterfall organisation. > "The idea behind Gas Town is to be the Kubernetes of multi-agents, where multiple roles work together to build software."
- **transformation vs accumulation** — Companies claim transformation but perform accumulation: Agile became a department plus JIRA, DevOps became a team plus AWS. > "All companies say they want to transform, but very few actually do. What actually happens is accumulation."
- **two-phase SDLC** — Discovery and delivery as separate phases, with AI helping designers, product and architects during discovery. > "Software development follows a two-phase SDLC (one for discovery and one for delivery)."
- **requirements as assumptions** — Requirements are treated as assumptions to be discovered and tested rather than fixed inputs. > "instead requirements are just an assumption that we will discover and learn if it’s true or not"
- **policies → tests → self-service platform** — Code-as-policy lets teams generate tests with AI, build self-service platforms and apply Terraform hands-off. > "We can, and we should be using more and more code as policy, but having policies, we can easily generate tests (using AI), and we build self-service platforms that unblock innovation."
GUIDELINES:
- Trigger a code-review agent on the engineer's machine via a git/GitHub pre-commit hook or a Claude hook before a PR is fired; "a code review agent in Claude's code is just a markdown file".
- Review code off-cycle rather than on every PR — "every 2 weeks or every 30 days".
- Expand AI-enabled testing "without much burden": unit, integration, chaos, stress, test induction, property-based, snapshot, contract and mutation testing.
- Generate more observability with AI, and halt deploys when the system does not add observability.
- Apply Terraform hands-off once policies and code are in place.
- Ask what was learned: if Claude generated an app in 2h, what did the team learn?
EVIDENCE: none — argumentative essay; the only figures are illustrative volumes (2023: 20 engineers × 2 PRs/week with 2–5 reviewers; now the same 20 engineers at 10–30 PRs/week with the same 2–5 reviewers).
LIMITS: Author's opinion ("IMHO") with no measurements; concedes the "new workflow" winner is unknown and that 2026 is a year of experimentation; the 2h app-generation claim is qualified as not hands-off or one-shot.
TOOLING: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, Google Nano Banana Pro, JIRA, AWS, Terraform, git hooks, Claude hooks.
LINKS: RUP; Gas Town (Steve Yegge); "The death of code review (again)"; "Environments and people"; Pacheco, "The Art of Sense" (randomness chapter).

## A012 · Study Finds AI Is a Priority for Software Testing Teams, but Confidence Hinges on Accuracy and Reliability
URL: https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/02/19/3241023/0/en/Study-Finds-AI-Is-a-Priority-for-Software-Testing-Teams-but-Confidence-Hinges-on-Accuracy-and-Reliability.html
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Leapwork's 2026 survey finds strong stated intent to use AI in testing, but adoption breadth is shallow and confidence is gated by accuracy, test stability and the time needed to keep tests current.
CONCEPTS:
- **AI as testing priority** — 88% call AI a priority for their future testing strategy, with 46% rating it critical or high priority. > "Most organizations now view AI as a priority for their future testing strategy."
- **confidence gating** — Trust depends on accuracy, reliability and the ability to keep tests current as applications change. > "Confidence in AI driven testing depends on accuracy, reliability, and the ability to keep tests current as applications change."
- **pilot-stage adoption** — 65% use or explore AI in one or more testing activities, but only 12.6% use it across key test workflows. > "65% said they currently use or explore AI across one or more testing activities, though only 12.6% use AI across key test workflows today"
- **fragile tests / test decay** — Tests that break too often are among the top reasons teams fail to automate more, eroding trust in results. > "Errors carry real business risk, and fragile tests or slow updates can quickly erode trust in results."
- **update latency** — Time needed to repair tests after a change in a critical system; 45% report three days or more. > "45% said it takes three days or more to update tests after a change in a critical system"
- **manual effort constraint** — Manual effort and time still bound automation: 54% cite lack of time as a barrier and only 41% of testing is automated on average. > "54% cited lack of time as a barrier to adopting or improving test automation"
- **test creation as top drag** — 71% name test creation as the biggest slowdown, with maintenance second at 56%. > "71% said test creation slows their teams down the most, followed by test maintenance at 56%"
- **agentic capability** — Leapwork's CEO frames agentic use as settled and leaves only confidence and predictability open. > "It is no longer a question of whether testing teams will leverage agentic capabilities in their work. The question is how confidently and predictably they can rely on it"
- **stable automation foundation** — The differentiator is pairing AI with reliable automation, which is what lets teams scale without losing trust in outcomes. > "The real opportunity lies in applying and integrating AI alongside stable automation, so teams gain speed and scale without sacrificing trust in outcomes."
GUIDELINES:
- Apply AI "alongside stable automation" rather than as a replacement for it.
- Treat accuracy as "table stakes" for any AI testing rollout.
- Prioritise reducing test-creation effort (named by 71%) and maintenance effort (56%) first.
- Expect adoption to track the maturity and stability of existing automation.
EVIDENCE: Survey of "more than 300 software engineers, QA leaders, and IT decision makers at large and midsize organizations worldwide": 88% priority / 46% critical-high; 80% expect positive impact within two years; 65% use or explore; 12.6% use across key workflows; 54% cite accuracy/quality concerns; 45% need three days or more to update tests; 41% automated; 71% test creation, 56% maintenance, 54% lack of time.
LIMITS: Vendor-commissioned, self-reported perceptions; the release reports no sampling method, margin of error or question wording; adoption figures measure claimed use, not measured outcomes.
TOOLING: Leapwork (AI-powered test automation platform, visual model-based approach); no third-party tools named.
LINKS: Leapwork 2026 AI and Test Automation Study (leapwork.com/resources/ai-testing-survey).

## A013 · AI Testing: What It Is, What It Isn't, and Why It Matters
URL: https://testgrid.io/blog/ai-testing/
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: AI testing means ML-based support for authoring, maintaining, prioritising and analysing tests; it amplifies an already-stable pipeline and cannot substitute for test architecture, deterministic guarantees or human judgement.
CONCEPTS:
- **AI testing** — Tools using machine learning to support and enhance testing: generating cases, finding flaky tests, auto-healing scripts, prioritising runs and flagging high-risk areas. > "It refers to tools that use Machine Learning (ML) and related techniques to support and enhance software testing."
- **AI in testing vs testing AI systems** — Two different jobs: supporting the QA workflow versus validating reliability, fairness and reproducibility of models. > "One helps testers work faster by improving automation and coverage; the other validates the reliability, fairness, and reproducibility of AI-driven products themselves."
- **AI-assisted vs AI-driven testing** — Assistance suggests and waits for approval, whereas driven mode acts automatically once permitted. > "AI-assisted testing supports the human tester. It helps you make decisions faster, spot patterns, or reduce repetitive work."
- **self-healing and flaky test management** — Repairing broken locators automatically while learning failure patterns to flag instability. > "Detects and repairs broken locators or element changes automatically, reducing test maintenance; also, identifies unstable or flaky tests by learning from failure patterns"
- **NLP-based test automation** — Plain-English instructions converted into executable scripts, bridging requirements and automation. > "Converts plain-English instructions into executable test scripts; allows QA engineers and product owners define test logic in natural language"
- **predictive/risk-based optimisation** — Historical data, commit history and usage analytics choose which tests to run. > "Leverages historical test data, commit histories, and usage analytics to predict high-risk areas and prioritize tests that matter most"
- **visual AI** — Computer vision ignores trivial pixel shifts while flagging layout breaks, missing elements and cross-device rendering issues. > "These tools ignore minor pixel shifts but flag layout breaks, missing elements, or inconsistent rendering across devices."
- **test environment orchestration** — Dynamic provisioning and scaling of environments, with predicted workload spikes. > "Dynamically provisions, configures, and scales test environments based on project needs; predicts workload spikes and allocates resources intelligently"
- **responsible AI testing** — Fairness, bias detection and reproducibility across user groups when the system under test is itself a model. > "Focuses on fairness, bias detection, and consistency in AI-driven systems; ensures that models behave ethically, produce reproducible outcomes, and maintain trust across diverse user groups"
- **signal quality ROI** — Value is measured by the quality of feedback produced, not by raw time or cost saved. > "The real ROI shows up in the quality of feedback your testing process produces."
- **decision relevance over coverage volume** — Run fewer, better-chosen tests and optimise for decision relevance instead of test count. > "You’re no longer optimizing for coverage volume, but for decision relevance."
- **guardrails / junior-tester framing** — Prompt libraries, reviewer checkpoints and approval flows, treating generative AI as a junior tester rather than a replacement. > "Teams are also building prompt patterns, adding reviewer checkpoints, and treating GenAI like a junior tester, not a replacement."
GUIDELINES:
- Map `3–5` critical user journeys (e.g. signup → onboarding → core action) as the first automation candidates.
- Pilot on a staging environment wired into CI/CD; "If the setup feels heavy or unnatural, it's a red flag."
- Define explicitly when AI may self-heal, when changes are flagged for review, and when repeated fixes indicate a product/test-design problem.
- Judge ROI by asking whether less time goes to investigating false failures, whether results are easier to act on, whether issues are caught earlier.
- Hold off if there is pressure to automate everything, no stable CI/reliable suite/clear QA ownership, regulated or mission-critical need for deterministic outcomes, or no ability to explain a misfire.
- Do not assume generation replaces review: generated tests "still need guidance, review, and prioritization".
EVIDENCE: PractiTest 2024 State of Testing: 50% expect GenAI to improve automation efficiency, 28% report measurable productivity gains. Fortune Business Insights: AI-enabled testing market USD 414.7 million (2024) → USD 2.3 billion by 2032. Cites arXiv 2409.05808 that ML can predict "up to 80% of likely failure points in large codebases".
LIMITS: Vendor blog promoting CoTester/TestGrid; the adoption and market figures are second-hand; five named adoption risks (weak baseline, cost/value misalignment, low explainability, false positives and missed defects, cross-environment inconsistency) are asserted without measurement.
TOOLING: CoTester, TestGrid, mabl, Testim, Testers.ai, Sauce Labs, Functionize.
LINKS: PractiTest STOT 2024; Fortune Business Insights AI-enabled testing market; arXiv 2409.05808.

## A014 · Shift-left testing | Shift left vs. shift right | SpecStory
URL: https://specstory.com/learning/ci-cd/shift-left-testing
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Shift-left testing places each check at the earliest point where it runs fast and produces a trustworthy result, and it adds earlier checks without removing later ones; coding agents move the earliest possible point into the agent session itself.
CONCEPTS:
- **shift-left testing** — An approach that moves testing and other quality checks earlier in development; the name comes from a timeline with requirements left and release right. > "Shift-left testing, often shortened to shift left, is an approach that moves testing and other quality checks earlier in development."
- **quality gate** — A checkpoint that a change must pass before it moves on to the next stage. > "a checkpoint that a change must pass before it moves on."
- **check ordering** — Each check is placed at the earliest point where it runs fast and gives a trustworthy result, from requirements through editor, hooks, CI, staging and production. > "Shift left puts each check at the earliest point where it runs fast and gives a trustworthy result."
- **four reasons early failure is cheaper** — The change is small, the context is fresh, nothing depends on the bug and no customer is affected. > "An early failure usually costs less to fix, for four reasons:"
- **agent session as the leftmost point** — Agents edit files through tools, so on-save editor checks may never run; checks fire only when the agent calls them or a hook runs. > "When a coding agent writes the change, the earliest point on the timeline is its session."
- **self-confirming tests** — An agent that writes code and its unit tests from one prompt can repeat the same mistake in both, so the tests pass. > "When the agent writes the code and its unit tests from the same prompt, the tests can repeat the code's mistake and pass."
- **CI as bottleneck** — Agents push more changes, so CI becomes the bottleneck and cheap checks must run before it, stopping some broken changes from reaching the shared pipeline. > "Agents also push more changes, so CI can become the bottleneck"
- **shift right / testing in production** — Checking software after release under real traffic, through monitoring, canary releases, feature flags and synthetic checks. > "a practice that checks software after release, under real traffic, alongside the tests that run before release"
- **continuous testing** — Automated testing early and often across the lifecycle, giving each release candidate fast feedback. > "Continuous testing is a test approach that tests early and often across the lifecycle, with automated tests that give each release candidate fast feedback."
GUIDELINES:
- Also verify requirements before code exists, e.g. that each one can be testable.
- After an agent's change run, in order: static checks (formatter, linter, type checker, "often finish in seconds"); the pre-existing tests, "not only the agent's own tests"; a build plus short smoke run; and the changed workflow (e.g. checkout).
- Keep hooks fast: "A hook that takes minutes delays each commit, so people often bypass it."
- Keep releases small and reversible when testing in production.
- Budget developer time for early testing work, otherwise "early tests stay shallow".
EVIDENCE: none — illustrative walkthrough (Acme Co. furniture checkout): `npm run lint` flags an unused import; `npm test` passes in 3 seconds; CI checkout test fails 6 minutes after push; under the old process a tester would have found the empty cart in staging days later.
LIMITS: Stated limits: early checks cover only part of the system; slow early checks get skipped; testing work shifts to developers; "Early passes are limited evidence" — a green pipeline shows only that the chosen checks passed. The example is explicitly simplified.
TOOLING: `npm run lint`, `npm test`, Git pre-commit and pre-push hooks, CI, staging, RunStory (private alpha, isolated sandboxes), agent hooks (Stop hooks).
LINKS: ISTQB glossary (shift left, shift right, continuous testing); SpecStory learning articles on CI/CD, pre-commit vs pre-push vs CI, quality gates.

## A015 · Software Testing Strategies: 12 Approaches Compared (2026)
URL: https://www.shiplight.ai/blog/software-testing-strategies
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: A testing strategy is the operating model above tactics — twelve established approaches exist, most teams combine three or four, and the agentic strategy is the newest mainstream addition since 2024.
CONCEPTS:
- **software testing strategy** — The operating model above tactics, answering six questions: what gets tested, how tests are authored, when they run, what happens on failure, how coverage is measured and who is accountable. > "A software testing strategy is a high-level operating model that answers six questions for a software product or team"
- **strategy vs plan** — Strategy is quarterly or annual and defines the framework; the plan is release-level and lists the specific tests. > "Strategy is quarterly / annual and defines the framework. Plan is release-level and lists the specific tests."
- **risk-based testing** — A matrix scores probability times impact, and the highest-scoring areas get the densest coverage. > "A risk matrix scores each area on probability × impact; the highest-scoring areas get the densest test coverage."
- **requirements-based testing** — At least one test per functional requirement, plus traceability matrices for auditors. > "Each functional requirement gets at least one test that validates it. Traceability matrices link requirements to tests so coverage gaps are visible."
- **model-based testing** — A state machine, decision graph or workflow diagram drives generated traversal of the application's paths. > "A formal model of the application (state machine, decision graph, or workflow diagram) drives test generation."
- **exploratory testing** — Iterative human probing where each session generates the questions that drive the next session, producing new tests rather than repeated scripts. > "Exploratory testing is iterative: each session generates new questions that drive the next session."
