- **agile/shift-left testing** — Testing embedded in the development cycle: commits trigger tests, PRs have a CI gate and sprints carry explicit quality goals. > "Testing is embedded in the development cycle: every commit triggers tests, every PR has a CI gate, every sprint has explicit quality goals."
- **BDD** — Given/When/Then statements in Gherkin, executed by Cucumber, acting as a living specification stakeholders can read. > "Tests are authored as Given/When/Then statements in Gherkin syntax, executed by frameworks like Cucumber."
- **TDD** — A failing test describing the desired behaviour, then the minimum production code to pass it, then refactoring. > "The engineer writes a failing test that describes the desired behavior, then writes the minimum production code to make the test pass, then refactors."
- **ATDD** — Acceptance criteria are agreed as executable tests before development starts, with customer, PM and engineer convening on them. > "Customer, PM, and engineer agree on acceptance tests before the feature is built."
- **pair testing** — Two people share a session, one driving and one observing and questioning, to surface assumptions the driver cannot see. > "Two people sit together (or share a screen): one drives the test, the other observes and questions."
- **crowdsourced testing** — A managed third-party network or user community covers devices, locales, accessibility profiles and edge cases the in-house team cannot replicate. > "A managed third-party network (or your own user community) tests the application across devices, locales, accessibility profiles, and edge cases the in-house team can't replicate."
- **AI-augmented testing** — AI features layered onto existing automation while the operating model stays human-led. > "AI features (smart locators, flakiness detection, visual diff scoring, assisted authoring, anomaly clustering on failures) are layered onto traditional automation."
- **agentic testing** — Agents author tests from intent, explore for untested flows, execute in real browsers, self-heal across UI change and feed results back into the coding loop. > "AI agents author tests from intent or specs, autonomously explore the application to discover untested flows, run tests in real browsers, self-heal across UI change, and feed results back into the coding loop."
- **maintenance ceiling** — The 100–200-test-per-engineer ceiling under traditional automation, after which the suite outgrows the team's maintenance capacity. > "teams that have hit the 100–200-test-per-engineer maintenance ceiling under traditional automation"
GUIDELINES:
- Combine `3–4` strategies; "almost none use exactly one".
- Re-score the risk matrix `quarterly`; review strategy `quarterly` (annual was the 2015 norm), moving to monthly or trigger-driven on any KPI breach "e.g., maintenance budget above 5%" or coding-agent adoption shift.
- Choose anchor strategies by dominant risk: payments → risk-based + exploratory + agentic; HIPAA/PCI/SOX → requirements-based + ATDD + risk-based; rapid UI iteration → agentic + exploratory + agile; complex workflows → model-based + BDD + risk-based; accessibility/locale breadth → crowdsourced + requirements-based; legacy automation → AI-augmented + risk-based; greenfield → agile + TDD + agentic.
- Map to lifecycle: pre-release exploratory + pair; per-PR agentic + AI-augmented; per-sprint agile + BDD; pre-launch crowdsourced + risk-based + exploratory; production risk-based monitoring + anomaly detection.
- Document which strategy applies to which scope, who owns it, and how it is measured; "Strategy first; tool second."
- Measure coverage with user-journey reach + coverage-decay rate + maintenance budget + PR-time verification density.
EVIDENCE: none — no study or measurement; the 100–200-test ceiling and the "5% maintenance budget" threshold are asserted vendor claims.
LIMITS: Vendor-authored guide that positions Shiplight's agentic stack as the 2026 default; tool mapping is self-declared; pitfalls are listed per strategy (e.g. stale models, over-engineered Gherkin, TDD on ambiguous research work).
TOOLING: TestFiesta, Xray, TestRail, DOORS, Jama, GraphWalker, ConformIQ, Cucumber, SpecFlow, Behat, Jest, JUnit, pytest, Concordion, Robot Framework, FitNesse, Applause, Testlio, Bugcrowd, Applitools, Shiplight (YAML + AI Fixer + MCP), QA Wolf.
LINKS: Heuristic Test Strategy Model (James Bach); ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119; Shiplight AI-native test strategy, agentic QA benchmark, agent-first testing.

## A016 · Beyond Shift Left: How "Shifting Everywhere" With AI Agents Can Improve DevOps Processes
URL: https://www.ibm.com/think/insights/ai-in-devops
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: "Shift everywhere" extends shift left by embedding security, monitoring and testing into every phase (coding, building, deployment, runtime), and agentic AI makes that breadth feasible while introducing governance, shadow-AI and trust risks that AI gateways can mitigate.
CONCEPTS:
- **shift left** — Moving testing, issue identification and security to earlier lifecycle stages, typically onto developers who may not have the bandwidth. > "It enables teams to discover problems (ideally) during coding, instead of deployment."
- **shift everywhere** — A DevSecOps practice that puts security, monitoring and testing into every phase, from coding through building, deployment and runtime. > "Whereas shift left focuses on integrating security and testing earlier in the development lifecycle, shift everywhere means incorporating security, monitoring and testing into every phase, including coding, building, deployment and runtime"
- **hybrid model** — Borrowing the best elements of both approaches per context rather than choosing one. > "But what we’re really seeing is a hybrid model emerging—one that borrows the best elements from each approach."
- **agentic AI** — A system that can accomplish a specific goal with limited supervision, executing multi-step work, adapting in real time, orchestrating with other agents and learning from experience. > "system that can accomplish a specific goal with limited supervision"
- **digital twin** — Multi-agent simulation of real-world conditions, so code behaviour and dependency interactions can be tested before coding starts. > "that simulate real-world challenges the robots might encounter, enabling developers to test code behavior and dependency interactions"
- **anomaly detection with dynamic baselines** — Agents learn normal behaviour, tune baselines autonomously and classify point, cluster and contextual anomalies instead of treating all equally. > "agents identify data patterns and link structures, learning what constitutes normal system behavior, dynamically tuning themselves over time, and tracking deviations from established baselines."
- **agentic test generation** — Agents read source, UI structure, requirements, flows, API responses, defect history and test artifacts to decide what to run, and can write tests before the code exists. > "Agentic AI analyzes application source code, user interface (UI) structure, software requirements, user flows, API responses, defect history and existing test artifacts to understand and decide which tests to run."
- **alert correlation** — Linking alerts by timing, source, event type and affected systems so one grouped notification can trigger remediation against the whole signal group. > "Agentic AI-assisted correlation features link related alerts across users, environments and API endpoints, parsing meaningful alerts from superfluous signals, reducing alert volume and alert fatigue for development and operations teams."
- **exploitability testing** — Multi-agent generation of proof-of-concept attacks that demonstrate the real risk of a vulnerability. > "Multi-agent systems can analyze vulnerability descriptions and corresponding source code to generate proof-of-concept attacks that demonstrate the actual risk of exploitation."
- **shadow AI** — Agents created and run without IT, security or governance visibility. > "Because AI gateways make agentic AI more observable, they also help businesses rein in the shadow AI issues and runaway costs that agentic AI deployment can create."
- **hallucinated build steps** — Invented parameters and configuration details that propagate errors through the codebase and pipelines. > "autonomous agents can sometimes hallucinate build steps or configuration details, inventing parameters that trigger accidental or malicious actions."
- **AI gateway** — A unified layer between agents and the models, APIs and tools they use, enforcing governance, authentication, monitoring and traceability. > "AI gateways act as a unified, lightweight layer between agentic AI applications and the models, APIs and tools they use."
GUIDELINES:
- Define goals and parameters with leaders, product and engineers; agents "can't (and shouldn't) operate without any human involvement" — use human-in-the-loop.
- Embed intelligence at the source: analyse raw data streams as they arrive for real-time correlation.
- Group correlated alerts into a single notification and trigger remediation against the whole signal group.
- Prioritise vulnerabilities by runtime, business impact and compliance context; simulate exploits in sandboxes.
- Add technical, cultural and ethical guardrails; use gateways to centralise policy and rein in shadow AI and runaway cost.
EVIDENCE: IBM IBV: 86% of executives say AI agents will make process automation reinvention more effective by 2027. PwC: nearly 80% of senior executives have adopted some agentic AI; 19% deploy at scale. Gartner: more than 40% of agentic AI projects cancelled by end of 2027. METR study: developers ~20% slower resolving code issues with AI. State of Software Delivery 2025: developers spend 67% more time debugging AI-generated code.
LIMITS: Vendor thought-leadership; several statistics are restatements of other vendors' surveys; the 2027 cancellation forecast and the METR/State of Delivery findings are cited without methodology; admits agentic AI "is still a new technology" with unresolved accountability.
TOOLING: IBM Instana, IBM Terraform, HCP Vault Dedicated, Vault Radar, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines, LLMs, MCP-adjacent API integration, AI gateways.
LINKS: IBM IBV agentic process automation report; PwC AI agent survey; Gartner press release (June 25, 2025); METR early-2025 experienced-OSS-dev study; State of Software Delivery 2025 report.

## A017 · AI-Native Test Strategy 2026: The 6-Component Template
URL: https://www.shiplight.ai/blog/ai-native-test-strategy-2026
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Under agent-speed development the 2015 test strategy (pyramid, separate QA team, nightly regression, stable selectors) collapses, and must be replaced by a six-component AI-native operating model in which the coding agent authors tests in the same session as the feature.
CONCEPTS:
- **AI-native test strategy** — The document and operating model that defines what a team tests, how tests are authored, who is accountable when they break and how coverage is measured, when agents ship faster than human-authored suites. > "The operating model a team uses to produce quality when AI coding agents ship features faster than tests keep up."
- **six components** — Test scope, authoring model, healing and maintenance posture, verification gates, coverage targets and ownership. > "The strategy has six components: test scope, authoring model, healing and maintenance posture, verification gates, coverage targets, and ownership."
- **2015 template failure modes** — The Selenium pyramid, separate QA team and nightly regression template collapses under agent-speed development. > "The 2015 test strategy template (Selenium pyramid, separate QA team, nightly regression) does not survive contact with agent-speed development."
- **authoring models** — Code-bound, no-code console, intent-based YAML/natural language and AI-generated candidates that a human approves. > "Tests describe user actions, runtime resolves to DOM. Survives most refactors. Authored by engineers OR coding agents."
- **healing posture** — An explicit decision about what happens when a test fails because the UI changed rather than the code. > "When a test fails because the UI changed (not because the code is broken), what happens? Your strategy needs an explicit posture:"
- **PR-time gate** — Unit, integration and E2E for affected flows under ten minutes and blocking, because a nightly-only gate lets bugs land and get reverted. > "If your nightly is blocking but your PR is not, bugs land in main, then get caught after, then get reverted"
- **four coverage metrics** — User-journey reach, coverage decay rate, PR-time verification density and maintenance budget, tracked on one dashboard with rolling four-week trends. > "Track these as a single dashboard with rolling four-week trends. They are the only metrics that tell you whether the strategy is working."
- **shared ownership** — The engineer or coding agent that ships a feature owns its test; a small QA function owns strategy, exploratory testing and policy. > "The engineer (or coding agent) who shipped the feature owns the test for the feature."
- **quarantine** — Tests that fail twice consecutively move out of the suite for weekly review by the QA function. > "A small QA function owns strategy, exploratory testing, quarantine review, and policy."
GUIDELINES:
- Target `> 60%` user-journey reach; `< 2% / week` coverage decay; `> 80%` PR-time verification density; `< 5%` of QA-engineering hours on maintenance (rolling 4-week).
- Gate table: pre-commit unit for touched files (seconds, optional); PR-time unit + integration + E2E (`< 10 minutes`, blocks merge); nightly full E2E (hours, informational); release smoke + critical journeys (`< 15 minutes`, blocks).
- Prefer PR-time blocking over nightly blocking; a nightly-only gate lets bugs land, get caught, then revert.
- Migrate one component per sprint over six sprints: coverage targets → authoring model (new tests only) → healing posture → gates → ownership → scope refresh. "Do not rewrite."
- Review the strategy `quarterly`; archive previous versions in version control; trigger review on tooling change, agent-adoption change or KPI breach.
- Keep E2E co-equal with unit/integration rather than a separate ceremony; expose the testing tool programmatically via MCP so agents can author.
EVIDENCE: none — figures are illustrative throughput claims: agents generate `50+ PRs per week per team` versus QA authoring `5–10 new E2E tests per week`; a suite needing `2 hours/week` of maintenance becoming `20 hours/week` at 10× UI churn; a 9am bug shipping at 5pm under 2am nightly regression ("16-hour latency"); `40–60%` of QA hours going to manual repair.
LIMITS: Vendor blog; performance and ratio figures are un-sourced estimates; the template is "opinionated toward AI-native operating models" and mapped onto Shiplight features.
TOOLING: Shiplight (YAML Test Format, AI Fixer, MCP Server, AI Skills, Cloud runners), GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenAI Codex.
LINKS: AI-native software testing; E2E vs integration testing; coverage decay glossary; agentic QA benchmark; MCP for testing; 30-day agentic E2E playbook; quality gate for AI pull requests.

## A018 · Use Self-Healing Agent for your Appium tests running on BrowserStack App Automate
URL: https://www.browserstack.com/docs/app-automate/appium/self-healing
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: BrowserStack Self-Heal detects a locator that no longer resolves during an Appium run, uses stored element context and AI signals to generate an alternate locator, continues the test and records the change so the healed locator can be pushed back into the script.
CONCEPTS:
- **Self-Heal** — Automatic recovery of failed Appium tests: a locator that stops resolving is replaced so the run continues and the change is recorded. > "Self-Heal automatically detects when a locator no longer works and intelligently finds the right element using historical context and AI signals."
- **element context capture** — Every interaction securely stores the locator, nearby attributes and DOM structure for later matching. > "Each time your test interacts with an element, Self-Heal Agent securely stores key information about that element — including its locator, nearby attributes and the structure of the DOM."
- **healing pipeline** — Detect a broken locator, evaluate the latest success context, generate an alternate healed locator, apply it and continue the run. > "If a locator no longer resolves during a test run, Self-Heal initiates the following process:"
- **elementIdentifier** — The identity used to match a failed locator to a prior success, so it must stay consistent across builds and the success case must run first. > "Self-Heal requires at least one successful test execution with the same elementIdentifier to capture the correct element context."
- **resilient locators as output** — Healed locators are written back into the script so the same failure does not recur; a heal alone keeps only one run green. > "BrowserStack recommends you to replace the locators in your test script with Self-Healed locators to improve the stability of your tests."
- **build-level healing report** — Every healed locator and the reason it was applied, reported per build. > "Every healed locator and the reason it was applied, per build."
- **findElement / findElements healing** — Broken locators in findElement calls are healed, with findElements support offered as beta. > "findElement command healing: Heals broken locators used in findElement commands."
- **MCP and GitHub PR writeback** — A build's healed locators can be applied to test files through the BrowserStack MCP server, or raised as a PR from the report for SDK users. > "If you use BrowserStack SDK, you can raise a GitHub PR directly from the Self-Healing report."
GUIDELINES:
- Enable BrowserStack AI in account settings first; Self-Heal Agent is available only on the **App Automate Pro plan**.
- Set capability `selfHeal: true` in `browserstack.yml` or under `bstack:options`.
- Toggle per execution with the JavaScript executor `browserstack_executor: {"action": "selfHeal", "arguments": {"enabled": true|false}}`; executors work only if `selfHeal: true` is already configured.
- Supported platforms: Android and iOS.
- Guarantee at least one successful execution with the same `elementIdentifier` before healing can work; `.text='Log in'` vs `.text='log in'` will not heal because the identifier differs — run the success case first.
- Replace script locators with the healed versions to improve stability; a heal "keeps a single run green" only.
- Review via build listing → build insights → test listing → text logs (filter to self-healed entries; the filter appears only when `selfHeal` is enabled); fetch build reports via REST API.
EVIDENCE: none — product documentation; no accuracy or recovery-rate figures published.
LIMITS: Some performance overhead from extra analysis during execution; "Not all failures can be healed" (system failures and WebDriver issues still fail); can misfire on negative assertions because it cannot distinguish a changed locator from an intentionally absent element, possibly substituting a similar element — disable Self-Heal before absence assertions and re-enable afterwards.
TOOLING: BrowserStack App Automate, Appium, BrowserStack SDK, JavaScript executors, BrowserStack MCP server, GitHub PRs, REST API (`get-self-healing-report`).
LINKS: BrowserStack AI activation docs; JS executors docs; MCP server overview; self-heal demo repo (testng-appium-app); test-reporting API reference.

## A019 · Use AI Self-Heal for your Playwright tests running on BrowserStack Automate
URL: https://www.browserstack.com/docs/automate/playwright/self-healing
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: BrowserStack Self-Healing recovers Playwright tests whose locators stop resolving by matching against stored element context and AI signals, then lets teams write the healed locator back into the script via MCP or an auto-generated GitHub PR.
CONCEPTS:
- **Self-Healing** — Automatic recovery of failed Playwright tests whose locators stop resolving, with a record of what changed to reduce false failures. > "Self-Healing automatically detects when a locator no longer works and intelligently finds the right element using historical context and AI signals."
- **stored element context** — The locator, nearby attributes and DOM structure saved at each interaction and reused when a locator breaks. > "Each time your test interacts with an element, Self-Healing Agent securely stores key information about that element — including its locator, nearby attributes and the structure of the DOM."
- **healing sequence** — Detect a broken locator, evaluate the latest success context, generate an alternate healed locator, then apply it and continue. > "During future test runs, if the original locator no longer resolves, Self-Healing steps in and the following process takes place:"
- **elementIdentifier consistency** — Success and failure runs must share the identifier, and the success case must run first, before healing can work. > "Self-Heal requires at least one successful test execution with the same elementIdentifier to capture the correct element context."
- **resilient locator output** — Healed locators are reusable in later runs and are meant to replace the script's original locators for stability. > "BrowserStack recommends you to replace the locators in your test script with self-healed locators to improve the stability of your tests."
- **build-level healing report** — A per-build record of every healed locator and the reason it was applied. > "Every healed locator and the reason it was applied, per build."
- **writeback paths** — Healed locators go back into test files through the BrowserStack MCP server, or as a GitHub PR raised from the report for SDK users. > "If you use BrowserStack SDK, you can raise a GitHub PR directly from the Self-Healing report."
- **Beta scope** — Playwright self-healing runs in limited capacity and does not cover all Selenium capabilities; findElements healing is beta. > "Self-Heal for Playwright is presently in limited capacity and does not support all the feature capabilities as Selenium"
GUIDELINES:
- Enable BrowserStack AI preferences; Self-Healing Agent requires the **Automate Pro plan**.
- Set `selfHeal: true` in `browserstack.yml` or under `bstack:options`.
- Supported browsers: Desktop Chrome `v126 and above`, Edge `v126 and above`, and all Playwright-bundled Chromium browsers.
- Do not use incognito mode: "AI Self Heal feature will not work on your Chrome tests if you have set the browser to operate in incognito mode."
- Toggle at runtime with `browserstack_executor: {"action": "selfHeal", "arguments": {"enabled": true|false}}`; executors require `selfHeal: true` in config.
- Run one successful execution per `elementIdentifier` before relying on healing; ensure the success case runs first.
- Replace script locators with healed ones; inspect healed entries via the Text Logs filter (available only when `selfHeal` is enabled) and the Build Insights widgets.
EVIDENCE: none — product documentation; no measured recovery or false-failure rates.
LIMITS: Performance overhead is "usually small" but healing "should complement — not replace — good test design and error handling"; system failures, WebDriver issues and genuinely removed elements still fail; Playwright Self-Heal is limited in capacity and does not support all Selenium capabilities; no support in incognito mode.
TOOLING: BrowserStack Automate, Playwright, BrowserStack SDK, JavaScript executors, BrowserStack MCP server, GitHub PRs.
LINKS: BrowserStack AI activation docs; self-heal demo repo (playwright branch); Selenium self-healing docs; Playwright REST API reference; capabilities generator.

# Batch ar03 — self-healing locators and LLM unit-test generation

## A020 · Use Self-Healing Agent for your Cypress tests running on BrowserStack Automate
URL: http://www.browserstack.com/docs/automate/cypress/self-healing
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: BrowserStack Self-Heal automatically detects a locator that no longer resolves in Cypress tests and substitutes an AI-derived resilient locator so the run continues instead of failing.
CONCEPTS:
- **`Self-Heal`** — BrowserStack recovers a test whose locator no longer resolves, substituting an element found from historical context and AI signals, and records what changed. > "Self-Heal automatically detects when a locator no longer works and intelligently finds the right element using historical context and AI signals."
- **`findElement` command healing** — heals broken locators used in `findElement` calls; the Cypress page lists this as the only command-level healing feature. > "`findElement` command healing: Heals broken locators used in `findElement` commands."
- **Resilient locators as output** — the heal is not just applied, it is emitted so future runs can reuse it. > "Resilient locators as output: Healed locators you can reuse in future runs."
- **`elementIdentifier`** — the key that ties a failing interaction to an earlier successful one; healing needs at least one recorded success with the same identifier. > "Self-Heal requires at least one successful test execution with the same `elementIdentifier` to capture the correct element context."
- **Healing pipeline** — a broken locator starts a sequence: detect, evaluate the latest success context, generate an alternate, apply and continue. > "If a locator no longer resolves during a test run, Self-Heal initiates the following process:"
- **Build-level healing report** — every build records each healed locator together with the reason it was applied. > "Every healed locator and the reason it was applied, per build."
- **Script maintenance via `MCP` or GitHub PR** — healed locators are pushed back into the test files instead of staying in the report. > "Apply healed locators to your test script directly through MCP, or create a GitHub PR for SDK users."
- **Text Logs filter** — narrows the log view to self-healed entries only, and appears only when healing is on for the session. > "The **Text Log** filter will only be available if `selfHeal` is enabled for your test session."
- **False-failure reduction** — the stated purpose is fewer false failures and green builds while the UI changes. > "BrowserStack recovers the test and records what changed - reducing false failures and keeping builds green as the UI evolves."

GUIDELINES:
- Set `browserstack.selfHeal` to `true` under `run_settings` in `browserstack.json`.
- Requires BrowserStack AI enabled on the account; Self-Heal Agent is "available only on **Automate Pro plan**".
- "Self-Heal is currently enabled only for Cypress v15.8. Newer Cypress versions do not have Self-Heal enabled by default" — contact support to enable elsewhere.
- Use consistent `elementIdentifier` values across successful and failed builds; run the success case first so element context is registered.
- Replace script locators with healed locators, via `MCP`/BrowserStack MCP server or "Raise Pull Request" from the report, to prevent recurrence — "A heal keeps a single run green."
- Use when flaky `NoSuchElement` failures are common or UI refactors are frequent.
EVIDENCE: none (product documentation).
LIMITS:
- "Some Performance overhead" — healing adds analysis during execution; small but "should complement, not replace, good test design and error handling".
- Not all failures healable: system failures and WebDriver issues fail as expected.
- "Can misfire on negative assertions" — Self-Heal cannot distinguish a changed locator from an intentionally absent element, so it may substitute a similar generic element and fail the check.
TOOLING: BrowserStack Automate, Cypress v15.8, `browserstack.json`, BrowserStack SDK, BrowserStack MCP server, REST self-healing report API.
LINKS: BrowserStack Self-Heal for Selenium; BrowserStack AI preferences activation; BrowserStack MCP server overview; self-healing report REST API.

## A021 · Use Self-Healing Agent for your Selenium tests running on BrowserStack Automate (self-healing-old, WebdriverIO)
URL: https://www.browserstack.com/docs/automate/selenium/self-healing-old?fw-lang=nodejs%2Fwebdriverio
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: Same Self-Heal mechanism documented for Selenium on Automate, adding `findElements` healing (beta), a browser/platform support matrix, and JavaScript-executor toggles.
CONCEPTS:
- **`selfHeal` capability** — boolean capability in the test configuration that turns healing on, set in `browserstack.yml` for SDK users or under `bstack:options` otherwise. > "To enable the Self-Heal feature, set the `selfHeal` capability to `true` in your test configuration file."
- **`findElement` and `findElements` healing** — the plural command is covered as a beta extension of single-element healing. > "`findElement` command healing: Heals broken locators used in `findElement` commands."
- **`selfHeal` JavaScript executors** — enable or disable healing inside a test run, but only if the configuration already enabled it. > "JavaScript executors work only when your configuration includes `selfHeal: true` in YAML or under `bstack:options` in your capabilities."
- **Historical element context** — at every interaction the agent stores the locator, nearby attributes and DOM structure. > "Each time your test interacts with an element, Self-Heal Agent securely stores key information about that element — including its locator, nearby attributes and the structure of the DOM."
- **Healing pipeline** — on a failed resolution the agent applies its last-success context to build a replacement locator and keeps running. > "During future test runs, if the original locator no longer resolves, Self-Heal steps in and the following process takes place:"
- **Healing report and Text Logs filter** — per-build record of what healed and why, surfaced through the self-heal icon and log filter. > "Every healed locator and the reason it was applied, per build."
- **Script maintenance via MCP or GitHub PR** — SDK users can feed healed locators back into the test script. > "Apply healed locators to your test script directly through MCP, or create a GitHub PR for SDK users."

GUIDELINES:
- Set `selfHeal` capability to `true` in the test configuration file.
- "AI Self-Heal feature will not work on your Chrome tests if you have set the browser to operate in incognito mode."
- Executors "work only when your configuration includes `selfHeal: true` in YAML or under `bstack:options`".
- Supported desktop browsers: Chrome v92 and above, Firefox v72 and above, Edge v92 and above.
- Supported mobile: iOS — "All browsers except Safari", minimum iOS 14; Android — all browsers.
- Requires BrowserStack AI enabled; Self-Heal Agent only on **Automate Pro plan**.
- Keep `elementIdentifier` consistent between passing and failing tests, and run the success case first; example: `.text='Log in'` vs `.text='log in'` prevents healing.
- Replace script locators with healed locators to improve stability.
EVIDENCE: none (product documentation).
LIMITS:
- Performance overhead from extra analysis during execution.
- Non-healable: system failures, WebDriver issues, "and situations where the element truly no longer exists cannot be recovered. These tests will (correctly) fail."
- Beta status of `findElements` healing.
TOOLING: BrowserStack Automate, Selenium, WebdriverIO/Node.js, BrowserStack SDK (`browserstack.yml`), JavaScript executors, MCP server, REST API.
LINKS: Automate sample repo `browserstack/selfheal-demo-browserstack` (testng-appium-app branch); BrowserStack AI activation docs; self-healing report API reference.

## A022 · Use Self-Healing Agent for your Appium tests running on BrowserStack App Automate
URL: https://www.browserstack.com/docs/app-automate/appium/self-healing?fw-lang=nodejs
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: Self-Heal applied to Appium mobile tests on App Automate, with the same capture-heal-record loop plus explicit guidance to disable healing around negative assertions.
CONCEPTS:
- **`Self-Heal`** — detects a locator that no longer works and finds the right element from history plus AI signals, so the test continues instead of failing. > "Self-Heal automatically detects when a locator no longer works and intelligently finds the right element using historical context and AI signals."
- **`selfHeal` capability** — enabled in the test configuration file, whether through the SDK or a non-SDK integration. > "To enable the Self-Heal feature, set the `selfHeal` capability to `true` in your test configuration file."
- **`findElement` and `findElements` healing** — single-element healing is the base feature, with `findElements` as its beta extension. > "`findElement` command healing: Heals broken locators used in `findElement` commands."
- **`selfHeal` JavaScript executors** — runtime enable/disable inside a test, valid only when the config already set `selfHeal: true`. > "JavaScript executors work only when your configuration includes `selfHeal: true` in YAML or under `bstack:options` in your capabilities."
- **Element context capture** — locator, nearby attributes and DOM structure are stored per interaction and later read as the latest success context. > "Each time your test interacts with an element, Self-Heal Agent securely stores key information about that element — including its locator, nearby attributes and the structure of the DOM."

## A024 · Reduce test maintenance and flaky tests | Katalon Studio
URL: https://www.katalon.com/test-maintenance-flaky-tests
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: Flaky tests come from a small set of causes (UI change, timing, environment noise, real bugs) and each cause needs its own fix; Katalon Studio pairs self-healing with Smart Wait, object repository, retries, and evidence capture, and nothing changes in tests until a fix is approved.
CONCEPTS:
- **Cause-matched remediation** — flakiness is treated as a handful of distinct causes, each with its own countermeasure rather than a rerun. > "Most flaky tests come from a few causes: locators that break when the UI changes, timing issues where an element isn't ready yet, test data or environment differences between runs, and shared state between tests."
- **`Object repository`** — locators are stored centrally so a single fix propagates to every test using them. > "Locators live in the object repository, so one fix reaches every test."
- **`Classic self-healing`** — falls back through the remaining locators in the author-defined order. > "Classic self-healing tries your other locators in the order you set."
- **`AI self-healing`** — runs only when every locator fails, reading page source, accessibility tree and screenshots. > "If they all fail, AI self-healing looks at the page source, accessibility tree, and screenshots to find the element."
- **`Smart Wait`** — synchronises on loading, visibility, animation and editability before each web step instead of fixed sleeps. > "Smart Wait waits for page loading, visibility, animations, and editability on web before each step."
- **`Self-healing Insights`** — proposals are queued for approval; the run may proceed on the alternative but nothing permanent changes until approved. > "The run can continue on an alternative locator, but the permanent change waits in Self-healing Insights."
- **Retry failed executions** — reruns are a configured policy, applied immediately or after the whole run. > "Retry failed executions immediately or after the whole run, and run in the same setup every time with the Katalon Docker Image or Test Cloud."
- **Environment pinning** — the same image or cloud browsers every run to remove local-versus-CI drift. > "Most “fails in CI, passes locally” failures come from environment drift. Pin it with a container, or let Test Cloud supply the browsers."
- **`Probabilistic Flakiness Score`** — computed from pass-to-fail patterns across run history in Katalon True Platform. > "It calculates a Probabilistic Flakiness Score from pass-to-fail patterns in your test history, so you can see which tests are unstable."
- **Evidence at point of failure** — screenshots and video are attached to failures and routed to Jira or Slack. > "Evidence at the point of failure, plus a flakiness score with True Platform"

GUIDELINES:
- Self-healing setup: (1) switch on self-healing for Web UI or Mobile in project settings; (2) "Order your locator methods (XPath, Attributes, CSS, Image, Smart Locator), most stable first"; (3) for AI self-healing, enable Execution Viewer and choose an AI model or use your own API key.
- Separately configure Web UI and Mobile self-healing.
- Run suites from any CI via `Katalon Runtime Engine` with retry rules applied on every run.
- Use `Smart Wait` instead of sleeps; use retries to separate one-off failures from real ones.
- Don't apply self-healing as a general fix: "It won't fix a timing issue, bad test data, or a real bug."
- Free plan includes object repository, Smart Wait, reports; self-healing, retries, AI self-healing are paid; True Platform is a separate product.
- Optional no-AI path: "Classic self-healing and Smart Wait use no AI."
EVIDENCE: none; claims are qualitative ("Trusted by 30,000+ quality teams", G2 **4.5**).
LIMITS:
- Self-healing scope limited to locator changes; timing, data, and real bugs need other mechanisms.
- Flakiness scoring requires the separate Katalon True Platform.
- Page is marketing copy (updated September 2026); no measurements given.
TOOLING: Katalon Studio, object repository, Smart Wait, AI self-healing, Self-healing Insights, Katalon Runtime Engine, Katalon Docker Image, Test Cloud, Katalon True Platform, integrations (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Azure DevOps, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Jira, Slack).
LINKS: Katalon docs "Self-healing tests in Katalon Studio"; blog posts on financial risk of flaky tests and flaky tests in test automation; Katalon AI features; Test Cloud.

## A025 · Self-healing tests in Katalon Studio | Katalon Docs
URL: https://docs.katalon.com/katalon-studio/maintain-tests/self-healing-tests-in-katalon-studio
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: Katalon Studio heals broken object locators in two stages — classic fallback through the project's other locator methods, then LLM-based AI self-healing over page source, accessibility tree and screenshots — with every proposal queued for human approval.
CONCEPTS:
- **`Classic self-healing`** — when the original locator fails, the other known locators for that object are tried, and the one that works is suggested as the replacement. > "When Katalon Studio can no longer locate a test object using the original locator, it triggers self-healing, trying other known locators associated with that object."
- **`AI self-healing`** — triggered only after classic healing fails, an LLM reads page source, accessibility tree and screenshots to propose an alternative locator. > "If none of the existing locators can recover the object through classic self-healing, Katalon Studio then moves to AI self-healing."
- **Locator priority** — methods are evaluated in the configured order, top down. > "Katalon Studio tries to generate the object locator with the method at the top first. If it fails, it will try alternative methods, from the top down."
- **Default locator strategies** — the strategy used when recording or spying is chosen per project type. > "Choose a default locator strategy: XPath (default), Attributes, CSS, Image, and Smart Locator"
- **Attribute-based locators** — selecting Attributes as default exposes the set of HTML attributes considered during detection. > "If you select Attributes as the default locator, you can configure attribute-based locators to specify which HTML attributes should be considered when detecting objects."
- **`Exclude keywords`** — objects used with a listed keyword skip healing entirely, which is how absence checks keep failing as expected. > "Katalon Studio allows you to exclude specific keywords from self-healing. When an object is used with one of these keywords, Katalon Studio skips the self-healing process."
- **Auto-excluded keywords** — `Verify*` and `Wait*` keywords are excluded from classic self-healing by default. > "The following keywords are automatically excluded from classic self-healing by default."
- **`Locator Override in Object view`** — a per-object selection method that overrides the global self-healing settings. > "In the locator selection setting for each object, you can decide the default selection method for detecting that object during execution. This configuration overrides the Self-Healing global settings."
- **`Self-healing Insights`** — a table of proposals with test object, broken and proposed locator, recovery method and screenshot; Approve makes it the default, Discard rejects it. > "Next to the Log Viewer tab, the Self-healing Insights tab displays a table containing suggestions for replacing broken locators, from either classic self-healing or AI self-healing."
- **Smart XPath** — when a screenshot locates the object, the proposal is a generated smart XPath. > "If the object was found using its screenshot, this value is a newly generated smart XPath."
- **Failure handling** — if both mechanisms fail, execution stops or continues per the configured option. > "If both fail to detect the test object, Katalon Studio may stop or continue, depending on the failure handling option you have configured."

GUIDELINES:
- Requires an active Katalon Studio license; AI self-healing additionally requires `Execution Viewer` enabled in `Project Settings > Execution`.
- Prioritize "attributes that are consistently used and unique (e.g., `id`, `name`)"; avoid dynamic values like `class` if they frequently change.
- "**XPath** is flexible but can be fragile in dynamic DOMs. **CSS** and **Smart Locator** may offer better resilience." Move the most stable/unique locators higher.
- Add `verifyElementPresent` to the exclusion list to keep absence checks failing as expected (worked example with `input_Username_username`).
- "Enabling Self-Healing for `Wait` and `Verify` keywords may lead to false positives and test flakiness. We recommend applying this capability only to interaction steps."
- More AI input sources "increases healing accuracy but may slightly increase processing time and cost"; Screenshots cost more than Accessibility tree or Page source.
- Model config: default falls back to `gpt-4o-mini`; set `SELF_HEALING_AI_MODEL` and `OPENAI_API_KEY` via `System.setProperty` using Global Variables in a test case or test listener; alternative `-DOPENAI_API_KEY=${{ YOUR_API_KEY }}` in Launch Arguments "risks exposing your OpenAI API key".
- Approve or discard each suggestion after verifying the captured screenshot.
EVIDENCE: none (product documentation).
LIMITS:
- "AI self-healing might have issues finding the element with the image locator."
- Unapproved Smart Locator suggestions from 9.3.1 are not visible when the project is opened in earlier versions.
- Model input breadth trades accuracy against processing time/cost.
- Known error `java.io.IOException` — `The filename or extension is too long` when the Katalon Studio path is too deep; fix by relocating to a higher-level directory.
TOOLING: Katalon Studio, Self-healing Insights, Execution Viewer, Global Variables, test listeners, AI Configurations, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `SELF_HEALING_AI_MODEL`, `gpt-4o-mini`.
LINKS: `katalon-studio/self-healing-demo` GitHub sample project; Katalon Academy "Self-Healing Mechanism in Test Automation"; Failure Handling docs; Selection methods for Web objects.

## A026 · Use AI self-heal for your Selenium tests running on BrowserStack Automate self-hosted
URL: https://www.browserstack.com/docs/automate-self-hosted/selenium/self-healing
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: Self-heal for self-hosted Automate monitors the DOM at runtime, logs the DOM path of successfully found elements, and regenerates locators for changed elements from those past references.
CONCEPTS:
- **`self-heal`** — described as automatic recovery from locator changes or poor locator strategies while tests execute. > "BrowserStack’s self-heal feature for automated tests enables automatic recovery from locator changes or sub-optimal locator strategies during test execution."
- **DOM monitoring** — the page is watched at runtime for changes to the document object model. > "During runtime, it continuously monitors the web page to detect changes in the Document Object Model (DOM)."
- **DOM path logging** — a successful lookup records the element's DOM path for later comparison. > "Once an element is successfully located on the page, its DOM path is logged for future reference."
- **`elementIdentifier` matching** — healing requires a prior success under the same identifier. > "Self-healing requires at least one successful test execution with the same `elementIdentifier` to capture the correct element context."
- **`Healed` filter** — builds and sessions can be filtered to the self-healed subset. > "You can filter the self-healed builds using the builds filter and selecting the **Healed** option under **Self-Healing** dropdown."
- **Text Logs filter** — shows only healed-locator entries, and only when `selfHeal` was enabled. > "The **Text Log** filter will only be available if `selfHeal` is enabled for your test session."
- **Claimed advantages** — stability, adaptivity and less manual script upkeep. > "BrowserStack’s self-heal feature automatically adjusts scripts, reducing manual intervention, time, and resource usage."

GUIDELINES:
- Set `selfHeal` capability to `true` in the test configuration; for SDK users add capabilities in `browserstack.yml`.
- Supported browsers: Chrome v92 and above, Firefox v72 and above, Edge v92 and above.
- Keep `elementIdentifier` values consistent across builds and run the success case first (same `.text='Log in'` vs `.text='log in'` example).
- Replace script locators with self-healed locators "to improve the stability of your tests".
- To use AI for self-healing, activate BrowserStack AI preferences.
- "Always review logs carefully to understand why tests require healing."
EVIDENCE: none (product documentation; no measurements).
LIMITS:
- Feature "is currently in beta".
- "Performance: Enabling self-heal may slightly impact test execution time due to additional checks and recovery mechanisms."
- "Non-recoverable errors: Self-heal cannot recover from specific errors, such as WebDriver initialization failures or system-level issues."
- "Test accuracy: Self-heal reduces test inconsistency but can mask genuine problems in your web application or scripts."
- Self-heal "is intended to complement good test design and error handling practices, not replace them."
TOOLING: BrowserStack Automate self-hosted, Selenium, BrowserStack SDK (`browserstack.yml`), Text Logs, builds/sessions filters.
LINKS: BrowserStack AI preferences activation docs; contact page for beta issues.

## A027 · How well LLM-based test generation techniques perform with newer LLM versions? (ICST 2026)
URL: https://www.computer.org/csdl/proceedings-article/icst/2026/330800a233/2iat1rHIAUM
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: LLM test-generation techniques were benchmarked against weak baselines (old models, weak prompts), so the authors replicate four state-of-the-art tools with current LLMs and find a plain LLM approach beats them on every effectiveness metric at comparable cost.
CONCEPTS:
- **`plain LLM` test generation** — direct prompting with no engineering scaffolding, used as the reference method the tooling must beat on both effectiveness and efficiency. > "evaluate their relative effectiveness and efficiency over a plain LLM test generation method"
- **Weak-baseline critique** — earlier evaluations compared against old models and weak prompts, which inflates the apparent contribution of the engineering on top. > "LLM-based test generation techniques have been evaluated against relatively weak baselines (for todays’ standards), i.e., old LLM versions and relatively weak prompts, which may exacerbate the performance contribution of the approaches."
- **Compilation/execution feedback** — the guidance components inside the replicated tools work by feeding compilation and execution feedback back into generation. > "include engineering components aimed at guiding the test generation process through compilation and execution feedback"
- **Replicated tools** — four tools are reimplemented rather than trusted as reported. > "We investigate this issue by replicating four state-of-the-art LLM-based test generation tools, HITS, SymPrompt, TestSpark, and CoverUp"
- **Effectiveness metrics** — line coverage, branch coverage and mutation score, all reported together. > "in all test effectiveness metrics we used: line coverage (by 17.72%), branch coverage (by 19.80%) and mutation score (by 20.92%)"
- **Efficiency metric** — cost is counted in LLM queries, so a gain only counts if it is not bought with more calls. > "and it does so at a comparable cost (LLM queries)"
- **Generation granularity** — whether the model is asked per class or per method materially changes the bill. > "We also observe that the granularity at which the plain LLM is applied has a significant impact on the cost."
- **Class-first strategy** — generate for classes first, then target the still-uncovered methods. > "We therefore propose targeting first the program classes, where test generation is more efficient, and then the uncovered methods to reduce the number of LLM requests."
- **Standalone-LLM insufficiency** — raw model output without post-processing often does not compile or cover much. > "the standalone use of LLMs without post-processing has proven insufficient, often producing tests that fail to compile or achieve high coverage."

GUIDELINES:
- Evaluate LLM test-generation techniques against current-generation models and strong prompts, not older models or weak prompts.
- Report both effectiveness (line, branch, mutation) and efficiency (LLM queries) so cost/benefit is visible.
- Prefer class-level generation first, then target uncovered methods to cut LLM requests (~20% fewer requests at comparable, slightly higher effectiveness).
- Do not assume scaffolding tools retain an advantage when the underlying model is upgraded; re-benchmark after model upgrades.
EVIDENCE:
- Experiment on **393 classes** and **3,657 methods**.
- Plain LLM outperformed prior state of the art on all effectiveness metrics: line coverage **by 17.72%**, branch coverage **by 19.80%**, mutation score **by 20.92%**.
- Cost was "comparable (LLM queries)".
- Class-first-then-uncovered-methods strategy: comparable (slightly higher) effectiveness with **about 20% fewer LLM requests**.
LIMITS:
- Abstract does not state the specific LLM versions, benchmark subject systems, or statistical tests; those details are in the paper body (paywalled at the source).
- Comparison is limited to four replicated tools plus a plain-LLM baseline.
- Coverage and mutation score are proxies for test quality; the abstract does not report defect-detection or developer-judgment studies.
TOOLING: `HITS`, `SymPrompt`, `TestSpark`, `CoverUp`; LLM query accounting.
LINKS: DOI 10.1109/ICST69053.2026.00040; ICST 2026 proceedings (pages 233–243); authors Michael Konstantinou, Renzo Degiovanni, Mike Papadakis (SnT University of Luxembourg / Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology); related: ASE 2024 "LLMs and Prompting for Unit Test Generation: A Large-Scale Evaluation", "ASTER", "Test Intention Guided LLM-Based Unit Test Generation".

## A028 · [2601.09695] How well LLM-based test generation techniques perform with newer LLM versions? (arXiv)
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.09695
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Same study as the ICST 2026 record — replication of four LLM test-generation tools with current LLM versions shows a plain LLM approach wins on all effectiveness metrics at comparable query cost.
CONCEPTS:
- **`plain LLM` comparison baseline** — direct prompting is the reference point, and both effectiveness and efficiency are measured against it. > "evaluate their relative effectiveness and efficiency over a plain LLM test generation method"
- **Four replicated tools** — earlier work is reimplemented with current models instead of cited. > "We investigate this issue by replicating four state-of-the-art LLM-based test generation tools, HITS, SymPrompt, TestSpark, and CoverUp"
- **Compilation/execution feedback components** — the scaffolding the replicated tools add is feedback-driven guidance of generation. > "include engineering components aimed at guiding the test generation process through compilation and execution feedback"
- **Effectiveness metric set** — line coverage, branch coverage and mutation score are taken together. > "in all test effectiveness metrics we used: line coverage (by 17.72%), branch coverage (by 19.80%) and mutation score (by 20.92%)"
- **Cost accounting in LLM queries** — efficiency is reported as request count against the plain method. > "and it does so at a comparable cost (LLM queries)"
- **Granularity effect** — applying the same model at class or method level changes cost significantly. > "We also observe that the granularity at which the plain LLM is applied has a significant impact on the cost."
- **Two-stage targeting** — classes first, then only the uncovered methods, to cut request count. > "We therefore propose targeting first the program classes, where test generation is more efficient, and then the uncovered methods to reduce the number of LLM requests."
- **Post-processing need** — tests that neither compile nor cover code are the failure mode the tooling claims to fix. > "the standalone use of LLMs without post-processing has proven insufficient, often producing tests that fail to compile or achieve high coverage."

GUIDELINES:
- Integrate current LLM versions into every compared approach before comparing; otherwise results reflect model vintage.
- Replicate rather than trust reported numbers, because earlier baselines used weak prompts and old models.
- Budget queries, not just coverage: report per-technique request counts alongside coverage and mutation score.
- Apply plain LLM generation at class granularity first, then method-level generation for uncovered methods.
EVIDENCE:
- **393 classes**, **3,657 methods**.
- Plain LLM gains: line coverage **17.72%**, branch coverage **19.80%**, mutation score **20.92%** higher, "at a comparable cost (LLM queries)".
- Class-first strategy: comparable (slightly higher) effectiveness, **about 20% fewer LLM requests**.
LIMITS:
- This page is the arXiv abstract only; no full text, tables, subject-project list, LLM version list, or threat discussion is included.
- Two versions exist: v1 submitted 14 Jan 2026; v2 revised 29 Jul 2026 (183 KB).
- Findings cover four replicated tools; generality to other pipelines is not established in the abstract.
TOOLING: `HITS`, `SymPrompt`, `TestSpark`, `CoverUp`; LLM query accounting.
LINKS: arXiv:2601.09695v2 (cs.SE, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2601.09695), CC BY 4.0; PDF, HTML (experimental), TeX source; ICST 2026 version.

## A029 · An Empirical Evaluation of Using Large Language Models for Automated Unit Test Generation
URL: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10329992
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Prompting an LLM with a function's signature, implementation and documentation usage examples — plus re-prompting with the failing test and error message — generates JavaScript unit tests that substantially exceed a feedback-directed search tool's coverage without model training or few-shot learning.
CONCEPTS:
- **Zero-training prompting** — no extra training and no few-shot examples of existing tests are required. > "This paper presents a large-scale empirical evaluation on the effectiveness of LLMs for automated unit test generation without requiring additional training or manual effort."
- **Prompt contents** — the model receives the function's signature, its implementation, and usage examples mined from documentation. > "the LLM is provided with prompts that include the signature and implementation of a function under test, along with usage examples extracted from documentation."
- **Iterative repair via re-prompting** — a failing test is not thrown away; it is fed back with its error message to request a fixed version. > "if a generated test fails, our approach attempts to generate a new test that fixes the problem by re-prompting the model with the failing test and error message."
- **`TestPilot`** — the adaptive tool that generates JavaScript unit tests for the methods of a project's API. > "We implement our approach in TestPilot, an adaptive LLM-based test generation tool for JavaScript that automatically generates unit tests for the methods in a given project's API."
- **Coverage metrics** — median statement and branch coverage per project are the reported effectiveness measures. > "The generated tests achieve a median statement coverage of 70.2% and branch coverage of 52.8%."
- **Feedback-directed baseline** — `Nessie` is the search-based comparator the LLM approach is measured against. > "In contrast, the state-of-the feedback-directed JavaScript test generation technique, Nessie, achieves only 51.3% statement coverage and 25.6% branch coverage."
- **Prompt-ablation analysis** — dropping any prompt component degrades the result, so all parts are load-bearing. > "experiments with excluding parts of the information included in the prompts show that all components contribute towards the generation of effective test suites."
- **Novelty measurement** — similarity to existing tests is quantified by normalized edit distance rather than eyeballed. > "92.8% of TestPilot's generated tests have ≤ 50% similarity with existing tests (as measured by normalized edit distance), with none of them being exact copies."

GUIDELINES:
- Prompt with signature + implementation + documentation-derived usage examples; each component contributes, so do not drop usage examples.
- Re-prompt with the failing test plus the error message instead of discarding failed generations.
- Evaluate at API level across whole projects, not single functions, to measure realistic coverage.
- Unless stated otherwise the paper's configuration uses few-shot learning on existing tests — avoid that requirement by design (this work needs none).
- Report median statement and branch coverage, and always compare against a search-based baseline (`Nessie`).
- Measure test similarity (normalized edit distance) to check outputs are not copies of existing tests.
EVIDENCE:
- Model: OpenAI `gpt3.5-turbo`; corpus: **25 npm packages**, **1,684 API functions**.
- TestPilot: median statement coverage **70.2%**, branch coverage **52.8%**.
- `Nessie`: **51.3%** statement coverage, **25.6%** branch coverage.
- **92.8%** of generated tests have ≤ **50%** similarity with existing tests by normalized edit distance; none were exact copies.
- Additional runs with OpenAI `code-cushman-002` and `StarCoder` (reported after the truncated point of the abstract).
LIMITS:
- Published abstract as captured is truncated mid-sentence in the additional-LLM discussion; the paper lists a "Threats to Validity" section but its content is behind the paywall here.
- Single language (JavaScript) and npm package subject set.
- Coverage and similarity are proxies; the abstract does not report mutation score or fault detection.
TOOLING: `TestPilot`, OpenAI `gpt3.5-turbo`, `code-cushman-002`, `StarCoder`, `Nessie`; JavaScript/npm; normalized edit distance.
LINKS: IEEE TSE vol. 50, issue 1 (January 2024), pages 85–105, DOI 10.1109/TSE.2023.3334955, published 28 November 2023; authors Max Schäfer, Sarah Nadi, Aryaz Eghbali, Frank Tip; sections I. Introduction, II. Approach, III. Research Questions and Evaluation Setup, IV. Evaluation Results, V. Threats to Validity.

## A030 · Evaluating LLM-Based Test Generation Under Software Evolution
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23443
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: LLM-generated unit tests largely reproduce surface-level patterns rather than reason about program behavior, so their coverage and pass rates collapse when the program evolves — even under semantics-preserving edits.
CONCEPTS:
- **semantic-altering changes (SAC)** — program mutations that change behavior, used as a probe for whether tests encode real expectations; the study varies them deliberately to see how newly generated suites respond. > "we analyze how generated tests react to semantic-altering changes (SAC) and semantic-preserving changes (SPC) across eight LLMs and 22,374 program variants"
- **semantic-preserving changes (SPC)** — refactorings that keep functionality identical, used to separate sensitivity to lexical/syntactic form from sensitivity to semantics; the author expects them not to matter. > "Performance also declines under SPCs despite unchanged functionality: pass rates fall to 79% and branch coverage to 69%."
- **mutation-driven framework** — an automated harness that produces program variants and re-runs generation on each, so the same generator is measured against a moving target. > "Using an automated mutation-driven framework, we analyze how generated tests react to semantic-altering changes"
- **residual alignment** — a failing test under SAC that still passes on the original program while executing the modified region, which shows the test still encodes the old behavior rather than the new one. > "More than 99% of failing SAC tests pass on the original program while executing the modified region, indicating residual alignment with the original behavior rather than adaptation to updated semantics."
- **regression awareness** — a suite's ability to keep detecting the behavior it was written for after the code changes; the author treats its loss as the core failure mode. > "current LLM-based test generation relies heavily on surface-level cues and struggles to maintain regression awareness as programs evolve"
- **baseline tests** — the tests generated on the original program, tracked to see whether later generations discard them in favour of fresh ones. > "Models generate more new tests while discarding many baseline tests, suggesting sensitivity to lexical changes rather than true semantic impact."
- **surface-level cues** — lexical or naming signals the model keys on instead of reasoning about semantics, which the author offers as the explanation for the observed degradation. > "our results indicate that current LLM-based test generation relies heavily on surface-level cues"
- **instability** — suite-to-suite variation in pass/fail caused by edits that do not change functionality, which the author attributes to the larger syntactic footprint of SPC edits. > "Although SPC edits preserve semantics, they often introduce larger syntactic changes, leading to instability in generated test suites."
GUIDELINES:
- When evaluating generated tests, judge them on evolved variants, not only on the original program: `SAC` and `SPC` must both be exercised.
- Measure `pass rate` and `branch coverage` separately on original, SAC, and SPC versions.
- Track test churn (how many baseline tests are discarded and how many new tests are emitted) as a signal of lexical sensitivity.
- Treat a test that still passes on the original program while covering the modified region as evidence of stale semantics, not of correctness.
EVIDENCE: Eight LLMs and 22,374 program variants. Baseline: `79%` line coverage and `76%` branch coverage with fully passing suites on original programs. Under SACs pass rate drops to `66%` and branch coverage to `60%`; "More than 99% of failing SAC tests pass on the original program while executing the modified region." Under SPCs pass rate falls to `79%` and branch coverage to `69%`. Models generate more new tests while discarding many baseline tests.
LIMITS: The extracted text is the arXiv abstract page only; no method section, threats-to-validity discussion, or per-model breakdown was available in the source.
TOOLING: Automated mutation-driven framework (unnamed in available text).
LINKS: none named in available text.

## A031 · Large Language Models for Unit Test Generation: Achievements, Challenges, and Opportunities
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.21382
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: A systematic review of 178 publications shows LLM test generation is best organized as a lifecycle of construction (context, prefix, oracle) plus quality assurance, where context enrichment and execution-feedback repair fix executability but leave oracle correctness, fault detection, benchmark validity, maintainability, and industrial reliability open.
CONCEPTS:
- **test prefix** — the artifact component that establishes objects, inputs and calls needed to exercise the code under test. > "a test prefix, which establishes objects, inputs, and calls needed to exercise the code under test (CUT)"
- **test oracle** — the artifact component that encodes expected behavior, usually through assertions rather than through execution success. > "a test oracle, which encodes expected behavior, commonly through assertions"
- **lifecycle-oriented taxonomy** — the review's organizing frame, splitting a generation phase that produces test artifacts from a quality-assurance phase that validates and refines them. > "it distinguishes a generation phase that produces test artifacts from a quality assurance and enhancement phase that validates and refines them"
- **SBST** — search-based testing frames generation as optimization, evolving test sets to maximize a fitness function that is usually a coverage metric. > "It employs metaheuristic algorithms, such as genetic algorithms, to evolve a set of test cases that maximize a fitness function, which is typically a code coverage metric like branch coverage"
- **symbolic/concolic execution** — solving collected path constraints to produce inputs; the author names path explosion as its principal scalability limit. > "Its principal scalability challenge is path explosion: the number of feasible paths can grow rapidly with program size, making exhaustive exploration computationally infeasible."
- **context enrichment** — supplying project information so the model stops failing on missing context, the review's main remedy for construction-phase errors. > "Across the reviewed studies, context enrichment addresses missing project information"
- **validation and repair** — feeding compiler and execution results back to revise generated tests, which the review credits mainly with making tests executable. > "iterative validation and repair use compiler and execution feedback to revise generated tests"
- **model-utilization approaches** — how a study brings a model to bear: prompting, fine-tuning or task-specific adaptation, and pre-training, with prompting dominating the corpus. > "Of the 178 publications, 164 (92.1%) used or centrally evaluated prompting"
GUIDELINES:
- Structure any review or tool evaluation around the three construction subtasks plus the three QA categories; treat the phases as analytical, not strictly linear, because systems feed execution results back into generation.
- Require reporting of model identity, access mode, configuration and role (`QC2`), of compilation/execution checks and flaky or invalid tests (`QC7`), of traceable metrics and denominators (`QC8`), of robustness checks (`QC9`), and of threats to validity (`QC11`).
- Score quality criteria `2` (fully met), `1` (partial), `0` (not met) over `11` criteria, maximum `22`; include only if QC1–QC8 each score `2` and total is `at least 18/22`.
EVIDENCE: `14,785` query hits → `6,536` base study families → `6,550` screened titles/abstracts → `495` full-text retrievals → `361` provisionally relevant → `345` search-derived candidates → `178` included. Publication years: 2020 `1`, 2021 `0`, 2022 `2`, 2023 `8`, 2024 `28`, 2025 `75`, 2026 `64` (through 31 July). Outlets: ICSE `16`, TOSEM `11`, PACMSE `10`, ASE `9`, ICST `8`, TSE `8`, IST `4`, ISSTA `3`, other formal `62`, preprints `47`. Approaches: prompting `164 (92.1%)`, fine-tuning `48 (27.0%)`, pre-training `5 (2.8%)`. Manual unit tests reported to consume "more than 15% of development" time.
LIMITS: Cutoff fixed at 31 July 2026; venue list used only to audit search coverage and "neither presented as exhaustive nor used as a ranking of venue quality"; some findings held at "moderate confidence because its direction was stable despite heterogeneous study designs, reported execution checks, and model versions."
TOOLING: Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, DBLP; EvoSuite, Pynguin, KLEE, Coyote C++, ASTER, CubeTesterAI, CasModaTest.
LINKS: SBST, symbolic/concolic execution literature; TOGA/TOGLL-era oracle work via citations.

## A032 · Supercharging Unit Test Generation with in-IDE TestSpark
URL: https://blog.jetbrains.com/research/2025/09/testspark-unit-test-generation
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: TestSpark, an open-source IntelliJ plugin built with TU Delft, makes LLM-based and search-based unit test generation usable inside the IDE by pairing IDE-derived context with a compilation-feedback loop.
CONCEPTS:
- **fitness function** — the objective function a metaheuristic search uses to score candidate solutions, which guides the algorithm through a very large or infinite search space. > "The technique includes one or more objective functions, called fitness functions, to evaluate the possible solutions."
- **genetic algorithms** — evolve a set of solutions across generations by mutating and recombining them, as in natural selection. > "Genetic algorithms evolve the solutions with mutated and recombined solutions in multiple generation cycles."
- **simulated annealing** — iterates on a single solution, accepting an improvement and discarding anything worse, analogous to controlled cooling in metallurgy. > "Simulated annealing involves changing the solution slightly or dramatically in each iteration."
- **dynamic symbolic execution** — runs the program with abstract inputs across every path; the author credits it with raising coverage while flagging where it stops paying off. > "This technique boosts testing coverage, but it is limited in complex scenarios."
- **LLM pipeline** — the shared three-step shape of LLM test-generation tools: collect context, issue the LLM request, then run a feedback loop over the first response. > "These particular tools are similar in their approach to test generation; the process comprises"
- **compilation feedback loop** — on a compile error the plugin builds a prompt containing the error and asks the model to fix it, the mechanism that guarantees compilable output. > "In case of a compilation issue, the algorithm prepares a prompt with the compilation error and asks the LLM to fix the problem."
- **mutation score** — how the author operationalizes fault-detection capability as one of the optimization objectives for test generation. > "Another objective for these algorithms is fault detection capability, which can be calculated by mutation score."
GUIDELINES:
- Start generation by right-clicking a unit and choosing TestSpark; the plugin first builds the project and, if it cannot compile, informs the user instead of generating.
- Choose generation technique (LLM-based or EvoSuite search-based) and, for LLM-based, choose the model.
- Review the generated-test view: per-test pass/fail border color, error messages on hover, per-test coverage impact, and a mutation-score/coverage tab; edit, rerun, and apply only selected tests via `Apply to test suite`, into a new or existing file.
- Control the feedback-loop threshold: the user can set it, and "the default value keeps the cost below that of an agentic approach."
- Supply your own LLM token: TestSpark "is not a part of the AI Assistant subscription."
- Evaluate generation tools by running each `ten times with different seeds`, with independent sessions, on data not in training (leakage risk), because LLM output is non-deterministic.
EVIDENCE: 2025 study (arXiv 2501.10200) comparing EvoSuite, Kex, and TestSpark on the GitBug Java dataset, with TestSpark configured to ChatGPT-4, ChatGPT-4o, Llama Medium, and Code Llama 70b. TestSpark "significantly outperformed" on mutation scores; EvoSuite and Kex were similar to each other on coverage and both beat TestSpark; all tools were mainly affected by class complexity and internal dependencies, with LLM approaches "especially sensitive to the class size"; ChatGPT-4o was the best LLM but its performance "still lagged behind traditional methods."
LIMITS: Reported study covers only the LLM-based configuration of TestSpark (not the hybrid), Java/Kotlin only; earlier evaluations' limitations cited include no Java evaluation, training-data leakage, and single runs ignoring non-determinism.
TOOLING: TestSpark, IntelliJ IDEA, EvoSuite, Kex, TestPilot, ChatUniTest, AthenaTest, SynPrompt, Junie, AI Assistant, GitBug Java, ChatGPT-4/4o, Llama Medium, Code Llama 70b.
LINKS: arXiv 2209.11515, 2302.06527, 2305.04764, 2401.06580, 2501.10200, 2402.00097, 2009.05617; Miller & Spooner 1976; ICSE 2024 tool demo.

## A033 · Improving LLM-Based Unit Test Generation Through Root-Cause-Driven Prompt Design
URL: https://www.computer.org/csdl/proceedings-article/aitest/2026/056200a076/2jgwi6yl4nC
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Prompt strategies should each be tied to an identified root-cause mechanism of test failure — explicit execution state, explicit semantic constraints, and pre-injected environment constraints — rather than to generic techniques like few-shot or chain-of-thought prompting.
CONCEPTS:
- **failure patterns** — eight classes derived from a prior analysis of Java unit test generation with GPT-4o, each traced back to one of three root-cause mechanisms. > "A prior failure analysis of Java unit test generation using GPT-4o classified 2980 trials into eight failure patterns and identified three root-cause mechanisms"
- **external context ignorance** — the model lacks knowledge of execution-environment dependencies, so it produces reference/resolution and mock errors. > "they frequently disregard semantic usage constraints and execution-environment dependencies, leading to assertion failures, mock-related errors, and reference/resolution errors"
- **internal context ignorance** — the model lacks the semantic usage constraints of the API it is calling, even when syntax is right. > "identified three root-cause mechanisms: external context ignorance, internal context ignorance, and a syntax–semantics gap"
- **syntax–semantics gap** — reproducing API syntax faithfully without getting semantics correct, the failure mode the prompt design targets first. > "Although LLMs often reproduce API syntax faithfully, they frequently disregard semantic usage constraints"
- **execution state explicitness** — writing the expected runtime state into the generated test so the model has a concrete target. > "(1) making the execution state explicit in the generated test"
- **semantic constraint statement** — declaring usage constraints literally in the prompt instead of hoping the model infers them. > "(2) stating semantic constraints explicitly, and (3) injecting environment constraints prior to generation"
- **environment constraint injection** — supplying environment facts before generation so the test does not assume dependencies it cannot resolve. > "semantic constraints explicitly, and (3) injecting environment constraints prior to generation"
- **root-cause correspondence** — every prompt rule is justified by mapping it to one specific failure mechanism, which separates the approach from generic prompting tricks. > "yielding a systematic design in which each rule is explicitly justified by its correspondence to a specific root-cause mechanism"
GUIDELINES:
- Derive prompt rules from a failure taxonomy: classify failures first, then design one rule per root cause.
- Use three strategies: (1) "making the execution state explicit in the generated test," (2) "stating semantic constraints explicitly," (3) "injecting environment constraints prior to generation."
- Prefer these over generic `few-shot learning` or `chain-of-thought prompting` when the target failure modes are assertion failures, mock-related errors, and reference/resolution errors.
- Report gains in absolute percentage points and per model, and report mock-error reduction as a relative percentage against a baseline prompt.
EVIDENCE: Prior failure analysis classified `2980` GPT-4o trials into eight failure patterns and three root causes. Experiments on `298` methods with five models (GPT-4o, GPT-5, GPT-5.1-Codex, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro) showed improved test execution success for every model, with "absolute gains ranging from 1.1 to 21.1 percentage points (pp)"; mock-related errors fell `61.9%–99.2%` relative to the baseline prompt.
LIMITS: The paper states LLM-based test generation "has not yet attained a quality level sufficient for practical use in industry"; it discusses conditions under which the strategies transfer to other code-generation tasks and "limitations on their scope." Only the abstract was available in the source.
TOOLING: GPT-4o, GPT-5, GPT-5.1-Codex, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro.
LINKS: the prior failure-pattern analysis of Java unit test generation it builds on (unnamed in available text).

## A034 · Effective test generation using pre-trained Large Language Models and mutation testing
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0950584924000739
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: MuTAP improves LLM-generated test effectiveness by augmenting prompts with surviving mutants and initial tests, optimizing for bug detection rather than code coverage.
CONCEPTS:
- **MuTAP** — a prompt-augmentation technique that uses mutation testing to push generated tests toward bug detection instead of coverage. > "In this paper, we proposed MuTAP as a means of improving and evaluating the ability of pre-trained LLMs to generate effective test cases."
- **PUT** — the Program Under Test; the author distinguishes the input half of a unit test from its oracle half. > "A unit test consists of two components: the first component is a set of test inputs for the Program Under Test"
- **mutation testing (MT)** — inject artificial changes modelled on real faults to create mutants; killing them is the effectiveness measure, and survivors expose what the tests miss. > "MT involves injecting artificial changes based on real faults into a PUT, resulting in mutated versions of the PUT known as mutants."
- **mutation score (MS)** — the ratio of killed mutants to total mutants, the paper's headline effectiveness number. > "the ratio of killed mutants by the total number of mutants"
- **surviving-mutant augmentation** — re-prompt with the surviving mutants plus the initial inadequate tests, since survivors point at what the tests failed to detect. > "by augmenting the initial prompt with both initial test cases and the surviving mutants"
- **syntax repair loop** — assess generated test syntax and re-prompt the model to fix what it detects before any behavioral check runs. > "MuTAP assesses the syntax of the generated test cases and re-prompts its LLMC to rectify any detected syntax issues."
- **return-value check** — after syntax is fixed, appraise intended behavior through return values, before mutation analysis starts. > "After identifying and correcting any potential syntax and return value errors in the generated test cases, MuTAP evaluates their effectiveness by conducting MT."
