- **LLMC** — the LLM used as MuTAP's main component, driven entirely by prompting rather than fine-tuning. > "Our proposed technique, MuTAP, employs an LLM as its main Component (LLMC) and starts by feeding a prompt to the LLMC in order to generate test cases."
- **zero-shot / few-shot** — the two initial prompt variants the pipeline starts from before any repair or augmentation. > "The initial prompt includes the PUT and instructions for generating test cases by using zero-shot and few-shot learning."
GUIDELINES:
- Prompt with the PUT plus instructions, starting from `zero-shot` and `few-shot` learning.
- After generation, check syntax and re-prompt to fix it; then check intended behavior via return values before mutation analysis.
- Run MT on the PUT and augment the prompt with surviving mutants; iterate until "the final test cases can effectively detect all mutants" or no unused surviving mutants remain.
- Optimize test cases for bug detection, not coverage: "coverage is weakly correlated with the efficiency of tests in bug detection."
- Operate without natural-language descriptions of the PUT.
- Apply post-processing: generated tests "may suffer from syntactic or functional errors and may be ineffective in detecting certain types of bugs and testing corner cases."
EVIDENCE: Two LLM back-ends (Codex, `llama-2-chat`); `164` PUTs with synthetic bugs plus buggy programs from a Python bug-repairing benchmark. Average MS `93.57%` on synthetic buggy code, outperforming Pynguin and zero-shot/few-shot baselines; detects "up to 468 (28%) more buggy code snippets written by humans" and identifies `79 (17%)` buggy snippets that no other technique detects. Cited by 114.
LIMITS: Internal validity — the study did not explore the impact of altering natural-language instructions or few-shot demonstrative examples; different examples "more closely aligned with the PUT's functionality could potentially enhance the results." Python-only. Only the abstract and section snippets were available in the extracted source.
TOOLING: Codex, llama-2-chat, Pynguin.
LINKS: Bareiß et al. few-shot test generation; ATHENATEST; TOGA; CODAMOSA; EvoSuite; Randoop; MuTAP artifact released publicly.

## A035 · LLM Test Generation via Iterative Hybrid Program Analysis
URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3744916.3764553
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Panta raises branch coverage by emulating a developer's loop — read coverage, analyze control flow, target uncovered paths, generate, validate — instead of prompting an LLM with static method fragments.
CONCEPTS:
- **Panta** — a technique that combines dynamic coverage analysis with static control-flow analysis to steer an LLM at under-tested paths. > "a novel approach that combines dynamic code coverage analysis and static control flow analysis to generate tests for under-tested execution paths"
- **static path approximation** — extract linearly independent paths from the method CFG, each adding at least one new edge, rather than enumerating every path. > "extract a set of linearly independent paths, ensuring that each path introduces at least one new edge"
- **cyclomatic complexity (CYC)** — the basis for bounding how many candidate paths a method can generate, which the author raises as the reason full path lists overflow the context window. > "For complex methods with high cyclomatic complexity, the large number of candidate execution paths poses a challenge"
- **MUT** — the method under test, deliberately excluding helper methods so generated tests target the real unit. > "we identify the methods under test (MUTs), excluding helper methods such as private methods, getters, and setters"
- **coverage deficiency score** — a per-path score summing missed statements and missed branches, used to rank which path to target next. > "we compute a coverage deficiency score for each candidate path: missedScore = num of missed statements in path + num of missed branches in path"
- **exploitation/exploration selection** — take the highest-scoring path and also the least-visited path each round, to improve coverage without losing diversity. > "For exploitation, we choose the path with the highest missedScore to maximize code coverage improvement. For exploration, we select the path that has been visited the least"
- **maxSelectedConst** — a cap on selection attempts per path; past the cap the author treats the path as invalid or too hard and excludes it. > "if a path has been selected multiple times without being covered, it may indicate that the path itself is invalid or that LLMs struggle to reason about it, making further attempts unproductive"
- **program analysis guided prompt template** — a five-section prompt carrying the numbered source, current tests, dependencies, failed tests, and the selected paths. > "Our program analysis-guided prompt template, shown in Figure 4, consists of five sections: source file, test file, test dependencies, failed tests, and methods under test."
GUIDELINES:
- Build the CFG for the file, then per-MUT CFGs; add `start` and dummy end nodes.
- Execute the current suite and parse the report for missed statements and branches.
- Filter candidate paths that are fully covered or have reached `maxSelectedConst` selections.
- Include only `two paths per method` in the prompt — one by highest missedScore, one least-visited — to stay inside the LLM context window; if both coincide, include it once and update `pathHistory`.
- Number source lines in the prompt so selected path lines map back to code.
- Pin test dependency versions in the prompt (example given: `junit:4.13.2`); for Maven extract them with `mvn dependency:list`.
- Feed failed tests from the previous iteration back into the prompt.
- Repair failing generated tests; if unrepairable, feed them back as failure feedback.
- Support both augmenting an existing test class and creating a new test file skeleton (class declaration plus imports) when none exists.
- Stop on `iterNoIncrease` (several consecutive iterations with no coverage gain), treating it as convergence.
EVIDENCE: Evaluation on high-cyclomatic-complexity classes from open-source projects in `Defects4J`; `26%` higher line coverage and `23%` higher branch coverage than the state of the art. In the motivating Cli project case, Llama 3.3 70b tests missed the true branch of `else if (ch == '!')` and the false branch of `if (opt != ' ')`; GPT-4o also missed the latter false branch.
LIMITS: The extracted text ends inside Section 3.4; the paper's own Section 6 threats-to-validity discussion was not available. Path approximation deliberately avoids enumerating all paths because loops make path counts "exponential or unbounded."
TOOLING: CFG generation technique, JaCoCo, Defects4J, Maven, Llama 3.3 70b, GPT-4o, JUnit.
LINKS: CoverUp; focal-method-slice and path-constraint prompting approaches; Cyclomatic complexity literature.

## A036 · From Business Requirements to Test Assertions: Evaluating LLM-Generated Oracles on Real Bugs
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10277
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: LLMs can generate non-trivial test oracles directly from natural-language business requirements without source code or example input-output pairs, but correctness varies strongly by bug and model, and requirement technicality or ambiguity does not linearly predict accuracy.
CONCEPTS:
- **oracle problem** — determining the correct expected outcome for a test, which the author frames as the standing bottleneck that motivates requirement-driven generation. > "The oracle problem (determining the correct expected outcome for a test) remains a major bottleneck in automated testing"
- **REQ** — a requirement-derived oracle constructed by hand and used as the gold standard against which generated oracles are scored. > "construct a requirement-derived oracle (REQ) as a gold standard, and (iv) prompt five LLMs"
- **business requirement translation** — converting a buggy/fixed diff into a natural-language requirement statement before any prompting happens. > "(ii) manually translate the change into a business requirement, (iii) construct a requirement-derived oracle (REQ) as a gold standard"
- **behavioral change extraction** — deriving what actually changed from the buggy and fixed diffs, the first step of the pipeline. > "For each of 10 real bugs from Defects4J Lang (Bugs 1 and 3-11), we (i) extract behavioral changes via buggy/fixed diffs"
- **dual-target evaluation** — score oracles twice, once against the gold-standard requirement and once against the system under test, because the two can disagree. > "We evaluate oracle correctness and generalization under two targets: agreement with REQ and agreement with the system under test (SUT)"
- **macro-averaged metrics** — accuracy, precision, recall and F1 averaged across cases so per-bug variance does not hide behind one aggregate. > "agreement with the system under test (SUT), reporting macro-averaged accuracy, precision, recall, and F1"
- **generalization** — oracle correctness on behaviors the model was never shown as input-output pairs, which the author finds non-trivial but uneven. > "LLMs achieve non-trivial generalization but with substantial bug- and model-level variance."
- **technicality/ambiguity ratings** — manual ratings of requirement properties, correlated against accuracy; the author expects them to predict quality and finds they do not. > "correlations between requirement technicality/ambiguity ratings and oracle accuracy are weak with wide confidence intervals"
GUIDELINES:
- Build the pipeline in four reproducible steps: (i) extract behavioral changes from buggy/fixed diffs, (ii) manually translate the change into a business requirement, (iii) construct a `REQ` oracle as gold standard, (iv) prompt the LLM to generate oracle code.
- Withhold source code and example input-output pairs from the model.
- Report both targets — agreement with `REQ` and agreement with `SUT` — with macro-averaged accuracy, precision, recall, and F1.
- Do not assume requirement wording quality predicts oracle quality; check correlations with confidence intervals.
EVIDENCE: Ten real bugs from `Defects4J Lang` (Bugs 1 and 3–11); five LLMs (DeepSeek-V3, Gemma-3n, Llama-3, Mistral-7B, Qwen-3) prompted to generate Java oracle code. Oracles "align more closely with REQ than with SUT"; correlations between requirement technicality/ambiguity ratings and accuracy are "weak with wide confidence intervals"; "No detectable linear relationship exists between requirement properties and oracle accuracy in this dataset."
LIMITS: Explicitly "a pilot proof of concept"; findings "are preliminary and are intended to establish feasibility and motivate larger-scale empirical investigation." Ten bugs from a single project and a single language; variance is "substantial" at bug and model level. Only the arXiv abstract was available in the source.
TOOLING: Defects4J (Lang), DeepSeek-V3, Gemma-3n, Llama-3, Mistral-7B, Qwen-3, Java.
LINKS: Defects4J benchmark; the oracle problem literature referenced by the abstract.

## A037 · Can we find bugs using LLM-generated oracles?
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21136v2
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: LLM-generated oracles mainly capture the program's actual behavior rather than its expected behavior, which limits automatic bug detection, though LLMs generate oracles better than they classify them and beat EvoSuite oracles on fault-detection potential.
CONCEPTS:
- **test oracle** — the part of a unit test that captures the developer's intended behaviour, as opposed to the inputs that exercise the code. > "Typically, a unit test consists of a test prefix and a test oracle which captures the developer's intended behaviour."
- **test prefix** — the input/setup portion of a unit test; the author treats it as separable from the oracle so each can be supplied or generated independently. > "a unit test consists of a test prefix and a test oracle"
- **actual vs expected behavior** — the distinction the study is built to test: an oracle that mirrors what the code does cannot detect a logic fault. > "assessing whether LLM oracles capture the actual or the expected behavior"
- **oracle classification** — judging whether a supplied assertion is correct for a given piece of code under test. > "by studying LLMs on two tasks, namely, test oracle classification and generation"
- **oracle generation** — emitting an assertion for a given prefix, the task the author finds models do better than classification. > "We also find that LLMs are better at generating oracles than classifying them."
- **fault detection potential** — oracle strength measured through the mutation score of suites built on LLM oracles versus EvoSuite oracles. > "LLM-generated oracles have a higher fault detection potential than the Evosuite ones"
- **clean program assumption** — traditional tools take the implementation as correct, so the oracles they emit encode actual behavior and cannot flag logic faults. > "often produce oracles that mirror the program's actual behavior rather than the expected one"
GUIDELINES:
- Separate oracle classification from oracle generation when evaluating models; a model can be strong at one and weak at the other.
- Compare generated oracles against EvoSuite oracles on fault detection, not only on compilability.
- Treat "the test passes" as insufficient: weak oracles may pass while constraining nothing.
EVIDENCE: Test cases and oracles written by developers and generated automatically for `24` Java repositories. Findings: LLM oracles "mainly capture the actual program behavior making bug detection difficult"; LLMs are "better at generating oracles than classifying them"; "LLM-generated oracles have a higher fault detection potential than the Evosuite ones."
LIMITS: Only the arXiv abstract page was available in the source; no threats-to-validity text or per-condition breakdown.
TOOLING: Randoop, EvoSuite.
LINKS: the companion full paper (arXiv 2410.21136v2).

## A038 · Code Review Agent Benchmark
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.23448
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Review quality should be judged by whether a review leads to a behaviorally correct fix, so c-CRAB converts human review comments into executable tests that serve as objective oracles.
CONCEPTS:
- **c-CRAB** — a benchmark dataset for reviewing agents on real pull requests, mined from open-source review discussions. > "a benchmark designed to assess how well automated review tools identify the same issues that human reviewers raise in realistic PR settings"
- **test-based evaluation** — replace comment similarity with executable tests: a review counts only if the issue it names corresponds to a failing test. > "Instead of evaluating reviews solely based on similarity to reference comments, c-CRAB adopts a test-based evaluation."
- **review filtering** — drop conversational comments (clarifications, acknowledgments, praise) because they cannot be mapped unambiguously to a test. > "only review comments that can be translated into high-quality test cases serving as benchmark targets"
- **execution environment construction** — build one isolated Docker image per pull request with the OS, dependencies and a checked-out repository, since a test must be runnable to serve as an oracle. > "as a generated test has to be executed and verified before being used as a reliable oracle for evaluating review comments"
- **NL-to-test conversion** — translate a human review comment into an executable test that encodes the concern the reviewer raised. > "human review feedback is systematically converted into executable tests that capture the underlying issues identified during the review process"
- **differential testing** — validate the synthesized test so it fails on the patch under review and passes once the issue is fixed, checking it against the forked and merged commits. > "Each test is constructed to fail on the original patch and pass once the corresponding issue has been resolved."
- **coding agent revision** — hand the generated review to a coding agent, let it revise the patch, then run the revised patch against the test. > "we provide the generated review to a coding agent, which revises the patch accordingly. The revised patch is then executed against the synthesized test."
GUIDELINES:
- Curate in four stages: `review filtering`, `executable environment construction`, `converting NL comments to executable tests`, and validation.
- Require each benchmark test to fail on the original patch and pass once the issue is resolved; validate with differential execution on the forked and merged commits.
- Filter remaining comments with a prompt calibrated on a gold set at a chosen precision threshold.
- Clone the repository and check out the exact commit to be reviewed, then preinstall dependencies, per PR, in Docker.
- Do not rely on n-gram or embedding similarity to score reviews, and do not rely on vanilla `LLM-as-a-Judge`: it cannot distinguish a trivial mitigation from a root-cause fix.
EVIDENCE: "current systems solve only about 40% of the benchmark tasks." On one PR, similarity scores were low: `BLEU-4 0.00`, `ROUGE-L 7.02`, `chrF 20.74`, embedding similarity `54.59` (all normalized to 0–100). Table 1 compares 10 prior benchmarks (Tufano-21/22, CodeReviewer, CRScore corpus, ContextCRBench, SWE-CARE, AACR-Bench, RovoDev, Qodo Benchmark, CR-Bench); only c-CRAB uses test-based evaluation.
LIMITS: The extracted text stops mid-Section 4.2.2, so evaluation details, agent selection, and threats to validity were unavailable. Raw review discussions are "inherently noisy"; environments must reproduce repository dependencies or tests "cannot be executed consistently."
TOOLING: Docker, SentenceTransformers (sbert.net), BLEU/ROUGE/chrF, Codex and Claude Code as review tools.
LINKS: python-telegram-bot PR #3514, posthog PR #10293; prior benchmarks in Table 1.

## A039 · Can we find bugs using LLM-generated oracles?
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.21136v2
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Under a controlled four-way split of code status and oracle correctness, LLM oracles mostly encode actual behavior; LLMs classify assertions less well than they generate them, and generated oracles detect more faults than EvoSuite's.
CONCEPTS:
- **four scenarios** — `CC+CA` (correct code, correct assertion), `CC+WA`, `WC+CA`, `WC+WA`, each `25%` of the dataset; the author splits accuracy this way because a combined figure hides the behavior that matters. > "we break the problem into four equal parts that capture all possible combinations, in order to examine the behaviour of LLMs under different versions"
- **oracle classification** — deciding whether an assertion captures intended behavior for the given code, tested as its own task. > "we design a controlled experiment in which we assess if LLMs can correctly classify a given test oracle assertion"
- **oracle generation** — producing one assertion for a given prefix, then checking it by executing the resulting test. > "we ask the LLM to generate one test assertion. We then evaluate their correctness by incorporating the generated assertions into the given test prefixes and executing them"
- **anonymous names** — test methods renamed to `testX` to test whether meaningful naming is what lets a model infer intent. > "(1) Anonymous names: Test method names are renamed to the pattern testX"
- **anonymous names + anonymous variables** — additionally rename every variable to `varX`, removing the last semantic hints from the test. > "In addition to the previous modification, all variable names are replaced with the pattern varX"
- **prompt variation** — three prompt combinations that include or exclude method implementations and documentation, following prior work. > "we make use of three different prompt combinations that contain different code information"
- **code quality dimension** — developer-written versus automatically generated test prefixes, so oracle behavior is checked across both code origins. > "The code under test may or may not contain descriptive comments and may or may not be automatically generated."
- **mutation score (MS)** — the adequacy measure used for oracle strength, computed from killed over generated mutants rather than from execution success. > "Mutants are used to assess the effectiveness and thoroughness of a test suite, by measuring how many of these artificial faults the suite is able to detect."
- **Acc@5** — the generation setup whose oracles are integrated into suites for mutation scoring against EvoSuite oracles. > "we compute the mutation score of the test suites that integrate Evosuite’s and the LLM generated test oracles (Acc@5 setup), respectively"
GUIDELINES:
- Do not report a single aggregate accuracy for oracle classification; break results into the four scenarios, since combined metrics are "not informative in this case."
- Build wrong code by mutation with `μBERT` applied to the method under test, so the fault is relevant to the associated test case.
- Build wrong assertions with GPT such that they are syntactically valid but cause the test to fail against the original implementation.
- Test prompt variations that include or exclude method implementations and documentation; prompts with method and prefix performed best previously.
- Check name sensitivity by comparing original vs `testX` vs `testX`+`varX` versions.
- Judge generated oracles by mutation score with `PiTest` (byte-code level mutants), not by successful execution alone: weak oracles "may still allow tests to pass while capturing only trivial or even irrelevant properties."
- Include buggy-code conditions, to avoid the `clean program assumption`.
EVIDENCE: `24` Java repositories; datasets from the TOGA and TOGLL evaluations (EvoSuite-generated prefixes with correct assertions). Findings: LLM approaches "mainly capture the actual program behavior making bug detection difficult"; LLMs are better at generating than classifying oracles; LLM oracles have "a higher fault detection potential than the Evosuite ones." Related benchmark figures cited: TOGLL generates "about 3.8 times more correct assertions and 4.9 times more exception oracles than TOGA," with about `25%` false positives for assertion oracles and about `5%` of assertions failing to compile.
LIMITS: Threats-to-validity section exists in the paper but its text was not captured in the extracted portion (extraction stopped inside Section 3.3); results depend on Java subjects and EvoSuite-generated prefixes.
TOOLING: EvoSuite, Randoop, Randoop-style feedback-directed generation, μBERT, PiTest, GPT, TOGA, TOGLL, ATLAS, KLEE.
LINKS: replication package at `https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13867480`; TOGA and TOGLL datasets and tools.

## A040 · [2606.18168] All Smoke, No Alarm: Oracle Signals in Agent-Authored Test Code
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18168
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Agent-authored test patches often execute code without asserting anything, so test-file counts overstate verification strength; explicit oracle signals still raise merge likelihood once confounders are controlled.
CONCEPTS:
- **oracle signal** — syntactic evidence in a test patch that the test verifies behavior rather than merely exercising it; the paper frames its goal as "characterizing oracle signals and their link to merge outcomes and review effort". > "characterizing oracle signals and their link to merge outcomes and review effort"
- **weak or no explicit oracle signals** — the dominant class, covering most agent test patches once the taxonomy is applied at scale. > "Applied at scale, 80.2% of test patches contain weak or no explicit oracle signals."
- **eight oracle signal categories** — an induced syntactic taxonomy of oracle signals, built from a qualitative reading of `384` stratified patches. > "A qualitative analysis of 384 stratified patches informs a syntactic taxonomy of eight oracle signal categories."
- **verification strength** — the property practitioners want; the authors argue it is not what current quality gates measure, because presence of a test file is read as proof of verification. > "Test files lacking explicit assertions execute code without verifying behavior, so quality gates based on test-file presence overestimate verification strength."
- **test-file patch** — the unit of analysis: a patch touching test files inside an agent-authored PR. > "We conduct an empirical study of 86,156 test-file patches from 33,596 agent-authored PRs across 2,807 GitHub repositories"
- **agent-authored PR** — a PR produced by one of five named coding agents: `OpenAI Codex`, `GitHub Copilot`, `Devin`, `Cursor`, or `Claude Code`. > "produced by five coding agents: OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor, and Claude Code"
- **stratified patch sample** — the sampling design that lets the induced categories span agents, languages and task types before they are applied at scale. > "A qualitative analysis of 384 stratified patches informs a syntactic taxonomy"
- **strong-oracle PR** — a patch carrying an explicit oracle, contrasted with weak or none; its raw merge rate runs against the regression result. > "While raw merge rates are lower for strong-oracle PRs, a regression analysis adjusting for agent, PR size, repository popularity, task type, and language shows strong oracles significantly improve merge likelihood"
- **adjusted merge likelihood** — the regression outcome measure, controlling for agent, patch size, repository popularity, task type and language. > "a regression analysis adjusting for agent, PR size, repository popularity, task type, and language"
- **raw merge rate** — the unadjusted outcome measure, which points the opposite way from the adjusted estimate. > "raw merge rates are lower for strong-oracle PRs, a regression analysis adjusting for agent, PR size, repository popularity, task type, and language"
- **oracle-aware quality check** — the proposed replacement for gates that count test files. > "practitioners can adopt oracle-aware quality checks to more accurately evaluate agent-authored contributions"
GUIDELINES:
- Do not credit a patch with behavior verification on file presence alone; require an explicit oracle first.
- Adopt `oracle-aware quality checks` for agent contributions, since counts "substantially overestimate verification strength".
- Adjust merge-outcome comparisons for `agent`, `PR size`, `repository popularity`, `task type`, and `language`; the unadjusted comparison reverses the conclusion.
- Build the taxonomy from a stratified sample (`384` patches) before applying its `8` categories at scale.
- Expect roughly `80.2%` of agent test patches to be weak/none, and a modest `OR = 1.28` (`p < 0.001`) merge advantage for strong oracles after adjustment.
EVIDENCE: `86,156` test-file patches from `33,596` agent-authored PRs across `2,807` GitHub repositories, from five agents. `384` patches coded qualitatively. `80.2%` of test patches contain weak or no explicit oracle signals. Raw merge rates are lower for strong-oracle PRs, but regression shows strong oracles significantly improve merge likelihood (`OR = 1.28`, `p < 0.001`). Cites prior scale of more than `932,000` agent PRs across more than `116,000` repositories.
LIMITS: Only the abstract is present in the extracted text, so category definitions, coding protocol, inter-rater agreement and regression specification are unobservable. Merge is a proxy for value, not defect detection. Scope is open-source GitHub PRs from five named agents.
TOOLING: OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor, Claude Code; GitHub PR data; regression reporting odds ratios.
LINKS: Prior study reporting 932,000+ agent-authored PRs across 116,000+ repositories; 8th IEEE International Conference on Artificial Intelligence Testing 2026.

## A041 · Automated Code Review Using Large Language Models at Ericsson: An Experience Report
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2507.19115v2
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: A lightweight, non-fine-tuned pipeline that prompts on the *enclosing method* of each diff yields reviews experienced Ericsson developers find time-saving, with Code Llama 13B preferred in blind pairwise comparison.
CONCEPTS:
- **enclosing method** — the Java method containing the changed lines; the context unit sent to the LLM, obtained by static program analysis rather than by passing the raw diff. > "Our solution then utilizes static program analysis to extract the enclosing method of the modified lines, thus ensuring that proper context is passed to the LLM."
- **lightweight approach** — no pre-training and no instruction fine-tuning; prompting only, followed by post-processing and human validation. > "we rely on a relatively light weight approach that avoided expensive pre-training and instruction fine tuning for generating code reviews"
- **adversarial prompting** — seeding bugs into snippets to test whether the model reports them. > "First was about adversarial prompting, where we introduced a few bugs in the code snippets and fed to the LLM."
- **pairwise comparison task** — blind preference judgment between two reviews of the same snippet, where reviewers are not told which model produced which. > "The experts were not informed which reviews were from the smaller models."
- **Issue Topics Prompt** — a prompt scoping the review to Code Design / Code I/O / Code Logic concerns for a large telecom system. > "In the role of a reviewer for a recent pull request within a large-scale real-time telecommunication system, evaluate the code snippet below for potential concerns"
GUIDELINES:
- Prompt on the enclosing method, not the bare diff: parse with `Tree-Sitter` for Java, build the AST, visit method declarations, select those containing the modified line numbers.
- The naive prompt "Please generate a code review for the following code" "do not work well in practice"; use structured prompts.
- Simple prompt: comment only on significant concerns; `Do not describe the functionality of the code`; `Avoid generating new code`; say nothing if the code is satisfactory.
- Detailed prompt: target runtime errors, edge cases, logic flaws, algorithm correctness, error handling, design, naming, performance, maintainability; cap at `approximately 200 words`; state explicitly when no issues exist. Survey variant: "include only things to improve in less than 50 words, and do not generate code".
- Validate prompts with humans, then re-calibrate from feedback; log generated reviews.
- Integrate at commit time through the `Gerrit` API and a `VS Code` plugin for early detection; latency is overhead-bound (`~6 s` for `100–300`-line snippets, `~5–6 s` for short ones).
EVIDENCE: 8 completed expert surveys over 10 methods — long snippets 3 positive / 2 neutral / 4 negative, medium 2/2/3, short 1/4/3. Pairwise: Code Llama 13B beat Llama 2 13B (2–1), Code Llama 7B (2–1) and Llama 2 7B (3–2). Field trial (9 developers, 15 days): 4 said it saved time; 4 effective/highly effective, 2 somewhat, 3 not very; 4 said reviews merely explain code, 2 factually incorrect, 3 off-target. Adversarial: bugs found in all `10` short and `5` medium snippets, but "relatively easy to catch logical bugs"; across `5` change IDs it commented only on changed lines.
LIMITS: Preliminary; 8–9 experts, one organization, experts as oracle; seeded bugs easy; no false-positive benchmark.
TOOLING: Llama 2 (7B/13B), Code Llama (7B/13B), Mixtral, `Tree-Sitter`, Gerrit API, VS Code plugin; SonarQube/Fortify as baselines.
LINKS: Cihan et al. "Automated Code Review In Practice" (arXiv:2412.18531); Pornprasit & Tantithamthavorn (IST 2024); CrewAI and RAG/Graph-RAG (planned).

## A042 · Improving Bug Detection in LLM-Generated Unit Tests: Revisiting Test-Oracle Reliability Across Modern Large Language Models
URL: https://njemcs.edu.iq/index.php/njemcs/article/view/123
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Replicating the "tests designed to pass" critique on newer models shows bug-revealing improved (22.9% → 39.1%) while bug-validating fell (41.1% → 26.2%), so the oracle-design defect resists model strength.
CONCEPTS:
- **test oracle derived from the code under test** — the root defect: expectations are read off the implementation instead of an independent specification of correct behavior. > "the test oracle is frequently derived from the very code under test rather than from an independent specification of correct behavior"
- **designed to pass** — tests whose assertions match whatever the code currently does rather than catching bugs. > "these tools may generate tests that are effectively "designed to pass" rather than designed to catch bugs"
- **Test-Oracle Reliability** — the paper's framing for whether assertions encode intended behavior; the authors probe whether model strength changes it. > "suggesting that the test-oracle design problem is significantly reduced but not eliminated by model strength"
- **Bug-Revealing Rate (BRR)** — share of buggy programs on which generated tests fail; the metric that improved across the four models. > "The Bug-Revealing Rate increases from 22.9% (GPT-4) to 39.1% (Qwen3-Coder) for all four models"
- **Bug-Validating Rate (BVR)** — share of correct reference solutions on which generated tests pass; the metric that fell for the strongest model. > "the ability of the strongest model (Qwen3-Coder) to validate bugs decreases from 41.1% to 26.2%"
- **four-class outcome model** — a formal model partitioning outcomes by generated-test result crossed with program correctness. > "This paper presents a formal mathematical model for categorizing the outcome of generated-tests into four classes"
- **McNemar test** — paired significance test used across model configurations. > "two basic statistical tests: McNemar test and Wilson confidence interval to ensure that the results are rigorous"
- **Wilson confidence interval** — interval estimator used alongside the paired test so reported rates are not bare point estimates. > "McNemar test and Wilson confidence interval to ensure that the results are rigorous"
- **Replication and Extension Study** — rerun of the prior "designed to pass" finding with newer models, plus the two new rates and the four-class model. > "This paper presents a Replication and Extension Study that re-examines this issue using a newer generation of large language models"
- **Refactory dataset** — real student-written buggy Python programs paired with correct reference solutions. > "the Refactory dataset, which contains 1,783 real buggy Python programs written by actual university students alongside 2,442 correct reference solutions"
GUIDELINES:
- Report `BRR` and `BVR` together; a single bug-detection number hides the oracle-reliability regression.
- Partition outcomes into the four classes before computing rates; never collapse pass/fail.
- Use paired tests (`McNemar`) and `Wilson confidence intervals`, not bare point estimates.
- Evaluate oracles against independent reference solutions, never the code under test.
- Treat stronger models as partial mitigation: gains in one rate can accompany losses in the other.
- Benchmarked at `1,783` buggy programs and `2,442` correct references; observed `BRR` span `22.9%` (GPT-4) to `39.1%` (Qwen3-Coder); strongest-model `BVR` drop `41.1%` to `26.2%`.
EVIDENCE: Four models including Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Qwen3-Coder and GPT-4 on Refactory (`1,783` buggy, `2,442` correct). Bug-Revealing Rate rises from `22.9%` (GPT-4) to `39.1%` (Qwen3-Coder) "for all four models". Bug-Validating Rate for the strongest model falls from `41.1%` to `26.2%`. Direction: detection up, validity down.
LIMITS: Abstract-only text; per-model figures beyond the two endpoints, effect sizes and class distributions unobservable. Single benchmark, Python only, student-authored single-function scale — industrial code out of scope.
TOOLING: Codium CoverAgent, CoverUp, GitHub Copilot (motivating tools); Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-4, Qwen3-Coder; McNemar; Wilson interval.
LINKS: Mathews & Nagappan (arXiv:2412.14137); Molina/Gorla/d'Amorim (TOSEM 34(5), 2025); TOGA (ICSE 2022); ASSERTIFY; AssertFlip; Schäfer et al. (TSE 2024); Yuan et al. (FSE 2024).

## A043 · [2608.17177] Grounding AI Agents in Contracts: An Empirical Evaluation of Spec-Driven Test Generation
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17177
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Making an agent document pre-conditions, post-conditions and undefined behaviors before generating tests — a semi-formal spec used as a cognitive scaffold — raises bug detection by 9.8 pp and branch coverage by 2.5 pp.
CONCEPTS:
- **Spec-Driven Test Generation** — the method: instruct the agent to reason about and write down the contract *before* writing tests. > "we propose Spec-Driven Test Generation, where we instruct an agent to first reason about -- and explicitly document -- code pre-conditions, post-conditions, and undefined behaviors"
- **pre-conditions, post-conditions, undefined behaviors** — the three documented elements of the contract. > "first reason about -- and explicitly document -- code pre-conditions, post-conditions, and undefined behaviors"
- **semi-formal specification** — the artifact produced: prose-plus-structure, sitting between natural language and machine-checkable contracts, and retained as the intermediate product of the method. > "This intermediate semi-formal specification acts as a cognitive scaffold to guide subsequent test generation."
- **cognitive scaffold** — the written spec steers subsequent reasoning so tests target boundaries instead of happy paths. > "acts as a cognitive scaffold to guide subsequent test generation"
- **behavioral boundaries and edge cases** — what directly-prompted agents miss; the paper attributes the misses to unreasoned contracts. > "thereby missing edge cases and behavioral boundaries that affect test quality"
- **contract reasoning failure** — the named limitation of "just generate tests" prompting. > "when directly prompted to generate tests, these agents can fail to reason about the code and its underlying contracts"
- **LLM-as-a-Judge** — evaluation protocol comparing suite quality beyond coverage, against both a plain agent baseline and human-authored tests. > "Using LLM-as-a-Judge, we further show that test suites generated by the spec-driven agent are superior to the baseline and human-authored tests in 77.8% and 56.7% of the cases"
GUIDELINES:
- Before test generation, have the agent explicitly document pre-conditions, post-conditions and undefined behaviors.
- Keep the spec as a reviewable artifact, not scratch reasoning; it is the scaffold that drives the tests.
- Evaluate suites against two references: a plain agent baseline and human-authored tests.
- Judge on several axes — best practices, readability, edge-case coverage — not coverage alone.
- Treat `LLM-as-a-Judge` as one signal beside bug-detection rate and coverage.
- Expect modest but significant gains: `9.8` pp bug detection (`p = 0.0352`), `2.5` pp branch coverage (`p = 0.0034`).
EVIDENCE: Evaluation on Google production bugs; spec-driven agent vs traditional test-generation agent baseline: `+9.8` pp bug detection (`p = 0.0352`), `+2.5` pp branch coverage (`p = 0.0034`). `LLM-as-a-Judge`: superior to baseline in `77.8%` and to human-authored tests in `56.7%` of cases; improvements on best practices, readability, edge-case coverage.
LIMITS: Abstract-only text; bug count, agent/model identity, judge model, judge-agreement validation and prompt wording unobservable. Judged superiority over human tests in `56.7%` is a model judgment, not executed fault detection. One industrial codebase.
TOOLING: LLM-based coding agent (unspecified); `LLM-as-a-Judge`; branch-coverage instrumentation; Google production bug corpus.
LINKS: SpecOps 2026 workshop (1st International Workshop on Specification-Driven Development Life Cycle), co-located with SPLASH 2026; DOI 10.1145/3842652.3843195; Cheng et al. on agentic bug-reproduction test co-generation.

## A044 · Test Oracle Automation in the Era of LLMs
URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3715107
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: LLM-based oracle generation inherits the accuracy, utility, applicability and expressivity limits of pre-LLM techniques; the field's blocking problem is evaluating whether generated oracles find real bugs.
CONCEPTS:
- **test oracle** — the artifact deciding whether an execution passed; suite effectiveness is stated to hinge on its quality. > "The effectiveness of a test suite in detecting faults highly depends on the quality of its test oracles."
- **test assertions** — in-test statements checking expected behavior in one scenario. > "Test assertions are statements included in test cases, that check the expected behavior of the SUT in a specific scenario"
- **contracts** — pre/post-conditions and invariants that are not tied to one test case. > "are logical constraints on a specific software element (method, class, etc.) and are usually captured in the form of pre- and post-conditions for methods"
- **metamorphic relations** — relations across executions, e.g. pop reverting push. > "a method that checks a metamorphic relation stating that the pop operation reverts the push operation for any given stack"
- **static oracle inference** — deriving oracles without executing the SUT, from comments, documentation or source. > "Static techniques are capable of inferring oracles without executing the SUT, extracting information by analyzing the SUT’s artifacts"
- **dynamic oracle inference** — observing executions and keeping candidate oracles consistent with those observations. > "Dynamic approaches, on the other hand, derive the oracles by observing the behavior of the SUT during execution"
- **regression assertions** — assertions over an observed result, as added by EvoSuite or Randoop. > "execute a given test case and then produce test assertions capturing some property of the execution result"
- **likely invariants** — template candidate oracles validated by execution, as in Daikon, and extended by grammar-based fuzzing in SpecFuzzer. > "is a well-known tool for inferring likely invariants using a template-based approach"
- **false positive** — a correct, expected state for which the oracle is false: a false alarm. > "is a correct and expected program state for which the oracle is false, i.e., a false alarm"
- **false negative** — an incorrect state for which the oracle is true: a missed fault. > "is an incorrect and unexpected program state for which the oracle is true, i.e., a missed fault"
- **expressivity limits** — restrictions inherited from the oracle language. > "languages that target specific kinds of constraints such as logical and arithmetic constraints (without quantified expressions)"
- **LLM-inherent threats (data leakage, dataset bias, reproducibility)** — properties of using an LLM that bear on oracle generation, treated separately from language expressivity. > "inherent challenges of LLMs, such as data leakage, dataset bias, and reproducibility, can impact LLM-based oracle generation"
GUIDELINES:
- Triage false positives first: "false positives are more critical, as they can lead to false alarms resulting in unnecessary debugging efforts"; a false negative can still be repaired.
- Measure with mutation testing *and* report false-positive rates; fault detection alone is insufficient. Report them explicitly — TOGA reached "up to 47%", dynamic techniques "up to 20%".
- Evaluate actual bug-finding capability, "a more realistic measure of the utility of the oracles", not lexical/functional similarity.
- Do not assume static comment-based techniques generalize: they need "very well documented and mature software projects". Dynamic techniques need an existing suite, else inference depends on generated-test quality.
- Adopt new evaluation practices (`LLM-as-a-Judge`, multi-agent approaches) and build leakage/bias-mitigating datasets.
EVIDENCE: Roadmap/survey, no new experiment. Literature base `37` LLM-based studies, `20` oracle-specific; `47%` and `20%` false-positive figures are quoted from cited work. Notes that generated assertions improve coverage and some lexical/functional metrics.
LIMITS: Position paper without new empirics; extracted text ends inside the survey table, so Sections 4–5 are known only via abstract and introduction. False-positive figures are quoted only.
TOOLING: Jdoctor, MeMo, CallMeMaybe, TOGA, EvoSuite, Randoop, Daikon, SpecFuzzer, SBES, MemoRIA, GAssert, EvoSpex, TOGLL, CoverUp.
LINKS: Wang et al. systematic review of LLMs for software testing; TOGA (ICSE 2022); Schäfer et al. (TSE 2024); Yuan et al. (FSE 2024); Alshahwan et al. (FSE Companion 2024); "Neural-Based Test Oracle Generation: A Large-Scale Evaluation and Lessons Learned"; "Towards More Realistic Evaluation for Neural Test Oracle Generation"; TOSEM 34(5) Article 150.

## A045 · [2609.24341] Evaluating the effectiveness of class-level LLM-generated test suites in Python
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24341
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: On ClassEval, structural coverage sits near its ceiling and discriminates nothing; executability varies widely and model choice explains more variance than prompt choice, so model selection should precede prompt tuning.
CONCEPTS:
- **executability as a gate** — a suite must run before coverage or mutation numbers mean anything. > "Reliable assessment of LLM-generated tests should treat executability as a gate and combine coverage with mutation testing and structural quality indicators."
- **structural coverage near ceiling** — line and branch coverage cluster at the top of their range, so they cannot rank configurations. > "Structural coverage is consistently near its ceiling and offers little discrimination among configurations."
- **mutation score** — class-level fault-detection proxy computed with `Cosmic Ray`, added to the evaluation alongside coverage. > "The evaluation combines execution outcomes, line and branch coverage, Cosmic Ray mutation scores, and structural quality indicators."
- **structural quality indicators** — the fourth evaluation axis besides executability, coverage and mutation. > "combines execution outcomes, line and branch coverage, Cosmic Ray mutation scores, and structural quality indicators"
- **prompt strategy** — the manipulated factor, varied across model configurations on the benchmark. > "We evaluate multiple prompt strategies across a diverse set of current LLM configurations on the ClassEval benchmark."
- **model choice** vs **prompt choice** — the two factors ranked by explained variation; model choice wins. > "Model choice explains more variation than prompt choice, and their interaction shows that prompt effectiveness depends on the selected model."
- **prompt × model interaction** — prompt effectiveness is model-conditional; no prompt dominates across models. > "their interaction shows that prompt effectiveness depends on the selected model"
- **unequal executable subsets** — human and LLM suites run on different class sets, which invalidates direct comparison. > "Human and LLM suites are evaluated on unequal executable subsets, so their relative mutation scores do not establish superiority."
- **paired comparison on shared classes** — the control: compare only classes present in both executable subsets. > "paired comparisons use only classes shared by the relevant executable subsets"
- **ClassEval** — the class-level Python benchmark used. > "a diverse set of current LLM configurations on the ClassEval benchmark"
GUIDELINES:
- Gate evaluation on executability; report execution outcomes before coverage or mutation.
- Do not offer coverage alone as quality evidence: near-ceiling coverage cannot rank configurations.
- Combine `line and branch coverage` with `mutation testing` and `structural quality indicators`.
- Choose the model before tuning the prompt: model choice explains more variation, and prompt effectiveness is model-conditional.
- When comparing human versus LLM suites, restrict to classes shared by the executable subsets, and do not claim superiority from unequal subsets.
- Instrument with `Cosmic Ray` mutants at class level, across multiple prompt strategies and multiple current LLM configurations on ClassEval.
EVIDENCE: Benchmark: ClassEval (class-level Python). Measured: execution outcomes, line coverage, branch coverage, Cosmic Ray mutation score, structural quality. Findings: coverage near ceiling and low-discrimination; executability varies substantially; the proposed prompt performs strongly for mutation score but no prompt dominates across models; model choice explains more variation than prompt; significant prompt×model interaction; human-versus-LLM mutation scores are not comparable because the executable subsets differ.
LIMITS: Abstract-only text; per-model and per-prompt mutation percentages, class counts and effect sizes unobservable. Single benchmark, Python only. The authors state the human-vs-LLM relative mutation scores "do not establish superiority".
TOOLING: `Cosmic Ray` (Python mutation testing); ClassEval benchmark; multiple current LLM configurations.
LINKS: ClassEval benchmark; mutation-testing literature via Cosmic Ray; arXiv non-exclusive distribution license.

## A046 · [2601.08998] On the Flakiness of LLM-Generated Tests for Industrial and Open-Source Database Management Systems
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.08998
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: LLM-generated database tests are slightly flakier than existing tests; reliance on unguaranteed ordering causes 63% of flaky cases, and both models transfer flakiness from prompt context — more in closed-source SAP HANA than open-source systems.
CONCEPTS:
- **flaky test** — inconsistent results across repeated runs on the same code, which breaks the assumption that a failure signals a defect. > "They produce inconsistent results when executed multiple times on the same code, invalidating the assumption that a test failure indicates a software defect."
- **test suite amplification** — using an LLM to extend an existing suite rather than author one from scratch. > "We amplified test suites with two LLMs, GPT-4o and Mistral-Large-Instruct-2407, to assess the flakiness of the generated test cases."
- **flakiness transfer** — flaky behavior present in the prompt's existing tests reappears in newly generated tests, observed for both models. > "both LLMs transferred the flakiness from the existing tests to the newly generated tests"
- **unordered collection** — root-cause category for a test relying on an order that is not guaranteed; the most common cause. > "the most common root cause of flakiness was the reliance of a test on a certain order that is not guaranteed"
- **prompt context** — the existing suite handed to the model; the mechanism through which flakiness is carried over. > "both LLMs transferred the flakiness from the existing tests to the newly generated tests via the provided prompt context"
- **tailored context** — the prescription: curate what suite content the model sees. > "the importance of providing LLMs with tailored context when employing LLMs for test generation"
- **closed-source vs open-source system** — the moderator of transfer prevalence. > "flakiness transfer is more prevalent in closed-source systems such as SAP HANA than in open-source systems"
- **manual inspection** — how root causes were assigned to flaky tests. > "Based on a manual inspection, we found that the most common root cause of flakiness"
GUIDELINES:
- Assume generated tests are flaky until shown otherwise; they show "a slightly higher proportion of flaky tests compared to existing tests".
- Before merging generated tests, inspect for order-dependent assertions on unordered collections — `63%` of flaky cases here.
- Curate prompt context: passing an existing suite teaches its flakiness, so strip or repair flaky exemplars before amplification.
- Apply stricter review in closed-source systems, where transfer was more prevalent.
- Scope: `115` flaky tests analyzed, `72` (`63%`) in the `unordered collection` class; two generators, four DBMS.
EVIDENCE: Four relational DBMS — SAP HANA (industrial, closed), DuckDB, MySQL, SQLite (open) — with suites amplified by `GPT-4o` and `Mistral-Large-Instruct-2407`. Generated tests show a slightly higher flaky proportion than existing tests. Manual inspection: `72 of 115` flaky tests (`63%`) caused by reliance on ordering that is not guaranteed. Both LLMs transferred flakiness from the existing tests via prompt context. Transfer more prevalent in SAP HANA than in the open-source systems.
LIMITS: Abstract-only text; absolute flaky rates, run counts, generated-test counts and annotator agreement unobservable. Flakiness judged by repeated execution, hence environment-sensitive. Confined to SQL/relational DBMS suites.
TOOLING: SAP HANA, DuckDB, MySQL, SQLite; GPT-4o; Mistral-Large-Instruct-2407.
LINKS: ICSE SEIP 2026 (48th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice); prior work flagging flakiness in LLM-generated tests.

## A047 · Testing with AI Agents: An Empirical Study of Test Generation Frequency, Quality, and Coverage
URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3793302.3793620
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Agents author 16.4% of test-adding commits in real repositories; their tests are longer with more assertions yet lower cyclomatic complexity, and deliver coverage gains comparable to or above human tests.
CONCEPTS:
- **Test Addition Commit** — a commit whose added lines match new test definitions, detected on `+` lines rather than by touched file path. > "A commit was classified as a “Test Addition Commit” only if its patch contained these specific markers of new test cases."
- **AI-authored commit** — classified only if every line of every added test method is AI-authored, traced with AST parsing plus `git blame`. > "A commit was classified as AI-authored only if all lines within all of its added test methods were authored exclusively by AI agents."
- **AI Test Method** vs **Human Test Method** — all lines AI-authored vs any line human-authored. > "we classified methods as either AI Test Method (all lines authored by AI) or Human Test Method (any line authored by a human)"
- **eLoC** — effective lines of code excluding comments and blanks; AI tests sit slightly higher but within a narrower range. > "AI-generated tests have a slightly higher median eLoC (12.0) compared to human-written tests (11.0)"
- **`# assertions`** — count of assertion calls such as `expect()`; AI tests carry a higher count. > "AI-generated tests are characterized by a higher number of assertions"
- **Cyclomatic Complexity (CC)** — decision-point nodes counted from a Babel AST. > "The median complexity for both groups is 1.00, but the mean for AI (1.09) is lower than for humans (1.31)."
- **Assertion Roulette** — the smell of multiple assertions per test hiding the failing cause; attributed to AI assertion density. > "a known bad practice where multiple assertions in a single test make it difficult to pinpoint the exact cause of failure"
- **Dispersed** vs **Localized Distribution** — t-SNE patterns of AI tests across the human embedding space; dispersed means spread across many human styles. > "where AI tests are broadly scattered throughout the entire human test distribution, indicating structural similarity to various human styles"
- **agent-heavy role** — AI dominates test creation in small projects, up to 100% of additions. > "AI-generated tests account for 100% and 83.3% of test additions, respectively."
- **auxiliary role** — in large projects the AI share of test additions settles near 10–15%. > "In the largest analyzed project, cal.com (876 contributors), the AI contribution is consistent but remains at 14.4%."
GUIDELINES:
- Standardize on one framework before measuring coverage; `vitest` covered `179` of `400` TypeScript projects with detectable frameworks (`44.8%`). Detect additions from added `+` lines, not file paths — touching a test file may be refactor or deletion.
- Attribute per method with AST extraction plus `git blame`; require all lines AI-authored.
- Expect AI share to scale inversely with project size: `100%` in a 5-contributor repo vs `14.4%` in the 876-contributor repo. Review AI tests for `Assertion Roulette`; density aids verification but raises debugging cost.
- Measure coverage at the parent and test-adding commits to attribute the delta; `531` commits were executed across `3` projects.
EVIDENCE: `2,232` test-related commits from `10` TypeScript `vitest` projects. RQ1: AI authored `16.4%` of test-adding commits; range `1.9%` (`azure-sdk-for-js`) to `100%` (`total-typescript-monorepo`, 5 contributors), `cal.com` (876 contributors) `14.4%`. RQ2 (`9` projects, Mann-Whitney U): eLoC median `12.0` vs `11.0` (`p < 0.001`, Cliff's `δ = −0.12`, max `87` vs `699`); assertions `2.00` vs `1.00`; CC median `1.00` both, mean `1.09` vs `1.31`, significant in `2 of 9`. RQ3: `liam` AI +0.072 statement / +0.074 branch vs human −0.090 / −0.142; `appkit` +0.030 / +0.183 vs −0.001 / +0.008; `helper` 0.000 / +0.006 vs 0.000 / +0.213.
LIMITS: Short paper. Coverage feasible for `3` of `10` projects; AI commit counts small (`18`, `28`, `13`). `total-typescript-monorepo` excluded from RQ2 (humans later removed/edited its AI tests). TypeScript plus `vitest` only; top-10 selection favors agent-heavy projects, so `16.4%` is not a population estimate.
TOOLING: `vitest`; GitHub API; `@babel/parser`, `@babel/traverse`; `CodeBERT`; t-SNE; Mann-Whitney U; AIDev dataset.
LINKS: AIDev dataset; EvoSuite; SWT-Bench; Assertion Roulette literature; cal.com, azure-sdk-for-js, primer-react, capgo repos; online appendix for complexity; MSR '26 Proceedings.

## A048 · [2607.22880] Do Coverage and Mutation Scores of LLM-Generated Test Suites Correlate with Their Effectiveness? (Replicability Study)
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22880
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Replicating the coverage/mutation findings on LLM suites, proxy validity proves context-dependent: meaningful for cross-model comparison in regression-style settings, unreliable when the code under test may itself be buggy.
CONCEPTS:
- **proxy metrics** — coverage and mutation score standing in for real-bug detection in evaluations of generated suites. > "Prior work commonly evaluates generated test suites using proxy metrics such as code coverage and mutation score."
- **real-bug detection effectiveness** — the target construct the proxies are validated against; the replication re-examines its relationship to coverage and mutation. > "re-examine the relationships among coverage, mutation, and real-bug detection effectiveness"
- **replicability study** — rerun of Inozemtseva et al. and Papadakis et al. under LLM-generation conditions. > "we conduct a large-scale replication study of these two prior works using a wide range of test suites generated by a diverse set of LLMs"
- **regression-style setting** — supplied code can reasonably be assumed bug-free, and the metrics yield meaningful cross-model signals. > "in regression-style settings where the code provided to the LLM can be reasonably assumed bug-free, these metrics can provide meaningful signals when comparing across models"
- **bug-exposing setting** — the code may already be buggy and the goal is exposing that bug, where the proxies stop being reliable. > "in another common scenario where the code-under-test may already be buggy and the goal is to expose the bug within the code-under-test, they no longer serve as reliable indicators"
- **test suite size confounder** — the control used by the prior works; the replication finds little evidence it dominates for LLM-generated tests. > "We also find little evidence that test suite size is a dominant confounder for correlations among coverage, mutation, and real-bug detection for LLM-generated tests."
- **context-dependence** — metric usefulness is a property of the setting, not of the metric. > "We show that the usefulness of coverage and mutation is highly context-dependent"
- **prior-result divergence** — the replication's findings do not reproduce the earlier conclusions, attributed to LLM workflows differing from traditional generation. > "Our findings diverge substantially from prior results. We show that the usefulness of coverage and mutation is highly context-dependent"
GUIDELINES:
- Classify the setting first: regression-style (bug-free assumption, compare models) or bug-exposing (buggy code, expose the defect).
- In regression-style settings, coverage and mutation may be reported for cross-model comparison.
- In bug-exposing settings, do not treat coverage or mutation as effectiveness indicators.
- Do not mechanically apply the human-test "control for suite size" correction; size was not a dominant confounder here.
- Condition prior studies' metric conclusions on the setting they actually measured.
- Use suites from "a diverse set of LLMs" rather than one model, since the conclusion is model-spanning.
EVIDENCE: Large-scale replication of two prior works over suites from many LLMs. Two settings distinguished: metrics meaningful across models in regression-style, unreliable in bug-exposing. Little evidence that suite size is a dominant confounder for coverage–mutation–bug-detection correlations in LLM-generated tests. Direction: prior conclusions do not transfer unchanged. Artifact: `24` pages, `4` figures, `14` tables.
LIMITS: Abstract-only in the extracted arXiv text; correlation coefficients, model list, benchmark projects and suite counts unobservable. Replication targets Java-centric human-test literature while LLM suites may span languages. Context-dependence means no single number summarizes validity.
TOOLING: Diverse unnamed LLMs; coverage instrumentation; mutation testing; correlation analysis controlling for suite size.
LINKS: Inozemtseva et al.; Papadakis et al. (incl. ICSE '17 "An empirical study on mutation, statement and branch coverage fault revelation that avoids the unreliable clean program assumption"); ISSTA 2026; PACMSE Vol. 3 No. ISSTA Article ISSTA002; DOI 10.1145/3832093.

## A049 · Do Coverage and Mutation Scores of LLM-Generated Test Suites Correlate with Their Effectiveness? (Replicability Study)
URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3832093
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Journal version of the replication study, concluding coverage and mutation are context-dependent proxies for LLM-generated suites and offering actionable guidance for interpreting prior evaluations.
CONCEPTS:
- **proxy metrics** — coverage and mutation score used in place of real-bug detection when evaluating generated suites. > "Prior work commonly evaluates generated test suites using proxy metrics such as code coverage and mutation score."
- **real-bug detection** — the effectiveness construct the proxies are validated against. > "re-examine the relationships among coverage, mutation, and real-bug detection effectiveness"
- **replicability study** — rerun of the two prior human-test studies on suites generated by a diverse set of LLMs. > "we conduct a large-scale replication study of these two prior works using a wide range of test suites generated by a diverse set of LLMs"
- **regression-style settings** — code assumed bug-free; the metrics still give meaningful cross-model signals. > "in regression-style settings where the code provided to the LLM can be reasonably assumed bug-free, these metrics can provide meaningful signals when comparing across models"
- **buggy code-under-test scenario** — an existing bug is to be exposed, and the metrics are no longer reliable indicators. > "the code-under-test may already be buggy and the goal is to expose the bug within the code-under-test, they no longer serve as reliable indicators"
- **suite size confounder** — little evidence that it dominates the correlations for LLM-generated tests. > "We also find little evidence that test suite size is a dominant confounder for correlations among coverage, mutation, and real-bug detection for LLM-generated tests."
- **context-dependence** — metric validity depends on the evaluation setting. > "We show that the usefulness of coverage and mutation is highly context-dependent"
- **actionable guidance for evaluating LLM-based test generation** — the stated deliverable of the paper, alongside a reinterpretation of prior results. > "we discuss how to interpret results from prior studies and provide actionable guidance for evaluating LLM-based test generation"
GUIDELINES:
- Classify the evaluation setting (regression-style vs. bug-exposing) before selecting metrics; do not carry validity across settings.
- Do not rely on coverage or mutation when the code under test may already contain the targeted bug.
- Re-examine the suite-size control before applying it; for LLM-generated tests it was not a dominant confounder.
- Re-read prior LLM test-generation results against the setting they measured before citing metric conclusions.
EVIDENCE: Abstract only on the extracted page. Reported: large-scale replication over suites from diverse LLMs; two settings distinguished; coverage/mutation meaningful across models in regression-style settings and unreliable in bug-exposing settings; little evidence of suite-size dominance. Publication record: received `30 January 2026`, accepted `25 June 2026`, published `1 October 2026`; PACMSE Vol. 3 Issue ISSTA, Article `ISSTA002`, pages `30–53`. Badges: `Artifacts Available / v1.1`, `Distinguished Paper`; reproduction package Zenodo `10.5281/zenodo.21437945`. `79` downloads, `0` citations at the metrics date (22 Oct 2026).
LIMITS: The extracted page holds only abstract, references and metadata; no numeric correlations, model list or benchmark description observable. Scope bounded by the two replicated constructs.
TOOLING: Code coverage tooling (references list `CodeCover`); mutation testing; Zenodo artifact; PACMSE artifact badge process.
LINKS: Inozemtseva et al.; Papadakis et al. (incl. ICSE '17 fault-revelation study); Abdullin, Derakhshanfar, Panichella, "Test Wars: A Comparative Study of SBST, Symbolic Execution, and LLM-Based Approaches to Unit Test Generation" (arXiv:2501.10200); A3Test (IST 2024); Andrews, Briand, Labiche, "Is mutation an appropriate tool for testing experiments?" (ICSE '05); CodeCover; PRIMG (EASE '25); NSERC funding.

## A050 · ASTER: Natural and multi-language unit test generation with LLMs
URL: https://research.ibm.com/blog/aster-llm-unit-testing
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: LLM prompting guided by lightweight program analysis can generate unit tests that are both high-coverage and "natural" — readable, human-like, and compilable — for multiple languages, including mocking of external dependencies.
CONCEPTS:
- **`ASTER` (Automated Test Case Generator)** — IBM Research's system realizing LLM-assisted test generation for Java and Python, built because usable generators exist for very few languages. > "That’s why our team at IBM Research decided to build the Automated Test Case Generator, or ASTER."
- **`naturalness`** — the property of generated tests having meaningful test names, variable names and assertions; conventional tools produce uninteresting sequences and "trivial or ineffective assertions". > "developers find automatically generated tests lacking in “naturalness” characteristics, suffering poor readability and comprehensibility, covering uninteresting sequences, and containing trivial or ineffective assertions."
- **`preprocessing via static analysis`** — extracting method signatures, call hierarchies and potential dependencies as context for prompts. > "The system performs a thorough static analysis of the application being tested to extract vital contextual information."
- **`LLM-guided test generation`** — crafting detailed prompts from static-analysis context so tests are syntactically correct and semantically rich. > "These prompts guide the models to generate unit tests that are not only syntactically correct but also semantically rich and aligned with human coding practices."
- **`postprocessing and refinement`** — validating that generated tests compile and execute, then iteratively fixing them through "targeted prompt enhancement". > "The generated tests undergo validation to ensure they compile and execute. ASTER iteratively refines these tests, addressing any errors through targeted prompt enhancement."
- **`coverage augmentation`** — identifying untested code paths and prompting the model for additional tests aimed at those paths. > "ASTER identifies untested code paths and instructs the LLMs to generate additional tests specifically targeting these areas, thereby improving overall code coverage."
- **`software mocking mechanisms`** — handling external dependencies such as database interactions or web service calls. > "ASTER incorporates software mocking mechanisms, enabling it to handle complex scenarios involving external dependencies, such as database interactions or web service calls."
- **`test smells / anti-patterns`** — cited as a known property of automatically generated tests that inhibits their adoption. > "All these factors inhibit the adoption of test generation tools in practice, as developers consider the tests generated by these tools to be hard to maintain"
GUIDELINES:
- Use `static analysis` before prompting; signature and call-hierarchy context is what makes prompts produce meaningful tests.
- Validate every generated test by compiling and executing it; feed errors back as "targeted prompt enhancement" rather than hand-fixing.
- Close the loop with coverage: find untested paths, regenerate for those paths specifically.
- Prefer smaller, internally hosted models when privacy/on-premises constraints exist; the reported loss was small relative to affordability gains.
EVIDENCE: Evaluated Granite-8B, Llama3-8B, Granite-34B, CodeLlama-34B, Llama3-70B, GPT4-turbo on Defects4J (Java SE), Java EE open-source/internal apps, and Python. Java SE: coverage "slightly lower in some cases (-7%) and considerably higher in other cases (4x-5x)" than EvoSuite. Java EE: ASTER exceeds EvoSuite "by 26.4%, 10.6%, and 18.5% in terms of line, branch, and method coverage". Python: "+9.8%, +26.5%, and +22.5%" over CodaMosa. Smaller models lost "0.1%, 6.3%, and 2.7%" line/branch/method versus larger models. Survey: 161 responses; "over 70%" willing to add ASTER tests with minor or no changes.
LIMITS: LLMs hallucinate and have limited access to the application under test, so tests "very often do not compile and run"; repair effort can exceed writing tests from scratch. Coverage results are language/framework specific (Java, Python). Blog-length technical note, not the full paper.
TOOLING: EvoSuite, CodaMosa, Granite-8B/34B, Llama3-8B/70B, CodeLlama-34B, GPT4-turbo, Defects4J, IBM watsonx Code Assistant.
LINKS: Fraser/Staats/McMinn/Arcuri/Padberg, "Does automated unit test generation really help software testers?" (TOSEM 2015); Panichella et al., "Revisiting test smells in automatically generated tests" (ICSME 2020); arXiv 2409.03093; ICSE 2025 SEIP Distinguished Paper.

## A051 · Prompt engineering in LLMs for automated unit test generation: A large-scale study
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-026-10840-4
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: The first large-scale empirical evaluation of LLM-generated unit tests at the full class level, comparing four models against EvoSuite under execution-driven assessment, reasoning-based prompting, and real-world testing scenarios.
CONCEPTS:
- **`full class level`** — generation/evaluation target, as opposed to single-method or single-function prompting. > "This study presents the first large-scale empirical evaluation of LLM-generated unit tests at the full class level"
- **`execution-driven assessment`** — one of three evaluation axes the authors say earlier LLM test-generation research lacks, and which their study covers. > "Although LLMs show promise for test generation, existing research lacks comprehensive evaluation across execution-driven assessment, reasoning-based prompting, and real-world testing scenarios."
- **`reasoning-based prompting`** — prompt strategies that elicit reasoning, named as the second axis previous work fails to evaluate. > "Although LLMs show promise for test generation, existing research lacks comprehensive evaluation across execution-driven assessment, reasoning-based prompting, and real-world testing scenarios."
- **`search-based software testing (SBST)`** — baseline paradigm producing efficient but poorly readable/maintainable tests. > "Although search-based software testing improves efficiency, it produces tests with poor readability and maintainability."
- **`test smells`** — quality defect category the paper invokes through the test-smells literature it cites. > "Revisiting test smells in automatically generated tests: limitations, pitfalls, and opportunities"
- **`readability / maintainability`** — the two qualities the abstract identifies as SBST's weakness and the reason LLM generation is worth studying. > "Although search-based software testing improves efficiency, it produces tests with poor readability and maintainability."
- **`CMD`** — a third benchmark dataset used alongside Defects4J and SF110, described only as "a dataset mitigating L…" in the accessible abstract. > "systematically analyzing four state-of-the-art models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Mistral 7B, and Mixtral 8x7B) against EvoSuite across 216,300 generated test cases targeting Defects4J, SF110, and CMD"
GUIDELINES:
- Evaluate generated tests at class level, not snippet level, if you want results that transfer to real codebases.
- Include a search-based baseline (`EvoSuite`) rather than only comparing LLMs with each other.
- Combine execution-driven metrics with readability/maintainability-oriented analysis; coverage alone is an incomplete criterion.
- Use benchmark sets that include contamination-mitigating data alongside `Defects4J` and `SF110`.
- Log token counts with `tiktoken` and parse Java with `javalang` when replicating the pipeline (from the paper's tooling notes).
EVIDENCE: 216,300 generated test cases; four models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Mistral 7B, Mixtral 8x7B) compared against EvoSuite; targets Defects4J, SF110, and CMD. Abstract reports "1002 Accesses" and "6 Citations"; no numeric outcome statements were accessible beyond the setup.
LIMITS: Only the abstract and front/back matter were retrievable (subscription paywall); the abstract itself is truncated mid-sentence in the accessible text, so detailed findings, effect sizes, and the eleven-guideline-style conclusions are not available from this source. No results can be quoted beyond the design.
TOOLING: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Mistral 7B, Mixtral 8x7B, EvoSuite, Defects4J, SF110, CMD, JaCoCo, javalang, tiktoken, Checkstyle, PMD, SpotBugs, TSDetect.
LINKS: Schäfer et al. (LLM unit test generation, TSE), Yuan et al. (ChatGPT unit tests), Tang et al. (ChatGPT vs SBST), Alshahwan et al. (Meta automated test improvement), Fraser & Arcuri (EvoSuite), Panichella et al. (test smells), anonymous.4open.science replication repository.

## A052 · What is Contract Testing? | JFrog
URL: https://jfrog.com/learn/devsecops/contract-testing/
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: Contract testing validates isolated interactions between a designated consumer and provider against a coded, predefined agreement about request and response specifications, giving fast, scalable test runs without deploying whole distributed environments.
CONCEPTS:
- **`contract testing`** — a methodology validating isolated interactions between a designated consumer and provider against a coded, predefined agreement. > "This practice verifies that a designated service consumer and service provider conform to a coded, predefined agreement outlining request and response specifications."
- **`consumer-driven`** — the consumer defines contract terms and judges whether the provider meets them; suited to projects where consumers change more often than providers. > "Consumer-driven testing is beneficial in projects where consumers change more frequently than providers."
- **`provider-driven`** — the provider defines the terms; suited to fast-changing providers and to proving backward compatibility across consumer versions. > "In provider-driven contract testing, the service that receives and responds to requests (the provider) defines contract terms."
- **`API mocking`** — simulating requests/responses from API design specifications, so contract tests can run before the API exists. > "API mocking makes it possible to perform contract tests even if developers haven’t fully implemented an API."
- **`boundary discrepancies`** — mismatches at service boundaries, caught early in the SDLC. > "Catching boundary discrepancies early in the software development lifecycle prevents integration bottlenecks, reduces pipeline maintenance overhead, and safeguards runtime architectural stability."
- **Root-cause clarity** — testing only two services localizes failures, unlike end-to-end runs. > "By testing just two services, it’s easier to pinpoint the source of a problem, such as a slow response to a certain type of request."
GUIDELINES:
- Follow three steps: `identify services to test` (services that commonly interact), `define a contract` in code, `execute the test` by generating requests/responses in a test environment and evaluating them.
- Prefer consumer-driven contracts when consumers churn faster; prefer provider-driven when the provider churns or when many consumer versions must keep working.
- Keep end-to-end integration tests for evaluating the whole user experience, typically late in development; use contract tests earlier.
- Do not treat contract testing as a replacement for API testing where security risks must be checked.
- Version and manage "contracts, stubs, and mocks" centrally alongside binaries, and automate compatibility checks inside CI/CD pipelines.
- Pick tooling by direction of control: `Pact` (consumer-driven, multi-language), `Spring Cloud Contract` (provider-driven, Java-centric, Groovy or YAML), `Dredd` (tests against API documentation), `RestAssured` (Java REST), `OpenAPI` (specification format for generating contracts).
EVIDENCE: none.
LIMITS: Promotional vendor page for the JFrog Platform; no measurements, no case data, and the platform section is product positioning rather than evidence.
TOOLING: Pact, Spring Cloud Contract, Dredd, RestAssured, OpenAPI (formerly Swagger), JFrog Platform/Artifactory, JFrog Xray.
LINKS: JFrog "integration tests", "continuous delivery", "API security" topic pages; JFrog webinar (Fannie Mae) and demo/trial links.

## A053 · Why contract testing can be essential for microservices | TechTarget
URL: https://www.techtarget.com/searchapparchitecture/tip/Why-contract-testing-can-be-essential-for-microservices
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: End-to-end integration testing of large microservice estates is unmanageable, so teams should adopt contract testing, which checks two services at a time against a shared contract using mocks.
CONCEPTS:
- **`end-to-end integration tests`** — spin up replica instances of services and test interactions; adequate for "a relatively simple application that only encompasses a handful of microservices". > "End-to-end integration tests evaluate how multiple services interact by spinning up replica instances of those individual services and running tests against each one."
- Failure mode: `too many integrations to test` — the number of interaction paths and dependencies outruns any test set. > "There are simply too many integration paths that exist within large collections of microservices -- and too many complex dependencies -- to ever be sure each possible interaction was tested."
