- **Conformance** — claimable as full or tailored, and the organization must say which. > "The organization or individual shall assert whether full or tailored conformance to this standard is claimed."
GUIDELINES:
- Techniques cover only `TD2` (derive test conditions), `TD3` (derive coverage items), `TD4` (derive test cases); TD1, TD5, TD6 are technique-independent.
- EP: partition inputs and outputs; conditions and coverage items coincide; use the `minimized` approach for valid items and separate cases for invalid items ("negative test cases").
- BVA: partition into ordered sets and subsets; choose two-value (boundary plus value each side) or three-value boundary testing; count duplicated values once (B.2.3.4.3).
- Syntax testing: express formats as sequences of, iterations of, or selections between; each selection option is a coverage item ("Blue", "Red", "Green"); for `+` derive "one letter" and "more than one letter"; for a 100-repetition maximum derive "100 letters" and "more than 100 letters"; mutate to an invalid value such as "Yellow".
- Classification tree: `minimized` = fewest coverage items covering all classes once; `maximized` = each possible combination.
- Conformance is `full` or `tailored`; the organization "shall assert whether full or tailored conformance" is claimed.
EVIDENCE: none in the extract (Annex F, "Test Design Technique Coverage Effectiveness," is titled only).
LIMITS: The standard "does not prescribe a process for test design and implementation"; Annex examples demonstrate manual application, with automation supporting only some techniques. The extract ends in clause 5.2.4, so clause 6 coverage measures appear only as table-of-contents entries.
TOOLING: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1/-2/-3; ISO/IEC 25010; BS 7925-2.
LINKS: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-1, -2, -3, planned Part 5 (keyword-driven testing); ISO/IEC 25010; BS 7925-2.

## A074 · Optimal test case generation for boundary value analysis
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11219-023-09659-9
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Because full boundary coverage is usually infeasible, the paper defines `boundary coverage distance (BCD)` — how far a test set lies from the boundaries — and generates optimal test inputs from it under random testing.
CONCEPTS:
- **`boundary coverage`** — the share of boundary values a suite actually executes. > "Boundary coverage is the percentage of boundary values that are executed by a test suite."
- **`boundary` (formal)** — the inputs where execution crosses from one equivalent partition into another, defined through a set of invertible input operations. > "Intuitively, the boundary is the input of software that crosses two equivalent partitions."
- **Partitions from outputs** — categories of output induce the input partitions, so `I_i` collects the inputs whose output falls in category `O_i`. > "Suppose that the output of software is divided into several categories."
- **`boundary coverage distance (BCD)`** — distance from suite `T` to boundary set `B`, where small values mean inputs sit near the boundaries. > "If BCD is small, the test inputs are placed close to the boundaries."
- **`expansion`** — a test input is credited with covering everything within a given operation distance. > "The expansion means that each test input covers the test inputs that are within a given distance."
- **BCD lower and upper limits** — sampling boundary points gives a lower bound, and covering the boundary with components (segments, triangles) gives an upper bound, both computable without enumerating every boundary value; an empty suite gives BCD `∞`. > "To compute BCD, we need to obtain all the boundary values. As mentioned before, it is not easy to get all the boundary values."
- **`Remark 1`** — which inputs count as boundary depends on the chosen operation set: adding diagonal ±1 moves makes `(-1,-1)` a boundary. > "In other words, the boundaries depend on the definitions of operations in the formal definition."
- **`Remark 2`** — boundaries also depend on how outputs are defined, so path-based (white-box) outputs change the partitions. > "if the output of software, the behavior of software, is defined by the execution paths, as in a white-box approach, the equivalent partitions are changed"
GUIDELINES:
- Judge BVA quality by distance to the boundary rather than by enumerating all boundaries.
- Use lower and upper BCD limits, computable "without extracting all the boundary values."
- Set BCD to `∞` for an empty test set: every partition needs an input.
- Generate inputs that `minimize BCD` under random testing (three algorithms proposed).
EVIDENCE: Worked example (English examination: listening and reading each out of 100; credit requires both `> 50` and total `> 120`) has three partitions and `963` boundary values despite being "a simple program." Metrics: 6,191 accesses, 15 citations; Software Quality Journal vol. 32, pp. 543–566 (2024). The extract stops in Section 3.2, so algorithm and experimental results are not quoted.
LIMITS: Stated challenges: no formal specifications; multidimensional spaces where boundaries miss "conventional notions of limits"; dynamic behavior producing shifting boundaries; combinatorial explosion of boundary combinations; and that "achieving complete boundary coverage might not always be the most efficient or cost-effective strategy."
TOOLING: none named.
LINKS: Reid (1997) on EP, BVA and random testing; White & Cohen (1980); Li & Miao (2012) model-based logic boundary coverage; Kosmatov et al. (2004) boundary coverage criteria for formal models; Zhu, Hall & May (1997).

## A075 · Data-oriented testing - TMAP
URL: https://www.tmap.net/building-blocks/data-oriented-testing
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: Data-oriented design starts from the data item: its equivalence classes (partitions) and the boundaries between them, with two-, three- or four-value BVA chosen by risk.
CONCEPTS:
- **`classes` (partitions) and `boundaries`** — the two terms that organise design once a data item is the starting point. > "When we take a data item as a starting point for test design, there are two important terms to consider: the classes (also called partitions) and the boundaries between these classes."
- **`Discrete values versus continuous value range`** — only a continuous range has boundaries between classes; discrete outputs such as admitted / not admitted have none. > "The difference between discrete values and continuous value range is that with a continuous range there are boundaries between the classes."
- **`Equivalence partitioning (EP)`** — determines all relevant classes for a data item and writes exactly one test case per class, treating the class as the test situation. > "This technique determines all relevant classes of values for a data item and creates one (and only one) test case per class."
- **`three-value boundary value analysis`** — a case for the boundary itself plus the values just below and just above it (99, 100, 101). > "This means you will make a test case for the boundary value itself, and for the values just below and just above the boundary value."
- **`two-value boundary value analysis`** — just one value per class (99 and 100). > "Another way of looking at it is just choosing one value for every class."
- **`four-value BVA`** — for high risk, adds a case for the output class that the boundary values covered only once (98). > "This would mean adding an extra test case for the output class that was just covered once."
- **Output-based coverage** — choosing cases from output classes instead of input classes can reach full coverage with two cases (50 kg, 200 kg), leaving sufficiency to the tester. > "Only two test cases, for example 50 kg and 200 kg, would then give 100% coverage."
- **`data combination test (DCoT)`** — the technique for combinations of values across several data items. > "When we want to test combinations of values of data items, the data combination test (DCoT) is a very useful technique."
- **`Syntactic test (SYN)`** — with the semantic test, establishes how far the system is proof against invalid or nonsensical input. > "This establishes the degree to which the system is proof against invalid, or “nonsense” input that is offered to the system."
GUIDELINES:
- State boundaries precisely: `between 100 and 300 kilograms` leaves `100 kg` ambiguous.
- EP example (total weight `100`–`300` kg): three classes, extended to six test situations — `0 kg <= x < 100 kg`, `100 kg <= x <= 300 kg`, `300 kg < x <= 999 kg`, `x < 1 kg`, `999 kg < x`, `Not numeric`.
- Choose `-200 kg`: "by choosing -200 we might get the result 'admitted' if the minus sign would not be considered by the system."
- Single boundary → three-value BVA; continuous range with multiple boundaries → two-value "will be sufficient": `99, 100, 300, 301`, since `300` gives the same confidence about boundary `100` as `101`.
- First boundary: `99` (not admitted), `100` and `101` (admitted).
- High risk → combine EP and BVA, testing boundaries plus mid-class values: "six test situations and ten test cases."
- Scale offsets to the unit: in grams the boundary is `99,999 kg`, not `99 kg`.
EVIDENCE: none (worked examples only).
LIMITS: EP suits "low risk, or as an additional technique," resting on an unverified within-class assumption; the BVA discussion omits invalid classes; whether two output-based cases suffice is left to the tester.
TOOLING: TMAP building blocks and glossary.
LINKS: TMAP pages on boundary value analysis, DCoT, SYN, elementary comparison test, orthogonal arrays and pairwise testing, CRUD and integrity rules, operational profiles; `[Tuinhout 2008]`.

## A076 · Boundary Value Analysis & Equivalence Partitioning with Examples
URL: https://people.scs.carleton.ca/~jeanpier/Fall2021/Topic%202%20-%20Beyond%20TDD/2-%20Equivalence%20Partitioning/2-%20More%20Examples%20-%20Boundary%20Value%20Analysis%20&%20Equivalence%20Partitioning%20with%20Examples.pdf
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: Exhaustive testing is infeasible, so two complementary techniques — equivalence partitioning to pick one value per class and boundary value analysis to probe class edges — select a small, effective test set.
CONCEPTS:
- **`Boundary testing`** — testing at the extreme ends or boundaries between partitions of the input values. > "Boundary testing is the process of testing between extreme ends or boundaries between partitions of the input values."
- **Boundary names** — the ends go by paired names: Start-End, Lower-Upper, Maximum-Minimum, Just Inside-Just Outside. > "So these extreme ends like Start- End, Lower- Upper, Maximum-Minimum, Just Inside-Just Outside values are called boundary values"
- **Five boundary picks** — per input variable, take the minimum, just above the minimum, a nominal value, just below the maximum, and the maximum. > "The basic idea in boundary value testing is to select input variable values at their"
- **`Equivalent Class Partitioning`** — a black-box technique, applied with code invisible to the tester, usable at unit, integration and system level. > "Equivalent Class Partitioning is a black box technique (code is not visible to tester) which can be applied to all levels of testing like unit, integration, system, etc."
- **`Equivalence Partitions` / `Equivalence Classes`** — the divided sets from which one value per partition is picked. > "The divided sets are called Equivalence Partitions or Equivalence Classes."
- **Partition hypothesis** — one value passing means all in the partition pass; one failing means all fail. > "The hypothesis behind this technique is that if one condition/value in a partition passes all others will also pass."
- **`Boundary Value Analysis`** — the companion technique that tests both valid and invalid boundaries, also called range checking. > "As you may observe, you test values at both valid and invalid boundaries. Boundary Value Analysis is also called range checking."
- **Ordering** — partitioning is done first, boundary testing on top of it. > "In Boundary Testing, Equivalence Class Partitioning plays a good role Boundary Testing comes after the Equivalence Class Partitioning."
GUIDELINES:
- Order Pizza field (valid `1 to 10`; `11 to 99` invalid, message "Only 10 Pizza can be ordered"): conditions include any number greater than `10` (say `11`), any number `0` or below, numbers `1 to 10`, and any 3-digit number such as `-100`.
- BVA values for an input box accepting `1 to 10`: `0` (not accept), `1`, `2`, `9`, `10` (accept), `11` (not accept).
- Password accepting `6` to `10` characters: partitions `0-5`, `6-10`, `11-14` are equivalent; scenario 1 enters `0` to `5` (not accept), scenario 2 `6` to `10` (accept), scenario 3 `11` to `14` (not accept).
- Test "values at both valid and invalid boundaries."
- Apply EP and BVA together, at all levels of testing.
EVIDENCE: none (tutorial examples). Motivation: testing all pizza-field values would need "more than 100" test cases.
LIMITS: Single-field, single-boundary illustrations only; no guidance on multi-boundary ranges or values per boundary. Partition diagrams are absent from the extracted text.
TOOLING: none named.
LINKS: sibling Guru99 tutorials (Testing Techniques, Decision Table Testing, Levels of Testing); no standards cited.

## A077 · Guideline: Equivalence Class Analysis
URL: https://swi.cs.vsb.cz/RUPLarge/core.base_rup/guidances/guidelines/equivalence_class_analysis_F89FE998.html
TYPE: official docs
THESIS: Equivalence class analysis reduces potential tests to a minimal, error-finding set, extended by boundary value analysis, special values and category-partition.
CONCEPTS:
- **`Equivalence class analysis`** (synonyms `equivalence partitioning`, `domain analysis`) — a black-box analysis that shrinks the potential test set to the tests most likely to expose errors; valid and invalid classes are distinguished. > "attempts to reduce the total number of potential tests to a minimal set of tests that will uncover as many errors as possible"
- **Representative equivalence** — a test built from a class representative is deemed equivalent to testing every other value of that class, so a clean run is generalised to the class. > "It is a method that partitions the set of inputs and outputs into a finite number of equivalence classes"
- **Sampling strategy** — classes exist to cut the combinatorial explosion of conceivable tests, giving a logical basis for selecting a subset. > "The power of Equivalence Classes lies in their ability to guide the tester using a sampling strategy to reduce the combinatorial explosion of potentially necessary tests."
- **`Boundary Value Analysis`** — boundary conditions find failures more often than non-boundary conditions, using `min`, `min+`, `max-`, `max`. > "In each of the equivalence classes, the boundary conditions are considered to have a higher rate of success identifying resulting failures than non-boundary conditions."
- **`Special Values`** — zero, time fields and date fields are singled out as rich sources of failure once class and boundary analysis are done. > "For an integer type, zero should always be tested if it is in the valid equivalence class."
- **`"Category-Partition" method`** (Ostrand and Balcer) — works from the specification rather than the code, so specification faults surface before implementation. > "The main benefit of this method is its ability to expose errors before the code has been written because the input source is the specification and the tests result from the analysis of that specification."
GUIDELINES:
- Range (`10 to 100`): one valid class, two invalid (less than `10`, greater than `100`).
- Enumerated set (`RED, WHITE, BLACK, GREEN, BROWN`): one valid, one invalid class; "Each value of the valid equivalence class should be handled distinctly."
- Ranges: floating valid `-1.0` to `1.0` → test `-1.0`, `1.0`, `-1.001`, `1.001`; integer valid `10` to `100` → test `9`, `10`, `100`, `101`.
- Uppercase letter: test `A`, `Z`, `@` and `[` — "`@` is just below A and `[` is just beyond the Z."
- Ordered set: "pay attention on the first and the last element"; sum to `n` → test `n-1`, `n`, `n+1`.
- List input: test list values; "All the other values are invalid." File I/O: check the "first and last characters in the file."
- Money range `a` to `b`: test `a - 0.01` and `b + 0.01`.
- Sub-ranges (non-overlapping): test values on the boundaries, beyond the upper, below the lower.
- Time fields: "59 and 0 should always be tested as the upper and lower bound for each field," plus `-1` and `60`; dates: days in a month, February in leap and non-leap years.
- Category-partition: decompose the specification, list parameters and environment conditions, classify into categories, partition into choices, add constraints; "If a choice causes an error, don't combine it with other choices."
EVIDENCE: none; the class-generalization claim is cited to Myers.
LIMITS: Boundary rules are labeled "recommendations"; effective special-value discovery depends on tester experience. No quantitative effectiveness data.
TOOLING: IBM Rational Unified Process (RUP) guidance set.
LINKS: Myers (1979); White & Cohen (1980); Clarke, Hassell & Richardson; Zeil, Afifi & White; Jeng & Weyuker; Jorgensen; Woodward & Al-khanjari; Hamlet; Kaner, Bach & Pettichord; Podgurski & Yang; Beizer; Howden; Ostrand & Balcer (1988).

## A078 · Practical Combinatorial Testing (NIST SP 800-142)
URL: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-C13-PURL-gpo14815/pdf/GOVPUB-C13-PURL-gpo14815.pdf
TYPE: official docs
THESIS: Because real failures are triggered by interactions among only a few parameters, covering all t-way value combinations for small t (roughly 4- to 6-way) yields high assurance at tractable cost — provided array generation and expected results are solved.
CONCEPTS:
- **`interaction failures`** — failures that appear only when two or more input values combine to drive the program to a wrong result. > "because they are only exposed when two or more input values interact to cause the program to reach an incorrect result"
- **`combinatorial testing`** — a cost-reducing, effectiveness-raising method built on the insight that not every parameter contributes to every failure. > "Combinatorial testing is a method that can reduce cost and increase the effectiveness of software testing for many applications."
- **`pairwise (2-way) testing`** — the accepted common approach, chosen because it is tractable and reasonably effective, not because it is sufficient. > "accepted as the common approach to combinatorial testing because it is computationally tractable and reasonably effective"
- **`covering array`** — the core artefact: columns are parameters, rows are tests, and all t-way combinations appear. > "The key component is a covering array, which includes all t- way combinations. Each column is a parameter. Each row is a test."
- **`t-way combinations`** — covering all t-way combinations is a century-old mathematical problem; efficient algorithms made beyond-pairwise practical, and 4- to 6-way coverage is the assurance-raising target. > "Testing all 4-way to 6-way combinations may therefore provide reasonably high assurance."
- **Discretization** — continuous parameters with ranges of `+/- 2³²` or more must be reduced to a few distinct values before arrays can be built. > "These values must be discretized to a few distinct values."
- **`test oracle problem`** — without a way to know the expected output, a large generated suite is useless. > "Generating 1,000 test data inputs is of little help if we cannot determine what the system under test (SUT) should produce as output for each of the 1,000 tests."
- **`configuration testing` / `input parameter testing`** — the two applications: platform stacks (OS, browser, protocol, CPU, DBMS) and input settings such as font options. > "Combinatorial testing can be applied to configurations, input data, or both."
- **Advanced extensions** — sequence covering arrays, combinatorial coverage measurement, assertion-based and model-based oracles, and fault localization by set-theoretic analysis, with formal models supplying expected results. > "discusses advanced topics such as the use of formal models of software to determine the expected results for each possible set of test inputs"
GUIDELINES:
- Set test strength from interaction data: failures were triggered by "a maximum of 4-way to 6-way interactions."
- Do not rely on pairwise alone: "pairwise testing may miss 10% to 40% or more of system faults."
- Coverage illustration: a 3-way array over binary parameters uses `13` tests "as compared with 1,024 for exhaustive coverage."
- Generate arrays with a tool (e.g. `ACTS`) rather than by hand.
- Establish an oracle — assertions or a formal model — before generating large suites.
EVIDENCE: A 2003 NIST report estimated inadequate testing costs the US economy `$59.5 billion` yearly while `50% to 80%` of development budgets go to testing. NIST interaction studies begun in `1999` across medical devices, a browser, a server and a NASA distributed database found all failures triggerable by at most 4- to 6-way interactions; Figure 2 plots cumulative detection rates for strengths `1` to `6`.
LIMITS: "While not conclusive, these results are interesting"; the interaction data spans limited domains; the pairwise gap is a range (10% to 40% or more); discretization remains a modeling judgement. The extract covers the front matter and Chapter 2 only; later chapters are summarized from the table of contents.
TOOLING: `ACTS` (free from NIST, csrc.nist.gov/acts); sequence covering arrays; assertion-based and model-based oracles.
LINKS: NIST 2003 cost-of-testing report; interaction-failure studies [34, 35, 36, 65]; Appendices A–D.

## A079 · Test doubles: mocks, stubs, and fakes
URL: https://principledcraft.dev/principles/testing/writing-good-tests/test-doubles
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: Test doubles replace external dependencies, and choosing among stub, mock and fake determines whether tests verify behaviour or mere choreography — so prefer stubs and fakes, and mock only to verify an interaction.
CONCEPTS:
- **`test double`** — the replacement used in tests for an external dependency such as a database, an API or the file system. > "When code depends on something external, a database, an API, the file system, you often need to replace that dependency in tests. The replacements are called test doubles, and they come in several flavours."
- **`stub`** — returns canned data and asserts nothing about how it was called, only supplying the answers the code needs. > "It doesn’t verify how it was called; it just provides the answers your code needs to keep running."
- **`mock`** — records its calls so the test can assert on them; it verifies interaction rather than result. > "A mock records how it was called and lets you make assertions about those calls."
- **`fake`** — a working implementation that takes a shortcut, e.g. an in-memory database instead of PostgreSQL or a local file instead of S3. > "A fake is a working implementation that takes a shortcut."
- **Stubs and fakes as the default** — given a choice, these produce more resilient tests because they check outcomes rather than interactions. > "When you have the choice, stubs and fakes tend to produce more resilient tests than mocks."
- **Choreography testing** — a heavily mocked test exercises the order of method calls, not the behaviour of the system. > "This test is really testing the choreography of method calls, not the behaviour of the system."
- **Implementation coupling** — reordering calls or renaming a method breaks the test even when the end result is identical. > "If you rearrange the order of calls, or rename a method, the test breaks, even if the end result is identical."
- **Dependency-count smell** — needing four mocks is a signal that the unit is doing too much. > "If a function needs four mocks to test, the function is doing too much."
- **False confidence** — a mocked test can pass while the real integration is broken, surfacing bad SQL or a schema change only in production. > "There’s another risk with mocks that’s easy to miss: a mocked test can pass while the real integration is broken."
- **Complementary kinds** — mocks test logic in isolation while integration tests check that the pieces fit, so both are needed. > "Mocks let you test logic in isolation. Integration tests verify that the pieces actually fit together."
GUIDELINES:
- Apply the hierarchy: "use the real thing when practical, a fake when the real thing is too slow or complex, a stub when you just need canned data, and a mock only when you specifically need to verify that an interaction happened."
- Treat heavy mocking as a design signal; the response "isn't usually to write better mocks; it's to restructure the code so it needs fewer dependencies."
- Flag tests that are "mostly mock setup with a thin assertion at the end."
- Keep both mocked unit tests and integration tests — "leaning too heavily on mocks means you're only getting half the picture."
EVIDENCE: none (guidance with illustrative Python snippets).
LIMITS: Prescriptive heuristics without measurements; the "four mocks" figure is a rule of thumb. Mocks remain legitimate for interaction checks, so the guidance is a preference, not a prohibition.
TOOLING: Python-style doubles (`Mock`, `assert_called_once`, stub repositories, in-memory stores).
LINKS: "Test Behaviour, Not Implementation," "Design for Testability," "Managing Dependencies," "Practical test tips," "Advanced Testing Techniques."

## A080 · Choosing the Right Test Double - Tanzu
URL: https://blogs.vmware.com/tanzu/choosing-the-right-test-double/
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Test doubles exist so a unit's tests pass or fail only on that unit's behavior, and choosing among the five kinds (dummy, stub, spy, mock, fake) follows from what the test needs to control or observe — with stateful dependencies requiring a fake that itself passes the dependency's own tests.
CONCEPTS:
- **test double** — a stand-in for a dependency, named after movie stunt doubles, that lets you control inputs and inspect how your code interacts with them. > "they allow you to control the inputs into your code and to inspect how your code interacts with them"
- **dummy** — a double that throws an exception when any method on it is invoked; used to prove a code path is *not* executed (branching logic). > "A dummy is a test double that throws an exception when a method on it is invoked."
- **stub** — returns pre-configured, hard-coded data when its methods are called, and must be configured *before* the SUT runs. > "A stub is a test double that returns pre-configured, hard-coded data when its methods are called."
- **spy** — records invocations and their parameters so you can ask afterwards whether and how methods were called; assertions come *after* the SUT executes. > "A spy is a test double that records the invocations of its methods, along with any parameters passed in, so that you can find out afterward whether and how its methods were called."
- **mock** — combination of stub and spy: control return data and record calls, then `verify()` that expected invocations with expected parameters happened. > "You use a mock for situations where you want to both control the data returned by a method and also confirm that the method was called with the correct values as arguments."
- **fake** — same business-logic behavior as the real component but a simplified implementation; used most often for stateful components (e.g., a database-backed service). > "A fake is a test double that has the same business-logic behavior as the real component it’s doubling, but using a simplified implementation."
- **stateful behavior** — a dependency whose method results change as other methods are called (`deposit()`/`withdraw()` change what `getBalance()` returns); no stub/mock/spy can model it. > "A stub only allows you to configure it to return a hard-coded piece of data, not one that can change along the way."
- **"behaves like a X" means precisely "passes the X tests"** — contract defined by a shared test suite, not interface conformance; `BadBankAccount` implements `BankAccount` yet always returns 0. > "“To behave like a BankAccount” means precisely “to pass the BankAccount tests”."
GUIDELINES:
- Set a stub's data *before* the SUT executes; ask a spy about calls only *after* it executes.
- For stateful dependencies use a fake, not stub/spy/mock — "the problem with using a spy ... doesn't resolve the problem with stubbing `getBalance()`".
- Write a reusable parameterized test (`testBankAccount(createBankAccount: () => BankAccount)`) with no opinion about which implementation arrives; run it against both `() => new RealBankAccount()` and `() => new FakeBankAccount()`.
- Fakes "must themselves be tested", ideally "using the same test cases as those used for the real component".
- Do not use a dummy where any code path must call the dependency (e.g., `getBalance()` must not throw).
- Write your own spy if the framework lacks one — "writing a spy isn't that difficult".
EVIDENCE: none (illustrative code only: 401K `4000 × 0.12 = 480`; 1000 + 500 refund = 1500; 1000 − 300 owed = 700).
LIMITS: notes only that some frameworks ship built-in spies and that the mock syntax shown is not Jest-supported, "for illustration purposes only"; no scale or maintenance claims.
TOOLING: Jest-style `expect`/`toHaveBeenCalledWith`; JavaScript/TypeScript examples.
LINKS: none external; "stunt doubles" analogy; no citations.

## A081 · Use cases of various types of test doubles for unit testing
URL: https://www.techtarget.com/it-infrastructure/tip/Use-cases-of-various-types-of-test-doubles-for-unit-testing
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: Test doubles should be used jointly with unit tests to limit interactions with systems outside the codebase, and teams should start with the simplest double (a mock) and escalate to stubs, fakes and spies only as tests demand more fidelity.
CONCEPTS:
- **test double** — a functional substitution for a dependency; also usable for load testing third-party services whose rate limits make scale testing impossible. > "Test doubles can be useful for load testing, as they can stand in as functional substitutions for third-party services whose rate limits make testing at scale impossible."
- **unit test** — a test of a small unit of code, exercising one method or function in an isolated scenario. > "Ideally, a unit test is just a test of a small unit of your code."
- **mock** — a bare-minimum shell object created by a library (Mockito or similar) so the SUT can be constructed; test asserts on SUT state, not the dependency. > "Mocking is a perfect solution here because we need only the bare minimum of a shell of the BookDBConnector object to get the code to run."
- **white box testing** — the failure mode of mocking: the tests define the implementation behind the class, so results are predetermined and the suite depends on that implementation. > "When a team mocks classes, the implementation behind the class or function being tested is defined by the tests, and the results from the mocked class are predetermined."
- **black box testing** — the ideal: validate classes/functions without knowing the implementation, so updating internals creates no dependent technical debt. > "Ideally, tests should validate classes and functions as a black box, where the implementation isn't known."
- **stub** — takes mocks a bit further by defining stubbed/hard-coded responses in the mocked class (`MockBookDBConnector.getListOfBooks()` returns three hard-coded titles). > "Stubs enable more in-depth testing than mocks since they are able to provide a bare minimum functionality over the mere placeholder of a mocked class."
- **fake** — a stubbed class with added functionality replicating production more closely (`FakeBookDBConnector` with `books`, `checkoutOutBooks`, `checkOutBook()`). > "Our FakeBookDBConnector class now emulates a production BookDBConnector class even closer by providing the functionality to check out books."
- **spy** — built from a production object with selected methods stubbed, leaving the rest of production behavior intact; "possibly the most complex type of test double". > "Testers create test spies from a production object but stub it to modify specific behaviors or methods, while leaving the rest of the production behavior untouched."
- **test spy** (alternate sense) — a recording method/class variable counting how often a stubbed method is called; useful for unintended race conditions or indeterminate behavior. > "it is also true that the term test spy can refer to a method that records some state about its usage"
- **BookStore/BookDBConnector** — running example: digital-book app where `BookStore` takes a `BookDBConnector` at instantiation. > "A simplified version of a class BookStore within the application may take an object during instantiation called BookDBConnector."
GUIDELINES:
- "Start with the simplest option of a basic mock before diving into higher-order test doubles."
- "mocking should be your first choice" over spies; "it may be best to avoid using spies if possible".
- Prefer black-box assertions so implementation changes create no "burdensome technical debt".
- Remember fake classes "may need to update with major changes to the corresponding production classes".
- Use doubles with unit tests while limiting interaction with systems outside the codebase.
EVIDENCE: none (worked example only).
LIMITS: states mocks "can make your tests less meaningful if the mocked class doesn't represent the production class well"; no measurement of how often this occurs. Article is explicitly a vendor tip, part 3 of a 3-part series.
TOOLING: Mockito and "other mocking libraries"; Python-like and Java-like pseudocode; `spy()`/`when(...).thenReturn(...)`.
LINKS: TechTarget definitions of unit testing and white box; "Stubs vs. mocks in software testing" (TheServerSide); related "Inside 5 types of test doubles".

## A082 · Use cases of various types of test doubles for unit testing
URL: https://www.techtarget.com/searchsoftwarequality/tip/Use-cases-of-various-types-of-test-doubles-for-unit-testing
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: Same TechTarget tip as A081, published under the Search Software Quality section: test doubles belong alongside unit tests to limit interaction with out-of-codebase systems, and the right double is the simplest one that gives the test the fidelity it needs.
CONCEPTS:
- **test double** — functional substitution for third-party services; also covers load testing where service rate limits block testing at scale. > "Test doubles can be useful for load testing, as they can stand in as functional substitutions for third-party services whose rate limits make testing at scale impossible."
- **unit test** — small unit exercised in an isolated scenario; mocks are a less common workaround to third-party services' rate limits because they target unit and lower-level integration tests. > "A unit test should be exercising some method or function from your application in an isolated scenario."
- **mock** — bare shell enabling construction of `BookStore(BookDBConnector)`; assertion is on `bookStore.booksCheckedOut == 0`. > "Mocking is the easiest and most widely known type of test double."
- **white box** dependency — mocking pins the implementation, so tests are predetermined and coupled to internals. > "When a team mocks classes, the implementation behind the class or function being tested is defined by the tests, and the results from the mocked class are predetermined."
- **black box** validation — the target: tests should not know implementation, avoiding technical debt on internal updates. > "Ideally, tests should validate classes and functions as a black box, where the implementation isn't known."
- **stub** — hardcoded responses layered on a mock (`getListOfBooks()` returns Moby Dick / The Count of Monte Cristo / The Road). > "Stubs enable more in-depth testing than mocks since they are able to provide a bare minimum functionality over the mere placeholder of a mocked class."
- **fake** — in-memory state plus real operations (`getNumberOfBooks()`, `checkOutBook(bookTitle)` moving titles between lists). > "Our FakeBookDBConnector class now emulates a production BookDBConnector class even closer by providing the functionality to check out books."
- **spy** — production object with only specific methods stubbed (`getNumberOfBooks()` forced to return 5), remaining methods untouched. > "Testers create test spies from a production object but stub it to modify specific behaviors or methods, while leaving the rest of the production behavior untouched."
- **spy-as-recorder** — conventional alternate meaning: recording invocation counts to expose race conditions or indeterminate behavior. > "the term test spy can refer to a method that records some state about its usage"
- **shell** — the minimum a mocked object must provide so the SUT can be instantiated. > "we need only the bare minimum of a shell of the BookDBConnector object to get the code to run"
GUIDELINES:
- "Start with the simplest option of a basic mock before diving into higher-order test doubles."
- Avoid spies where possible; mixing mocks and production code "can quickly lead to unintended consequences".
- Mock "only the functionality necessary for testing" rather than duplicating an entire class with a spy.
- Prefer black-box tests so implementation edits do not cascade.
- Update fakes when corresponding production classes change materially.
EVIDENCE: none (worked example with three-book list and a `5` return value).
LIMITS: acknowledges mocks can be "less meaningful" when the mocked class poorly represents production; no data on frequency or cost. Content identical to A081 apart from site section and navigation.
TOOLING: Mockito; `mock(...)`, `spy(...)`, `when(...).thenReturn(...)`; Python-style `def` pseudocode.
LINKS: TechTarget unit-testing, white-box and technical-debt articles; companion tips "Inside 5 types of test doubles" and "How to implement mock objects for simpler testing".

## A083 · Choosing the Right Test Double | Labs Practices Site
URL: https://labspractices.com/guides/test-doubles
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: Authored version of the Tanzu "Choosing the Right Test Double" guide (Alex Basson): five double types, with the argument that for stateful collaborators the only usable double is a fake proven by the same contract test as the real implementation.
CONCEPTS:
- **test double** — stand-in that isolates SUT behavior from dependency behavior, avoiding false positives/negatives from the dependency. > "They do this by helping you isolate the behavior of the code you’re testing from the behavior of the components that code depends on."
- **dummy** — throws on any method invocation; proves a branch is not taken. > "A dummy is a test double that throws an exception when a method on it is invoked."
- **stub** — returns pre-configured hard-coded data; set up before execution. > "A stub is a test double that returns pre-configured, hard-coded data when its methods are called."
- **spy** — records invocations and parameters; queried after execution; frameworks may supply them, but hand-writing is viable. > "A spy is a test double that records the invocations of its methods, along with any parameters passed in, so that you can find out afterward whether and how its methods were called."
- **mock** — stub + spy; `verify()` checks expected calls and arguments after a stubbed return value was supplied beforehand. > "You use a mock for situations where you want to both control the data returned by a method and also confirm that the method was called with the correct values as arguments."
- **fake** — simplified implementation with the same business-logic behavior; must itself be tested with the real component's test cases. > "A fake is a test double that has the same business-logic behavior as the real component it’s doubling, but using a simplified implementation."
- **stateful behavior** — the property stubs/mocks cannot express, because they return fixed data rather than one that changes "along the way". > "A stub only allows you to configure it to return a hard-coded piece of data, not one that can change along the way."
- **contract test** — `testBankAccount(createBankAccount: () => BankAccount)` taking a factory, encoding balance starts at 0, deposit(1000) → 1000, withdraw(250) → 750. > "Notice that testBankAccount has no opinions as to what kind of BankAccount it is testing, only that the BankAccount it receives implements the BankAccount interface."
- **`RealBankAccount` vs `FakeBankAccount` vs `BadBankAccount`** — DB-backed, in-memory-balance, and interface-conforming-but-behaviorless implementations. > "BadBankAccount correctly implements the BankAccount interface, but implementing the interface isn’t enough to make it usable in our Accountant tests."
- **`injection`** — doubles passed into `Accountant(bankAccount, taxCalculator, clientNotifier)`. > "When you write the tests for Accountant , obviously you won’t want to inject an instance of a client’s real bank account."
GUIDELINES:
- Define behavior as "to pass the `BankAccount` tests"; run the same parameterized suite for real and fake implementations.
- Use a fake, not stub/spy/mock, for stateful collaborators (database-backed services are the typical case).
- Test your fakes; a wrong fake (always returns 0) makes SUT tests permanently red.
- Configure stubs before the SUT runs; assert spy/mock calls after it runs.
- Prefer writing your own spy when no framework support exists.
EVIDENCE: none (worked examples: 1000 + 500 = 1500 refund; 1000 − 300 = 700 owed; balance sequence 0 → 1000 → 750).
LIMITS: example mock syntax explicitly marked as unsupported by Jest; the guide covers only unit-level doubles and gives no guidance on scale, performance, or test-suite economics.
TOOLING: TypeScript interfaces; Jest-style matchers (`toEqual`, `toHaveBeenCalledWith`).
LINKS: labspractices "Modern Development Practices" track; companion guide "Architectural Decision Records"; GitHub repo `joemoore/labs-practices-site`.

## A084 · Stubs vs Mocks · Enterprise Craftsmanship
URL: https://enterprisecraftsmanship.com/2015/07/27/stubs-vs-mocks
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: Interaction correctness can be verified without mocks: hand-written stubs that record interactions concentrate fragility in one place, so tests stay one level of abstraction above the code and survive refactoring; mocks are only justified when a single test uses the dependency.
CONCEPTS:
- **mock** — a "dynamic wrapper for dependencies used in tests", programmed with expectations of what exact method calls in what sequence the dependency must receive. > "They are programmed with expectations of what exact method calls in what sequence the dependency should receive from a system under test (SUT)"
- **stub** — a hand-written class mimicking the dependency "with significant shortcuts" (in-memory repository; email gateway that records sends), possibly minimal to satisfy the interface. > "Stubs are hand-written classes that mimic the dependency’s behavior, but do that with significant shortcuts."
- **test double** — generic term for dependency substitution; the author declines to subdivide stubs into fakes and spies because the distinctions are less important than the mock/stub difference. > "Test double is a generic term used for indicating some kind of dependency substitution for the test purposes"
- **SUT** — system under test. > "Programming a mock for a particular order of operations and verifying that order afterward helps us to check that the SUT interacts with the callback correctly."
- **record-and-assert stub** — `HandlerStub : IHandler` accumulating `List<Tuple<Action,string>> actionsCalled` (DocumentStarted, ElementStarted, ElementEnded, DocumentEnded) with fluent checks `WasCalled().WithStartDocument().WithStartElement("outer")...`. > "The stub basically records all the interactions that come from the outside world and provides methods to validate those interactions."
- **cascade failure** — replacing the interface's mock in every test duplicates the interface, so any `IHandler` change breaks many tests. > "Every change in IHandler would cause cascade failures throughout all tests that use it."
- **fragility concentration** — the stub absorbs change: adjust one stub, touch no tests. > "If you change the Handler interface, you need to adjust the stub only once; you don’t have to touch any tests that use it."
- **most important TDD rule** — keep tests one level of abstraction above the code they check. > "the most important TDD rule, which is keeping the tests one level of abstraction above the code they check"
- **domain model** — usually free of external dependencies, so enterprise apps can unit test with real classes and reserve doubles for integration tests. > "The domain model usually don’t contain any external dependencies, hence no need for test doubles."
- **callback object** — the case where sequence of invocations matters (`Parser.ParseXml(xml, handler)`). > "An example here could be a callback object, methods of which the SUT has to invoke in an exact sequence."
GUIDELINES:
- "whenever you see you start having more than one test that substitute the same dependency using mocks, you should switch to a hand-written stub instead".
- With exactly one test using the dependency, prefer mocks: "less up-front effort" and no effective difference on refactoring.
- Verify "the end result of those interactions, not the behavior that led to that result".
- Use real classes for unit tests of a domain model; use doubles in integration tests.
- Accept extra up-front cost of stubs for refactoring resilience.
EVIDENCE: none (single worked example: `Parser_parses_xml_in_correct_order` with `<outer><inner /></outer>`, mock version vs stub version).
LIMITS: author concedes mock/stub classifications "inconsistent across different authors"; the recommendation is argued from refactoring cost, not measured; .NET-specific tooling.
TOOLING: xUnit `[Fact]`; `MockRepository`, `CreateMock<IHandler>()`, `ReplayAll()`, `VerifyAll()` (RhinoMocks-style); Moq and RhinoMocks named.
LINKS: series posts — "Test-induced design damage", "How to do painless TDD", "Integration testing or how to sleep well at nights", "The most important TDD rule", "TDD best practices"; code gist by vkhorikov; Pragmatic Unit Testing Pluralsight course.

## A085 · Understanding Test Doubles - Fakes, Stubs, Mocks, and Spies
URL: https://blog.nimblepros.com/blogs/understanding-test-doubles/
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: The four double types are distinguished by what they do — fakes supply specific values, stubs control responses without verification, mocks verify interactions, spies record calls for later inspection — and matching the type to the test's question produces maintainable suites.
CONCEPTS:
- **test double** — object that mimics real objects but executes no real work; umbrella over fakes, stubs, mocks, spies. > "Test doubles are objects that mimic the behavior of real objects but don’t execute any real work."
- **fake** — interface implementation designed for a specific test scenario, possibly very basic, using concrete values and no `Any`/generic matching. > "Fakes are implementations of interfaces or classes that are designed to work in a specific test scenario."
- **stub** — pre-programmed responses that do not verify interactions; used to control the behavior of a dependency. > "Stubs provide pre-programmed responses to calls made during the test. They do not verify the interactions with the object."
- **mock** — records calls and asserts they happened with specific parameters; the example sets no `Returns`, focusing on the interaction and not the result. > "Mocks are objects that verify the interaction with them during the test."
- **spy** — records calls and exposes the recorded data while leaving verification to ordinary assertions (`Assert.Equal(1, spyUserRepository.CallCount)`). > "Spies are similar to mocks but do not verify the interaction; instead, they record the calls and provide access to the recorded data."
- **`IUserRepository` / `UserService.IsUserActive`** — running example returning `_userRepository.GetUser(userId)?.IsActive ?? false`. > "This code shows how to use a version of IUserRepository for testing whether a user’s active state is being returned."
- **`IExternalService` / `UserStatusChecker.IsUserActive`** — second example for the stub case. > "In this example, the UserStatusChecker class depends on an IExternalService."
- **`SpyUserRepository`** — hand-written class with `CallCount` incremented in `GetUser`. > "This takes the approach of Assert.Equal to ensure that the method is getting called a specific number of times using a spy."
- **NSubstitute idioms** — `Substitute.For<T>()`, `.Returns(value)`, `.Received(1).GetUser("123")`. > "We are setting a controlled call to a method with a specific input - GetUser("123"). We are also setting a controlled return value using Returns()."
- **convenience trap** — choosing a `FakeUserRepository` merely because it needs no dependencies, producing tests hard to maintain and understand. > "You might find yourself tempted to use a simple FakeUserRepository class because it’s quick and doesn’t require any additional dependencies."
GUIDELINES:
- Fake: "Use when a simple implementation is sufficient for the test scenario, and you don't want to use external frameworks."
- Stub: "Use when you need to control the behavior of a dependency in a specific way during the test."
- Mock: "Use when you need to verify that certain methods were called with specific parameters or to assert interaction patterns."
- Spy: "Use when you need to record calls and provide access to the recorded data."
- Keep fakes free of `Any`/generic matching — use concrete values (`"123"` active, `"456"` inactive).
- With a stub, deliberately omit assertions that the method was called; with a mock, deliberately omit `Returns` setup.
EVIDENCE: none (four runnable C# examples, one per double type).
LIMITS: explicitly a conceptual primer; no measured maintenance or defect data; classification is presented as usage-based rather than as a formal taxonomy.
TOOLING: C#, NSubstitute, xUnit `[Fact]`/`Assert`.
LINKS: NimblePros "Testing Techniques" series; adjacent posts "Null-Conditional Assignment" and "Santa's AI Chat App".

## A086 · Mock vs. Stub: Key Differences According to Experts | Built In
URL: https://builtin.com/software-engineering-perspectives/mock-vs-stub
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: Mocks verify behavior (call counts and order) while stubs supply canned responses for state-based tests, and four practitioners converge on a discipline: mock only boundary services, never domain/model objects, and keep higher-level tests to catch the false positives mocks can create.
CONCEPTS:
- **mock testing** — replacing code with mock code to isolate and test the real code's behaviors; ideal for testing the order in which functions are called. > "Mock testing refers to the process of replacing code with mock code to isolate and test the real code’s behaviors."
- **stub** — imitates a service or object by responding to specific inputs and ignoring anything else, producing the same value during each test. > "That’s because a stub is programmed to respond to specific inputs and ignore anything else."
- **behavior verification** — expectations established before the test states which methods get called, with which arguments, in which order; failure reported if unmet. > "With a mock, you’re trying to test more of the behavior side of things."
- **state verification** — classicist style: assert whether a specific state occurred (e.g., inspect a Kafka queue for a purchase message) rather than asserting an email service call. > "the classicist style would be more about asserting whether a specific state has occurred"
- **mockist / London style** vs **classicist** — two schools; classicists reach for stubs and spies, not mocks, and only when setup is awkward. > "With the [classicist] school, more often than not, they’re going to reach for stubs and spies, not mocks"
- **domain/model object** — objects that live in the heap (an email with sender, recipients, CC/BCC, subject, body, attachments); strict rule: never mock these. > "I have a very strong rule of not mocking any domain objects or any model objects"
- **service (mockable)** — things that have data flowing through them on the stack, e.g., the messaging queue or the sender service handling the email object. > "The mocks should be services, so things that have data flowing through them on the stack, but nothing that lives in the heap gets mocked."
- **false positive from mocks** — a collaborator changes, the mock still behaves as scripted, the test passes while reality broke. > "the test is going to pass because it’s using a mock that is behaving in a specific way"
- **inside-outside mocking** — Freed's approach: mock only third parties and other people's systems outside your boundary. > "What I am writing and designing is “inside,” and I don’t want to mock anything there, and everything else — third parties, other people’s systems — I want to keep some sort of boundary."
- **implementation coupling** — mock style digging into the implementation, e.g., asserting warehouse gets called first and then email next. > "I have to set up all these tests against the internals of the implementation — with the mock style, you’re digging into the implementation a lot."
GUIDELINES:
- Mock services and boundaries; do not mock domain/model objects — "The moment you start doing that, that's when you get into trouble."
- If you use mocks, declare methods, arguments and order beforehand and let the test complain when they do not happen.
- Pair mock-based units with higher-level tests: "how am I going to know if the code underneath changes?".
- Prefer starting at an integration level with one integration test covering every code path, then refactor before unit-testing or mocking new classes.
- Avoid classes depending on "17 other classes" — otherwise a collaborator bug fails your unit test.
EVIDENCE: none quantitative; qualitative testimony from four engineers (Solomon, Benham, Freed, Riley) plus the author.
LIMITS: responses "edited for length and clarity"; opinion-based, no measurements; concedes both schools are "kind of right".
TOOLING: JMock, Mockito, JustMock; Kafka (as state-verification target); no versions cited.
LINKS: Built In pieces on unit testing, integration testing, software testing data.

## A087 · Use cases of various types of test doubles for unit testing
URL: https://www.testingmind.com/use-cases-of-various-types-of-test-doubles-for-unit-testing/
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: Syndicated reprint of Matthew Grasberger's TechTarget tip (source credited to searchsoftwarequality.techtarget.com): escalate from simple mocks to stubs, fakes and spies only as the test needs more production fidelity, while keeping tests black-box.
CONCEPTS:
- **test double** — functional substitution, also for load testing services whose rate limits prevent scale testing. > "Test doubles can be useful for load testing, as they can stand in as functional substitutions for third-party services whose rate limits make testing at a scale impossible."
- **unit test** — exercise one method/function in an isolated scenario; test doubles should be used jointly with unit tests, limiting calls to systems outside the codebase. > "A unit test should be exercising some method or function from your application in an isolated scenario."
- **mock** — library-created shell (`mock(BookDBConnector)`) purely to construct `BookStore`; assertion on `bookStore.booksCheckedOut == 0`, data held in the class not the DB. > "Mocking is a perfect solution here because we need only the bare minimum of a shell of the BookDBConnector object to get the code to run."
- **white box testing** — what mocking encourages: the tests define the implementation behind the class and results are predetermined, creating a dependency on that implementation. > "When a team mocks classes, the implementation behind the class or function being tested is defined by the tests, and the results from the mocked class are predetermined."
- **black box testing** — ideal validation where the implementation isn't known, so internal updates create no technical debt. > "Ideally, tests should validate classes and functions as a black box, where the implementation isn’t known."
- **stub** — `MockBookDBConnector` returning a hardcoded three-book list from `getListOfBooks()`. > "Test stubs take mocks a bit further by simply defining stubbed or hardcoded responses in a mocked class."
- **fake** — `FakeBookDBConnector` with `books`, `checkoutOutBooks`, `getNumberOfBooks()`, `getListOfBooks()`, `checkOutBook(bookTitle)`. > "Our FakeBookDBConnector class now emulates a production BookDBConnector class even closer by providing the functionality to check out books."
- **spy** — built from a production object with only chosen methods stubbed (`getNumberOfBooks()` → 5); other methods remain intact and untouched. > "Testers create test spies from a production object but stub it to modify specific behaviors or methods, while leaving the rest of the production behavior untouched."
- **test spy** (recording sense) — a class variable counting invocations of a stubbed method; useful for race conditions and indeterminate behavior. > "it is also true that the term test spy can refer to a method that records some state about its usage"
- **realistic facade** — the fake's role: a mock that maintains a realistic facade of a working production class. > "Fakes implement actual functionality to create a mock that maintains a realistic facade of a working production class."
GUIDELINES:
- "Start with the simplest option of a basic mock before diving into higher-order test doubles."
- "mocking should be your first choice"; "it may be best to avoid using spies if possible".
- Mock "only the functionality necessary for testing" instead of duplicating a whole class.
- Treat fake classes as production representations that "may need to update with major changes".
- Design tests as black boxes so implementation changes cause no downstream test debt.
EVIDENCE: none (illustrative Python snippets only).
LIMITS: no measurements; warns only that mocks can make tests "less meaningful" when the mocked class misrepresents production. Reprint of third-party content, so authority rests on the TechTarget original.
TOOLING: Mockito/other mock libraries; `mock()`, `spy()`, `when(...).thenReturn(...)`; Python-style syntax.
LINKS: TechTarget origin URL for the same tip; TechTarget white-box definition and technical-debt news item; staging-environment best-practices tip.

## A088 · Integration Tests vs End-to-End Tests
URL: https://blog.openreplay.com/integration-vs-end-to-end-tests
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Frontend integration tests render your own modules together with the network mocked in milliseconds; E2E tests drive the deployed app in a real browser and mock nothing; the sound budget is mostly integration plus three-to-five E2E tests on revenue journeys.
CONCEPTS:
- **integration test** — renders a tree of your own components together, network stubbed, in Node or jsdom; milliseconds to low seconds; no browser, no real server. > "An integration test renders a tree of your own components together and asserts their combined behavior with the network stubbed out"
- **end-to-end test** — drives the deployed/staging app in a real browser as a user, mocking nothing; seconds to minutes per test. > "An end-to-end test drives your actual deployed application in a real browser, exactly as a user would, and asserts on what the user sees — with nothing mocked."
- **testing pyramid** — many unit tests, fewer integration, very few E2E; a sound default for keeping a suite fast. > "The classic testing pyramid prescribes many unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and very few slow E2E tests at the top."
- **testing trophy** — Kent C. Dodds's model fattening the integration layer for best confidence-per-cost, a counterpoint to the pyramid. > "which fattens the integration layer because integration tests give the best confidence-per-cost for web applications"
- **resemblance principle** — Testing Library's guiding principle: the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you. > "The reasoning rests on Testing Library’s guiding principle that the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you"
- **contract bugs between modules** — `user.name` vs `user.fullName`, a 401 path that never re-renders the error banner, a loading flag that never clears. > "This is the layer where contract bugs surface: the component expects user.name but the handler returns user.fullName"
- **E2E-unique bugs** — auth, redirects, environment config, third-party scripts, CSP violations, cross-page state surviving navigation. > "E2E tests catch the bugs that only exist in a real deployment: authentication and redirects, environment configuration, third-party scripts, content-security-policy violations, and cross-page state that survives a navigation."
- **MSW** — Mock Service Worker; intercepts at the network layer via `setupWorker` (Service Worker API) in browsers and `setupServer` (request interception, no worker file) in Node. > "It intercepts requests at the network layer in both environments — via the Service Worker API in the browser (setupWorker), and via low-level request interception in Node"
- **frontend spectrum** — the integration/E2E boundary is a spectrum, not a wall; drawing it is a budget decision, not a law. > "The frontend integration/E2E boundary is a spectrum, not a wall — where you draw it is a budget decision, not a law."
- **session replay** — records the untested journey that broke (DOM state, network calls, console errors), converted into the missing test. > "a replay of a real failure shows the exact untested journey that broke — the DOM state, the network calls, and the console errors at the moment it failed"
GUIDELINES:
- "keep a small suite of three-to-five E2E tests on your highest-value journeys, and don't try to E2E everything".
- Choose by bug prevented: new module interaction or contract → integration; critical cross-stack journey → one E2E; everything else → integration.
- In MSW tests use `beforeAll(server.listen())`, `afterEach(server.resetHandlers())`, `afterAll(server.close())`; MSW v2 `http` + `HttpResponse`, not v1 `res`/`ctx`.
- Keep E2E stable: role/label selectors over CSS paths, Playwright auto-waiting "instead of fixed sleeps", isolated test data, capped count.
- Delete E2E tests that no longer protect revenue; an E2E test for a tooltip is "a maintenance liability".
- `mockServiceWorker.js` is needed only for the browser `setupWorker` path, not Node `setupServer`.
EVIDENCE: none quantitative; timing claims are ranges ("milliseconds to low seconds" vs "seconds to minutes").
LIMITS: E2E worth its cost only for certain journeys; Jest "does not currently support" async React Server Components, so Next.js recommends E2E there; trophy view "widely adopted modern view ... not a universal replacement".
TOOLING: Vitest 4, Jest, @testing-library/react 16, MSW 2 (`msw`, `msw/node`), Playwright 1.6x (Chromium/Firefox/WebKit), Cypress, Next.js, jsdom.
LINKS: testing-library.com guiding principles; vitest.dev; jestjs.io; mswjs.io; playwright.dev; docs.cypress.io; Next.js Jest guide; Kent C. Dodds's testing trophy.

## A089 · E2E vs Integration Testing: When to Use Each | Shiplight AI
URL: https://www.shiplight.ai/blog/e2e-vs-integration-testing
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Integration tests verify two or more components at a boundary with externals stubbed and give fast, targeted feedback; E2E tests validate whole user workflows with nothing mocked and give holistic confidence, so use both in defined proportions rather than choosing.
CONCEPTS:
- **integration testing** — verifies that two or more components or services work correctly together, scoped to the boundary; externals outside the boundary are mocked or stubbed. > "Integration testing verifies that two or more components or services work correctly together."
- **E2E testing** — validates complete user workflows across the whole stack with nothing mocked, hitting the same browser, APIs, databases and third-party services as a real user. > "End-to-end testing validates complete user workflows across the entire application stack. Nothing is mocked."
- **scope** — the primary differentiator: boundary vs full workflow. > "The scope is intentionally limited: you test the boundary between components rather than the entire system."
- **feedback loop** — integration: fast, seconds in CI, pinpoints the failing location; E2E: slightly slower, increasingly fast with modern frameworks. > "Integration tests provide fast, targeted feedback that pinpoints the exact failure location in seconds."
- **confidence level** — integration proves components connect correctly; E2E proves the product works as users experience it. > "Integration tests verify that components connect correctly at their boundaries, but they cannot confirm that a complete user workflow functions end-to-end."
- **mocking axis** — integration stubs external dependencies; E2E uses real services and infrastructure. > "Integration tests typically mock or stub external dependencies outside the boundary being tested."
- **E2E coverage ladder** — prioritization device that ranks high-value paths (auth, onboarding, checkout, account management) first. > "Authentication, onboarding, checkout, and account management are workflows where failure has direct business impact."
- **cross-service regression** — a change in one service breaking a multi-service workflow; only E2E catches it. > "When a change in one service breaks a workflow that spans multiple services, only an E2E test will catch it."
- **deployment verification** — E2E against staging proves config, migrations and infra changes did not break user-facing functionality. > "E2E tests running against staging verify that deployment configuration, migrations, and infrastructure changes have not broken user-facing functionality."
- **test-layer duplication** — repeating in E2E an error path already covered by an integration test, violating the rule that each layer adds unique value. > "If an integration test already verifies that the API returns the correct error for invalid input, you do not need an E2E test that exercises the same error path through the browser."
- **intent-based YAML** — Shiplight's agent-maintained authoring format, positioned against code-based Playwright/Cypress. > "Playwright and Cypress do this in code; Shiplight does it with intent-based YAML the agent maintains."
GUIDELINES:
- Run unit tests on every save, integration tests on every commit, E2E tests on every pull request.
- "Use E2E tests for happy paths and critical journeys. Push edge cases down to integration and unit tests."
- Expect "a ratio of roughly five to ten integration tests for every E2E test".
- Start a new project with integration tests for core API boundaries, then add E2E for sign-up or the primary conversion flow.
- Use recorded responses for third-party APIs (payment gateways, email providers) instead of real network calls.
- Verify ORM behavior, transaction boundaries, and REST/gRPC/message-queue communication at the integration layer.
- Do not skip integration tests when jumping from unit tests to E2E — that gap hides contract and data-layer bugs.
EVIDENCE: none (comparison table of nine dimensions; no measured datasets).
LIMITS: E2E reliability given as "Moderate to high (depends on tooling and patterns)"; the ratio is "Most projects benefit from", not measured; author is a vendor of E2E tooling.
TOOLING: Playwright, Cypress, Shiplight (intent-based YAML), contract tests for backend-only seams.
LINKS: Martin Fowler's Test Pyramid; Google Testing Blog; Shiplight posts "complete guide to E2E testing in 2026", "e2e coverage ladder", "best AI testing tools in 2026".

## A090 · End-to-end testing: Definition, benefits, and tools (2026)
URL: https://katalon.com/resources-center/blog/end-to-end-e2e-testing
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: E2E testing verifies an entire application from start to finish by simulating real user journeys, and it earns its high cost only when reserved for critical paths inside a balanced test pyramid.
CONCEPTS:
- **End-to-end (E2E) testing** — verifying the functionality and performance of a whole application from start to finish by simulating real user scenarios with live-like data, to catch bugs that surface only once components are integrated. > "End-to-end testing is a software testing technique that verifies the functionality and performance of an entire software application from start to finish by simulating real-world user scenarios and replicating live data."
- **Test pyramid** — unit at the base, integration in the middle, E2E at the top; E2E gives the highest confidence in business requirements but must be confined to critical workflows. > "These give the highest confidence in business requirements but are slower and more complex — so they should focus on critical workflows only."
- **Horizontal E2E** — outside-in testing that puts the tester in the user's place and verifies each workflow through UI interactions and customer-facing functionality. > "Testers put themselves in the user's position and verify that each individual workflow in the application works correctly from start to finish."
- **Vertical E2E** — a technical approach that works across system layers — backend services and APIs, databases and data integrity, internal and external integration — tracing depth rather than breadth. > "This tests the depth of one part of the system rather than the breadth of a user journey."
- **Flaky tests** — failures that are not actual regressions; they cost engineering velocity by generating noise and eroding trust in the suite. > "Failures that are not actual regressions create noise, erode trust, and introduce risk fatigue."
- **Setup complexity** — the more external dependencies a system has, the more fragile and bloated test orchestration becomes, most painfully in production-mirroring environments. > "When systems depend on multiple microservices, cloud APIs, or external providers, test orchestration becomes fragile and bloated."
- **Test data management** — E2E scenarios need specific accounts, listings and history, and keeping that data consistent and reset across runs is hard once tests write to a database or call external systems. > "Keeping data consistent and resetting state between runs is difficult, especially when tests modify a database or call external systems."
- **Four-phase process** — planning (begun after integration testing completes), design, execution, and results analysis ending in a retrospective. > "Test planning. Starts once integration testing is complete. Outline test objectives based on the initial client requirements and the application architecture."
GUIDELINES:
- E2E tests should be `5-10%` of total tests, integration `15-20%`, unit `70-80%`.
- Automate critical workflows first: `login`, `checkout`, `onboarding`.
- "Avoid hardcoded delays. Use dynamic waits"; write modular tests; "Prefer API-level tests where they fit."
- Run in CI/CD "on every pull request," including in ephemeral preview environments per PR.
- Use "isolated, seeded datasets and reset state between runs."
- Do not use E2E for exhaustive edge cases; use E2E "to bootstrap legacy codebases" lacking lower-level tests; bring QA in early.
EVIDENCE: none (practitioner guidance). Cites the 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter loss — "a $125 million spacecraft" — where no test verified the journey from data generation to thruster execution. Comparison table claims integration testing runs "200 tests" in "less than 1 hour," while E2E "may take up to 4 - 8 hours."
LIMITS: States the trade-off — E2E is "slower, more complex, and more expensive to maintain"; flakiness "is sometimes inevitable." Vendor-authored, ending in product promotion.
TOOLING: Katalon (Studio, TestOps, TestCloud), Autify, testRigor (codeless), CircleCI, Jenkins, GitLab, Playwright.
LINKS: Wikipedia Mars Climate Orbiter; StackExchange on scaling integration testing; Medium "I'm so done with E2E testing."

## A091 · End-to-end testing vs integration testing
URL: https://bug0.com/knowledge-base/end-to-end-testing-vs-integration-testing
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: Integration tests check one seam at a time from inside the system, E2E tests check whole user journeys from where the user stands; they fail differently, so keeping both is the argument rather than choosing one.
CONCEPTS:
- **Seam** — the boundary an integration test stands inside and checks, such as one service with its database or one API with its consumer. > "An integration test stands inside the system and checks one seam: this service and its database, this API and its consumer."
- **Vantage point** — because both test types use real components rather than mocks, the real distinction between them is scope and standpoint rather than the presence of fakes. > "Both test types use real components instead of mocks, which is why they blur together in conversation. The difference is scope and vantage point."
- **Better detector vs better proof of consequence** — an integration failure localizes the defect, while an E2E failure proves the product is broken; the asymmetry is the reason to keep both layers. > "The integration test is the better detector; the E2E test is the better proof of consequence. This asymmetry is the whole argument for keeping both."
- **Emergent failures** — bugs no single seam owns, where every pairwise check passes but the assembled journey breaks. > "A session cookie set by one service is dropped by a redirect three steps later. No single seam owns that bug; only the assembled flow exposes it."
- **Two precisions on "real"** — an integration test's real is the seam under test and anything beyond it may be stubbed; an E2E test's real is the user's path with only third-party edges sandboxed. > "An integration test's real is the seam under test; everything beyond that seam can be stubbed."
- **Ice cream cone** — the inverted pyramid produced by leaning entirely on E2E, giving slow suites whose failures are vague. > "Teams that lean entirely on E2E build slow suites that fail vaguely."
- **Vertical E2E variant** — one action traced down the full stack, the shape most often mistaken for a deep integration test. > "The vertical E2E variant, one action traced down the full stack, is the shape most often confused with a deep integration test"
- **API-level end-to-end testing** — chaining API calls to replay a whole workflow without a browser, as against testing one endpoint against a running service, which is integration testing. > "Chaining API calls to replay a whole user workflow without a browser is API-level end-to-end testing"
GUIDELINES:
- "Put an integration test on every seam you own": each service pair, each external API, the database layer.
- "Put E2E tests on the journeys where failure costs revenue or trust."
- "Let the integration layer absorb detail and keep E2E focused on the handful of flows that define whether the product works."
- Small team with no suite: "E2E first, on the two or three journeys the business cannot survive breaking," then add integration tests "at the seams that E2E failures keep tracing back to."
- Selector-healing tooling "cuts E2E maintenance, not diagnosis time and not runtime."
EVIDENCE: none. Illustrative case: `total_cents` renamed to `amount_cents` in orders while billing is not updated — the integration test fails "within seconds" naming the missing field; without it the nightly E2E run reports only "checkout journey failed at the confirmation step," and "someone spends an hour tracing it."
LIMITS: Admits E2E is "taxonomically" a type of integration testing; the distinction is operational. Speed claims are qualitative ("Seconds" vs "Seconds to minutes"); the one-hour diagnosis figure is unmeasured.
TOOLING: none named.
LINKS: Bug0 entries on end-to-end testing, regression testing, testing pyramid, unit-vs-integration testing, API functional testing.

## A092 · End-to-End Testing Strategy: Implementation Guide
URL: https://ardura.consulting/blog/e2e-testing-strategy-implementation-guide
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: E2E tests are the most expensive test type, so they must be scoped to critical journeys, written to mirror user behavior, and maintained via page objects, stable selectors and quarterly review.
CONCEPTS:
- **Right/wrong fit** — right for critical journeys that span services and UI, frontend-backend integration risk, and sequence-dependent flows; wrong for business logic, API contracts, visual appearance and high-variation edge cases. > "E2E tests are the wrong choice for business logic validation (use unit tests), API contract verification (use integration tests), visual appearance (use visual regression tools)"
- **Inverted pyramid** — a suite dominated by E2E runs slowly, delays feedback, and consumes the QA team in maintenance; the target starting ratio is 70% unit, 20% integration, 10% E2E. > "If 80% of your tests are E2E and 5% are unit tests, you have an inverted pyramid. Execution will be slow, feedback will be delayed, and maintenance will consume your QA team."
- **User-story assertions** — each E2E test should read as a user story and assert what the user perceives, not implementation internals such as store state or status codes. > "Each E2E test should read like a user story. Navigate to a page, interact with elements as a user would, verify the outcome the user would see."
- **Smoke E2E suite** — 10-20 tests covering critical paths, run on every pull request and capped in duration so feedback arrives fast. > "Run the smoke E2E suite (10-20 tests covering critical paths). This suite must complete in under 10 minutes."
- **Quarantine** — a chronically flaky test is moved to a separate non-blocking job, with a two-week deadline to fix or delete it. > "If a test fails more than twice in 30 days without a corresponding code change, quarantine it. A quarantined test runs in a separate job that does not block the pipeline."
- **Test-data options** — API-driven setup for most tests, UI-driven setup only when the setup is the thing under test, and database seeding for slow-changing reference data. > "Before each test, create the required data through API calls (create user, create product, set inventory). This is fast, reliable, and independent of UI changes."
- **Page Object Model** — one object per page or component, with methods naming user actions and properties naming page state, so a UI change is absorbed in one place. > "A page object encapsulates all selectors and interactions for a single page or component. When the UI changes, update the page object once."
- **Selector priority** — `data-testid` first, then accessible roles and labels, then text; CSS classes and XPath are to be avoided entirely. > "Use data-testid attributes first (most stable, explicitly for testing). Use accessible roles and labels second (stable and improves accessibility testing)."
GUIDELINES:
- Target `70% unit, 20% integration, 10% E2E`; FAQ variant `5-15%` E2E — "30-80 E2E tests" typical, "More than 150 usually indicates" misplacement.
- "10-20 critical journeys cover the highest-risk areas."
