- PR smoke suite "must complete in under 10 minutes"; full suite on merge to main "20-40 minutes"; smoke suite on staging before production.
- "A 40-minute sequential suite runs in 10 minutes across 4 parallel runners."
- Flake threshold: "if a test fails more than twice in 30 days without a corresponding code change, quarantine it"; team gets "2 weeks to fix or delete."
- Allow "one automatic retry" in CI and flag passes-on-retry as unstable.
- Reliability bar "less than 2% flake rate"; delete tests that caught no defect in 6 months (FAQ: 12 months).
- Add `data-testid` during development and "Include them in the Definition of Done for UI components."
- Run in Docker; use tags/path filtering; save screenshots, video, traces and logs.
EVIDENCE: none for engineering claims. Vendor self-metrics only: "500+ senior specialists," "2-week onboarding," "40% average cost savings."
LIMITS: Vendor author (Chief Growth Officer at a staff-augmentation firm); cost claims are marketing.
TOOLING: Cypress (time-travel debugging; Chromium-only free tier; no native multi-tab; single-origin limit; paid Cloud for Firefox/WebKit; Percy, Applitools), Playwright (three engines, out-of-process parallelism, trace viewer, JS/TS/Python/Java/C# SDKs), Docker, Selenium.
LINKS: ARDURA post on Selenium vs Cypress vs Playwright; Definition of Done.

## A093 · What is End-to-End Testing and When Should You Use It?
URL: https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/end-to-end-testing-tutorial
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: E2E testing validates the whole application including dependencies but is commonly over-favored by developers; respecting the testing pyramid keeps tests fast to write and cheap to maintain.
CONCEPTS:
- **End-to-end testing** — validating the entire application from start to finish with its dependencies, in an environment identical to production, exercising every action users might perform. > "In E2E testing, you create an environment identical to the one that will be used by real users. Then you test all actions that your users might perform on your application."
- **Inverting the testing pyramid** — covering most cases with E2E, or using E2E alone; the author planned exactly this on a past project before changing course. > "I was in a situation like this. In one of my projects, I was planning to cover most cases with E2E tests – or even worse, use only the E2E test."
- **Three layers** — unit tests cover the smallest unit with no external dependencies, integration tests cover the interaction between two distinct entities, and E2E tests cover flows as a multi-step integration test. > "Lastly, E2E tests focus on flows, from the simplest up to the most complex. They can be viewed as a multi-step integration test."
- **Layer gradient** — moving up the pyramid each layer loses speed and gains scope, complexity and maintenance burden. > "From the bottom to the top, each layer of testing represents a decrease in **speed** and an increase in **scope, complexity** and **maintenance.**"
- **Failure range** — the set of places a failure could have come from; narrowest for unit tests and widest for E2E, where anything along the path may have broken. > "If E2E tests fail, finding the issue is often difficult because now the failure range is expanded to the entire application. Basically, along the path, anything could have broken."
- **Hourglass** — an observed deviation from the pyramid with many unit and E2E tests but few integration tests. > "Or it will look like an hourglass, where there are a lot of unit tests and E2E tests, but not many integration tests."
- **Codeless testing** — AI-powered record-and-replay tools with drag-and-drop panels, contrasted with writing test code in browser-automation frameworks. > "In a **codeless** testing situation, you use frameworks powered by Artificial Intelligence that record your actions."
- **E2E as extension** — E2E supplements the other test types rather than replacing them, and should not be stretched past its defined purpose. > "E2E testing cannot replace other methods – it is meant to extend them. The purpose of E2E testing is well-defined, and the tests should not extend beyond that boundary."
GUIDELINES:
- Maintain "a good balance of various tests"; treat the pyramid as "an industry-standard guideline" that "has endured since the mid-2000s."
- "Ideally, tests should catch bugs as close to the root of the pyramid as possible."
- Use E2E to "validate buttons, forms, changes, links, external processes, and generally an entire workflow's function without problems."
- Codeless fits simple flows; "if the target application has some very complex flows that include multiple moving parts, then a classic testing situation is the way to go."
- Avoid spending "more time writing tests and maintaining them than developing the application itself."
EVIDENCE: none. Anecdotal: the author's own near-miss project planning to cover most cases with E2E. Illustrative steps from Cypress docs: visit `https://example.cypress.io`; click the `type` link; assert URL includes `/commands/actions`; type `fake@email.com` into `.action-email`; assert value.
LIMITS: Teaching article without measurement. The codeless comparison is qualitative: "these solutions are still new. Therefore, they can't yet reach the complexity of test suites that you can develop by writing the code yourself."
TOOLING: Selenium, Cypress (JavaScript), TestCraft (codeless, built on Selenium).
LINKS: Automation Panda "The Testing Pyramid" (2018); freeCodeCamp Selenium-and-Docker E2E guide; TutorialsPoint unit and integration testing entries; Cypress "writing your first test."

## A094 · What is End-to-End (E2E) Testing? | IBM
URL: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/end-to-end-testing
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: E2E testing validates an entire application workflow from beginning to end and is best run as a seven-step process from planning through CI/CD automation, at the cost of more time and resources than narrower testing.
CONCEPTS:
- **E2E testing** — a methodology that validates an entire application workflow from beginning to end, confirming that front end, back end, databases and third-party services work smoothly together. > "Because E2E testing is ambitious enough to stake out the entire application development lifecycle, it’s not surprising to discover that E2E testing requires more commitment, resources and time."
- **Black box contrast** — E2E differs from a pass/fail assessment because it evaluates each stage of app performance rather than only whether the app works as billed. > "For this reason, E2E isn’t the ideal choice for every purpose. It’s typically a time-consuming testing process that’s best used in situations when testers genuinely require an evaluation of each stage of app performance."
- **Test suites** — the organizing device that groups test cases by user journey, feature, module or component so the work can be managed. > "Test suites fulfill this function, grouping test cases according to user journeys, certain features or modules and components."
- **Staging environment** — an environment that strongly resembles production, populated with the normally integrated components such as APIs and databases, using synthetic data when real performance data is unavailable. > "Ideally, testers should develop a staging environment that strongly resembles the production environment."
- **Automation step** — wiring automated tests into the CI/CD pipeline so they run routinely, which moves performance detection earlier in development. > "Testers that use the CI/CD pipeline can then detect performance issues earlier in the software development process, when they are able to mitigate them quickly and easily."
- **Selectors** — patterns that address the reactive elements of the DOM, letting a framework locate input fields, text and buttons. > "Selectors are patterns that call out the reactive elements within the Document Object Model (DOM) of a webpage."
- **Self-healing tests** — tests that recognize UI changes and correct themselves instead of breaking. > "This approach includes “self-healing” tests that can correct themselves based on system recognition of UI changes."
GUIDELINES:
- Follow the seven steps: `test planning and management`, `test environment setup`, `testing tool selection`, `test creation and execution`, `result validation`, `defect resolution`, `automation`.
- "Triage essential workflows" — test the most important journeys first, then break workflows into manageable steps.
- "Choose stable selectors": prefer "`data-*` attributes or other stable identifiers"; avoid `class names`; use DOM structure "carefully."
- "Ensure test independence": tests must be repeatable and "run free and unencumbered by external influences, such as third-party availability and network timing issues."
- "Make tests manageable": offload logic verification to unit and integration testing so E2E stays on user behavior and system synchronization.
- "Establish test environments" with "deep isolation to protect test results from undue interference from outside sources."
- "Dedicate time to API testing" to weed out logic problems "before testers ever evaluate the functionality of the UI."
- Run tests in parallel, especially in cloud configurations, to cut execution time and speed feedback.
- "Revisit and revise tests as needed."
EVIDENCE: none. Purely definitional and prescriptive.
LIMITS: No measurement, sample, or comparison data. The AI section is generic: benefits are "roughly like the advantages AI introduces to other forms of software testing."
TOOLING: Cypress, Selenium (web), Appium (mobile), Playwright (open source, CI/CD), cloud testing services, test management systems.
LINKS: IBM Think topics on software testing, unit/functional/integration testing, API, data integrity, CI/CD pipeline, DevOps, AI; IBM Engineering Lifecycle Management test management docs.

## A095 · Integration Testing: How-to, Examples & Free Test Plan (2025)
URL: https://katalon.com/resources-center/blog/integration-testing
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Integration testing progressively combines parts of a system and tests them as a group, and the choice among Big Bang, incremental and hybrid approaches — plus a pyramid-shaped test ratio — determines whether defects are found early and localized.
CONCEPTS:
- **Integration testing** — a type of testing in which multiple parts of a system are gradually integrated and then tested as a group, to check whether components work seamlessly together. > "Integration testing is a type of testing in which multiple parts of a software system are gradually integrated and then tested as a group."
- **Post-integration failure modes** — components that pass in isolation can still clash once combined, through inconsistent code logic, inconsistent data rules, third-party conflicts or inadequate exception handling. > "Conflicts can always arise — just like how people who work well individually may not always work well as a team."
- **Big Bang** — all modules integrated and tested at once, permitted only after every component has passed unit testing; simple to coordinate but poor at localizing defects. > "Big Bang Integration testing is an approach in which all modules are integrated and tested at once as a single combined system."
- **Incremental** — group two or more modules with closely related logic, test them, then keep expanding until the system is covered; more strategic because it demands detailed up-front planning. > "an approach in which 2 or more modules with closely related logic are grouped and tested first, then gradually expanded to other modules"
- **Bottom-up / top-down / hybrid** — bottom-up integrates from the lowest-level modules upward, top-down starts at the highest level and moves down, and hybrid (sandwich) runs both in parallel. > "With bottom-up integration testing, you start integrating modules at the lowest level, then gradually move to higher-level modules."
- **Low-level vs high-level components** — low-level parts do fundamental tasks such as data structures, input validation or database connection; high-level parts do system-wide work such as user management, catalog, checkout, payment and orders. > "Low-level components handle fundamental or simple tasks (e.g., data structures, utility functions). High-level components handle complex, system-wide operations such as processing, managing data, or securing workflows."
- **Stubs and drivers** — temporary substitutes created for components that do not exist yet when integrating incrementally. > "Some components may not be developed yet, requiring the creation of **stubs** and **drivers** as temporary substitutes."
- **Test pyramid** — E2E sits at the top with fewer tests because they are more complex, slower and more brittle than the layers below. > "They are fewer in number because they are more complex, slower, and more brittle."
GUIDELINES:
- Ratios: "**70–80% unit tests**, **15–20% integration tests**, and **5–10% end-to-end (E2E) tests**"; "Around 80% coverage is both realistic and effective" for unit tests.
- Choose Big Bang for simple, low-dependency systems; pair it with "detailed logging for easier fault localization" and defined expected interactions; "Reserve Big Bang testing for small and simple applications."
- Choose bottom-up when complexity sits low, low-level components are built first, bug localization matters, and higher modules still change.
- Choose top-down when complexity sits high, you want to "simulate real-world workflows and user journeys," and lower modules are stable.
- Practices: unit test all modules first; plan for "scope, objectives, cases, and required resources"; automate repetitive/complex cases; "Validate input test data"; "Run regression tests after each integration step."
EVIDENCE: none. No studies, samples, or measured results.
LIMITS: Katalon marketing (product section on browser coverage, page-object repository, Jira integration). Ratios are "a helpful guideline" with no source; cost claims about Big Bang are unquantified.
TOOLING: Katalon Platform / Studio (object repository, page-object model, API testing, cloud execution), Jira integration, Excel plan template.
LINKS: Katalon guides on Big Bang, bottom-up, top-down, unit, and E2E testing.

## A096 · What is the difference between unit, integration and end-to-end tests?
URL: https://specstory.com/learning/testing/unit-vs-integration-vs-e2e-tests
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: The levels differ in how much real software each test runs at once: each level up catches failures between parts a lower level replaces, at the price of speed, cost and precision of diagnosis.
CONCEPTS:
- **Unit test** — the smallest testable part, run in the same process with no network or database, with slow or outside parts replaced by a test double. > "It runs in the same process as the code, with no network or database, so it usually finishes in milliseconds."
- **Integration test** — real code at a boundary, typically a database or another service's API, with the database usually real while a local fake may stand in for another service. > "It runs the real code at a boundary instead of replacing that code with a test double. The boundary is often a database or another service's API."
- **Narrow vs broad integration tests** (Fowler) — narrow tests check one boundary such as database code; broad ones run against live versions of other services. > "narrow integration tests, which check one boundary, e.g. database code, from broad ones that run against live versions of other services."
- **End-to-end test** — the whole system exercised through its real interface the way a customer uses it: a headless browser for web, the built program for a CLI. > "An end-to-end test runs the whole system through its real interface, the way a customer would use it."
- **Level boundaries are conventions** — where unit ends and integration begins is set per team, so the same test can be classified differently elsewhere. > "A test that runs a function with the real classes it calls is a unit test on some teams and an integration test on others."
- **Names vs purposes** — smoke and regression tests are named for their purpose rather than a scope, so smoke usually runs at integration or E2E level and regression at any level. > "Smoke and regression tests name a purpose, not a scope."
- **Agent-level bias** — a coding agent tends to write tests at the level its own session can execute, which is not necessarily where the change can break. > "A coding agent often tests at the level its session can run, not where a change can fail."
- **Evidence, not proof** — every level checks only the behaviour its tests name, and the pyramid itself is a heuristic rather than a rule. > "Even all three levels together check only the behavior their tests name, so passing tests are evidence, not proof."
GUIDELINES:
- "Test each failure at the lowest level that can catch it": unit for rules inside one function, integration "wherever code writes to or reads from another part," "a few" E2E for customer journeys such as checkout from cart to confirmation.
- Unit tests "on every save" and in a `pre-push hook`; CI re-runs them with integration tests "on each push"; E2E "before merge or release."
- "Reviewers can check what each test replaces, not only its file name."
- Give the agent a test database; "require one test above the unit level, written from the request before the agent starts."
EVIDENCE: none measured; a worked case: `update_address` passes against `StubOrderStore` but the integration test fails with `assert 0 == 2` — the new `REPLACE` deletes the order row and a cascade deletes its items, so "the address saved, but the cart emptied."
LIMITS: "An illustrative example," simplified — "A real checkout would also need tests for payment and for stock levels." Boundaries differ per team, making counts incomparable.
TOOLING: Playwright, headless browsers, test doubles, CI, pre-push hooks, coding agents.
LINKS: Fowler, "The Practical Test Pyramid"; ISTQB glossary; SpecStory pages on mocks vs stubs and flaky tests.

## A097 · Session Based Test Management による 探索的テストの実践 1
URL: https://www.ipa.go.jp/archive/files/000064281.pdf
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: A system integrator applied Session Based Test Management (SBTM) on two outsourced projects to make exploratory testing manageable and reportable, by giving exploration a countable unit — the chartered, time-boxed session — plus explicit rules.
CONCEPTS:
- **SBTM** — a test-management concept that divides testing into sessions of roughly 30 minutes to 2 hours, each with a defined purpose, thereby giving exploratory testing a management unit. > "Session Based Test Management では、テストをセッションと呼ばれる時間枠に分割し、管理単位としている。セッションは 30 分～2 時間程度の時間枠であり、セッションごとにテストの目的を定義する。"
- **Session sheet** — a form that serves as both charter and report template, prepared per time box so the manager can direct the content before testing and review it afterwards. > "時間枠（セッション）ごとにテストチャーターとレポート様式を兼ねたセッションシートを準備することで、図 88-1 のように、テストの実施前にテスト管理者がある程度テストの内容を指示することや、テストの実施後に内容を振り返れる状態を目指した。"
- **Test charter** — a document organizing the scope, purpose and viewpoints of a test; setting one per session makes the tested range, volume and viewpoints graspable after the fact. > "Session Based Test Management では、セッションごとにテストチャーターを設定することで、探索的テストであっても、テストを実施した範囲や総量、観点などを後から把握することができる。"
- **Planned vs actual** — progress is tracked as consumption of session sheets against the target session count, and plotting remaining sessions weekly surfaces delay quickly. > "残存セッション数を週次単位でグラフによって図示することを試みて、進捗の遅れ具合を素早く察知できるようにした。"
- **Bugs-per-session by function** — plotting defects per session per feature exposes where bugs and severe bugs concentrate, allowing later sessions to be redirected. > "1 セッションあたりの摘出バグ数を機能ごとに図 88-5 のようにグラフで整理した。この結果、特定の機能でのバグが多く摘出されていることや、重大バグの発生状況の偏りを把握することができ"
- **Dispersion (ブレ)** — sessions that spend longer on preparation run at a different density, so per-session bug counts can diverge from the real situation. > "同じ 1 時間のセッションであっても、テスト実施のための準備（テストデータの作成や、環境の変更など）を行う時間が長いセッションと、短いセッションでは実施できたテストの濃度が異なる。"
- **Direction control** — the manager reads the daily reports, draws on them for new session sheets, and steers the direction of testing as the work proceeds. > "テスト管理者は、図 88-3 のように、日々セッションシートのレポートを確認し、テスターのレポートから気づきを得ることで、新たなセッションシートを作成し、随時テストの方向性を制御できる。"
GUIDELINES:
- Max `3 sessions per tester per day`, from SBTM's `2-hour` maximum session plus tester concentration limits, set by interviewing experienced testers.
- Target session count = testers × test days × 3; track progress as consumption against it.
- Rule (1): if a session needs more than `2 hours`, report it, and the manager splits the session.
- Rule (2): "do not perform work other than exploratory testing during a session."
- Rule (3): report approximate testing time; the manager judges density and removes obstacles.
- Rule (4): testers may leave charter scope when bugs seem findable, but must report an approximate `%` of charter adherence, and the manager rewrites the sheet to match.
- Train managers and testers; fold SBTM into the development standard via a guideline document.
EVIDENCE: Two projects — (1) maintenance of a financial-institution screening system; (2) redevelopment of a student management system, client-server to packaged web. In (2) consumption fell behind on workload; the PM added testers and revised the schedule. Both improved bugs found per unit time versus exploratory testing without the approach; all goals were judged achieved.
LIMITS: Two case studies in one company; evaluation by questionnaire and interview, not controlled measurement; the bugs-per-time gain is "confirmed" without figures; one project's data is masked.
TOOLING: session sheets, remaining-session and defects-per-session graphs, daily information-sharing meetings.
LINKS: Bach, "Session-Based Test Management" (2000); JSTQB Foundation Level Syllabus; IPA/SEC report SEC-2017-88-01.

## A098 · Session-Based Test Management | SQRBOK - Handbook
URL: https://sqrbok.github.io/content/verif/exploratory/session-based.html
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: SBTM organizes exploratory testing into chartered, time-boxed sessions each ending in a written report and a short debriefing, so exploration can be planned, counted and reviewed like any test work.
CONCEPTS:
- **Four parts of a session** — a charter, an uninterrupted block of about 90 minutes, a session report, and a debriefing that produces the next charter. > "Charter, then an uninterrupted session of about 90 minutes, then a session report, then a debriefing that produces the next charter"
- **Charter** — one mission expressed in the three-slot form: explore a target using resources to discover information. > "One mission, in the form _explore target using resources to discover information_"
- **Time box** — an uninterrupted block of testing, about 90 minutes by default, with 60 to 120 minutes counted as a normal session, under 60 short and over 120 long. > "A **normal session** lasts about 90 minutes (this handbook counts 60 to 120 minutes as normal, under 60 as short and over 120 as long)"
- **Session report** — the reviewable written outcome of a session, which Bach calls the session sheet and the handbook calls the report. > "Bach calls the written outcome the session sheet; this handbook calls it the session report."
- **Debriefing** — tester and test lead walk through the report in minutes, covering what was done, found and not reached, and settle the next charter. > "The tester and the test lead go through the report in a few minutes: what was done, what was found, what was not reached, and what the next charter should be."
- **Five levels of exploration** (Ghazi et al.) — freestyle, high, medium, low and fully scripted, each adding one element to what the tester receives. > "Ghazi et al. describe five levels, from freestyle to fully scripted, each adding one element to what the tester receives"
- **Freestyle still has a mission** — even at the freest level the charter names the test object, so a mission, time box and report remain; a three-part charter starts at level 2. > "at freestyle it names only the test object, so freestyle still has a mission, a time box and a report, which ad hoc testing lacks."
GUIDELINES:
- Record the session type: it "keeps session counts comparable."
- Choose levels by need: freestyle for "learning a new product, hunting for unknown problems"; high for "finding defects fast, under time pressure"; medium when "known risks must be checked, but the path is open"; low when "traceability matters"; scripted when "conformance must be shown."
- Ericsson reference mix: `16%` freestyle, `18%` high, `23%` medium, `22%` low, `21%` scripted; that team ran about `20%` at the two most exploratory levels against the recommended `34%`. "The point is not the numbers but the mix."
- Use SBTM when exploration "must be planned, estimated or reported to someone outside the team," or when several testers cover one product.
- Skip it when "one developer explores their own feature for half an hour."
EVIDENCE: Afzal et al. "used Bach's 90 minutes in their experiments"; Hendrickson recommends "one to two hours." Ericsson rated the levels against 17 self-elicited criteria, top-weighted being checking requirements, reproducing defects and finding unknown defects — "which pull in opposite directions." "No controlled study compares sessions with and without SBTM."
LIMITS: "The report records what the tester says they covered; there is no automatic coverage measure." Debriefs "cost the test lead time for every session." Levels and the mix come from "one focus group each." AI used for summarization.
TOOLING: none.
LINKS: Bach, STQE 2(6):32–37, 2000; Afzal et al., EMSE 20(3), 2015; Hendrickson, *Explore It!* 2013; Ghazi et al., IEEE Access 6, 2018; Ghazi et al., arXiv:1704.00994.

## A099 · Charters, Heuristics and Tours | SQRBOK - Handbook
URL: https://sqrbok.github.io/content/verif/exploratory/techniques.html
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: A charter, a heuristic and a tour are the three tools that tell an exploratory tester what to try next — mission, next input, and whole-session strategy — and none lists test steps; they direct attention.
CONCEPTS:
- **Charter** — the device that sets a session's mission, in Hendrickson's three-slot template, as against a script that prescribes steps. > "the charter sets the mission of a session, a heuristic suggests the next input, and a tour names a strategy for moving through the product"
- **Target / resources / information** — the part of the product to explore, what the tester brings to it (tools, data, configuration, a named heuristic or tour), and what counts as a finding. > "The **target** is the part of the product to explore; the **resources** are what the tester brings to it: tools, test data, a configuration, or a named heuristic or tour"
- **Heuristic** — a rule of thumb for choosing inputs, used to suggest the next input rather than plan a whole session. > "A heuristic is a rule of thumb for choosing inputs."
- **Tour** — a strategy that governs a whole session, where a heuristic governs only the next single input; Whittaker groups his tours into six districts of a city. > "A **tour** sets one strategy for a whole session, where a heuristic suggests the next single input."
- **Nightmare Headline Game** — asking what headline a failure would produce, then aiming the next session at that risk. > "The **Nightmare Headline Game** asks what headline a failure would produce, and points the next session there"
- **Level mapping** — a goal-only charter is level 2; naming starting points such as a tour or heuristic moves it to level 3, medium exploration, and a charter listing steps is a script. > "a charter with only a goal is level 2; naming starting points, such as a tour or heuristic, moves it to level 3, medium exploration"
- **Dynamic test design** — testers were observed applying equivalence partitioning, boundary values and combinations while executing, without writing them down first. > "Observations of eleven industrial testers found them applying equivalence partitioning, boundary values and combinations _during_ execution, without writing them down first"
GUIDELINES:
- Write charters in the three-slot form: `Explore checkout using the Saboteur tour (cut the network during payment) to discover lost or double payments.`
- Match heuristic to artifact: "input fields suit Goldilocks; lists, Beginning, Middle, End; prices, Never and Always."
- Named heuristics: `Some, None, All` ("no permissions, some, all"); `Goldilocks` (too big, too small, just right); `Beginning, Middle, End`; `CRUD` (every entity "in unusual orders"); `Follow the Data` (one value from entry to every screen and report); `Never and Always`.
- Use these when "a feature is new or changed and the specification is thin" and "you need test ideas fast"; not alone when "a regulator requires a predefined, traceable test record," or when "the tester does not know the domain."
EVIDENCE: "Observations of eleven industrial testers found them applying equivalence partitioning, boundary values and combinations during execution, without writing them down first" (Itkonen et al., ESEM 2009).
LIMITS: "They do not guarantee any coverage: two testers with the same charter will try different things. Coverage is known only from the session report." "Which heuristics work best has not been compared experimentally." Authors hold summaries, not full text. AI used for summarization.
TOOLING: none.
LINKS: Hendrickson, *Explore It!* 2013; Whittaker, *Exploratory Software Testing*, Addison-Wesley 2009; Itkonen, Mäntylä, Lassenius, ESEM 2009; SQRBOK pages on Tours, Session Report, SBTM.

## A100 · Exploratory Testing
URL: https://docs.tricentis.com/tosca-2026.1/en-us/content/tosca_commander/exploratory_testing.htm
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: Exploratory testing is "a plan-as-you-test approach" in which learning the product, designing tests, and executing them happen simultaneously, and session-based testing is the framework that makes it workable at scale.
CONCEPTS:
- `exploratory testing` — A single activity in which the tester learns the product, designs and runs tests, and reads the results together, rather than in separate phases. > "Exploratory testing is about learning the product, designing and executing tests, and interpreting the test results, all at the same time."
- Formal vs exploratory purpose — Formal manual testing monitors risks already known, while exploratory testing targets risk that has not yet been named, starting from assumptions that lack evidence. > "This means that exploratory testing starts with a focus on the things you do not know, and the illusions you are holding true without any empirical evidence."
- Feedback-driven sequencing — Each test is chosen from what the previous result revealed, so the more unpredictable the right next test is, the more exploratory the cycle. > "In exploratory testing, your next test is always influenced by the result of the last test you did."
- `session-based testing` — The named framework (also called session-based test management) that gives exploratory testing a structured form usable when several agile teams are involved. > "Session-based testing (aka session-based test management) is a framework allowing the idea of exploratory testing to unfold in a structured fashion."
- `session` — The core object of the framework, which supplies the entry point for exploration and lets testers choose what and how to test. > "This can be attributed to its core object: the session. A session identifies a starting point for exploratory testing."
- `session charter` — The artefact that states the goals and agenda of a session, and the reason the approach works for testers of different skill levels. > "All this is achieved with the session charter which represents the goals and agenda of a session."
- `session owner` — The role that sets up Exploratory Sessions in Tosca Commander and allocates exploratory testers, and may assign their tasks. > "The session owner is responsible for setting up Exploratory Sessions in Tosca Commander and allocating exploratory testers to these sessions."
- `scenario` — The artefact testers build while exploring, using videos, screenshots and TestSteps to document the scenario and any errors found in the test object. > "Upon exploratory testing, exploratory testers create scenarios, where they make use of videos, screenshots and steps (TestSteps) to document both the scenarios and any found errors in the test object."
- TestCase-as-template — A scenario need not start empty; an existing TestCase can serve as its template. > "Existing TestCases can also be used as a template for scenarios"
- `Exploratory Testing Agent` — Tests can run either inside Tosca Commander or stand-alone through this agent. > "Testers are able to run their tests either in Tosca Commander or in stand-alone mode via the Exploratory Testing Agent"
- Scenario-to-manual-test-case conversion — Session results are collected in Tosca Commander and manual TestCases can be generated from the scenarios recorded during the session. > "Manual TestCases can then be created out of the scenarios that the testers created earlier"
GUIDELINES:
- Assign a `session owner` who creates sessions and allocates testers before testing begins.
- Work from a `session charter` stating goals and agenda; do not treat a session as unbounded exploration.
- Document findings in-session using videos, screenshots and `TestSteps` so errors are attached to the test object.
- Reuse existing `TestCases` as templates when recording a scenario.
- Choose execution mode per tester: Tosca Commander or stand-alone via the `Exploratory Testing Agent`.
- Convert proven scenarios into manual `TestCases` after the session so discovery becomes regression coverage.
EVIDENCE: none (vendor conceptual/feature documentation).
LIMITS: Product documentation for Tosca 2026.1; describes Tosca capabilities, not measured outcomes; no data on defect yield or session effectiveness. The flowchart implies tooling prerequisites.
TOOLING: Tricentis Tosca 2026.1, Tosca Commander, Exploratory Testing Agent, TestSteps, Exploratory Sessions.
LINKS: Internal Tosca docs chapters — "Create session", "Add testers", "Record scenario", "Perform standalone testing", "Generate manual test case".

## A101 · Get Started With Session-Based Testing | Hindsight | Guides
URL: https://help.hindsightsoftware.com/en/articles/941309-get-started-with-session-based-testing
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: Session-based Test Management gives exploratory testing reportable results and coverage, and it runs as a three-step cycle — planning, executing, debriefing — attached to individual Jira issues.
CONCEPTS:
- `test session` — The practice is not new: a session is simply a time slot of roughly 45 minutes to two hours aimed at one test objective. > "They’re simply the periods of time, usually between 45 minutes and two hours, devoted to fulfilling specific test objective."
- `charter` — The session's scope, combining test objective and time period; it fails if it collapses into one test case or sprawls beyond the allotted time. > "A good Session Charter isn't so precise it's essentially a single test case but it also shouldn't be so broad and vague that the session can never be completed within the time period assigned."
- Risk-driven charter derivation — When session ideas are hard to find, enumerate the important risks of the story and of the application, then create one session per risk. > "Identify important and relevant risks to the Story or Issue and the application under test, and create sessions for each of them"
- Risk checklist — A starting list of risk areas — capability, reliability, usability, security, scalability, performance, installability, compatibility — used as prompts rather than as an exhaustive set. > "A basic list of risks to consider: capability, reliability, usability, security, scalability, performance, installability (Software installation process) and compatibility."
- Session states — A session moves through Open, In progress and Ended, and the charter is editable only in the first state. > "sessions have three self explanatory states; Open, In progress, and Ended"
- `Report defect` — Defects are filed from inside the session, which pre-selects the right issue types, counts defects, and shows the parent issue and the session on the defect. > "Report defect creates Jira Issues but automatically selects 'Defect' or 'Bug' Issue types for the user."
- Note labels — Notes can be typed with labels such as Ideas, Questions, Surprises, Issues and concerns, and Positives. > "Behave Pro allows you to add one or more labels to a note"
- Session close fields — Ending a session asks for a short summary, a quality rating of the work tested, a coverage rating, and an optional time breakdown. > "the user will be prompted to write a short summary of the session, rate the quality of work that was tested and the session coverage, and optionally record how their time was spent"
- `debrief` — The handback makes the session and the testing effort accountable to the team rather than merely sharing findings. > "Debriefs don't just share information with the team, but also makes the session and testing effort accountable to the team"
- `session improvement` — A fellow tester or test coach reviews the session notes and proposes alternative techniques, framed as a retrospective on the session. > "You can think of this as running a retrospective on the Test Session."
GUIDELINES:
- Timebox every session to `45 minutes`–`2 hours`.
- Give each session a short `Title` in addition to charter and time, for discussion references.
- Do initial planning as early as possible (sprint planning or development), then review sessions before testing: "Are additional sessions required? Is an specified session still relevant?"
- Assign testers when the story moves into testing, not at creation, to adapt to availability.
- Create one or two sessions for a simple change; many sessions for a complex change, in proportion to risk.
- Keep notes during the session so the close-out summary is accurate and can serve as regulatory evidence.
- If drifting off charter: "take note of current diversion and create a new session charter for it."
- Debrief on: defects found (triage them), coverage gaps, risks/questions, and positives.
- Typical Definition-of-done rule: all defects related to the story must be fixed before it is "done".
EVIDENCE: none (vendor how-to; no measurements).
LIMITS: Behave Pro/Jira-specific workflow; no empirical data; recommendations presented as vendor practice.
TOOLING: Hindsight Behave Pro for Jira, Jira issue types and issue linking, agile boards, Jira gadgets/dashboards.
LINKS: SBTM lineage (sessions/charters), Hindsight articles on enforcing triage, linking user stories and defects, building a session-based testing dashboard.

## A102 · What is Session-Based Test Management (SBTM)? | Testpad
URL: https://testpad.com/session-based-test-management
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: SBTM is a formalization of exploratory testing built from sessions, charters, note-taking and debriefing, sitting between rigid test case management and unstructured exploration — and many teams end up with something more pragmatic than either.
CONCEPTS:
- `SBTM` — A structured form of exploratory testing in which testers receive an area and a session length, explore freely inside that scope, and then document what they covered and found. > "Session-based test management (SBTM) is a formalization of the more general idea of exploratory testing."
- `test case management (TCM)` — Test cases are detailed instructions plus expected outcomes and any supporting data a tester needs, used mainly by large QA organisations needing rigid KPI reporting. > "detailed instructions for completing a test, along with expected outcomes and any other data a tester might need to know or capture."
- Fundamental TCM limit — Test Case Management can only detect the defects that the test author already imagined. > "There is a major downside to Test Case Management, though: it only catches the bugs you can anticipate."
- `exploratory testing` — Testing driven by observation, where the tester decides the next step from what the product just did and modifies tests as they go. > "We like to describe it as testing with your brain switched on: deciding what to try next based on what you just observed."
- Unknown unknowns — SBTM keeps the tester's freedom to choose how to test, which is what lets unexpected classes of defect surface. > "testers still have the freedom to decide how to test, which can reveal unknown unknowns"
- `sessions` — Session length is budgeted from the complexity of the area and the probability that defects live there. > "The idea is to budget time according to the complexity of the topic and the likelihood that there will be bugs in it."
- `charters` — A charter is a test plan reduced to an allocation of minutes per area of functionality. > "Testers are to spend a certain amount of time in each area of functionality, testing as they see fit."
- `note-taking` — Written notes are the session's output and must make the tested and untested areas distinguishable. > "Testers should journal what they tried during their sessions (in accordance with the charter) and what happened as a result."
- `debriefing` — The debrief turns notes into bugs and improvements, and into the next set of sessions and charters. > "Debriefs are a chance to analyze and act on testers’ notes."
- Pomodoro analogy — Fixed sessions are claimed to hold attention the way the Pomodoro productivity technique does. > "Stayed focused – sessions are similar to the popular"
- Pragmatic hybrid — Where full SBTM is too loose, a templated grid keeps testers on track while still letting them add tests they think of. > "This keeps your testers on track while giving them the option to add in more tests as they think of them."
GUIDELINES:
- Budget longer sessions for new, high-risk features; shorter sessions for "established, stable, old features that haven't changed".
- Example charter allocation: `Set up and login - 20 minutes`, `Social sharing - 10 minutes`, `Account deletion - 15 minutes`.
- Write charters detailed enough to prevent missed areas, but keep items as high-level prompts — "Stick to high-level prompts using words like 'look at'" rather than binary checks.
- Define explicit pass/fail criteria: pass = "Yes, we looked at this, and there are no problems"; fail = "This particular thing failed, and I have comments in the next cell over explaining what went wrong."
- Reuse charters across releases but "iterate on them from release to release" so updated areas are re-reviewed and regression testing is not forgotten.
- Avoid over-broad charters: "Explore login for 10 minutes" may omit forgotten-password functionality.
EVIDENCE: none — explicitly "we don't have data to back it up" for the claim that SBTM is underused.
LIMITS: Vendor editorial with product promotion; acknowledges note-quality variance, less predictable coverage, and subjectivity as SBTM drawbacks; reporting "depends on note quality"; "There is no one single best way to test."
TOOLING: Testpad, spreadsheets, Pomodoro technique.
LINKS: James Bach and Jonathan Bach (2000), "Session-Based Test Management" paper at satisfice.com (called "the canonical description"); Testpad articles on writing test cases, test plans, exploratory testing, manual regression testing.

## A103 · Exploratory testing - Service Manual - GOV.UK
URL: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/technology/exploratory-testing
TYPE: official docs
THESIS: Exploratory testing explores a system as a user would, without a script chasing a predetermined outcome, and despite sounding ad hoc it is "a disciplined approach" requiring stated goals, documented evidence and deliberate techniques.
CONCEPTS:
- Definition — The tester works through the system as a user would, with no script predicting the outcome, relying on knowledge, experience and intuition. > "The goal of exploratory testing is to explore a system as a user would, without a script to test a predetermined outcome."
- Complement to automation — Exploratory testing hunts problems not yet known, whereas automation demonstrates that already-written scripts complete without defects. > "Exploratory testing aims to find new and undiscovered problems. It contrasts with other more prescribed methods of testing, such as test automation"
- `test charter` — The charter states the session's mission and scope without specifying which problems to look for. > "Test charters give exploratory testing sessions a mission without being prescriptive."
- `mind maps` — A diagram-based way of recording information, chosen because it is fast to write and does not impose a linear order. > "Mind mapping is a visual thinking tool that involves organising information in a diagram, instead of writing it in sentences."
- `timeboxing` — A time limit is what keeps an unscripted session on its goals instead of wandering. > "Timeboxing your session (or setting a time limit) can help you focus on specific goals rather than drift into unfocused exploration."
- `inspect and adapt` — Because the work is unscripted, each test follows from the results of the previous one. > "following an ‘inspect and adapt’ model (where the next test you do is based on the previous test results)"
- Evidence capture — Notes, screenshots and logs are the record that allows the testing to be repeated or investigated later. > "capture the evidence as notes, screenshots and log files so that the testing can replicated or investigated further"
- Bug-to-scenario conversion — A defect found during exploration can be turned into a test scenario and then automated so it is not repeated. > "An exploratory test that discovers a bug can be developed into a test scenario and automated."
- Activity-time reporting — A session can be reported as time split across creating and executing tests, investigating and reporting bugs, and setting up. > "You can also report how much of the exploratory testing session you spent on each different activity"
GUIDELINES:
- State a goal for each testing session.
- Document all queries and observations during the session, capturing evidence as notes, screenshots and logs.
- Note down ideas for further testing as you go.
- Apply the three techniques: `test charters`, `mind maps`, `timeboxing`.
- A charter should record mission scope, testing goals (e.g. "making sure a system is secure enough for people to use"), who is testing, when and where, the test environment, and any test data such as a mock username or password.
- Run exploratory testing when the system has "enough functionality for you to interact with it in a meaningful way" — e.g. before releasing a first MVP in beta or a major new feature.
- Prefer experienced QA testers; business analysts, product managers and subject matter experts also work if they have the necessary testing skills.
- "the only tools you really need are a pen and some paper" — do not postpone testing for lack of tooling.
- Report the charter, features tested, testing approach notes, bugs found, issue list, supporting materials, and per-activity time.
EVIDENCE: none (guidance, no measurements).
LIMITS: Government service-manual guidance from 2016; no empirical data; oriented to public-sector digital services; tooling advice is deliberately minimal.
TOOLING: video capture and logging tools, planning tools, process diagrams; pen and paper as the minimum.
LINKS: Jonathan Bach, "Session-based test management" (satisfice.com/sbtm); related GOV.UK guides on quality assurance/testing regularly, performance testing, vulnerability and penetration testing, accessibility testing.

## A104 · Exploratory testing in Test Management | BrowserStack Docs
URL: https://www.browserstack.com/docs/test-management/overview/exploratory-testing
TYPE: vendor docs
THESIS: Exploratory Sessions make unscripted, time-boxed testing a first-class, auditable entity in a test management platform, removing the need to invent throwaway test cases before you can log findings.
CONCEPTS:
- Problem being solved — Structured runs demand test cases before anything can be executed, which is friction for new features, bug bashes and unstable areas. > "Structured test runs in Test Management require you to define test cases before you can execute anything."
- Consequence of workarounds — Generic placeholder cases and off-platform spreadsheets leave no coverage record and undermine a single source of truth. > "These workarounds produce no auditable coverage data and break the single-source-of-truth promise of a test management platform."
- `Session` — The core entity, describing one time-boxed exploratory effort with a title, mission, duration, assignee and optional metadata. > "Session is the core entity. It represents a single time-boxed exploratory testing effort."
- `Session Log` — The timeline of timestamped entries is the actual deliverable of an exploratory session. > "The log is the primary output of an exploratory session."
- Entry statuses — Every log entry carries a status drawn from Pass, Fail, Bug, Note, Blocked or Retest. > "Each entry has rich text content, a status (Pass, Fail, Bug, Note, Blocked, or Retest), and a timestamp."
- `Timebox` — A planned duration with an elapsed-time counter that never halts or locks the session. > "The counter does not auto-stop or lock the session when time runs out. It is a guide, not a gate."
- `Mission` — The charter equivalent: it must narrow testing enough to focus it yet stay open enough for discovery. > "A good mission is specific enough to focus your testing but broad enough to allow discovery."
- `Session logging` style — A complete audit trail of every action, typical where regulated work or stakeholder proof of coverage is required. > "This approach is common in regulated environments or when stakeholders need proof of coverage."
- `Bug bashing` style — Successful actions go unlogged; only defects and their issue links are captured as the deliverable. > "You skip logging successful actions and focus on capturing bugs and linking them to your issue tracker."
- Session vs Test Run split — The two entities answer different needs, and because sessions are excluded from Test Run Reports, Test Plan Reports and dashboard widgets, per-case pass/fail reporting still requires Test Runs. > "Test Runs and Exploratory Sessions serve different testing needs. Understanding the distinction helps you pick the right tool for the job."
GUIDELINES:
- Create the session with title, timebox, mission, configurations, tags and assignee before testing.
- Set the timebox in minutes at creation and watch the elapsed-time counter for adherence; do not expect enforcement.
- Write missions as scope-plus-goal statements rather than step lists.
- Choose per-effort which style to log: full session logging for audit/coverage proof, bug bashing for defect yield; both can coexist in one session or be split into separate sessions.
- Link requirements before testing and defects during testing via Jira, Azure DevOps and other supported integrations.
- Prefer Exploratory Sessions over generic placeholder test cases for feature discovery, bug bashes, ad-hoc investigation and smoke testing; keep Test Runs for regression, compliance verification and repeatable execution.
- Use Test Runs when per-case pass/fail reporting in dashboards is required, since sessions do not feed those reports.
EVIDENCE: none (product documentation).
LIMITS: Documentation for one vendor's feature; explicitly notes sessions are excluded from existing reports; no outcome data.
TOOLING: BrowserStack Test Management (Exploratory Sessions, Test Cases, Test Runs, Test Plans), Jira, Azure DevOps integrations.
LINKS: BrowserStack sub-pages — Create an Exploratory Session, Run an Exploratory Session, Link issues to an Exploratory Session, Edit/close/delete, Manage Exploratory Sessions.

## A105 · Exploratory Testing
URL: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ExploratoryTesting.html
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: Exploratory testing emphasizes a rapid cycle of learning, test design and execution to probe the boundaries of what scripted tests cover; even excellent automated testing is scripted and therefore insufficient alone.
CONCEPTS:
- Definition — A style built on a fast loop of learning, designing tests and executing them, exploring characteristics rather than verifying a script and sorting discoveries afterwards into acceptable behaviour or failures. > "Exploratory testing is a style of testing that emphasizes a rapid cycle of learning, test design, and test execution."
- `scripted testing` — Test designers write each manipulation together with the expected behaviour, and the scripts are run separately, repeatedly, usually by people other than their authors. > "In scripted testing, test designers create a script of tests, where each manipulation of the software is written down, together with the expected behavior of the software."
- Automation shift — Moving scripted tests into automation, under Extreme Programming influence, made them faster and removed human error from judging expected behaviour. > "This allows the tests to be executed faster, and eliminates the human error involved in evaluating the expected behavior."
- The `net` metaphor — A scripted suite is a net that catches bugs passing through it, and the open question is whether the net is spread where it should be; exploratory testing probes that boundary. > "Such tests can be a fine net that catches any bugs that try to get through it, but how do we know that the net covers all it ought to?"
- Known vs unknown conditions — A script can only confirm the conditions somebody already wrote into it. > "Scripted testing can only verify what is in the script, catching only conditions that are known about."
- Benign discoveries — Exploration also surfaces behaviour that was never considered and turns out to be acceptable or desirable. > "sometimes it exposes behaviors that are benign, even welcome, but not thought of before"
- `time-boxed sessions` — Discipline is supplied by sessions with a fixed length, each aimed at one aspect of the software. > "A good way to do this is to carry out exploratory testing in time-boxed sessions."
- `charter` — The charter names the target and the information sought, and that is enough focus for a session. > "A charter that identifies the target of the session and what information you hope to find is a fine mechanism to provide this focus."
- Skill requirement — The work needs testers who are curious and can invent test designs mid-session, though they need not test full-time. > "Exploratory testing requires skilled and curious testers, who are comfortable with learning about the software and coming up with new test designs during a session."
- Escape analysis — Bugs that reach production are evidence of gaps, and examining each escape shows whether more exploratory testing is warranted. > "It's worth looking at any bug that escapes to production and thinking about what measures could be taken to either prevent the bug from getting there, or detecting it rapidly when in production."
GUIDELINES:
- Carry out exploratory testing in time-boxed sessions with a charter naming the target and desired information.
- Do not let the charter prescribe the session's details; allow questions outside the charter to spawn later sessions.
- Start with a `one hour` session `every couple of weeks` and see what information surfaces (author's suggestion, since guidelines are scarce: "it's hard to find any guidelines on how much should be done").
- Alternative cadence some teams use: `half-an-hour` or so of exploratory testing whenever a story is completed.
- Make exploratory testing "a regular activity occurring throughout the software development process".
- Treat "a team isn't doing exploratory testing at all" as "a red flag", even with excellent automation.
- Expect a ramp-up: "it will take time to build up the skill to do exploratory testing well".
- When a bug escapes, ask what would prevent it or detect it rapidly in production.
EVIDENCE: none (practitioner opinion/bliki).
LIMITS: Author states guidelines on how much exploratory testing to do are hard to find and his cadence is a suggestion; explicitly informal; relies on cited book for method depth.
TOOLING: none named.
LINKS: Elisabeth Hendrickson's book *Explore It!* (source of the net metaphor); Extreme Programming.

## A106 · Test flakiness' causes, detection, impact and responses: A multivocal review
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0164121223002327
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: A multivocal review of 200 flaky-test articles — 109 academic and 91 grey literature — organizes the field along four dimensions (causes, detection, impact, responses) and shows research has concentrated on Java, on order-dependency and concurrency, and on rerun-based detection.
CONCEPTS:
- `flaky tests` — Tests whose outcome is not deterministic, treated by the authors as a major problem for testing as a whole. > "Flaky tests (tests with non-deterministic outcomes) pose a major challenge for software testing."
- `multivocal review` — The paper's method is to trace a topic through both scholarly work and practitioner writing so research and practice are examined together. > "This paper presents a multivocal review that investigates how flaky tests, as a topic, have been addressed in both research and practice."
- Four analysis dimensions — The literature is organised under causes, detection, impact and responses, with existing research, discussions, methods and tools classified in each. > "structured the body of relevant research and knowledge using four different dimensions: causes, detection, impact and responses"
- Impact framing — Flakiness is described as damaging how effective and how fast testing is, and as pushing releases out. > "They are known to cause significant issues, such as reducing the effectiveness and efficiency of testing and delaying software releases."
- Language skew — The reviewed work concentrates overwhelmingly on one programming language. > "Most studies covering test flakiness have focused more on Java."
- Cause concentration — Two causes in particular have attracted most of the research attention: dependence on test order, and concurrency. > "Flakiness due to test order dependency and concurrency are widely studied."
- Dynamic rerun-based detection — Rerunning tests to observe the same test pass and fail is the dominant detection approach in the reviewed body of work. > "Dynamic rerun-based approaches are the most common methods of flaky test detection."
- Mitigation strategies — Responses to flakiness are treated as a separate strand of work, alongside causes, detection methods and impact. > "increased interest in flaky tests, with research focusing on different aspects of flakiness, such as identifying causes, detection methods and mitigation strategies"
- Practitioner discourse — The topic is argued to be live outside academia because its effects are felt by working teams. > "Test flakiness has also become a key discussion point for practitioners (in blog posts, technical magazines, etc.) as the impact of flaky tests is felt across the industry."
GUIDELINES: none stated in the available text beyond the review's own structuring method (screen 560 articles, retain those focused on flaky tests, then bucket by the four dimensions).
EVIDENCE: Out of 560 articles reviewed, 200 focused on flaky tests, composed of 109 academic and 91 grey literature articles/posts. Reported highlights: majority of studies focus on Java; order dependency and concurrency widely studied; dynamic rerun-based approaches the most common detection method.
LIMITS: The extracted text contains only highlights, abstract, keywords and author biographies — the full categorization tables are not present. Because flakiness research skews to Java, generalization to other languages is a stated gap; the review identifies "limitations and opportunities for future research" rather than resolving them.
TOOLING: none named in available text.
LINKS: Journal of Systems and Software vol. 206 (Dec 2023), article 111837, DOI 10.1016/j.jss.2023.111837; open access under CC BY 4.0.

## A107 · Surveying the Developer Experience of Flaky Tests
URL: https://www.computer.org/csdl/proceedings-article/icse-seip/2022/959000a253/1EhscHlWGdi
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Combining a 170-response developer survey with analysis of 38 StackOverflow threads, the study finds developers strongly agree flaky tests hinder continuous integration, frequent flaky-test experience breeds failure-ignoring, and setup/teardown issues are rated the most common cause.
CONCEPTS:
- `flaky` — A test that changes outcome while the code under test stays the same. > "Test cases that pass and fail without changes to the code under test are known as flaky."
- Research gap — A decade of growing interest in flaky tests had left developers' own views and experiences largely unexamined. > "The past decade has seen increasing research interest in flaky tests, though little attention has been afforded to the views and experiences of software developers."
- Multi-source design — StackOverflow discussion is used alongside the survey precisely because it is not self-reported. > "We also searched on StackOverflow and analyzed 38 threads relevant to flaky tests, offering a distinct perspective free of any self-reporting bias."
- Developer definition — One of the study's inquiry areas is how practitioners themselves define flakiness, rather than how papers define it. > "we utilized a multi-source approach to obtain insights into how developers define flaky tests"
- Impacts, causes and responses — The remaining inquiry areas cover what developers say flakiness does to them, what they believe causes it, and what they do when they hit it. > "their experiences of the impacts and causes of flaky tests, and the actions they take in response to them"
- `CI hindrance` — The strongest attitudinal result is agreement that flaky tests obstruct continuous integration. > "this study reveals a number of findings, including (1) developers strongly agree that flaky tests hinder continuous integration"
- `failure-ignoring` — Habituation is reported: the more often a developer meets flakiness, the more likely they are to discount failures that may be real. > "developers who experience flaky tests more often may be more likely to ignore potentially genuine test failures"
- `setup and teardown` — Practitioners rank test setup and teardown as the leading cause, which is put in contrast with the research emphasis on concurrency and order. > "developers rate issues in setup and teardown to be the most common causes of flaky tests"
GUIDELINES: none stated in the available abstract; no thresholds or practices are prescribed.
EVIDENCE: Survey deployed on social media yielding `170` total responses; `38` StackOverflow threads analysed; mixture of numerical and thematic analyses. Three named findings: (1) strong agreement that flaky tests hinder CI; (2) more-frequent flaky-test experiencers more likely to ignore potentially genuine failures; (3) setup and teardown issues rated the most common cause.
LIMITS: Survey distribution via social media implies self-selection; the paper frames StackOverflow analysis specifically as a counter to self-reporting bias, implying the survey results carry that bias; findings are perceptual/attitudinal rather than measured failure data.
TOOLING: none named in available text.
LINKS: ICSE-SEIP 2022, pages 253–262, DOI 10.1109/ICSE-SEIP55303.2022.9793965. Related works listed include "A Survey on How Test Flakiness Affects Developers" (ICST 2022), FlakyCat, FlakeSync, and "A Study on the Lifecycle of Flaky Tests" (ICSE 2020).

## A108 · A survey of flaky tests
URL: https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/230095/1/parry2021.pdf
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: A systematic survey of 76 papers splits flaky-test knowledge into causes, costs and consequences, detection, and mitigation/repair, positioning flaky tests as "a threat to the validity of any methodology that assumes the outcome of a test only depends on the source code it covers".
CONCEPTS:
- `flaky test` — The survey's working definition: a test observed both passing and failing with the code under test unchanged, with narrower definitions restricted to timing or concurrency and broader ones including external factors. > "a test that can be observed to both pass and fail without changes to the code under test"
- `order-dependent tests` — Tests whose result hinges on execution order but is otherwise deterministic, and which matter because several techniques deliberately reorder or isolate tests. > "one whose outcome depends upon the test execution order, but is otherwise deterministic"
- Platform dependency — A test that passes on one machine and fails on another, which becomes effectively non-deterministic under cloud CI where runs land on different physical machines. > "a test with a platform dependency may be considered flaky since it might pass on one machine but fail on another"
- Underdetermined specification reliance — Reliance on unspecified behaviour, such as assuming an iteration order the specification never mandates, produces results that vary by implementation. > "it relies on the behavior of a particular implementation of an underdetermined specification"
- `intermittent tests` — Strandberg et al.'s broader class: a history of passing and failing regardless of software or hardware changes, of which flaky tests are the no-change special case. > "defined intermittent tests as those with a history of passing and failing, regardless of software or hardware changes"
- False-alarm failures — Flakiness breaks the inference from failure to bug, which the survey names as a leading source of false alarms. > "Flaky tests challenge the assumption that a test failure implies a bug, constituting a leading cause of false alarm test failures"
- Four-part structure — The analysis is divided into causes, costs and consequences, detection strategies, and mitigation and repair. > "We split our analysis into four parts, addressing the causes of flaky tests, their costs and consequences, detection strategies, and approaches for their mitigation and repair."
- Research milestones framing — 2014 is treated as the turning point after which a small set of heavily cited papers appeared, and later tools are dated against that sequence. > "Until 2014, research in the area was fairly limited, at which point several now heavily cited papers emerged."
- Victim/polluter — Most order-dependent failures come from tests that are fine alone and break only after particular other tests run. > "The majority of order-dependent tests are victims, passing in isolation but failing after the execution of certain polluter tests."
- Static-field state pollution — Shared in-memory state reached through static fields is reported as the mechanism behind most Java order dependencies. > "Shared access to in-memory resources via static fields was the facilitator of 61% of order-dependent tests in the Java programming language."
- Timing-based UI dependencies — In user interface testing, too little waiting for elements to render is named as a strong domain-specific cause, which the survey classes with timing dependencies. > "Insufficient waiting for elements to be rendered in user interface testing appears to be a strong factor"
- ML non-determinism — Algorithmic non-determinism, not timing, dominates flakiness in machine learning projects, so general mitigation advice may not transfer. > "Algorithmic non-determinism accounts for 60% of flaky tests in machine learning projects."
GUIDELINES:
- Ensure "test outcomes are consistent across the platforms targeted by their software, especially when using cloud-based continuous integration".
- Prefer eliminating state pollution during test execution: this "would indirectly repair most order-dependent tests".
- Be careful "not to introduce test cases that may induce a failure in other tests in the test suite".
- Detector designers should assume "complex networks of dependencies are an unlikely occurrence" (most order-dependent tests involve one other test).
- Expect that "a significant minority of cases cannot be identified by analyzing program state alone".
- Do not transfer general flakiness mitigation wholesale to ML projects, where algorithmic non-determinism dominates.
- Check the top venues regularly: ESEC/FSE, ICSE, ISSTA, ASE, ICST account for ~`64%` of studies.
EVIDENCE: `76` papers: `168` unique query results → `56` after screening, + `6` from 2021 accepted papers, + `14` via backward snowballing. `63%` (just under) published 2019–2021. Developer survey: `59%` deal with flaky tests monthly/weekly/daily; `20%` monthly, `24%` weekly, `15%` daily; of the `91%` who face them at least a few times a year, `56%` call them a moderate problem and `23%` a serious one. Platform dependencies = `34%` of sampled bug reports; order-dependent = up to `16%` of flaky bug reports and `9%` of repairs; `76%` of order-dependent tests depend on only one other test; `61%` of Java order-dependent tests facilitated by static fields; `60%` of ML flakiness is algorithmic non-determinism; Android cause distribution roughly matches general Java projects.
LIMITS: Peer-reviewed-only scope excludes preprints, theses, blogs and grey literature; redundant "dependent tests" excluded by definition; no additional quality assessment — "we consider that the peer-review process constitutes a sufficient quality bar"; 2021 data partial; the 2015–2016 dip "may be" a sampling artefact. The available extraction ends mid-Section 3, so later sections' details are not captured.
TOOLING: ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, SpringerLink; DTDetector, VmVm, PolDet, NonDex, DeFlaker, iDFlakies, iFixFlakies, FLAST, FLASH.
LINKS: Luo et al. 2014 (flakiness categories), Zhang et al. 2014 (DTDetector), Bell & Kaiser VMVM, Shi et al. NonDex/iFixFlakies, Lam et al. iDFlakies, Eck et al. 2019 developer perspective, Zolfaghari et al. 2020 review; public BibTeX repository on GitHub.

## A109 · A large-scale longitudinal study of flaky tests
URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3428270
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Applying two state-of-the-art detectors longitudinally to 55 Java projects, the study finds 75% of flaky tests are already flaky when added and 85% are flaky when added or directly modified — so running detectors at first commit captures most, but not all, flakiness.
CONCEPTS:
- `flaky tests` — Tests that can both pass and fail on one code version, which makes a failure's origin — a recent change or flakiness — ambiguous and so degrades regression testing. > "Flaky tests are tests that can non-deterministically pass or fail for the same code version."
- `detectors` — Tools that organisations including Mozilla and Netflix run in order to find flaky tests quickly. > "Some software organizations, e.g., Mozilla and Netflix, run some tools—detectors—to detect flaky tests as soon as possible."
- Cost problem — Non-determinism makes detection expensive enough that even the best detectors cannot practically run over every test on every change. > "detecting flaky tests is costly due to their inherent non-determinism, so even state-of-the-art detectors are often impractical to be used on all tests for each project change"
- Common industry mitigation — The workaround is to restrict a detector to new or directly modified tests, leaving out unmodified tests and every other kind of change. > "these organizations typically run a detector solely on newly added or directly modified tests"
- `first-commit flaky` — Most flaky tests already flake in the version where they were introduced, so running detectors on new tests has real value. > "We find that 75% of flaky tests (184 out of 245) are flaky when added"
- `longitudinal` design — The method follows each test across project history to establish when it began flaking and which change did it, instead of sampling one snapshot. > "we conduct a large-scale longitudinal study of flaky tests to determine when flaky tests become flaky and what changes cause them to become flaky"
- Change categories examined — The study asks about unmodified tests, test-suite changes, changes to the code under test, and library dependency changes. > "not on unmodified tests or when other changes occur (including changes to the test suite, the code under test, and library dependencies)"
- Detection coverage envelope — Restricting detection to new tests leaves a quantified remainder undetected. > "running detectors solely on newly added tests would still miss detecting 25% of flaky tests"
- Compile-and-run filter — Only flaky tests that could be built and executed in their introduction version are counted. > "identifying a total of 245 flaky tests that can be compiled and run in the code version where each test was added"
GUIDELINES:
- Run detectors on newly added tests: this alone yields `75%` (`184/245`).
- Extend detector runs to newly added *or directly modified* tests to reach `85%`.
- Accept that `15%` (the remaining flaky tests) become flaky through other changes and "can be detected only when detectors are always applied to all tests".
- Treat the 25% residual from new-tests-only as the quantified argument against that cheapest strategy.
- Evaluate a flaky test in the code version where it was added when judging whether it was born flaky.
EVIDENCE: 2 detectors applied to `55` Java projects; `245` flaky tests identified that compile and run in their introduction version; `75%` (`184` of `245`) flaky when added; `85%` detectable when detectors run on newly added or directly modified tests; `15%` require always-on runs. The paper claims to be "the first to empirically evaluate when tests become flaky and to recommend guidelines for applying detectors in the future."
LIMITS: Java-only, Maven-based open-source projects; findings depend on the two chosen detectors and on the compile-and-run filter, so the 25%/15% residuals are conditional on that detector set; historical checkout builds may not reflect industrial CI configurations.
TOOLING: Detectors including iDFlakies, DeFlaker, NonDex, VmVm/VMVM, iFixFlakies; Maven and Maven Surefire; Git bisect; testrunner (TestingResearchIllinois); Infer; Flakiness Dashboard (Chromium).
LINKS: Lam et al. iDFlakies (ICST 2019), Lam et al. lifecycle study (ICSE 2020), Lam et al. root-causing in industry (ISSTA 2019), Luo et al. empirical analysis (FSE 2014), Shi et al. NonDex/iFixFlakies, Bell et al. DeFlaker (ICSE 2018), Memon et al. Google-scale continuous testing (ICSE SEIP 2017), Ziftci & Reardon "Who broke the build?" (ICSE 2017), Eck et al. developer perspective (ESEC/FSE 2019).

## A110 · A Survey of Flaky Tests
URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/fullHtml/10.1145/3476105
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: First systematic survey of the flaky-test literature, arguing that flaky tests threaten the validity of any method that assumes test outcome depends only on covered source code, and organising the field around four research questions on causes, costs, detection, and repair.
CONCEPTS:
- **flaky test** — A test that can both pass and fail with no change to the code under test; the survey notes definitions differ between sources, some of which count only timing-driven flakiness. > "is generally considered to mean a test that can be observed to both pass and fail without changes to the code under test"
- **false alarm test failures** — Flaky tests break the inference from a failure to a bug, making them a leading source of spurious failure signals. > "Flaky tests challenge the assumption that a test failure implies a bug, constituting a leading cause of false alarm test failures"
- **intra-test family** — The grouping for flakiness that originates inside the test's own execution or in the code it directly covers. > "The intra-test family describes flakiness wholly internal to the test, in other words, stemming from issues isolated to the execution of the test code itself, or the direct code under test."
- **inter-test family** — Flakiness that shows up only relative to the execution of other tests in the suite. > "The inter-test family contains tests that are flaky with respect to the execution of other tests, for example, those with test order dependencies."
- **external family** — Flakiness whose source lies outside the test's control, such as how long a remote response takes. > "The flakiness of tests in the external family stems from factors outside of the test's control, such as the time taken to receive a response from a web sever."
- **order-dependent test** — A test that relies on a shared value or resource another test modifies, so a change of run order breaks it. > "Test that depends on some shared value or resource that is modified by another test that impacts its outcome."
- **victim / polluter** — Most order-dependent tests are victims: they pass alone and fail only after particular polluter tests have run. > "The majority of order-dependent tests are victims, passing in isolation but failing after the execution of certain polluter tests."
- **state pollution** — Shared in-memory state, static fields above all, left modified by an earlier test. > "Shared access to in-memory resources via static fields was the facilitator of 61% of order-dependent tests in the Java programming language."
- **asynchronicity and concurrency** — The survey records async and concurrency issues as the leading general cause, so any mitigation has to address them to be impactful. > "Issues regarding asynchronicity and concurrency appear to be the leading causes of flaky tests."
- **platform dependency** — Outcomes differing across target platforms and environments, aggravated by cloud-based continuous integration. > "Platform dependencies represented 34% of sampled bug reports indicative of flaky tests."
- **algorithmic non-determinism** — In machine-learning projects this is the dominant source of flakiness, unlike projects where async waits and concurrency lead. > "Algorithmic non-determinism accounts for 60% of flaky tests in machine learning projects."
- **flakiness categories** — The reusable taxonomy introduced by Luo et al.'s empirical study, against which later work classifies flaky tests. > "Luo et al.’s An Empirical Study of Flaky Tests, that introduced a widely used set of flakiness categories"
GUIDELINES:
- Treat test outcomes as needing consistency `across the platforms` your software targets, especially under cloud-based CI.
- Avoid introducing test cases that may induce failure in other tests; eliminating `state-pollution` would indirectly repair most order-dependent tests.
- Detection techniques for order dependence should assume `complex networks of dependencies are an unlikely occurrence`.
- Do not assume techniques tuned for async-wait/concurrency flakiness transfer to machine-learning projects.
- Do not classify redundant tests as `dependent tests`; the article excludes that literature.
EVIDENCE:
- Developer survey: `59%` deal with flaky tests monthly, weekly or daily; `20%` monthly, `24%` weekly.
- Collection: `168` unique results; `56` selected; `+6` from ICSE/ICST/MSR 2021; `+14` by backward snowballing.
