- Platform dependencies were `34%` of sampled bug reports; order-dependent tests up to `16%` of bug reports and `9%` of repairs; `76%` of order-dependent tests depended on only `one other test`; static-field sharing explained `61%` of Java order-dependent tests.
- ML projects: `60%` of flaky tests from algorithmic non-determinism; Android distribution roughly matches general Java projects.
- Top five venues hold roughly `64%` of papers.
LIMITS:
Scope restricted to peer-reviewed work; searches run on a single date (15 April 2021), so 2021 coverage is incomplete; Scopus/SpringerLink restricted to CS venues; two studies of the same Apache subjects report different findings, which the survey notes without resolving.
TOOLING: ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, SpringerLink; `DTDetector` for order-dependent detection; PySyft example.
LINKS: Luo et al. *An Empirical Study of Flaky Tests*; Zhang et al. *Empirically Revisiting the Test Independence Assumption*; Shi et al. on library-specification assumptions; public BibTeX bibliography repository.

## A111 · What Made This Test Flake? Pinpointing Classes Responsible for Test Flakiness
URL: https://www.computer.org/csdl/proceedings-article/icsme/2022/795600a352/1JeFkXgEsrC
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Re-targets fault localisation to *flaky component localisation* — pinpointing the program classes that cause non-deterministic behaviour — showing that Spectrum-Based Fault Localisation augmented with change history and static code metrics ranks the guilty class highly enough to cut inspection effort sharply.
CONCEPTS:
- **flaky component localisation** — A reformulation of fault localisation: instead of locating a fault, locate the classes responsible for a flaky test's non-determinism. > "we propose re-targeting Fault Localisation techniques to the flaky component localisation problem, i.e., pinpointing program classes that cause the non-deterministic behaviour of flaky tests."
- **Spectrum-Based Fault Localisation (SBFL)** — The coverage-based localisation technique the authors adopt for its simplicity and effectiveness, fed here with spectra from flaky-test executions. > "we employ Spectrum-Based Fault Localisation (SBFL), a coverage-based fault localisation technique commonly adopted for its simplicity and effectiveness."
- **localisation augmentation** — Additional data sources layered on the SBFL ranking to sharpen it. > "We also utilise other data sources, such as change history and static code metrics, to further improve the localisation."
- **technical debt of non-determinism** — Developers in large codebases need the sources of non-determinism in order to keep quality from decaying into non-deterministic behaviour. > "developers working with large codebases often need to know the sources of non-determinism to preserve code quality, i.e., avoid introducing technical debt linked with non-deterministic behaviour"
- **top-k suggestion** — The evaluation metric: whether the flaky class lands among the first k ranked classes. > "augmenting SBFL with change and code metrics ranks flaky classes in the top-1 and top-5 suggestions, in 26% and 47% of the cases"
- **classes inspected** — The cost metric: how many classes a developer must read to reach the first flaky one. > "we successfully reduced the average number of classes inspected to locate the first flaky class to 19% of the total number of classes covered by flaky tests"
- **flakiness categories as evaluation strata** — Effectiveness is checked across flakiness categories rather than on one narrow kind of non-determinism. > "localisation methods are effective in major flakiness categories, such as concurrency and asynchronous waits, indicating their general ability to identify flaky components"
GUIDELINES:
- When a test flakes, localise the responsible `classes` rather than only detecting/re-running the test; detection alone leaves the fix undone.
- Combine SBFL scores with `change history` and `code metrics`; SBFL alone was not what produced the reported top-k results.
- Expect usefulness across `concurrency` and `asynchronous waits` categories rather than one narrow flakiness class.
- Prioritise the ranked class list in order; practitioners should start inspection at the top-ranked class.
EVIDENCE:
- Augmenting SBFL with change and code metrics ranks flaky classes in the `top-1` in `26%` and `top-5` in `47%` of cases.
- Average number of classes inspected to locate the first flaky class reduced to `19%` of the total classes covered by flaky tests.
- Localisation shown effective in major categories (`concurrency`, `asynchronous waits`).
LIMITS:
The extracted text states only that the approach "employs" SBFL plus extra sources; the number of subject projects, tests, and the statistical treatment are not given in the available text. Threats noted at the framing level: developers rarely fix flaky tests at all because localisation is hard, so ranking quality is the binding constraint.
TOOLING: Spectrum-Based Fault Localisation; change-history mining; static code metrics; evaluated on a Ubisoft industrial codebase context.
LINKS: DeFlaker; *A Multi-factor Approach for Flaky Test Detection and Automated Root Cause Analysis*; *Static Test Flakiness Prediction*; Google's *De-Flake Your Tests*; prior Python and JavaScript flakiness studies.

## A112 · A Study on the Lifecycle of Flaky Tests
URL: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/a-study-on-the-lifecycle-of-flaky-tests/
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Studies the previously unexamined lifecycle (reoccurrence, runtimes, time-before-fix) of flaky tests in six large proprietary Microsoft projects and introduces FaTB, an automated balancer that shortens async-flaky test runtimes without increasing their failure frequency.
CONCEPTS:
- **flaky test lifecycle** — Reoccurrence, runtime and time-before-fix treated as measurable properties, which the authors present as unstudied territory. > "Although flaky tests are the focus of several existing studies, none of them study (1) the reoccurrence, runtimes, and time-before-fix of flaky tests, and (2) flaky tests indepth on proprietary projects."
- **proprietary-project evidence** — Closed-source industrial projects as a study population distinct from the open-source corpora earlier work used. > "we study the lifecycle of flaky tests in six large-scale proprietary projects at Microsoft"
- **asynchronous call** — Confirmed as the leading cause of flakiness in these Microsoft projects, reproducing the prior open-source finding. > "We find, as in prior work, that asynchronous calls are the leading cause of flaky tests in these Microsoft projects."
- **FaTB (Flakiness and Time Balancer)** — The paper's automated remedy for async-caused flakiness: it targets the frequency of failures rather than their presence. > "we propose the first automated solution, called Flakiness and Time Balancer (FaTB), to reduce the frequency of flaky-test failures caused by asynchronous calls"
- **claimed fix** — A developer-asserted repair; empirically many such changes neither fix nor reduce the failure frequency. > "our study finds several cases where developers claim they “fixed” a flaky test but our empirical experiments show that their changes do not fix or reduce these tests’ frequency of flaky-test failures"
- **time-before-fix** — Elapsed time between a flaky test appearing and being repaired, measured here as a lifecycle property. > "none of them study (1) the reoccurrence, runtimes, and time-before-fix of flaky tests"
GUIDELINES:
- Re-run flaky tests empirically before accepting a `fix`; do not trust commit messages or bug resolutions that claim flakiness was fixed.
- Study reoccurrence and runtime, not just presence, when triaging a flaky suite.
- Target `asynchronous calls` first; they are the leading cause in both open and proprietary settings.
- Researchers building on repositories should be cautious when basing results on changes developers claim to be `"fixes"`.
EVIDENCE:
- Six large-scale proprietary Microsoft projects.
- Five flaky tests evaluated with FaTB: running times reduced by up to `78%` without empirically affecting the frequency of flaky failures.
- Several cases found where claimed fixes neither fixed nor reduced the failure frequency.
- Async calls identified as the leading cause, consistent with prior work; prior categorisation schemes were checked for applicability to proprietary projects.
LIMITS:
Small FaTB evaluation (five tests); the source is a publication landing page containing only the abstract, so methodology, statistics, and lifecycle distributions are unavailable here; proprietary projects limit external generalisation even though the async-cause finding replicated.
TOOLING: FaTB; Microsoft proprietary regression-testing infrastructure; ICSE 2020 venue.
LINKS: Prior flaky-test categorisation work (Luo et al. and successors); flaky-test studies the paper says omit lifecycle and proprietary contexts.

## A113 · On the Impact of Flaky Tests in Automated Program Repair
URL: https://store.computer.org/csdl/proceedings-article/saner/2021/963000a295/1twfpvD7jaM
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Flaky tests are quietly removed from repair benchmarks, and restoring them to Defects4J shows they propagate into bug localisation and repair results, so the repair community should drop the assumption that benchmark suites are flake-free.
CONCEPTS:
- **imperfect oracle** — Test suites used to validate generated patches can be both incomplete and contaminated by flaky tests. > "beyond the widely-discussed concern that test suites are an imperfect oracle because they can be incomplete, they can include tests that are flaky"
- **flaky test** — The paper's working definition: outcome decided non-deterministically for the same program. > "A flaky test is one that can be passed or failed by a program in a non-deterministic way."
- **benchmark curation by removal** — Repair benchmarks such as Defects4J are built by stripping flaky tests out; the study reverses that removal to observe the effect. > "Such tests are generally carefully removed from the repair benchmarks."
- **threat to validity of APR evaluation** — Flakiness distorts localisation and repairability measurements, and the authors frame the omission of it as an unexamined validity threat. > "no study has discussed this threat to validity for evaluation of program repair"
- **environment-dependent determinism** — Most flaky tests turn deterministic once the environment is fixed, with the JDK version influencing the outcome. > "most flaky tests (98%) actually provide deterministic results under specific environment configurations (with the jdk version influencing the results)"
- **spectrum-based fault localisation (SBFL) ranking** — Restored flaky tests reorder and degrade bug rankings, never improving them. > "flaky tests drastically hinder the effectiveness of spectrum-based fault localization"
- **partial-fix patches** — A proposed alternative acceptance rule: treat patches that fix some tests while failing others as worthwhile, since the failures may be the flaky ones. > "One direction that we propose is to consider developing strategies where patches that partially-fix bugs are considered worthwhile"
GUIDELINES:
- Do not assume a benchmark test suite is free of flaky tests; relax that artificial assumption explicitly.
- Pin and record environment configuration (`jdk version`) when deciding whether a test is flaky, since many "flaky" tests are deterministic under one configuration.
- Consider `partially-fixing patches` worthwhile rather than discarding them when failures may be flaky.
- Report flaky-test handling as part of APR evaluation methodology; the omission is a validity threat.
EVIDENCE:
- Flaky tests are few — approximately `0.3%` of total tests — yet affect experiments on `98.9%` of Defects4J real-world faults.
- `98%` of flaky tests give deterministic results under specific environment configurations.
- SBFL: rankings of `90` bugs drop while `none` improve compared with flake-free results.
- `10` state-of-the-art APR tools fix significantly fewer bugs when flaky tests are restored.
LIMITS:
Single benchmark family (Defects4J); only abstract-level detail is available in the source text — no per-tool numbers, no statistical tests; the paper explicitly notes flaky-test detection is still nascent, so reverted flaky tests cannot all be identified reliably.
TOOLING: Defects4J; spectrum-based fault localisation; ten unnamed state-of-the-art APR tools.
LINKS: APR + test-overfitting work; *What Do Developer-Repaired Flaky Tests Tell Us About the Effectiveness of Automated Flaky Test Detection?*; FlakeSync.

## A114 · An Empirical Study of Flaky Tests in Python
URL: https://www.computer.org/csdl/proceedings-article/icst/2021/683600a148/1tRP8lWaACc
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Flakiness is as prevalent in Python as in Java, but its causes differ sharply — order dependency dominates and a previously undocumented category, test-infrastructure problems, accounts for over a quarter of flaky tests.
CONCEPTS:
- **order dependency** — The dominant Python cause, far more prominent than in the Java studies the work compares against. > "Order dependency is a much more dominant problem in Python, causing 59 % of the 7 571 flaky tests in our dataset."
- **test infrastructure problems** — Failures originating in the test framework or harness layer rather than in test logic or product code; the authors report it as a new cause category. > "Another 28 % were caused by test infrastructure problems, which represent a previously undocumented cause of flakiness."
- **network and randomness APIs** — The residual cause class, which the authors read as characteristic of the kind of software Python projects are. > "The remaining 13 % can mostly be attributed to the use of network and randomness APIs by the projects, which is indicative of the type of software commonly written in Python."
- **degree of flakiness** — How often a flaky test fails, measured alongside prevalence and causes. > "we empirically study the prevalence, causes, and degree of flakiness within software written in Python, one of the currently most popular programming languages"
- **PyPI sampling** — The package index supplies the population frame for the study. > "we sampled 22 352 open source projects from the popular PyPI package index, and analyzed their 876 186 test cases for flakiness"
- **rerun budget for confidence** — The number of reruns needed before a passing test can be trusted as non-flaky. > "finding flaky tests requires more runs than are often done in the literature: A 95 % confidence that a passing test case is not flaky on average would require 170 reruns."
GUIDELINES:
- Do not assume Java-derived flakiness distributions transfer to Python; re-measure per language.
- Investigate `test infrastructure` first in Python suites, not only product code.
- Budget enough reruns: a `95%` confidence that a passing test case is not flaky on average requires `170 reruns`, more than literature often performs.
- Treat order dependency as the primary Python target.
EVIDENCE:
- `22,352` open-source PyPI projects sampled; `876,186` test cases analysed; `7,571` flaky tests identified.
- Order dependency caused `59%` of flaky tests; test infrastructure `28%`; remaining `13%` mostly network and randomness APIs.
- Flakiness prevalence in Python comparable to Java.
- `170` reruns needed for `95%` confidence per passing test.
LIMITS:
Only the abstract is present in the source text: sampling procedure, failure-detection method, and per-project variance are not described; results cover PyPI open-source projects only, and the paper frames language generalisation as the open question it addresses rather than as settled.
TOOLING: PyPI; Python test suites; automated reruns to detect flakiness.
LINKS: Java flakiness studies (Luo et al. lineage); *iPFlakies* for Python order-dependent tests; *An Empirical Study of Flaky Tests in JavaScript*; *Test Flakiness Across Programming Languages*.

## A115 · Continuous Fuzzing: A Study of the Effectiveness and Scalability of Fuzzing in CI/CD Pipelines
URL: https://www.computer.org/csdl/proceedings-article/sbft/2023/018200a025/1P7EiXpnwv6
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Fuzzing is worth running inside CI/CD for security bugs, but large fractions of per-commit fuzzing effort are wasted on commits that cannot expose new bugs, and campaigns far shorter than field defaults still find important bugs.
CONCEPTS:
- **continuous fuzzing** — Running fuzzers as part of CI/CD security testing rather than as long standalone campaigns. > "it is only natural to look for effective ways of incorporating fuzzing into continuous security testing."
- **commit triage** — Deciding which commits need no fuzzing, which the paper treats as the main optimisation lever. > "seek optimization opportunities to triage commits that do not require fuzzing"
- **campaign duration vs. effectiveness** — The trade-off between short campaigns that keep pipelines fast and long campaigns that reach sophisticated bugs. > "a significantly shorter fuzzing campaign facilitates a faster pipeline for developers, while it can still uncover important bugs"
- **recent-change concentration** — Most reported bugs come from recent code changes, which is the argument for testing every change continuously. > "A recent study on bug reports from OSS-Fuzz observed that recent code changes are responsible for 77% of all reported bugs, stressing the importance of continuous testing."
- **security-related bugs** — Effectiveness is measured on security-relevant findings rather than on crashes in general. > "it has proven to be a fundamental technique in uncovering bugs (often security related) in many applications."
GUIDELINES:
- Prioritise fuzzing on commits that touch fuzz-relevant code; triage the rest.
- Accept short per-commit campaigns when pipeline latency matters, while accepting reduced power against sophisticated bugs.
- Expect real reduction potential: fuzzing effort reducible by `63%` in three of nine libraries, `55%` on average.
EVIDENCE:
- Prior OSS-Fuzz bug-report study: recent code changes responsible for `77%` of all reported bugs.
- Nine libraries analysed; effort reduced by `63%` in three of them, `55%` on average.
- Shorter campaigns still uncovered important bugs, with a documented loss of capability for sophisticated ones.
LIMITS:
Only the abstract is present in the source text: nine libraries is a small sample, the triage heuristic and its false-negative risk are not stated here, and the duration study is described qualitatively without per-duration figures.
TOOLING: CI/CD pipelines; fuzzers (unnamed in the abstract); OSS-Fuzz as the motivating corpus.
LINKS: Böhme and Zhu on regressions from recent changes; OSS-Fuzz bug-report study; SBFT 2023 workshop.

## A116 · Large-Scale Empirical Analysis of Continuous Fuzzing: Insights from 1 Million Fuzzing Sessions
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16433
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Across roughly 1.12 million OSS-Fuzz sessions, continuous fuzzing finds most of its bugs early because latent bugs predate integration, but coverage keeps growing and coverage changes are what drive later bug discovery.
CONCEPTS:
- **continuous fuzzing** — Fuzzing folded into continuous integration so that it runs in short, frequent cycles. > "the main approach to vulnerability detection, fuzzing, has been integrated into the continuous integration process to run in short and frequent cycles."
- **fuzzing session** — The unit of analysis: one campaign run inside the continuous pipeline. > "Through an empirical study of a total of approximately 1.12 million fuzzing sessions from 878 projects participating in OSS-Fuzz"
- **pre-existing bug pool** — Bugs already present when continuous fuzzing is adopted, which explains the high early detection rate. > "a substantial number of fuzzing bugs exist prior to the integration of continuous fuzzing, leading to a high detection rate in the early stages"
- **coverage growth** — Coverage keeps rising as continuous fuzzing proceeds instead of flattening out quickly. > "code coverage continues to increase as continuous fuzzing progresses; and (iii) changes in coverage contribute to the detection of fuzzing bugs"
- **coverage change as detection driver** — It is the shift in coverage, not the absolute level, that is associated with finding bugs. > "changes in coverage contribute to the detection of fuzzing bugs"
- **issue reports, coverage reports, fuzzing logs** — The three OSS-Fuzz data sources the study mines. > "We collect issue reports, coverage reports, and fuzzing logs from OSS-Fuzz, an online service provided by Google that performs fuzzing during continuous integration."
GUIDELINES:
- Interpret an early spike in bugs after onboarding as backlog burn-down, not as a sustained rate.
- Keep campaigns running to sustain coverage growth rather than concluding saturation from the early spike.
- Track coverage *deltas* per session, since changes in coverage predict bug detection.
- Mine `issue reports`, `coverage reports`, and `fuzzing logs` together when evaluating a continuous-fuzzing deployment.
EVIDENCE:
- Approximately `1.12 million` fuzzing sessions from `878` projects in OSS-Fuzz.
- Findings: (i) substantial numbers of fuzzing bugs exist prior to integration, giving a high early detection rate; (ii) coverage keeps increasing over time; (iii) coverage changes contribute to bug detection.
LIMITS:
Abstract-only source: no per-project distributions, no statistical tests, no effect sizes beyond the qualitative direction of each finding. Population is OSS-Fuzz participants, i.e. projects that already adopted continuous fuzzing, so adoption-selection bias is unaddressed in the available text.
TOOLING: OSS-Fuzz (Google continuous fuzzing service); coverage instrumentation.
LINKS: OSS-Fuzz issue tracker and coverage tooling; prior continuous-fuzzing studies of CI/CD integration (Klooster et al.).

## A117 · Effectiveness and Scalability of Fuzzing Techniques in CI/CD Pipelines
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14964
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Continuous fuzzing in CI/CD is beneficial, and its cost can be cut by triaging commits plus shortening campaigns from the 24-hour field default to 15 minutes, at the price of weaker detection of sophisticated bugs; resource assignment can be prioritised automatically.
CONCEPTS:
- **commit triage** — Identifying commits that do not require fuzzing; the paper's primary optimisation. > "we study an optimization opportunity to triage commits that do not require fuzzing"
- **campaign duration** — Short CI campaigns measured against the long field default. > "A shorter fuzzing campaign such as 15 minutes (as opposed to the wisdom of 24 hours in the field) facilitates a faster pipeline"
- **prioritisation strategy** — Automatic assignment of resources to campaigns from a set of predefined priority rules. > "we discuss a prioritization strategy that automatically assigns resources to fuzzing campaigns based on a set of predefined priority strategies"
- **regressions** — Bugs introduced by recent code changes, the phenomenon that makes per-commit fuzzing pay off. > "a recent study by Böhme and Zhu shows that four in every five bugs have been introduced by recent code changes (i.e. regressions)"
- **scalability** — The cost and latency of fuzzing under high code-change velocity and automated delivery. > "there are many optimization opportunities to improve the effectiveness and scalability of fuzz testing"
GUIDELINES:
- Triage commits and skip fuzzing where a commit cannot affect the fuzz target.
- Run `15 minutes` per campaign instead of `24 hours` when pipeline latency dominates; accept reduced capability against sophisticated bugs.
- Select fuzz targets rather than fuzzing everything; compute save is substantial.
- Use a predefined `priority strategy` to allocate resources across campaigns.
EVIDENCE:
- Average fuzzing effort in CI/CD reducible by approximately `63%` in three of nine libraries analysed, `>40%` for six libraries.
- Böhme and Zhu: four in every five bugs introduced by recent code changes.
- `15`-minute campaigns still uncovered important bugs while reducing sophisticated-bug capability.
- Paper length `12 pages`, `5 figures`.
LIMITS:
Only nine libraries; triage false negatives and how they were measured are not stated in the abstract; the duration result is qualitative about sophistication; prioritisation strategies are discussed rather than quantitatively validated here.
TOOLING: CI/CD pipelines; fuzzers (unnamed in abstract); 12-page arXiv v2 (7 Jun 2022).
LINKS: Böhme and Zhu on regression-prone fuzzing; the companion SBFT 2023 paper on the same nine-library study; Magma-style CI simulation work in follow-ups.

## A118 · Compiler Fuzzing in Continuous Integration: A Case Study on Dafny
URL: https://www.computer.org/csdl/proceedings-article/icst/2025/10988954/26S4GK2n9vO
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: A brief fuzzing campaign can run on every pull request to a compiler if you solve deduplication, regression bisection across changing interfaces, and complementarity with existing regression tests — demonstrated by CompFuzzCI for the Dafny compiler.
CONCEPTS:
- **CompFuzzCI** — The framework that puts compiler fuzzing inside Dafny's CI workflow. > "We present the design of CompFuzzCI, a framework for incorporating compiler fuzzing into the continuous integration (CI) workflow of the compiler for Dafny"
- **per-pull-request campaign** — Fuzzing runs on each pull request instead of as a long standalone job. > "CompFuzzCI explores the idea of running a brief fuzzing campaign as part of the CI workflow of each pull request to a compiler project."
- **bug deduplication** — Deciding whether reported crashes are new or duplicates, without which per-PR fuzzing would flood developers. > "Making this effective involved devising solutions for various challenges, including how to deduplicate bugs"
- **revision bisection** — Bisecting project history to attribute a regression to its commit, complicated by interfaces that change over time. > "how to bisect the project's revision history to find the commit responsible for a regression (challenging when project interfaces change over time)"
- **complementarity with regression testing** — Making fuzzing add coverage rather than duplicate what the existing suite already checks. > "how to ensure that fuzz testing complements existing regression testing efforts"
- **fuzz-d** — The fuzzer the framework is built around and prioritises support for. > "CompFuzzCI prioritises support for the Dafny compiler and the fuzz-d fuzzer"
- **generalisable design** — Internal interfaces kept separable so other fuzzers can be substituted with modest modification. > "with modest modification to its internal interfaces, it could be adapted to work with other fuzzers"
GUIDELINES:
- Run fuzzing as part of the CI workflow of `each pull request`, not as a separate nightly-only job.
- Deduplicate crash reports automatically; without dedup a per-PR campaign floods developers.
- Implement bisection that tolerates interface drift across revisions.
- Design the integration so fuzzing `complements` existing regression testing instead of shadowing it.
- Keep internal interfaces narrow so swapping the fuzzer requires only `modest modification`.
EVIDENCE:
- Three previously-unknown bugs found and reported in the Dafny compiler, discovered as a by-product.
- A controlled experiment simulated long-term CompFuzzCI use over a range of Dafny commits to assess historic-bug discovery; per-commit hit rates are not stated in the available text.
- Concrete engineering engagement with the Dafny team at Amazon shaped the design.
LIMITS:
Single compiler and single language (Dafny); `fuzz-d`-specific support means portability is asserted by design argument rather than demonstrated by a second deployment; source text is the abstract only, so experiment scale and thresholds are unavailable.
TOOLING: CompFuzzCI; `fuzz-d`; Dafny compiler; Amazon-internal CI; git-history bisection.
LINKS: Dafny open-source project; prior compiler-fuzzing and CI-fuzzing literature referenced by the paper (not named in the available text).

## A119 · Directed or Undirected: Investigating Fuzzing Strategies in a CI/CD Setup (Registered Report)
URL: https://www.carolemieux.com/cicd_fuzzing24.pdf
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: Because 24-hour fuzzing advice cannot fit a CI pipeline, this registered report sets out to test whether *directed* fuzzers beat undirected ones at reaching and triggering injected bugs under a 10-minute budget, starting from a saturated corpus and one bug per simulated commit.
CONCEPTS:
- **CI/CD fuzzing simulation** — Emulating a commit by injecting one Magma bug at a time and fuzzing it for a short budget. > "we simulate the commits in CI/CD by injecting one bug in each commit instead of injecting all bugs at the same time"
- **directed fuzzing** — Fuzzing aimed at a specific program location rather than at the program as a whole. > "Directed fuzzing, as the name suggests, focuses on testing a specific program location of the PUT rather than the whole."
- **directed grey box fuzzing** — The variant the paper studies: coverage-guided fuzzing steered toward a set of target locations. > "We are interested in the directed grey box fuzzing that generates inputs with the goal to reach a specific set of program locations."
- **AFLGo** — A directed fuzzer that derives basic-block distances to the targets from compile-time call graphs and intraprocedural CFGs, a static analysis that can take hours. > "AFLGo first calculates the distance of each basic block to the targets from the call graphs and intraprocedural control flow graphs (CFGs) generated at compile time."
- **Fuzz Factory Diff (FFD)** — A lighter directed fuzzer that rewards inputs hitting the targets and then finding new coverage, avoiding distance computation. > "FFD uses a simpler heuristic that rewards generating inputs that can both exercise the target code locations and explore new coverage after hitting these targets"
- **saturated corpus** — A seed corpus built by a 24-hour AFL++ campaign so per-commit budgets are spent on changed code. > "We use the recommended timeout of 24 hours, hoping to get a saturated initial corpus that can cover most of the reachable code of the target library."
- **reached vs. triggered vs. detected** — Magma's three instrumentation levels: the buggy line executed, the faulty condition satisfied, and faulty behaviour observed. > "The source-code instrumentation in Magma reports a bug is reached when the line of the inserted buggy code is reached. A bug is triggered when the input satisfies the faulty condition"
- **commit bloat / target sensitivity** — Augmented commits whose extra non-buggy target lines test whether directed fuzzers still find the injected bug. > "we will add additional lines of code, beyond the buggy patch, as targets for each “commit”, and run directed fuzzers on these augmented commits."
GUIDELINES:
- Use `10 minutes` per campaign as the CI-compatible budget, and validate short-campaign claims rather than assuming them.
- Build the seed corpus with a `24-hour` AFL++ campaign before per-commit fuzzing.
- Inject `one bug` per simulated commit rather than all Magma patches, since real commits rarely contain ~20 bugs.
- Add extra non-buggy target lines as a sensitivity experiment when directed fuzzers would otherwise be handed the bug location.
- Select only fuzz targets affected by the change, e.g. by checksumming the target before and after the commit.
- Generate AFLGo/FFD target files automatically with `showlinenum` from `git diff` output.
- Exclude compiled-binary-only targets when using libFuzzer, which requires a function entry point.
EVIDENCE:
- Preliminary run: `5` benchmarks, `4` fuzzers (AFL, AFL++, libFuzzer, AFLGo), `10` repetitions each.
- Mean survival time to reach (R) was `5` seconds for AFL, AFL++, and AFLGo on most benchmarks; libFuzzer reached libpng001 at `13` s and libtiff012 at `22` s.
- Trigger only observed for libtiff012: `456` s AFL, `504` s AFL++, `485` s libFuzzer, `592` s AFLGo; libxml003 triggered at `140` s by AFL++.
- Only openssl001 showed AFL++ reaching at `170` s; all bugs reached were not triggered otherwise.
- Context figures: `21` commits/day across `575` projects; OSS-Fuzz discovered over `8,800` vulnerabilities and `28,000` bugs; `75%` of errors appear in the first year after release; maintenance `60%`–`80%` of lifecycle costs; Magma provides `9` libraries and `138` bugs.
LIMITS:
Registered report — preliminary results cover a subset of benchmarks and omit FFD and all sensitivity experiments; Magma patches give directed fuzzers too-precise bug locations, a threat the augmented-commit design only partly addresses; injecting synthetic single patches may not represent real commits; Magma's default seeds were replaced, so results are not comparable with prior work's starting conditions.
TOOLING: Magma (9 libraries, 138 bugs); AFL, AFL++, libFuzzer, AFLGo, FFD; `showlinenum`; sanitizers; git diff.
LINKS: Klooster et al. on CI/CD fuzzing (the prior study disputed here); Klees et al. fuzzing-benchmarking practices (24-hour recommendation); Böhme et al. directed grey-box fuzzing (AFLGo); Rangnau and Fowler on ~10-minute build times; OSS-Fuzz; a 2021 Magma issue on AFLGo integration.

# Batch ar13 — fuzzing in CI/CD and mutation testing in practice

## A120 · Effective Fuzzing within CI/CD Pipelines (Registered Report)
URL: https://srg.doc.ic.ac.uk/files/papers/pazzer-fuzzing-24.pdf
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: AFLGo-style directed greybox fuzzing suits CI/CD, but its distance computation is too expensive for short runs; PaZZER drops the CFG distance component and computes call-graph distances incrementally.
CONCEPTS:
- **directed greybox fuzzing** — Most inputs reach targets by being prioritised by estimated distance rather than by exhaustive exploration, which is what makes the technique a fit for short CI/CD runs. > "Directed greybox fuzzing techniques such as AFLGo are a good match for the CI/CD context. These techniques prioritise inputs based on estimated distances to the changed code."
- **function-level target distance** — A per-call-graph distance computed before fuzzing starts, giving each function a distance to the target functions it can reach. > "The distance from a basic block to a target is pre-computed before the actual fuzzing campaign begins. Each pre-computed distance has two components"
- **basic-block-level target distance** — An intraprocedural distance for blocks that only reach a target by calling through other blocks, and it depends on which blocks call a target function. > "the latter computes the distance between the basic block and all other basic blocks that call a target function"
- **CG distance vs CFG distance** — Two names the paper uses for the call-graph component and the control-flow-graph component of a block's distance estimate. > "In the rest of the paper, for brevity, we refer to the first kind of distance as CG (Call Graph) distance, and to the second one as CFG (Control-Flow Graph) distance."
- **c** — A tuning constant that scales the call-graph distance when a block can reach a target directly. > "with 𝑐 a configurable constant (with default value 10 in AFLGo)"
- **Time-to-Exposure (TTE)** — The measured time needed to produce an input that triggers a known crash, used to compare AFLGo with PaZZER. > "For each crash, we measure the Time-to-Exposure (TTE) for both AFLGo and PaZZER"
- **incremental shortest-path classes** — The three algorithm families PaZZER draws from, chosen to represent different optimality/time trade-offs. > "We have picked one algorithm to represent each of the three classes of algorithms based on optimality: optimal, sub-optimal and near-optimal."
- **patch coverage** — The fraction of the patch's target blocks that the produced inputs actually reach; for a single-block patch it is simply 0% or 100%. > "For patches consisting of multiple target basic blocks, this metric is defined as the fraction of basic blocks reached by executing the input set."
- **patch proximity** — The fallback measure when the patch is never reached: how near the inputs got, by call-graph distance to the target. > "If a tool does not manage to generate inputs that reach the patch, we will measure patch proximity, i.e. how close the generated inputs got to the patch."
GUIDELINES:
- Budget `10 min` per fuzzing run including distance computation, because the technique must run on every single commit.
- Drop the CFG distance component; keep only CG distance, and reuse prior distances via an incremental algorithm instead of full Dijkstra recomputation.
- Give each of five configurations (AFLGo, PaZZER-No-Increment, PaZZER-LPA*, PaZZER-Anytime-D*, PaZZER-HPA*) the same budget; run on `27 commits` per SUT.
- Mark as targets the method calls from the crash stack trace; repeat experiments `20 times`; choose `3 small`, `3 medium`, `3 large` SUTs by LOC.
EVIDENCE: Distance computation: Giflib 7,259 LOC — 1 s CG + 32 s CFG = 33 s; Jasper 28,256 — 2+181 = 183 s; Libming 82,303 — 2+192 = 194 s; Objdump 570,040 — 154+1,866 = 2,020 s (34 min), dominated by CFG. TTE: Giflib 122→109 s (1.1x), Jasper CVE-2015-5221 245→68 s (3.6x), Libming CVE-2018-8962 370→194 s (1.9x), Objdump CVE-2017-8392 2,263→438 s (5.2x). LPA* vs Dijkstra: Objdump call graph 21,596 nodes / 51,318 edges, 154 s → 14 s; small/medium graphs stay at 1–2 s.
LIMITS: registered report — results are preliminary and the full evaluation is planned, not executed. One crash per benchmark; incrementality measured with a synthetic bug-injecting commit; single machine class.
TOOLING: AFLGo (with its artifact examples), Python NetworkX Dijkstra, Ubuntu 20.04, Intel Core i3-8100 @3.60GHz, 32GB RAM.
LINKS: AFLGo; LPA*, Anytime D*, HPA*, D* Lite, DynamicSWSF-FP; OSS-Fuzz; CIFuzz; Giflib, Jasper, Libming, Objdump/Binutils, Libbpf, Selinux, Libjpeg-turbo, Systemd, OpenSSL.

## A121 · An Empirical Study of OSS-Fuzz Bugs (Registered Report)
URL: https://www.computer.org/csdl/proceedings-article/msr/2021/871000a131/1tB7jeDBsQM
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: The first empirical study of OSS-Fuzz finds that continuous fuzzing is often effective at quickly finding bugs and developers patch them quickly, but flaky bugs, timeouts and out-of-memory errors are problematic.
CONCEPTS:
- **continuous fuzzing** — Fuzzing run as an ongoing automated service rather than as isolated campaigns, positioned as a quality and security assurance technique. > "Continuous fuzzing is an increasingly popular technique for automated quality and security assurance."
- **OSS-Fuzz** — Google's hosted continuous fuzzing service for open source software, and the subject of this first empirical study of its kind. > "Google maintains OSS-Fuzz: a continuous fuzzing service for open source software."
- **fault characteristics** — The study asks what kinds of faults fuzzers actually find, alongside their lifecycles and campaign evolution. > "We examine the characteristics of fuzzer-found faults, the lifecycles of such faults, and the evolution of fuzzing campaigns over time."
- **fault lifecycle** — The paper's empirical base is a large corpus of fuzzer-reported bugs tracked through their resolution, not a synthetic benchmark. > "We conduct the first empirical study of OSS-Fuzz, analyzing 23,907 bugs found in 316 projects."
- **evolution of fuzzing campaigns** — Bug discovery is studied as a time series over a project's participation, not as a single aggregate rate. > "the lifecycles of such faults, and the evolution of fuzzing campaigns over time"
- **punctuated equilibria** — Campaigns stay stable for long stretches and then spike, so a sudden burst of findings is normal behaviour rather than a signal of regression. > "However, flaky bugs, timeouts, and out of memory errors are problematic, people rarely file CVEs for security vulnerabilities, and fuzzing campaigns often exhibit punctuated equilibria"
- **flaky bug** — Non-reproducible reports form one of the three fault categories the authors call problematic, together with timeouts and OOM errors. > "However, flaky bugs, timeouts, and out of memory errors are problematic"
GUIDELINES: none stated in the available text (the extracted page carries only the abstract and bibliographic metadata; no prescriptions, thresholds or practices are given).
EVIDENCE: sample of `23,907` bugs found in `316` projects; MSR 2021, pages `131-142`. Direction of findings: OSS-Fuzz "often effective at quickly finding bugs"; developers "often quick to patch them"; flaky bugs, timeouts and out-of-memory errors are "problematic"; CVEs are "rarely" filed for security vulnerabilities; campaigns exhibit punctuated equilibria. No further metrics are present in the extract.
LIMITS: the artifact is the IEEE Computer Society Digital Library landing page; full text, tables and threats-to-validity sections were not captured, so per-finding magnitudes cannot be quoted.
TOOLING: OSS-Fuzz.
LINKS: cited in the page's related-work list: T-Fuzz, SMARTIAN, BugOss benchmark, "What Happens When We Fuzz? Investigating OSS-Fuzz Bug History" (MSR 2023), ASanity, "Continuous Fuzzing: A Study of the Effectiveness and Scalability of Fuzzing in CI/CD Pipelines" (SBFT 2023), BazzAFL, "Compiler Fuzzing in Continuous Integration: A Case Study on Dafny" (ICST 2025), Slicer (ACSAC 2025).

## A122 · An Empirical Study of OSS-Fuzz Bugs
URL: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9463112
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Same MSR 2021 study: continuous fuzzing via OSS-Fuzz finds bugs quickly and they are patched quickly, but flaky bugs, timeouts, OOM errors, missing CVEs and punctuated campaign dynamics are problems.
CONCEPTS:
- **continuous fuzzing** — Fuzzing embedded in a continuous testing strategy, adopted in both industry and open-source engineering. > "Continuous fuzzing — using fuzz tests as part of a continuous testing strategy — is increasingly popular in both industry"
- **OSS-Fuzz** — The Google-run continuous fuzzing service that the paper treats as the main provider of continuous fuzzing. > "To improve the quality and security of open-source, Google maintains OSS-Fuzz"
- **fault characteristics** — The study characterises the faults fuzzers report, examined alongside lifecycle and campaign evolution. > "We examine the characteristics of fuzzer-found faults, the lifecycles of such faults, and the evolution of fuzzing campaigns over time."
- **fault lifecycle** — The empirical basis is a corpus of fuzzer-found bugs tracked over time across many projects. > "We conduct the first empirical study of OSS-Fuzz, analyzing 23,907 bugs found in 316 projects."
- **punctuated equilibria** — Campaigns report bugs in bursts, with stability broken by large spikes rather than smooth growth. > "people rarely file CVEs for security vulnerabilities, and fuzzing campaigns often exhibit punctuated equilibria"
- **flaky bug, timeout, out of memory error** — Three fault types the authors single out as problematic in practice, beyond the headline finding that bugs are found and fixed quickly. > "However, flaky bugs, timeouts, and out of memory errors are problematic"
- **CVE filing for fuzzer-found vulnerabilities** — Security-relevant findings rarely receive CVE identifiers, so CVE counts understate what fuzzing discovers. > "However, flaky bugs, timeouts, and out of memory errors are problematic, people rarely file CVEs for security vulnerabilities"
GUIDELINES: none stated in the available text; the extract contains the abstract, document outline and metadata only.
EVIDENCE: `23,907` bugs analysed across `316` projects; DOI `10.1109/MSR52588.2021.00026`; MSR 2021 (17–19 May 2021, Madrid); pages 131–142; page metrics report `44` cites in papers and `1225` full-text views. Directional findings as in the abstract: bugs found quickly, patched quickly, flaky/timeout/OOM problematic, CVEs rarely filed, punctuated equilibria.
LIMITS: IEEE Xplore landing page only — abstract and section headings ("I. Introduction" through "V. Fault Lifecycle") without body text; references "is not available for this document"; so no per-finding numbers, effect sizes or validity discussion can be cited.
TOOLING: OSS-Fuzz.
LINKS: the same related-work set as A121 (T-Fuzz, SMARTIAN, BugOss, OSS-Fuzz bug history study, ASanity, SBFT 2023 continuous-fuzzing study, BazzAFL, Dafny CI fuzzing, Graph Attention Network vulnerability detection).

## A123 · Large-Scale Empirical Analysis of Continuous Fuzzing: Insights From 1 Million Fuzzing Sessions
URL: https://www.computer.org/csdl/journal/ts/2026/07/11480921/2fEJErOefgk
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Across ~1.12 million OSS-Fuzz sessions in 878 projects, many fuzzing bugs pre-exist continuous-fuzzing adoption, coverage keeps rising with sessions, coverage *changes* (up or down) drive detection, and developer-provided seed corpora stay effective long term.
CONCEPTS:
- **continuous fuzzing** — Many short sessions repeated as code changes, contrasted with one long campaign on a fixed commit, so bugs surface near real time. > "In contrast, continuous fuzzing adopts a different strategy by conducting brief but frequent fuzzing sessions, aiming to identify fuzzing bugs in near real-time as the software evolves."
- **coverage-guided fuzzing (CGF)** — The fuzzer steers toward executing more source lines on the assumption that more coverage raises the chance of hitting a vulnerability. > "CGF refers to a fuzzing strategy where the fuzzer tries to maximize the coverage (i.e., the number of source code lines executed) during fuzzing to increase the chances of finding vulnerabilities."
- **fuzzing bug** — An umbrella term for issue-tracker entries found by fuzzing, used because those differ from general bugs. > "we refer to them collectively as “Fuzzing Bug” to explicitly indicate that they were detected through fuzzing"
- **fuzzing session** — Session counts are reconstructed from build logs, which record each compilation of a project and its fuzz targets. > "to measure the number of fuzzing sessions, we collected over 3.95 million build logs generated up to January 2025 from the compilation of the fuzzers and projects"
- **coverage report** — Daily automated reports give three coverage views, with region coverage standing in for branch coverage. > "The coverage reports include “line coverage,” “function coverage,” and “region coverage.”"
- **corpus pruning** — ClusterFuzz shrinks the input corpus to a minimal set that preserves coverage, which is why long-run corpus growth has to be interpreted carefully. > "which removes unnecessary inputs from the corpus while preserving coverage with a minimal set of test cases"
- **seed corpus** — Project-provided starting inputs that the study tests for lasting value against automated pruning and generation. > "In OSS-Fuzz, developers are encouraged to explicitly specify a set of inputs known as a “seed corpus”."
- **regression range / fixed range** — Commit ranges in each issue report bracket when the bug appeared and when it stopped reproducing. > "which shows the commit SHAs when the bug was detected and when the bug could not be reproduced"
GUIDELINES:
- Fuzz each project at least daily; the default per-session duration is `10 minutes`.
- Keep sessions short and frequent rather than long and single-shot; a `10 min` session has been shown effective for critical bugs.
- Select projects with at least `365` coverage measurements (about a year of fuzzing) for trend analysis.
- Treat "Bug" and "Vulnerability" labels collectively as fuzzing bugs.
- Maintain developer-provided seeds: they retain long-term value despite automated pruning.
- Keep issue reports private for `90 days` after detection or until fixed.
EVIDENCE: `~1.12 million` sessions, `878` projects (68% of all OSS-Fuzz projects), `>3.95 million` build logs to January 2025, `1.04 million` coverage reports, `72,660` issue reports from `1,201` projects → `56,173` fixed reports from `1,125` projects, and `49,470` reports from `808` projects. Abstract findings: (i) many bugs pre-date adoption, giving a high early detection rate; (ii) coverage keeps increasing; (iii) coverage changes contribute to detection; (iv) seeds are effective long term. Example report: 76.66% line, 72.40% function, 79.21% region coverage.
LIMITS: only publicly available GCS data; some build logs missing due to build errors or download failures, so the dataset "is not exhaustive"; projects joined at different times; validity threats not captured.
TOOLING: OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzz, CIFuzz, Fuzz Introspector, AFL++, libFuzzer, Corpus Pruning, Google Cloud Storage, Zenodo replication package.
LINKS: Böhme et al. (coverage reliability), Liyanage et al. (7-day coverage growth, logarithmic), Nourry et al. (fuzzing-expert survey), Klooster et al. (10-minute sessions), Zhu et al. (77% of fuzzing bugs from recent changes), Heartbleed, Log4Shell, RegreSSHion.

## A124 · Mutation Testing in Practice: Insights From Open-Source Software Developers
URL: https://www.computer.org/csdl/journal/ts/2024/05/10472898/1VpY3do6cyA
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: A survey of 104 open-source practitioners shows high satisfaction with mutation testing across languages and tools, with performance as the overwhelming limitation and popularity, usability and configurability as the adoption drivers.
CONCEPTS:
- **mutation operator** — A syntactic rewrite rule applied wherever its pattern matches, such as swapping a relational operator or negating a condition. > "Such faults are generated by applying mutation operators, which introduce simple syntactic changes into the source code of a computer program."
- **mutant / mutation** — The injected fault is the mutation and the resulting faulty program version is the mutant; both are distinct from real defects. > "The injected faults are known as mutations, and the new faulty versions of the program under test are known as mutants."
- **mutation score (mutation coverage)** — The share of non-equivalent mutants the suite detects, used as the headline adequacy measure. > "The adequacy of test suites is measured by the mutation score (a.k.a mutation coverage), which is the ratio of detected (a.k.a. killed) mutants over the total number of mutants."
- **killed vs alive** — Surviving mutants are treated as useful information rather than noise, because each names a gap in the suite. > "Mutants that are not killed by the employed test cases, i.e., that remain alive, are considered valuable as they showcase ways for improving the test suites."
- **semantically-equivalent mutants** — Some mutants behave exactly like the original and therefore cannot be killed, which is why the score is defined over non-equivalent mutants. > "a mutant can turn out to be functionally equivalent to the original program; these are the so-called semantically-equivalent mutants"
- **Competent Programmer Hypothesis** — The assumption that real programs are mostly right and err in small ways resembling mutants, justifying mutants as fault proxies. > "which states that programmers tend to write programs that are largely correct, in some sense missing simple cases, similar to mutants in mutation testing"
- **Coupling Effect Hypothesis** — The assumption that catching simple mutants generalises to complex faults, which is what makes a score meaningful. > "which states that tests detecting simple mutants are also able to detect others, including the majority of the more complex ones"
- **adoption factors** — Practitioners adopt tools for popularity, usability and configurability rather than for research pedigree. > "The adoption of mutation tools is mostly driven by their popularity, usability, and configurability."
- **reported uses** — Respondents value mutation for test-suite improvement and bug finding, and also for deciding when testing can stop. > "Developers find the technique beneficial for enhancing their test suites, identifying bugs, and deciding when to stop testing."
GUIDELINES:
- Treat mutation coverage as a refactoring guide, not only a test metric.
- Integrate mutation tools into CI/CD workflows and build tools, as respondents commonly do.
- Participant-contact recipe: use the word "questionnaire" not "survey"; ask for help; avoid spam filters (no `info@`/`noreply@`); personalise; appealing subject line; explain purpose; publish results; be grateful.
- Sample the most popular repositories (`up to 100` per tool, by stars) and most active contributors (`up to 100` per repo, by commits); exclude bots and contributors without email.
- Use divergent stacked bar charts for Likert data and the Matthews correlation coefficient for co-answered multiple-choice groups.
EVIDENCE: prior mining covered `127` tools and `3,581` repositories; filtering to development-purpose repos with industry/public owners cut this to `1,574` (44%), then `1,468`, then `503` repositories with `3,375` contributors → `3,207` non-bot → `1,192` with email. `1,192` emails and `503` GitHub issues sent; `127` responses = `10.65%` response rate (email basis); `23` excluded → `104` valid. Questionnaire: `21` questions (`17` closed-ended, `4` open-ended), 5-level Likert. Literature context: `400+` papers, `~130` tools. `26` congratulatory replies; `8` complaints about issue creation.
LIMITS: extract stops at the methodology section, so findings percentages and validity threats are not captured; self-selection (104 of 1,192 contacted); only the ten most-used tools are covered (MuJava, Major excluded).
TOOLING: PIT, MuJava, Major, Infection (PHP), Humbug (PHP), Mutant, Mutmut, MutPy, StrykerJS, Stryker.NET, GitHub REST API.
LINKS: DeMillo et al. (1970s origin), Kintis et al. (three Java tool comparison), Delahaye and du Bousquet (teaching/research/industry profiles), Petrović et al. (long-term effects), Google mutation system for seven languages, Beller et al. (Facebook), Sánchez et al. (prior mining study), Creswell (qualitative guidelines).

## A125 · Mutation Testing in Practice: Insights From Open-Source ...
URL: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10472898
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: Same TSE article: 104 open-source practitioners report high satisfaction with mutation testing, valuing it for test-suite quality, bug detection and maintainability, while naming performance as the primary impediment.
CONCEPTS:
- **mutation testing** — A fault-based adequacy technique: how well tests detect deliberately injected faults, not just whether code runs. > "Mutation testing assesses the adequacy of tests based on their ability to detect artificial faults."
- **mutation operator / mutant / mutation score** — Operators produce mutants; the score counts killed mutants over non-equivalent ones. > "The adequacy of test suites is measured by the mutation score (a.k.a mutation coverage), which is the ratio of detected (a.k.a. killed) mutants over the total number of mutants."
- **killed and alive mutants; semantically-equivalent mutants** — An undetected mutant is alive and worth analysing, unless it is behaviourally identical to the original. > "when the output is the same, the mutant remains alive and requires further analysis, as it can point out a deficiency in the fault detection ability of the test suite"
- **Competent Programmer Hypothesis and Coupling Effect Hypothesis** — The two assumptions the technique rests on: programmers err simply, and simple-mutant detection transfers to complex faults. > "which states that programmers tend to write programs that are largely correct, in some sense missing simple cases, similar to mutants in mutation testing."
- **mutation tools** — Tool support spans the main languages but is dominated by research prototypes rather than production systems. > "more than one hundred mutation testing tools have already been developed and these cover most of the widely-used programming languages, including Java, C/C++, Python or C#."
- **adoption drivers** — Popularity, usability and configurability explain uptake more than technique quality. > "The adoption of mutation tools is mostly driven by their popularity, usability, and configurability."
- **impediments** — Runtime cost is the dominant blocker, with IDE integration a secondary friction point. > "Performance stands out as the primary impediment to the practical implementation of the technique"
- **reported benefits** — Practitioners report gains in suite quality, defect detection and decisions about when to stop testing. > "Developers find the technique beneficial for enhancing their test suites, identifying bugs, and deciding when to stop testing."
GUIDELINES: none beyond the reported practice that tools are "commonly integrated into continuous integration/deployment workflows and build tools"; the extract is abstract plus the introduction and background, without the findings or threats sections that carry the actionable detail.
EVIDENCE: `104` valid survey responses from contributors identified via `>3.5K` GitHub repositories showing mutation-tool use; publication metadata: TSE vol. 50, issue 5, May 2024, pages `1130-1143`, published 18 March 2024, DOI `10.1109/TSE.2024.3377378`, open access under CC BY 4.0; `2,564` full-text views and `18` cites-in-papers at capture time. Prior-work figures quoted: `400+` research papers, `~130` tools, `127` tools mined by the earlier repository study.
LIMITS: IEEE Xplore landing page; only abstract, introduction and background are captured ("Background and Related Work" partially, breaking at Habchi et al.), so percentages, per-tool satisfaction and validity threats cannot be quoted.
TOOLING: PIT, MuJava, Major, Infection (PHP), Humbug (PHP).
LINKS: DeMillo et al.; Kintis et al.; Delahaye and du Bousquet; Chekam et al.; Google's seven-language mutation system; Beller et al. (Facebook); Sánchez et al. (GitHub mining); Prado and Vincenzi; Beller et al. (416 engineers, five months); Habchi et al. (14 practitioners, flaky tests); Perry et al. (47 participants, AI code assistants).

## A126 · Extreme mutation testing in practice: An industrial case study
URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.08480
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: In an industrial Java project, extreme (method-level) mutation testing runs and is analysed far faster than traditional mutation testing while still exposing weaknesses that line coverage hides; it best supplements unit testing when results appear while tests are written.
CONCEPTS:
- **mutator / mutant / survived / killed / mutation score** — The standard vocabulary: change types, altered program versions, detection outcomes, and the ratio of killed mutants. > "For mutation testing, small controlled changes in the source code of the software under test are introduced to change its behavior."
- **extreme mutation testing** — Mutations replace whole method bodies instead of single instructions, trading granularity for far fewer mutants. > "In contrast to traditional mutation testing, where mutations are usually performed on an instruction level"
- **pseudo-tested method** — A method whose whole body can be deleted while the suite still passes, despite the method showing as covered. > "The goal is to find pseudo-tested methods, which are methods where their whole functionality can be removed, and still, no test will fail."
- **mutator shapes** — Each return type gets a replacement that is obviously wrong: empty body for void, true/false for booleans, 0/1 for integers, ""/"A" for strings, null for objects. > "One mutator replaces the method-body with a single return statement that returns true and one that only returns false."
- **side-effect method** — A method exercised by tests but never asserted on, because it only logs or stores unused metadata. > "The remaining 14 methods are methods that are called during testing but are not subject to be tested and do not have an impact on the test result."
- **weak tests with no assertions and incomplete tests** — Two of the three pseudo-test causes: tests that assert nothing, and tests with strong assertions that miss properties of the class. > "We found eight tests that had no assertions, which caused them to be pseudo-tested."
GUIDELINES:
- Run extreme mutation testing **while writing unit tests** (IDE or command-line build), not in a decoupled session; that is where developers said they would fix findings.
- Highlight pseudo-tested code inside existing **code coverage reports**, marking those lines as uncovered.
- Do not chase the mutation score in extreme mode; strengthen only `weak tests with no assertions` and `incomplete tests`, and merely surface side-effect methods in coverage reports.
- When PIT runs a suite containing parallel/static-state tests, set the number of execution threads to `1` and remove parallel tests where possible.
- Repeat runs to check stability (extreme and default traditional runs were each repeated `three times`).
EVIDENCE: Java project, `11,424` unit tests finishing in `12 s`, `2,041` methods, ~`12,500` LOC. Extreme: score 85%, 2,297/2,706 killed, 409 survived, 19 mutators, 597,877 tests, `13 min`. Traditional default: 73%, 5,813/7,989, 2,176 survived, 7 mutators, 4,228,169 tests, `37 min`. Traditional all: 70%, 55,515/79,350, 23,835 survived, 66 mutators, 34,391,374 tests, `4 h 1 min`. `291` of `2,041` methods (14%) pseudo-tested; 1,129 lines affected, 835 covered (7% of 11,189; 9% of 12,572). Adjusted line coverage drops from `89%` to `82%`. Causes in the 25 sampled methods: no assertions (8), incomplete (3), side-effects (14). At 5 min/method, 291 methods ≈ `24 hours` vs ~`7 days` for 2,176 traditional mutants.
LIMITS: numbers depend on PIT's correctness; parallel/static-state tests distort results (nine methods remained in a class named "parallel"); only `two` developers interviewed, both largely agreeing.
TOOLING: PIT 1.4.10 with Gregor engine, PIT Descartes engine 1.2.6, JaCoCo 0.8.6, Python script for access-modifier labelling.
LINKS: Niedermayr/Juergens/Wagner (2016); Niedermayr thesis (2019; 19 projects, median 10.1% pseudo-tested); Coles et al. (PIT); Vera-Pérez/Monperrus/Baudry (Descartes); Vera-Pérez et al. (pseudo-tested methods); Jia and Harman; Papadakis et al.

## A127 · Mutation Testing in Continuous Integration: An Exploratory Industrial Case Study
URL: https://greg4cr.github.io/pdf/23mutationci.pdf
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: At Zenseact (automotive), Dextool and Mull are the C++ mutation tools usable in a GitHub Actions CI workflow, and interviews plus literature yield guidelines for applying mutation testing at commit level.
CONCEPTS:
- **mutant, mutation operator, mutation score** — Mutation testing scores a suite by whether its tests detect small injected changes, not merely by whether code runs. > "Mutation Testing judges the quality of a test suite by evaluating the ability of the tests to detect subtle changes in the code"
- **sensitivity** — Structural coverage only says code ran, so a suite can be insensitive to subtle defects even at high coverage. > "A challenge with traditional coverage metrics is that they mandate that code be executed, but only lightly constrain how that code is executed"
- **valid and useful mutants** — A mutant must compile to be usable, and must add value; equivalent, trivially failing and debug-print mutants do not. > "Mutants are introduced with the intent that they are syntactically valid and semantically useful. Effective mutants will compile (“valid”), and will be “useful” for improving the test suite"
- **mutation schema** — Multiple mutants are embedded in one program so it compiles once and each variant is instantiated, cutting generation cost. > "The tool has partial support for mutant schema, where multiple (but not all) mutants are embedded in a single file"
- **diff-only mutation** — A push-triggered workflow mutates only the changed lines, paired with a periodic whole-project run to cover the rest. > "One workflow is triggered by pushes to the repository and only mutates the git diff."
GUIDELINES:
- Require a CLI, plus the ability to mutate only changed code.
- Use the CI-relevant features: operator-subset selection, specify-lines-to-mutate, only mutate covered code, stop after N live mutants, skip previously killed mutants when relevant code is unchanged, resume after interruption, parallel execution, ignore-flags, configurable `timeout`.
- Visualise mutation score trends over time so practitioners can see test quality evolving.
- Balance fast feedback against keeping or flagging relevant mutants; treat mutation score as a coverage and acceptance criterion.
- Train developers inexperienced with mutation testing; apply mutation at commit level.
- Borrow Google's limits: mutate only new covered lines, `one mutant per line`, present few mutations to avoid fatigue, use a minimal test set, omit logging code, use only simple arithmetic/conditional/relational operators, limited by historical data.
EVIDENCE: five C++ tools (Dextool, Mull, MuCPP, Mutate++, CCmutator) on six projects; `seven` semi-structured interviews (developers, architects, SCRUM master, chief safety manager). Mutants/time: Corrade 15,359 LOC — Dextool 9,573 (4.12e-03 s each), Mull 2,314; FMT 42,229 — 9,815, 1,998; JSON 60,366 — 6,407, 528 (MuCPP 9,266); TimSort 1,584 — 1,073, 279; TinyXML-2 5,581 — 1,907, 698; yaml-cpp 18,210 — 6,235, 2,147. Mull was often orders of magnitude faster (TimSort `2.25 s` vs Dextool `5,398.9 s`); scores ranged 1.43%–82.00% (Mull), 2.30%–77.00% (Dextool). Mutate++ and CCmutator failed with errors.
LIMITS: one company, seven interviews; two tools unusable; Mull accepts one test binary and under-reports mutants with template functions; MuCPP needs a Makefile.
TOOLING: Dextool, Mull (Clang plugin over LLVM bitcode), MuCPP, Mutate++, CCmutator, Clang/LLVM, GitHub Actions, Docker, Ubuntu 20.04, Intel Core i9-10885H/32GB.
LINKS: Google mutation work, Facebook ML-derived operators, Ramler et al., mutation schemas, Usaola et al. (reach-based test selection, loop counters), Offutt et al. (operator subsets), Ma et al. (ML operator prediction), PIT, MuJava, Git, Makefile.

## A128 · Mutation Testing in Practice: Insights From Open-Source ...
URL: https://idus.us.es/server/api/core/bitstreams/9d3fb0c4-9373-4ecd-9b15-abcec39624b7/content
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: The authors' survey of open-source mutation-testing practitioners (104 valid responses from 1,192 contacted contributors) documents how tools are used, the perceived value, and the benefits/limitations that should steer tool research.
CONCEPTS:
- **mutation operator, mutant, mutation score, killed/alive, semantically-equivalent mutants** — The technique's vocabulary: operators inject faults, mutants are the altered programs, and the score counts killed non-equivalent mutants. > "The adequacy of test suites is measured by the mutation score (a.k.a mutation coverage), which is the ratio of detected (a.k.a. killed) mutants over the total number of mutants."
- **Competent Programmer Hypothesis and Coupling Effect Hypothesis** — The two assumptions justifying mutation analysis: programmers err simply, and detecting simple mutants transfers to complex ones. > "which states that programmers tend to write programs that are largely correct, in some sense missing simple cases, similar to mutants in mutation testing."
- **mutation tools** — Many tools exist across mainstream and emerging domains, so tool choice is a real decision rather than a default. > "more than one hundred mutation testing tools have already been developed and these cover most of the widely-used programming languages, including Java, C/C++, Python or C#."
- **adoption drivers and limitation** — Uptake follows popularity, usability and configurability, while performance is the dominant limitation. > "Popularity, usability, and configurability emerge as key factors for the adoption of mutation tools, whereas performance stands overwhelmingly as their main limitation."
- **per-tool selection funnel** — Recruitment was capped per tool and per repository, keeping the sample comparable across tools. > "we considered up to 100 repositories for each tool (ordered by popularity, i.e., number of stars) and up to 100 contributors for each repository (ordered by their number of commits to the project)"
- **survey instrument** — A fixed questionnaire with mostly closed questions and an optional comment field, plus a few open questions. > "The final version of our questionnaire, included in the Appendix (see the supplemental material), contains 21 questions, 17 closed-ended, in which additional comments can also be included, and 4 open-ended."
- **analysis devices** — Responses were analysed narratively with charts and a correlation measure over co-answered option groups. > "we used a combination of narrative analysis, different kinds of charts, and correlation computed using the Mathews coefficient"
GUIDELINES:
- Ask about role, invocation mode and frequency of mutation coverage, whether computed results are restricted to a test-case type, whether tool configuration was modified, and whether the respondent chose the tool.
- Recruit only "development purposes" repositories owned by industry or public institutions; exclude teaching and research repositories.
- Cap sampling at `100` repositories per tool by stars and `100` contributors per repository by commit count.
- Apply the eight participant-contact recommendations (word "questionnaire", ask for help, avoid spam filters, personalise, appealing subject line, explain purpose, publish results, thank participants).
- Send one reminder only to those who said they were away or would reply later.
EVIDENCE: `3,581` → `1,574` (44%) → `1,468` → `503` repositories; `3,375` → `3,207` → `1,192` contributors; `1,192` emails and `503` issues; first send-out 29 Nov 2022, reminder 15 Dec 2022, additional send-out 7 Dec 2023 (448 emails, 330 issues), responses closed 2 Jan 2024; `127` responses = `10.65%`; `23` excluded (1 no consent, 3 no tool acknowledged, 19 unable to identify the tool) → `104` valid; `26` congratulatory replies, `8` complaints.
LIMITS: extract ends inside the qualitative-analysis paragraph, so findings percentages, per-RQ results and Section V validity threats are absent; repository availability checked 10 Oct 2022; only the ten most-used tools are covered.
TOOLING: GitHub REST API, PIT, StrykerJS, Stryker.NET, Mutmut, MutPy, Mutant, Infection, Humbug.
LINKS: Sánchez et al. (prior mining study, 127 tools), Kintis et al., Delahaye and du Bousquet, Chekam et al., Petrović et al., Google and Facebook mutation reports, Beller et al. (416 engineers), Habchi et al., Perry et al., Creswell (qualitative research guidelines), survey-participation literature and Likert/divergent-chart recommendations.

## A129 · Extreme mutation testing in practice:An industrial case stud
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2103.08480v1
TYPE: conference preprint
THESIS: The HTML edition of the same industrial case study: extreme mutation testing is ~3x faster to execute and far cheaper to analyse than traditional mutation testing, and should be surfaced inside coverage reports while tests are written.
CONCEPTS:
- **mutator, mutant, survived, killed, equivalent mutants, mutation score** — The base vocabulary is unchanged from traditional mutation testing; only the mutation granularity differs. > "For mutation testing, small controlled changes in the source code of the software under test are introduced to change its behavior."
- **extreme mutation testing** — Mutation happens at method level rather than instruction level, so the number of mutants drops sharply. > "In contrast to traditional mutation testing, where mutations are usually performed on an instruction level, extreme mutation testing performs these mutations on a method level."
- **pseudo-tested methods** — Full functionality can be removed without a failing test, and such methods turn out to be common rather than exceptional. > "The goal is to find pseudo-tested methods, which are methods where their whole functionality can be removed, and still, no test will fail."
- **partially-tested** — When only one of the required replacement mutants survives, the method is flagged as partially rather than pseudo-tested. > "If both resulting mutants survive, the method is categorized as pseudo-tested. If only one survives, the method is categorized as partially-tested."
- **replacement defaults** — Void methods get an emptied body; other types get obviously wrong default returns such as true/false, 0/1, ""/"A" or null. > "One mutator replaces the method-body with a single return statement that returns `true` and one that only returns `false`."
- **pseudo-test causes** — Analysis of sampled methods yields three causes: missing assertions, incomplete tests, and side-effect methods. > "We analyzed 25 methods in more depth and found the following three reasons why methods are pseudo-tested"
- **line coverage inadequacy** — Covered lines that no test actually verifies understate the gap, which is why adjusted coverage is lower than reported coverage. > "when counting pseudo-tested lines as “uncovered”, the total line coverage would have to be adjusted from 89% to 82%"
GUIDELINES:
- Report extreme mutation results by highlighting pseudo-tested code in code coverage reports.
- Perform extreme mutation testing while writing unit tests rather than in a decoupled session; CI-produced reports are only acted on "depending on available time and priorities".
- Treat the mutation score as largely irrelevant in extreme mode; remediate no-assertion and incomplete tests, and merely reflect side-effect methods in coverage.
- Set PIT to a single execution thread for suites with parallel or static-state tests, and remove parallel tests where possible.
- Verify stability by repeating extreme and default traditional runs `three times`.
- Scope findings to the package under test: developers said they would not act on pseudo-tested methods from unrelated packages.
EVIDENCE: `11,424` unit tests normally finishing in `12 s`; `2,041` methods, ~`12,500` LOC, Java, multiple sub-projects. Extreme: 85% score, 2,297/2,706 killed, 409 survived, 19 mutators, 597,877 executed tests, `13 min`. Traditional default (7 mutators): 73%, 5,813/7,989, 2,176 survived, 4,228,169 tests, `37 min`. Traditional all (66 mutators): 70%, 55,515/79,350, 23,835 survived, 34,391,374 tests, `4 h 1 min`. `291`/`2,041` methods (14%) pseudo-tested; 835 of 11,189 covered lines (7%); 1,129 of 12,572 total lines (9%). Cause counts: 8 no-assertion, 3 incomplete, 14 side-effect. Analysis cost at 5 min/method: ≈`24 h` vs ≈`7 days`. Company policy of `80%` line coverage did not motivate test writing.
LIMITS: relies on PIT correctness; parallel and static-class-coupled tests distort results (nine methods remained in a "parallel"-named class); only `two` developers interviewed, both largely agreeing, so generalisability is limited; the HTML rendering may differ from the PDF (LaTeXML-generated, a build-log link is offered for errors).
TOOLING: PIT 1.4.10 (Gregor engine), PIT Descartes 1.2.6, JaCoCo 0.8.6, Python labelling script, LaTeXML HTML rendering.
LINKS: Niedermayr et al. (2016), Niedermayr thesis (2019; 19 projects, median 10.1% pseudo-tested), Coles et al. (PIT), Vera-Pérez/Monperrus/Baudry (Descartes), Vera-Pérez et al. (pseudo-tested methods study), Jia and Harman, Papadakis et al.

## A130 · An Empirical Evaluation of Property-Based Testing in Python
URL: https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~mcoblenz/assets/pdf/OOPSLA_2025_PBT.pdf
TYPE: peer-reviewed paper
THESIS: A corpus study of 426 Python programs using Hypothesis formalizes 12 categories of property-based test and uses mutation testing on 40 projects to show that, per test, property-based tests kill far more mutants than example-based unit tests.
CONCEPTS:
- **`property-based testing (PBT)`** — developers state the whole class of valid inputs plus one property that must hold for all of them; a generator supplies random instances and the property is checked on each. > "In property-based testing, developers specify all the possible valid test inputs and a particular property that is supposed to hold of the tested code."
- **`generated arguments`** — the values Hypothesis randomly produces for a test function's parameters, which the analysis treats as the sources of dataflow. > "the data source is the input values randomly generated by Hypothesis (the generated arguments), and the data sinks are the assert statements of the test function"
- **`influenced expression`** — an expression reachable from a generated argument through assignments, calls, conditionals or loops. > "Expressions within these statements are considered influenced by an argument generated by Hypothesis if there is some sequence of dataflows from that argument to the expression."
- **`property-based test assertion`** — an assertion whose tested expression carries dataflow from a generated argument. > "We defined a property-based test assertion as one that involves an expression that has been influenced by an argument generated by Hypothesis."
- **`PBT function` vs `unit test`** — a purely structural distinction: a test function with at least one property-based assertion versus one with none. > "A PBT function is a test function that contains one or more property-based test assertions, and a test function that does not contain any is called a unit test."
- **`detector`** — a category's classifier, implemented as an intraprocedural dataflow analysis from generated arguments to assert statements. > "Each test classification function (or detector) consists of an intraprocedural dataflow analysis."
- **12 categories** — e.g. `constant equality`, `generated-expression and constant non-equality`, `type checking`, `inclusion`, `constant inclusion`; five came from novice-facing advice and covered 48% of tests, the rest were added after inspecting unclassified assertions. > "The definitions inspired by the informal property recommendations accounted for five of the 12 property categories we defined and 48% of the tests in our corpus."
- **`partial correctness property`** — the usual shape of a property, because asserting equality with a known-correct value needs an oracle the developer does not have. > "often, the properties expressed are only partial correctness properties, since testing whether the output of the function under test equals some known-correct value requires a (usually unavailable) oracle."
- **`mutation testing` / `mutation score`** — small syntactic edits are made to the source and the suite is rerun; a mutant no test fails on is left uncaught. > "In a mutation test, small changes are made to a program’s source code, called mutations."
- **`mutation operators`, `mutmut`** — mutmut edits AST nodes (numbers, strings, lambdas, function arguments, operators, decorators) and reruns the suite against each mutant. > "The mutmut tool adds mutations to source code by editing specific nodes of the AST, including numbers, strings, lambdas, function arguments, operators, and decorators according to certain rules."
- **`parameter sweep`** — rerunning the same projects over many inputs to locate the input index at which a mutation is caught. > "To conduct the parameter sweep experiments, we tested the same projects on 100 randomly selected mutations and ran the property-based tests with 500 inputs."
