- **Deploy/release split** — Code ships dark, then is enabled for a cohort before reaching 100%. > "The point of a feature flag is that deploy and release stop being the same event: code ships to production dark, then you turn it on for a cohort"
- **Sticky bucketing** — A 5% flag must reach the same users on every request rather than a fresh random 5%. > "A flag enabled for 5% of users reaches the same users on every request (sticky bucketing), not a random 5% each time."
- **Canary progression** — Traffic steps up 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%, holding at each step while metrics stay healthy. > "The classic progression is 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%, holding at each step while metrics stay healthy."
- **Shadow traffic / dark launch** — Requests are mirrored to the new version while users still receive the stable response. > "In shadow testing, production requests get mirrored to the new version — but the response users see still comes from the stable one."
- **Synthetic monitoring** — Scripted probes hitting login, search and checkout from multiple regions all day. > "Synthetic probes are scripted tests that keep hitting production — login, search, checkout — from multiple regions, all day."
- **RUM** — Real page loads, JS errors, API latencies and click paths cut by browser, device and region, used to corroborate synthetics. > "RUM is the other half of the picture: what real users actually experience — page loads, JS errors, API latencies, click paths — cut by browser, device and region."
- **Game day** — Failure practice for the team, where the deliverable is corrected playbooks rather than the drill. > "The drill itself isn't the deliverable; corrected playbooks and a team that has already seen the failure once are."
- **Symptom-based alerting** — Alerts fire on symptoms users feel, not on causes engineers infer. > "Alerts should fire on symptoms users feel, not causes engineers infer."
GUIDELINES:
- Require three preconditions: observability, a rollback measured in minutes, and blast-radius-bounding techniques.
- Define canary pass/fail before starting — e.g. fail if p99 latency rises more than `10%` over baseline or errors exceed `0.1%`; route on consistent criteria (user ID hash, region, stickiness).
- Automate rollback on threshold breach; verify it completes inside the SLA, "typically under five minutes", without dropping sessions. Weigh duration: `five minutes` misses slow-burn issues like memory leaks; a week at `50%` extends exposure.
- Keep mirroring async/fire-and-forget; route shadow writes to separate schemas, make them idempotent, or strip side effects — "no shadow request should ever charge a card".
- Start chaos with one reversible fault, with abort condition, rollback plan and monitoring; give every experiment its own dashboard first.
- Start read-only, graduate to idempotent writes, then stateful operations — with a rollback you have run in a drill.
- Test in low-traffic windows; never without observability or a rollback, or where the domain forbids it (payment ledgers, PHI, audit trails).
- Argo example: `setWeight` `5`, `25`, `50` with `10m` pauses; `AnalysisTemplate` fails when the 5xx rate over `5m` exceeds `0.01`, `failureLimit: 2` — two consecutive failures roll back automatically.
EVIDENCE: none (worked configuration only).
LIMITS:
- Anecdotal: teams found their "instant" switch "actually propagated in ten minutes because it polled a config file".
- Production tests "complement unit, integration and staging tests; they don't replace them".
TOOLING: OpenFeature, LaunchDarkly, Flagsmith, Unleash, Argo Rollouts v1.8, Prometheus, kubectl argo rollouts.
LINKS: Canary Deployment Testing Guide, Feature Flags Testing Guide, Observability-Driven Testing, Google SRE Book — Release Engineering, Principles of Chaos Engineering.

## A149 · Testing in Production to Stay Safe and Sensible | LaunchDarkly
URL: https://launchdarkly.com/blog/testing-in-production-for-safety-and-sanity
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Testing in production runs code on production servers with real data and real users without showing new behaviour to most of them; feature flags make it safe, and it extends QA into the most realistic environment rather than replacing other testing.
CONCEPTS:
- **Definition** — Running code on production servers with real data and real users while hiding the new behaviour from most of them. > "“Testing in production” refers to the practice of running code on production servers, using real data from real users, without showing the new behavior to the majority of users."
- **Two implementations** — Either proving a stated hypothesis, or confirming that nothing negative happened. > "In the first, the test exists to prove or disprove a stated hypothesis—“If we make this change, customers will convert at least 10% more often”."
- **Not a QA substitute** — An extension of QA control points into the most realistic environment, not a replacement for other testing. > "Instead, it is an extension of testing and QA control points into the most realistic environment possible—the real-world."
- **Three production phases (Cindy Sridharan)** — Deploy, release and post-release; tests in any phase count as production testing. > "describes three phases of production—deploy, release, and post-release. Tests taking place in any of these phases can be considered testing in production."
- **Blue-green deployment** — Two identical instances, one live and one CI-fed, so testing the inactive one is testing production. > "At any time, the system not receiving traffic could become the production environment, hence the testing you are conducting on the inactive application is a production environment."
- **Canary testing** — A percentage of real users see the new feature or version in production. > "the process of testing out new features or software versions with a percentage of real users in a production environment."
- **Experimentation / a/b/n tests** — End-user data on conversions, performance or other metrics used to fine-tune before full release. > "With a/b testing, you can collect user data on conversions, performance, or other metrics to determine which version has the most impact on the business."
- **Progressive Delivery** — Slow rollout judged by observability data, starting with trusted, low-risk customers. > "The idea of slowly rolling out a feature and using observability data to determine if things are running smoothly are two core tenets of Progressive Delivery."
- **Kill switch / flag trigger** — Turning the offending feature off without redeploying, optionally automatically on an APM signal. > "A feature flag allows you to immediately reverse any change that is going poorly. Turn the feature off completely, or leave it on for developers and engineers only."
GUIDELINES:
- Keep the pre-production suite: unit, integration, performance (load and stress), regression, functional, lint, usability tests.
- "don't bypass running tests in staging because you will be testing in production".
- Wrap features in flags to deploy without visibility, then let test/software engineers run tests or experiments.
- Rerun integration or load tests in production during the deploy phase where staging configuration or scale is insufficient; use blue-green or canary in the release phase, chaos engineering and experimentation post-release.
- Plan for: "Wider or narrower distribution than intended", "Unforeseen interactions or impacts on other production systems", "Runaway processes", "Pages and alerts to people on-call".
EVIDENCE:
- Total Economic Impact study cited for two savings: less duplicate staging infrastructure ("this is very expensive to build and maintain") and less developer time on integration issues.
- Quote (Chris Guidry, VP Engineering, O'Reilly Media): "if a feature causes problems on the day of the launch, we can just turn it off with a kill switch—no rollbacks."
LIMITS:
- Vendor advocacy for feature management; savings claims rest on a vendor-commissioned TEI study.
- Concedes risk persists "even if you follow all the best practices and have safety mechanisms in place".
- No error budgets, rollout percentages or rollback time targets are given.
TOOLING: LaunchDarkly (Code References, Flag Triggers, APM integrations), blue-green, canary releases, a/b/n experimentation.
LINKS: Cindy Sridharan, "Testing in Production, the safe way"; LaunchDarkly posts on canary releases, blue-green, Progressive Delivery; TEI study.

## A150 · Testing in Production -- Canary Deployments, Feature Flags, and Synthetic Monitoring
URL: https://qaskills.sh/blog/testing-in-production-strategies
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: Testing in production is a disciplined addition to pre-production testing: passing pre-production tests is "necessary but not sufficient", so canaries, flags, and monitoring validate the last mile.
CONCEPTS:
- **`staging is a lie`** — no amount of effort makes a staging environment mirror production; data scale, traffic, integrations, infrastructure, and configuration drift all differ in ways that matter. > "No matter how much effort you invest in making your staging environment mirror production, it will always differ in ways that matter."
- **`canary deployment`** — route a small share of real traffic to the new version while most traffic stays on the stable one, then compare metrics against baseline. > "A canary deployment is a production testing strategy where you route a small percentage of real traffic to a new version of your application while the majority of traffic continues hitting the current stable version."
- **`feature flags`** — decouple deployment from release so code can ship dark and be enabled for dogfooding, beta cohorts, or percentage rollout. > "Feature flags (also called feature toggles) are a production testing strategy that decouples deployment from release."
- **`flag hygiene`** — every flag needs an owner, an expiration date, and a removal plan, because permanent flags become technical debt. > "Every feature flag should have an owner, an expiration date, and a plan for removal. Flags that live forever become technical debt."
- **`synthetic monitoring`** — scheduled scripts replay critical journeys against production, so regressions surface before real users hit them. > "Synthetic monitoring is a production testing strategy where automated scripts simulate user interactions against your live production environment on a scheduled basis."
- **`chaos engineering`** — deliberately inject faults into production systems to prove that resilience mechanisms work under real conditions. > "Chaos engineering takes testing in production to the next level by deliberately injecting faults into your production systems to verify that your resilience mechanisms work under real conditions."
- **`GameDay`** — a structured drill in which the team injects a failure scenario and practices incident response with defined roles. > "A GameDay is a structured team exercise where engineers deliberately inject failures into production (or a production-like environment) while the team practices their incident response."
- **`observability-driven testing`** — instead of explicit assertions, instrumentation so complete that anomalous behavior is detected and surfaced automatically; latency budgets and call-graph checks act as assertions. > "Instead of writing explicit test assertions, you instrument your system so thoroughly that anomalous behavior is automatically detected and surfaced."
GUIDELINES:
- Canary flow: deploy to `1-5%` of fleet, route `1%` of traffic, monitor `15-30 minutes`, step to `5%`, `10%`, `25%`.
- Canary thresholds: error rate `> 1%` over baseline; p99 latency `> 20%`; saturation `> 80%`; business metrics `> 2%` decrease.
- "A canary that requires a human to decide whether to roll back is a canary that will fail at 3 AM on a Saturday" — automate rollback.
- Synthetic monitors run every `1 to 5 minutes`; alert after `2-3 consecutive failures`, routed to the owner with failing step, screenshot, timing, trace link.
- RUM gates: `LCP > 2.5s` for `> 5%` of users; JS error rate `> 0.5%`; API failure rate `> 1%` per endpoint; `CLS > 0.1` for `> 10%` of views.
- Progressive rollout: internal `1-3 days`; beta `1-5%` for `3-7 days` (advance below `baseline + 0.1%`, rollback above `+ 0.5%`); canary `1%` for `1-2 days` (advance within `5%`, roll back at `> 20%`); then `10%`/`25%`/`50%` with tolerances `15%`, `10%`, `10%`.
- Automatic rollback: error rate `5x` baseline, p99 `3x`, `> 10` new crash signatures in `5 minutes`, data corruption, health failures on `> 50%` of instances.
- Manual rollback: error rate `2x` baseline, business metric drop `> 3%`, `> 5` customer reports within `30 minutes`; never for transient fluctuations under `2 minutes`, documented known issues, or expected feature consequences.
EVIDENCE: none.
LIMITS: none stated; practice superiority asserted without measurement; FAQ truncated.
TOOLING: Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Istio, AWS CodeDeploy, LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Checkly, Datadog, Playwright, web-vitals, Sentry, OpenTelemetry, Chaos Monkey, Litmus.
LINKS: QASkills chaos-engineering and smoke-vs-sanity guides; `production-smoke-suite`, `audit-website` skills.

## A151 · Testing strategies: pyramids, trophies, and honeycombs
URL: https://howitworks.dev/testing-strategies/
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: No shape is universally correct; each optimizes for a different kind of system, so ask which shape fits which code.
CONCEPTS:
- **`pyramid` (Mike Cohn)** — many unit tests, fewer integration, few end-to-end; the premise is that each step up costs speed and diagnosis clarity. > "The premise is that unit tests are cheap to write, fast to run, and isolate failures precisely; integration tests are slower and harder to debug; end-to-end tests are slowest and flakiest."
- **pyramid fit** — complexity in pure logic: algorithms, business rules, calculations, state machines, libraries, rich domain layers. > "aggregates with real invariants, value objects with real behavior, policies with real complexity — unit tests at the bottom of a pyramid will catch a huge percentage of bugs cheaply"
- **pyramid failure mode** — mocking everything in glue code yields tests that verify the glue matches the mocks, not that it works. > "Unit testing glue by mocking everything it touches produces tests that verify the glue matches the mocks, not that it works."
- **`trophy` (Kent C. Dodds)** — static base, modest unit layer, thick integration layer, small E2E cap; bets multi-layer tests near real boundaries carry the most signal. > "a small base of static checks (types, linters), a modest layer of unit tests, a thick layer of integration tests, and a small cap of end-to-end tests"
- **trophy failure mode** — rich logic tested through integration is slow and misses edge cases. > "reproducing all the cases of a complex rule through integration tests is slower and more expensive than unit-testing the rule directly"
- **`honeycomb` (Spotify)** — the service, not the function, is the unit of meaning: the service is tested through its real API and real database, with dependencies mocked only at the network boundary. > "a thick middle of integrated-service tests (the service tested through its real API, against a real database, with its real dependencies mocked only at the network boundary)"
- **`ice cream cone`** — thin unit layer, moderate integration, huge manual/E2E cap; a symptom of untestable code, not a strategy. > "a thin layer of unit tests, a moderate layer of integration tests, and a huge cap of manual or end-to-end tests on top"
- **`fake`** — a simpler working implementation that behaves like the real thing within a bounded scope. > "A fake is a working implementation that is simpler than production — an in-memory database, a fake mail sender that records what was sent."
- **`stub`** — a hard-coded response that does not verify how it was called. > "A stub is a hard-coded response. “When called with this input, return this output.” Does not verify how it was called."
- **`mock`** — a stub that additionally verifies how it was called, turning the test into an assertion about implementation details. > "A mock is a stub that additionally verifies how it was called. “Was this method invoked exactly once, with these arguments?”"
- **`spy`** — records calls but passes through to the real implementation. > "A spy is like a mock but passes through to a real implementation — it records calls without replacing behavior."
- **`contract testing`** — the consumer tests against a mock specified by a contract file that the producer's CI verifies against the real producer; neither side needs the other running. > "The consumer writes a test that exercises its client code against a mock of the producer — but the mock’s behavior is specified in a contract file that is shared with the producer’s test suite."
- **`property-based testing`** — verify properties that should hold for all inputs by generating random ones (empty, huge, Unicode, negatives, zero, NaN). > "Property-based tests — QuickCheck, Hypothesis, fast-check — verify properties that should hold for all inputs, by generating many random inputs and checking the property on each."
GUIDELINES:
- Diagnostic: if most business logic can be exercised by calling a function and checking its return value with no I/O, the pyramid fits.
- Prefer `fakes` over `stubs`, `stubs` over `mocks`; use mocks only when the interaction itself is what you test.
- Every consumer-producer pair should have a contract, verified automatically on both sides.
- Keep end-to-end tests few, focused on critical journeys — "A large number drowns."
- Add property-based tests where mathematical structure exists; a handful can find bugs thousands of examples miss.
- Every test should earn its keep on two of three: catching bugs, documenting behavior, enabling refactoring.
EVIDENCE: none.
LIMITS: Asserts each shape fits a different system and no universal answer exists; the adoption cost of contract testing is called real (workflow learning, broker infrastructure, producer-team friction).
TOOLING: `@testing-library/react`, TypeScript, mypy, clippy, Pact, Spring Cloud Contract, Specmatic, OpenAPI, QuickCheck, Hypothesis, fast-check.
LINKS: Cohn's pyramid, Dodds' trophy, Spotify honeycomb, Pact, Spring Cloud Contract, Specmatic.

## A152 · Pyramid or Crab? Find a testing strategy that fits | Articles | web.dev
URL: https://web.dev/articles/ta-strategies
TYPE: official docs
THESIS: Test types combine into named shapes whose suitability depends on application size, team composition, and reliance on manual testing; the goal is serving users, not coverage.
CONCEPTS:
- **strategy matrix** — application size × team composition × manual reliance → recommended shape, presented as a lookup table rather than a single prescription. > "You can compare the strategies to a number of shapes to better grasp their meaning. Here's a list of strategies with respective sizes and development scopes."
- **`test pyramid` (Mike Cohn, *Succeeding with Agile*; expanded by Fowler and Vocke)** — unit base, integration middle, E2E/UI top. > "As shown in this drawing, the test pyramid consists of three layers"
- **`confidence versus resources`** — E2E is closest to users but needs a full stack and simulated user, so confidence competes with execution resources. > "they require a complete application stack and a simulated user, therefore, they are also potentially the most expensive"
- **Cohn's two essential points** — write tests at different granularity; the higher the level, the fewer tests. > "The more high level you get, the fewer tests you should have."
- **`test diamond`** — unit layer cut because unit tests erode after refactors; integration widest; E2E only for critical cases. > "the next time you refactor, you will have to update many of these unit tests and you might be tempted to skip them"
- **`testing honeycomb` (Spotify)** — microservice specialization where complexity sits in interaction rather than inside the service. > "Due to their small size, the most considerable complexity in a microservice is not within the service itself, but in how it interacts with others."
- **`integrated test` (J. B. Rainsberger via Spotify)** — a test whose pass/fail depends on another system's correctness; use only for essential cases. > "A test that will pass or fail based on the correctness of another system."
- **`testing trophy` (Kent C. Dodds)** — static analysis, unit, integration as main focus, UI tests. > "the testing trophy adaptation that takes static analysis into account while maintaining the focus on integration tests"
- **`testing ice cone`** — reversed pyramid, heavy manual/UI, least unit; an anti-pattern; without the manual step it is the `testing pizza`. > "The ice cone has bigger focus on manual or UI testing and the least focus on unit testing."
- **`testing crab`** — ice cone variant emphasizing E2E and visual testing; verifies that the application functions and looks good. > "The test crab is similar to the test ice cone, but with more emphasis on E2E and visual testing"
GUIDELINES:
- Mapping: small + developers only + high manual → Ice Cone or Crab; small + developers only + low manual → Pyramid; large + developers only + high manual → Trophy or Diamond; large + developers + QA + high manual → Trophy or Crab; large + developers only + low manual → Trophy or Honeycomb.
- Define the goal first: "When do you consider that your application has been sufficiently tested?"
- Do not make `100% coverage` the goal; unprioritized testing creates heavy maintenance.
- Prioritize E2E for crucial user journeys and defect-prone places.
- Ice cone and crab suit small projects where an integration-focused strategy is over-engineered.
- Aim for tests that "establish clear boundaries, run quickly & reliably, and only fail for useful reasons" (Justin Searls).
EVIDENCE: none.
LIMITS: The answer is explicitly "It depends"; acknowledges the pyramid oversimplifies, omits test types, and that definitions differ between teams.
TOOLING: Jest (unit example), Cypress (API test, real-world app), Nuxt component test, Cypress visual testing.
LINKS: Cohn's *Succeeding with Agile*, Fowler's *Practical Test Pyramid* and 2021 test-shapes article, Dodds' static/unit/integration/E2E post, Spotify microservices testing, Rainsberger, Guillermo Rauch, Searls tweet, `web.dev/articles/ta-types`, changelog.com crab article.

## A153 · Determine testing goals: What do you want to achieve with these tests?
URL: https://web.dev/articles/ta-strategies?hl=id
TYPE: official docs
THESIS: The same web.dev test-strategy article (localized variant) argues strategy should follow the testing goal, application size, and team composition, aiming to ship working software for users rather than maximize coverage.
CONCEPTS:
- **`testing goal`** — the prior question is when the application counts as "sufficiently tested"; coverage is one answer, serving users' needs the better one. > "Before you can start building a good strategy, figure out your testing goal. When do you consider that your application has been sufficiently tested?"
- **`test pyramid` (Cohn; Fowler expanded)** — unit (fast, isolated, smallest units), integration (API and component tests, acceptable speed), E2E/UI (simulated genuine user, slowest). > "You find these tests at the base layer of the pyramid because they are fast to execute and simple to maintain."
- **`confidence versus resources`** — E2E gives most confidence at highest cost, hence a unit-heavy base with strictly prioritized E2E cases. > "they require a complete application stack and a simulated user, therefore, they are also potentially the most expensive"
- **`test diamond`** — unit layer cut because unit tests erode when refactors make updating them unattractive. > "Imagine that you have reached 100% coverage on unit tests. However, the next time you refactor, you will have to update many of these unit tests and you might be tempted to skip them."
- **`testing honeycomb`** — microservice specialization; complexity is in interactions, not inside the service. > "Due to their small size, the most considerable complexity in a microservice is not within the service itself, but in how it interacts with others."
- **`integrated tests`** — pass or fail based on another system's correctness; use only for essential cases. > "A test that will pass or fail based on the correctness of another system."
- **`tests on implementation details`** — unit-like tests for naturally isolated code with its own internal complexity. > "These tests resemble unit tests---tests that focus on parts of the code that are naturally isolated and thus have their own internal complexity."
- **`testing trophy`** — adds `static analysis` as a base layer missing from the pyramid; integration is the main focus; UI and visual tests on top. > "Static analysis is missing from the test pyramid and in most of the adaptations you have seen so far."
- **`testing ice cone` / `testing pizza`** — reversed pyramid, costly in resources and manual work, an anti-pattern. > "The ice cone has bigger focus on manual or UI testing and the least focus on unit testing."
- **`testing crab`** — ice cone plus visual testing; component and API testing move further into the background. > "The test crab is similar to the test ice cone, but with more emphasis on E2E and visual testing"
GUIDELINES:
- Choose by size/team/manual reliance: small + low manual → Pyramid; large + high manual → Trophy or Diamond; large + developers + QA + high manual → Trophy or Crab; large + low manual → Trophy or Honeycomb.
- Decompose Rauch: "Write tests" (trust, less maintenance); "Not too many" (`100%` coverage is not always good); "Mostly integration" (business value at reasonable execution time).
- Automate routine work to free QA engineers for crucial areas; automation complements manual testing.
- Focus on tests that report real-life errors users might encounter, not coverage percentages.
- Fit the strategy to architecture, requirements, and users rather than a textbook definition.
EVIDENCE: none.
LIMITS: Explicitly "It depends"; acknowledges the pyramid oversimplifies and that definitions vary between teams.
TOOLING: Jest, Cypress, Cypress visual testing.
LINKS: Cohn *Succeeding with Agile*, Fowler's *Practical Test Pyramid* and test-shapes article, Dodds' static/unit/integration/E2E post, Spotify microservices testing, Rainsberger, Rauch, Searls tweet, `ta-types`.

## A154 · The Test Pyramid: How to Balance Unit, Integration and End-to-End Testing
URL: https://shiftasia.com/column/the-test-pyramid-how-to-balance-unit-integration-and-end-to-end-testing
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: The pyramid models the cost of feedback, not a quota; a balanced suite is designed from risk, pushed to the lowest layer that catches each check, and governed by time budgets and flake rates.
CONCEPTS:
- **cost-of-feedback model** — each layer up raises run cost, nondeterminism, and diagnosis difficulty while raising realism. > "The shape exists because tests get slower, flakier, and harder to debug as they cover more of the system."
- **ratio provenance** — Google's blog offered `70/20/10` in 2015 as an opening estimate; *Software Engineering at Google* describes roughly `80% unit / 15% integration / 5% E2E` by count, varying per team. > "Google has offered 70/20/10 as a first estimate and describes a rough 80/15/5 mix for its own code, while noting that each team’s mix differs."
- **test `size` versus `scope`** — size is what a test can do (process and machine span); scope is how much code is verified; size rules are CI-enforceable. > "Size describes what a test can do. Small tests run in a single process, medium tests stay on one machine, and large tests can span machines and networks."
- **`solitary` versus `sociable` unit tests** — solitary replaces collaborators with doubles; sociable runs real ones, stubbing only slow or external parts. > "Solitary unit tests replace every collaborator with a test double. Sociable unit tests let real collaborators run and only stub out slow or external things."
- **middle-layer jobs** — split the middle into narrow integration (one real dependency), contract (verified on each side), and component/service (whole service via public API) because their costs differ. > "It helps to split the middle of the pyramid into three separate jobs"
- **`hourglass` / `ice cream cone`** — a hollow middle between unit and E2E layers, or too many E2E/manual tests with too few unit tests. > "the hourglass, a suite with many unit tests, many end-to-end tests, and very little in between"
- **`mutation score` / oracle risk** — gate AI-generated tests on fault detection; one model writing code and tests from one prompt confirms what code does, not what it should. > "do not judge AI-generated tests by how many there are or how much coverage they add. Judge them by whether they catch faults, which is what mutation testing measures."
GUIDELINES:
- Start from where failure hurts (billing, permissions, data validity, key journeys, compliance); give each behavior the cheapest reliable layer.
- Push each check to the lowest layer that can catch it; when a high-level test finds a bug, add a lower-level reproducing test first.
- Time budgets: commit stage "a few minutes on every push"; pull-request stage "under 15 minutes"; release stage "under 30 minutes" against production-like infrastructure.
- Measure three ways plus flake rate: tests per layer, CI minutes per layer, layer where each escaped defect belonged.
- E2E covers revenue journeys, access paths, cross-service flows with no lower seam, config-sensitive paths; many SaaS products need `10 to a few dozen` journeys; judge AI tests by `mutation score` with human acceptance criteria.
EVIDENCE: 2026 Stack Overflow survey — `58%` use AI to write or improve tests; Google — about `1.5%` of test runs flaky, nearly `16%` of tests showed some flakiness; flakiness near `1%` makes tests lose value; DORA 2025 — AI adoption related positively to throughput, negatively to stability.
LIMITS: No universal ratio and no agreed definitions; survey and DORA figures second-hand; vendor-authored.
TOOLING: Playwright test agents (planner, generator, healer), TypeScript, linters, mutation testing, Docker.
LINKS: Cohn's "forgotten layer" post, Fowler bliki, *Practical Test Pyramid* (Vocke 2018), Google "Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests", Spotify honeycomb, Dodds trophy.

## A155 · What is the testing trophy and how does it help better test software?
URL: https://symflower.com/en/company/blog/2023/what-is-the-testing-trophy/
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: The testing trophy is a lesser-known alternative to the pyramid that adds static analysis as a foundation and shifts emphasis to integration testing, because fewer integration tests identify problems and depend less on implementation details.
CONCEPTS:
- **speed/confidence trade-off** — testing is "cheaper" at the base; more components mean costlier tests; you cannot skip a level but choose how much focus each gets. > "there is a trade-off between speed and confidence, so you can’t really skip any level of testing – but you can decide how much focus you place on the different levels of testing"
- **`testing pyramid`** — unit, integration, system tests building on each other; many unit, fewer integration, only necessary system tests, to catch problems cheaply and early. > "The testing pyramid has unit tests at the bottom, meaning that those following the testing pyramid will carry out a lot of unit tests"
- **`testing trophy`** — static testing as foundation, integration testing most emphasized, unit tests less emphasized. > "When compared to the pyramid, the testing trophy introduces static testing as the foundation of all testing activities."
- **static layer** — linters catching typos and syntactical errors. > "static tools like linters to catch problems like typos and syntactical errors"
- **integration rationale** — fewer tests needed to find problems, less dependent on implementation details, relatively fast to write and run; unit tests need maintenance as implementation changes. > "you generally need fewer integration tests to identify problems in the application, and they are not as dependent on the details of the implementation"
- **`testing trophy applies to an individual codebase`** — serverless functions, microservices, and other concepts are not considered. > "the concept of the testing trophy applies to the development of an individual codebase, with serverless functions, microservices, and other concepts not considered"
- **shape choice depends on context** — the distribution depends on project, language, and other factors rather than a fixed diagram. > "depends on the individual project, the programming language applied, and a range of other factors"
GUIDELINES:
- Put static tooling (linters) at the base to catch typos and syntax errors.
- Favor integration tests for framework behavior, e.g. "testing Spring Boot controllers".
- Keep a "good unit testing base" but do not overlook a solid level of integration testing.
- Use unit test generation tooling to offset the manual cost of a comprehensive unit suite.
- Consider architecture (serverless, microservices) before assuming a trophy shape.
EVIDENCE: none.
LIMITS: States the trophy ignores serverless functions and microservices by design; concedes distribution depends on project and language; ends with an unrelated fictional passage.
TOOLING: Symflower test generation (IntelliJ IDEA, VS Code, CLI, Android Studio plugins), linters, Spring Boot.
LINKS: Fowler's test-shapes article, Dodds' testing trophy post, Symflower's earlier pyramid post, Symflower unit-vs-integration post.

## A156 · On the Diverse And Fantastical Shapes of Testing
URL: https://martinfowler.com/articles/2021-test-shapes.html
TYPE: practitioner blog
THESIS: The pyramid-versus-honeycomb/trophy debate is largely definitional: what critics call excessive unit testing is what Fowler calls solitary unit tests, and what they call integration testing resembles his sociable unit tests.
CONCEPTS:
- **`test pyramid`** — the older image arguing most testing effort should be unit tests. > "The pyramid argues that you should have most testing done as unit tests"
- **honeycomb and trophy** — "misshapen blobs" arguing few unit tests and mostly integration tests. > "the honeycomb and trophy instead say you should have a relatively small amount of unit tests and focus mostly on integration tests"
- **`unit test` ambiguity** — the split between unit and integration tests is opaque because neither term is well defined. > "The terms “unit test” and “integration test” have always been rather murky, even by the slippery standards of most software terminology."
- **Kent Beck's usage** — "unit test" meant anything written by programmers rather than a separate testing team. > "Kent used “unit test” to indicate tests written by developers as part of their day-to-day work."
- **C3 practice** — tests focused on a single class's behavior, with a fixture creating the object and necessary dependencies, assuming the other code works. > "When we wrote a unit test, we'd usually focus on a single class's behavior"
- **`sociable` and `solitary` unit tests (terms from Jay Fields)** — sociable lets real collaborators execute; solitary replaces them with mocks, stubs, or other `Test Double`s. > "This led to a different style of writing unit tests, where any collaborating object would be replaced with a mock, stub or other kind of Test Double."
- **`classic` and `mockist` XP schools** — classic follows the sociable approach; mockist favors solitary tests. > "Classic XP unit testing follows the sociable approach we originally used, while mockist style favors solitary tests."
- **`integration test`** — even murkier term; its definition makes "unit test" look tightly defined. > "The second biggest issue I have with this discussion is that it's rendered opaque by the fact that it's not clear what people see as the difference between unit and integration tests."
GUIDELINES:
- When anyone discusses testing categories, "dig deeper on what they mean by their words, as they probably don't use them the same way as the last person you read did."
- Do not argue percentages; instead "write expressive tests that establish clear boundaries, run quickly & reliably, and only fail for useful reasons" (Justin Searls).
- Take automated testing seriously (endorsing Tim Bray).
EVIDENCE: none; anecdotal (a test expert "covers 24 different definitions of unit test" in his course).
LIMITS: Author names semantic confusion his "second biggest issue" and the percentage debate the biggest; he infers rather than verifies what honeycomb advocates mean. Very short essay.
TOOLING: Xunit family of testing tools.
LINKS: Tim Bray "Testing in 2021", Fowler bliki `TestPyramid`, `UnitTest`, `IntegrationTest`, `TestDouble`, `Xunit`, `ExtremeProgramming`, `C3`; Kent Beck *Extreme Programming Explained*; Jay Fields; Fowler "Mocks Aren't Stubs"; Searls tweet; Spotify and Dodds diagrams.

## A157 · Pyramid or Crab? Find a testing strategy that fits | Articles | web.dev for China
URL: https://web.developers.google.cn/articles/ta-strategies
TYPE: official docs
THESIS: The web.dev strategy article as mirrored on the China developer site: shapes (pyramid, diamond, honeycomb, trophy, ice cone, crab) suit different application sizes, team compositions, and manual-testing reliance, with user needs as the goal.
CONCEPTS:
- **strategy matrix** — application size × team composition × manual reliance → shape. > "Here's a list of strategies with respective sizes and development scopes."
- **`test pyramid` (Cohn; Fowler's *Practical Test Pyramid*)** — unit base (fast, maintainable, isolated), integration middle (API and component tests), E2E/UI top (simulated user, slowest). > "As shown in this drawing, the test pyramid consists of three layers"
- **`confidence versus resources`** — E2E gives most confidence but requires a complete stack and simulated user, so it competes with execution cost. > "they require a complete application stack and a simulated user, therefore, they are also potentially the most expensive"
- **Cohn's two points** — different granularities; the higher the level, the fewer tests. > "The more high level you get, the fewer tests you should have."
- **`test diamond`** — unit layer cut because tests erode; integration widest; E2E only for critical cases. > "the next time you refactor, you will have to update many of these unit tests and you might be tempted to skip them"
- **`testing honeycomb` (Spotify)** — microservices; complexity in interaction, so integration dominates. > "Due to their small size, the most considerable complexity in a microservice is not within the service itself, but in how it interacts with others."
- **`integrated tests` (Rainsberger)** — pass or fail based on another system's correctness. > "A test that will pass or fail based on the correctness of another system."
- **`testing trophy` (Dodds)** — static analysis base, unit, integration as main focus, UI and visual tests on top. > "the testing trophy adaptation that takes static analysis into account while maintaining the focus on integration tests"
- **`testing ice cone` / `testing pizza` and `testing crab`** — manual/UI-heavy shapes; crab stresses visual testing. > "The test crab is similar to the test ice cone, but with more emphasis on E2E and visual testing"
GUIDELINES:
- Mapping: small + high manual → Ice Cone or Crab; small + low manual → Pyramid; large + developers only + high manual → Trophy or Diamond; large + developers + QA → Trophy or Crab; large + low manual → Trophy or Honeycomb.
- Define the goal first: "When do you consider that your application has been sufficiently tested?"
- Interpret Rauch: write tests; not too many (`100%` coverage is not always good); mostly integration.
- Automate routine work so QA focuses on crucial areas; automation complements manual testing.
- Focus tests on real errors users might encounter; choose by architecture, requirements, and users.
EVIDENCE: none.
LIMITS: Answer is "It depends"; acknowledges the pyramid oversimplifies and that test-type definitions differ across teams.
TOOLING: Jest, Cypress, Nuxt component tests, Cypress visual testing.

## A158 · The test pyramid and its discontents, or, why no one agrees on anything
URL: https://qase.io/blog/the-test-pyramid-and-its-discontents
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: The pyramid is a metaphor, not a model, framework, or even a heuristic; treating it as a target produces cargo-cult proportions, so prefer reality-driven testing measured by team confidence and code quality.
CONCEPTS:
- **origin story** — 2003-2004 discussions (Fowler), an independent 2006 idea by Jason Huggins, popularized by Cohn's *Succeeding With Agile* (2009). > "Martin Fowler, one of the co-authors of the Agile Manifesto, participated in some of the first discussions that led to the test pyramid in 2003 and 2004."
- **dual purpose** — model what a suite should look like and show deviations (Google's two anti-pattern diagrams). > "a way to model what a test suite _should_ look like, and two, a way to show how a test suite can deviate from that ideal form"
- **`Beyoncé rule` (Google)** — "If you liked it, then you shoulda put a test on it." > "If you liked it, then you shoulda put a test on it."
- **size versus scope (Bender)** — tests vary in size (small, medium, large) and scope (narrow, medium, large). > "Bender explaining that tests vary in size (small, medium, and large) to scope (narrow, medium, and large)"
- **`narrow` versus `broad` integration tests** — 1980s integration testing conflated "separately developed modules work together" with "a system of modules works as expected". > "these conflated two different things: testing that separately developed modules worked together properly and testing that a system of multiple modules worked as expected"
- **`testing trophy` (Dodds)** — write more integration tests than any other type; `testing honeycomb` (Spotify) as an alternative balance. > "That leads to a different model, a “testing trophy.” Dodds is not alone in allowing a different balance to lead to a different model."
- **alternative labels** — some keep the pyramid shape but substitute different layers, such as developer, consumer, and user interface tests. > "Some people use the test pyramid shape but add different layers."
- **"The pyramid is not a model..."** — Seb Rose's weaker-than-heuristic framing of the image. > "The pyramid is not a model. It’s not a framework. It’s not even a heuristic. It’s something much weaker than that — it’s a metaphor."
- **`reality-driven testing` (Holub)** — let practical realities of code, product, industry, and users lead. > "testing can be a tool where you let the practical realities of your code, your product, your industry, and your users lead the way"
- **`Goodhart's Law`** — "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." > "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."
GUIDELINES:
- Do not gather per-category test statistics, nor enforce "acceptable values ... 'derived' from the pyramid" as build rules.
- Do not report unit-test counts or coverage upward as progress; pressure toward `100%` coverage follows immediately.
- Keep the original nuance: many more low-level unit tests than high-level broad-stack GUI tests, with balance varying per team.
- Replace model conformance with confidence in the team and quality of code as the only measures; derive your own model from the work.
- Prefer deliberately broad, thought-through advice or local contextual advice over the pyramid's "messy middle".
EVIDENCE: none conducted; cites GetDX data that over half of developers see flaky tests monthly, and that pseudo-tested methods create false coverage confidence.
LIMITS: Argumentative essay relying on quotations; offers no replacement model beyond "reality-driven testing"; concedes the pyramid "served its purpose".
TOOLING: GitHub Copilot (cited for test writing), Docker, modern framework API layers for simulation.
LINKS: Fowler bliki `TestPyramid`/`IntegrationTest`, *Practical Test Pyramid*, Huggins 2006 talk, *Software Engineering at Google* ch. 11, Google "Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests", Dodds, Spotify, Riviere, Holub, Seb Rose/Cucumber blog, George Box, Sústrik, Tim Bray, Atwood, GetDX survey, Increment.

## A159 · Is the Test Pyramid Dead? Agent-Native Coverage Explained
URL: https://www.augmentcode.com/guides/is-the-test-pyramid-dead
TYPE: vendor blog
THESIS: The four classic coverage shapes are static, author-set ratios that stop serving when AI agents author tests; a fifth "agent-native" shape computes distribution from runtime adequacy signals like mutation score.
CONCEPTS:
- **`static shapes`** — pyramid, trophy, honeycomb, diamond ask a human to pick a layer distribution before the suite proves it detects defects. > "the pyramid, trophy, honeycomb, and diamond ask a human to choose a layer distribution before the suite proves whether tests detect defects"
- **pyramid economics** — Cohn's 2009 model encoded era tooling costs: UI automation "expensive to run, expensive to write, and brittle". > "Cohn's 2009 model encoded the tooling economics of its era: unit tests were cheap, UI tests were expensive, so the bulk of tests should sit at the bottom."
- **`confidence coefficient` (Dodds)** — confidence rises with test level; the trophy adds static analysis as a base. > "Explicit "confidence coefficient": higher layers yield more confidence per test"
- **trophy scope** — built for monoliths, "not microservices or serverless functions"; Dodds later noted E2E may become as cheap as integration. > "He designed it for monoliths, "not microservices or serverless functions.""
- **honeycomb boundary shift** — service interaction is the unit; implementation-detail tests shrink; `integrated tests` ideally zero. > "Service interaction becomes the center of the suite, while implementation details move to a smaller role."
- **`diamond`** — thin unit and E2E, dominant integration middle; sourcing thinner, and may treat a symptom of misapplied unit testing. > "The testing diamond thins both unit and end-to-end tests to critical cases while making integration tests the dominant middle band."
- **`oracle gap`** — tests execute paths but omit assertions separating correct from observed behavior, driven by incentive misalignment. > "The mechanism is an oracle gap: tests run paths but omit assertions that distinguish correct behavior from observed behavior."
- **`agent-native coverage`** — runtime-computed distribution; the loop measures execution, verification strength, new behavior, change relevance, then sets the next target. > "Agent-native testing replaces fixed ratios with runtime-computed coverage grounded in mutation scores and fault detection."
- **`checked-code adequacy`** — names the gap between code executed and code actually asserted on. > "mature test suites exhibit gaps of up to 51 percentage points between executed and checked code"
GUIDELINES:
- Add mutation testing to the highest-value domain logic "this sprint", compare mutation score with the coverage dashboard, and use the mismatch to pick the next test-writing task.
- Judge agent-authored tests by fault detection, not count per layer or coverage added; review failing mutants first.
- Treat green coverage as an execution signal, not release evidence.
- Use dependency graphs, call-flow analysis, and CI data to compare declared coverage intent with what CI executes; watch weak oracles, deleted tests, and hollow assertions.
EVIDENCE: `86,156` test-file patches from `33,596` agent-authored PRs across `2,807` repositories — `80.2%` contain weak or no explicit oracle signals; gaps "up to 51 percentage points" between executed and checked code; Inozemtseva & Holmes (2014, `31,000` suites, five systems) found "a low to moderate correlation between coverage and effectiveness when the number of test cases in the suite is controlled for"; one suite reaches "100% coverage but only 4% mutation score".
LIMITS: Vendor-authored with a product call-to-action; diamond sourcing is thinner; the fifth shape requires mutation, edge, or change-relevance signals.
TOOLING: Augment Cosmos (Environments, Experts, Sessions), Context Engine (`400,000+` files, `6`-minute index, `45`-second increments), E2E Testing Expert, AFL++, MCP integrations, mutation testing.
LINKS: Cohn *Succeeding with Agile*, Fowler `TestPyramid` and 2021 test-shapes, Dodds trophy, Spotify honeycomb (Schaffer and Dybeck 2018), Inozemtseva & Holmes ICSE 2014, arXiv mutation-guided and hybrid LLM/evolutionary papers, web.dev `ta-strategies`.
